explanation: BW = f_r/Q = 455/50 = 9.1 kHz. For a high-Q circuit f₁ ≈ f_r − BW/2 = 450.45 kHz and f₂ ≈ f_r + BW/2 = 459.55 kHz.

questionText: The half-power frequencies of a series RLC circuit are 40 kHz and 90 kHz. The resonant frequency and the quality factor are:
explanation: For a series RLC circuit f_r is the geometric mean: f_r = √(f₁f₂) = √(40 × 90) = 60 kHz. BW = 50 kHz, so Q = f_r/BW = 60/50 = 1.2. The arithmetic mean (65 kHz) is only an approximation for high Q.

questionText: A coil of inductance 0.2 H and resistance 20 Ω is connected in parallel with a 10 µF capacitor across a 200 V supply at the resonant frequency. The line current is:
explanation: Dynamic impedance Z_r = L/(CR) = 0.2/(10⁻⁵ × 20) = 1000 Ω, so the line current is 200/1000 = 0.2 A.

questionText: A coil with L = 0.1 H and R = 60 Ω is connected in parallel with a 10 µF capacitor. The resonant frequency of the combination is approximately:
explanation: f_r = (1/2π)√(1/(LC) − R²/L²) = (1/2π)√(10⁶ − 3.6 × 10⁵) = 800/(2π) ≈ 127 Hz, lower than the ideal value 1/(2π√(LC)) ≈ 159 Hz because of the coil resistance.

questionText: A series RLC circuit has R = 10 Ω, L = 0.1 H and C = 10 µF. When it is supplied at twice its resonant frequency, its impedance and nature are:
explanation: At f_r, X_L = X_C = √(L/C) = 100 Ω. At 2f_r, X_L = 200 Ω and X_C = 50 Ω, so Z = √(10² + 150²) ≈ 150 Ω; X_L > X_C, so the circuit is inductive.

questionText: An ideal parallel RLC circuit (R, L and C each in a separate branch) has R = 10 kΩ, L = 1 mH and C = 10 nF. Its quality factor and bandwidth are:
explanation: For the three-branch parallel circuit Q = R√(C/L) = 10⁴ × √(10⁻⁵) ≈ 31.6 and BW = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 1.59 kHz. The series formulas (1/R)√(L/C) and R/(2πL) do not apply here.

questionText: A coil of inductance 2 mH and resistance 25 Ω is used at 100 kHz. Its quality factor at this frequency is approximately:
In terms of energy, the quality factor of a resonant circuit is defined as:
options: (maximum energy stored) / (2π × energy dissipated per cycle)
explanation: Q = 2π × W_stored/W_lost per cycle. For a series circuit this reduces to ω₀L/R, the familiar X_L/R.

questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 50 Ω is fed from a 100 V variable-frequency supply. The power dissipated at either half-power frequency is:
explanation: Maximum power at resonance is V²/R = 100²/50 = 200 W. At a half-power frequency it is half of this, 100 W.

questionText: The maximum current of a series RLC circuit at resonance is 4 A. The current at the lower half-power frequency is approximately:
explanation: At a half-power frequency I = I_max/√2 = 4 × 0.707 ≈ 2.83 A, which makes the power I²R exactly half the maximum.

questionText: At the upper half-power frequency of a series RLC circuit, the current:
options: Is in phase with the supply voltage
explanation: Above f_r the circuit is inductive, and at f₂ the net reactance X_L − X_C equals R, so tan φ = 1 and the current lags by 45°.

questionText: At series resonance, the net voltage across the series L-C combination (measured across both together) is:
options: Zero, because V_L and V_C are equal and 180° apart
explanation: V_L and V_C are each Q × V but in antiphase, so their phasor sum is zero and the whole supply voltage appears across R.

questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 5 Ω resonates at 1 kHz. With 10 V applied at resonance, the voltage across the capacitor is 250 V. The inductance is approximately:
explanation: I = V/R = 10/5 = 2 A, so X_C = V_C/I = 125 Ω. At resonance X_L = X_C = 125 Ω, so L = 125/(2π × 1000) ≈ 19.9 mH (Q = 25).

questionText: A series RLC circuit must resonate at 10 kHz with a bandwidth of 100 Hz using a 10 mH inductor. The required R and C are approximately:
A radio tuning circuit uses a fixed inductor with a variable capacitor adjustable from 30 pF to 300 pF. The ratio of the highest to the lowest resonant frequency is approximately:
A tuned circuit with a fixed inductor must cover 550 kHz to 1650 kHz. The ratio C_max/C_min of the variable capacitor must be:
explanation: C ∝ 1/f², so C_max/C_min = (f_max/f_min)² = (1650/550)² = 3² = 9.

questionText: A parallel tank circuit with Q = 40 draws a line current of 5 mA at resonance. The current in the capacitor branch is approximately:
explanation: At parallel resonance each branch current is about Q times the line current: I_C ≈ 40 × 5 mA = 200 mA.

questionText: A coil (L = 200 µH, R = 10 Ω) is connected in parallel with a 200 pF capacitor. Its resonant frequency and dynamic impedance are approximately:
explanation: Since R² ≪ L/C, f_r ≈ 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π × 2 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 796 kHz. Z_r = L/(CR) = 200 × 10⁻⁶/(200 × 10⁻¹² × 10) = 100 kΩ (equivalently Q²R with Q = 100). 5 MHz is ω₀ in rad/s, not f.

questionText: Which statement about series resonance is NOT correct?
options: The current is in phase with the supply voltage
Increasing R raises the resonant frequency
The voltages across L and C can each exceed the supply voltage
explanation: f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)) is independent of R. The other statements are all true at series resonance.

questionText: In an ideal (lossless) parallel LC circuit at resonance:
options: The line current is zero although the branch currents are not
The branch currents are both zero
explanation: The inductor and capacitor currents are equal in magnitude and 180° apart, so they cancel at the junction; the impedance is infinite and no current is drawn from the supply.

questionText: A wave trap is used to block one interfering frequency from reaching a receiver. It is:
options: A series LC circuit tuned to the unwanted frequency, connected in series with the signal path
A parallel LC circuit tuned to the unwanted frequency, connected in series with the signal path
A parallel LC circuit tuned to the unwanted frequency, connected across the signal path
A resistor connected in series with the signal path
explanation: A parallel resonant circuit has maximum impedance at its resonant frequency, so placed in series with the line it blocks that frequency while passing others.

questionText: An ideal parallel LC circuit is operated above its resonant frequency. It behaves as:
options: An inductive load, because X_L is larger than X_C
A capacitive load, because the capacitor branch draws the larger current
An inductive load, because the inductor branch draws the larger current
explanation: Above f_r, X_C is smaller than X_L, so the capacitor branch current dominates and the net line current leads: the parallel circuit looks capacitive (the opposite of a series circuit).

questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 10 Ω has a bandwidth of 50 Hz. If R is increased to 25 Ω with L and C unchanged, the new bandwidth is:
explanation: BW = R/(2πL) is proportional to R: 50 × (25/10) = 125 Hz.

questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 10 Ω and L = 20 mH is supplied with 20 V (rms) at its resonant frequency. The maximum energy stored in the inductor is:
explanation: I = V/R = 2 A rms, so I_m = 2√2 A. W = ½ L I_m² = ½ × 0.02 × 8 = 0.08 J. Using the rms current gives 0.04 J.

questionText: A series RLC circuit has R = 100 Ω, L = 0.1 H and C = 10 µF. Its exact upper half-power frequency is approximately:
explanation: ω₂ = R/(2L) + √((R/2L)² + 1/(LC)) = 500 + √(250 000 + 10⁶) ≈ 1618 rad/s, so f₂ ≈ 257.5 Hz. Q = 1 here, so f_r + BW/2 ≈ 238.7 Hz is not accurate.

questionText: A resonant circuit has f_r = 2 MHz and a bandwidth of 40 kHz. Its quality factor is:
A practical coil (L with series resistance R) is connected in parallel with a capacitor C. Resonance (unity power factor) is possible only if:
options: R has any value, because the resonant frequency does not depend on R
explanation: f_r = (1/2π)√(1/(LC) − R²/L²) is real only when 1/(LC) > R²/L², that is R < √(L/C).

questionText: Apparent power in an AC circuit is expressed in:
explanation: Apparent power S = VI is the product of rms voltage and rms current, measured in VA (or kVA).

questionText: A 200 V supply delivers 5 A to a load at a power factor of 0.6. The active power is:
explanation: P = VI cos φ = 200 × 5 × 0.6 = 600 W. VI = 1000 VA is the apparent power, and 800 would be VI sin φ (in VAR).

questionText: The instrument that directly measures the active power drawn by an AC load is the:
explanation: A wattmeter responds to the product of voltage, current and the cosine of the angle between them, so it reads VI cos φ directly.

questionText: A load draws an apparent power of 10 kVA and an active power of 6 kW. Its reactive power is:
explanation: Q = √(S² − P²) = √(100 − 36) = 8 kVAR. Subtracting 10 − 6 = 4 or adding 6 + 10 are the usual slips.

questionText: A load takes 12 kW of active power and 5 kVAR of reactive power. The apparent power is:
explanation: S = √(P² + Q²) = √(144 + 25) = 13 kVA. Active and reactive powers are at right angles, so they cannot be added arithmetically.

questionText: An induction motor running on load normally operates at:
explanation: An induction motor needs magnetizing current, so it is an inductive load that draws current lagging the voltage (typically 0.7 to 0.9 lagging at full load).

questionText: For a 50 Hz supply, the instantaneous power drawn by a single-phase load pulsates at:
explanation: p = VI cos φ − VI cos(2ωt − φ), so the power varies at twice the supply frequency: 2 × 50 = 100 Hz.

questionText: A current of 4 A flows through a series circuit with R = 10 Ω and impedance Z = 20 Ω. The active power is:
explanation: Active power is dissipated only in the resistance: P = I²R = 4² × 10 = 160 W. I²Z = 320 is the apparent power in VA.

questionText: A series circuit has R = 12 Ω and X_L = 5 Ω. Its power factor is approximately:
explanation: Z = √(12² + 5²) = 13 Ω, so pf = R/Z = 12/13 ≈ 0.923, lagging because the reactance is inductive. 5/13 = 0.385 is sin φ.

questionText: When a capacitor bank is connected in parallel with an inductive load to improve its power factor, the active power taken by the load:
explanation: The capacitor only supplies reactive power; the load's voltage is unchanged, so it takes the same active power. Only the reactive power, apparent power and line current fall.

questionText: A circuit in which the current leads the applied voltage is said to have:
options: A leading power factor, as in a capacitive load
A lagging power factor, as in a capacitive load
A leading power factor, as in an inductive load
A unity power factor, as in a resistive load
explanation: The power factor is named after the current: when the current leads the voltage the pf is leading, which happens with a net capacitive load.

questionText: Large power transformers and alternators are rated in kVA rather than kW because:
options: Their output is always at unity power factor
Their losses depend on voltage and current, not on the load power factor
kVA is always smaller than kW
explanation: Copper loss depends on current and iron loss on voltage, so heating is set by VA. The manufacturer does not know the load pf, so the machine is rated in kVA.

questionText: A load operates at a power factor of 0.8. Its reactive factor (sin φ) is:
explanation: sin φ = √(1 − cos²φ) = √(1 − 0.64) = 0.6. The reactive factor is Q/S.

questionText: A 230 V load draws 10 A at a power factor of 0.8 lagging. The reactive power is:
explanation: sin φ = 0.6, so Q = VI sin φ = 230 × 10 × 0.6 = 1380 VAR. 1840 is VI cos φ, the active power in W.

questionText: A single-phase load of 11.5 kW is supplied at 230 V with a power factor of 0.5. The line current is:
explanation: I = P/(V cos φ) = 11 500/(230 × 0.5) = 100 A. At unity pf the same power would need only 50 A.

questionText: A series circuit with R = 30 Ω and X_L = 40 Ω is connected to 200 V. The active power consumed is:
explanation: Z = √(30² + 40²) = 50 Ω, I = 200/50 = 4 A, P = I²R = 16 × 30 = 480 W. 800 VA is the apparent power and 640 VAR the reactive power.

questionText: A series circuit with R = 8 Ω and X_C = 6 Ω is connected to 100 V. The reactive power is:
explanation: Z = √(8² + 6²) = 10 Ω, I = 10 A, Q = I²X_C = 100 × 6 = 600 VAR. The load is capacitive, so the reactive power is leading (supplied by the load).

questionText: A 50 µF capacitor is connected to a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. The reactive power it supplies is approximately:
What capacitance is needed to supply 5 kVAR at 400 V, 50 Hz?
explanation: C = Q_C/(2πfV²) = 5000/(2π × 50 × 400²) ≈ 99.5 µF. Leaving out 2π gives 625 µF.

questionText: A 4 kW heater (unity pf) and a motor taking 3 kW at 0.6 pf lagging are supplied from the same source. The overall power factor is approximately:
explanation: Motor Q = 3 × tan(cos⁻¹0.6) = 4 kVAR. Total P = 7 kW, Q = 4 kVAR, S = √(49 + 16) ≈ 8.06 kVA, so pf = 7/8.06 ≈ 0.87 lagging. Averaging the pfs (0.8) is wrong.

questionText: A load draws 10 A (rms) from a 100 V (rms) supply with the current lagging by 60°. The minimum value of the instantaneous power is:
explanation: p = VI cos φ − VI cos(2ωt − φ) swings between VI cos φ ± VI. P = 1000 × 0.5 = 500 W, so p_min = 500 − 1000 = −500 W: for part of each cycle energy flows back to the source.

questionText: A wattmeter, voltmeter and ammeter connected to a single-phase load read 1200 W, 240 V and 8 A. The power factor of the load is:
A 100 kW load operates at 0.6 pf lagging. The capacitor kVAR needed to raise the power factor to unity is approximately:
explanation: Q_C = P(tan φ₁ − tan φ₂) = 100 × (1.333 − 0) ≈ 133 kVAR. 167 kVA is the apparent power, and 80 kVAR (P sin φ) is not the load's reactive power.

questionText: A 50 kW load has a power factor of 0.8 lagging. The capacitor kVAR required to improve the power factor to 0.95 lagging is approximately:
explanation: tan φ₁ = 0.75 and tan φ₂ = tan(cos⁻¹0.95) ≈ 0.329, so Q_C = 50 × (0.75 − 0.329) ≈ 21.1 kVAR. 37.5 kVAR is the load's whole reactive power.

questionText: For a fixed active power and supply voltage, the power factor of a load is improved from 0.6 to 0.9. The I²R loss in the supply cable falls to about what fraction of its original value?
explanation: I ∝ 1/cos φ, so loss ∝ 1/cos²φ. New/old = (0.6/0.9)² = 0.444, about 44 %. 67 % is the ratio of the currents, not the losses.

questionText: The voltage and current of a load are V = 100∠30° V and I = 5∠−15° A (rms). The active and reactive powers are approximately:
explanation: S = V I* = (100∠30°)(5∠+15°) = 500∠45° VA = 354 + j354. Positive Q means an inductive (lagging) load; the current lags the voltage by 45°. Using I instead of I* gives the wrong angle 15°.

questionText: The complex power of a load is S = P + jQ with P positive and Q negative. The load is:
options: Inductive, with a lagging power factor
Capacitive, with a leading power factor
explanation: With S = V I*, a negative Q means the current leads the voltage, which is a capacitive load. The positive P shows it still absorbs active power.

questionText: A workshop takes 45 kW at a power factor of 0.75 lagging from a 400 V single-phase supply. Its kVA demand and line current are:
explanation: S = P/cos φ = 45/0.75 = 60 kVA and I = S/V = 60 000/400 = 150 A. Multiplying by the pf instead of dividing gives 33.8 kVA.

questionText: A 500 kVA transformer is fully loaded. How much additional active power can it supply if the load power factor is raised from 0.7 to 0.9 at the same kVA?
explanation: At 0.7 pf: P = 500 × 0.7 = 350 kW; at 0.9 pf: P = 450 kW. The extra capacity is 450 − 350 = 100 kW with no change in the transformer's current or kVA.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT a consequence of a low power factor, for the same active power and voltage?
options: More active power is converted into useful work by the load
Larger copper losses in cables and transformers
explanation: The load's active power is the same; a low pf raises the current, which increases I²R losses and voltage drop. It does not give the load more useful power.

questionText: Besides static capacitors, which machine can supply leading reactive power for power-factor correction?
explanation: An over-excited synchronous motor draws leading current, so it behaves like a capacitor; run without load for this purpose it is called a synchronous condenser.

questionText: Power-factor correction in practice is usually stopped at about 0.95 rather than taken to exactly unity because:
options: Unity power factor would make the active power zero
Capacitors cannot supply reactive power at unity power factor
The line current increases as the power factor approaches unity
The capacitor kVAR needed rises steeply near unity for a small further reduction in current
explanation: For 100 kW, going from 0.9 to 0.95 needs about 15.6 kVAR, but 0.95 to 1.0 needs about 32.9 kVAR for only about 5 % less current, so the last step is uneconomical; overshooting also gives a leading pf.

questionText: A pure inductor with X_L = 46 Ω is connected to a 230 V supply. The active and reactive powers are:
explanation: I = 230/46 = 5 A. A pure inductor dissipates no energy, so P = 0, and Q = I²X_L = 25 × 46 = 1150 VAR (lagging).

questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 10 Ω and X_L = X_C = 20 Ω is connected to 100 V. The reactive power absorbed by the inductor alone is:
explanation: At X_L = X_C the circuit is resonant: I = V/R = 10 A, so Q_L = I²X_L = 100 × 20 = 2000 VAR. The capacitor supplies an equal 2000 VAR, so the net reactive power from the source is zero.

questionText: A 50 Ω resistor and an inductor of reactance 25 Ω are connected in parallel across a 100 V supply. The power factor is approximately:
explanation: P = V²/R = 200 W and Q = V²/X_L = 400 VAR, so pf = 200/√(200² + 400²) ≈ 0.447. Treating them as a series pair (R/Z = 50/55.9) wrongly gives 0.894.

questionText: A 230 V, 50 Hz single-phase load takes 5 kW at 0.6 pf lagging. The parallel capacitance needed to raise the power factor to unity is approximately:
explanation: Q_C = P tan φ₁ = 5000 × 1.333 = 6667 VAR; C = Q_C/(2πfV²) = 6667/(2π × 50 × 230²) ≈ 401 µF. Using Q = P (5 kVAR) instead gives about 301 µF, and Q = S (8.33 kVA) about 501 µF.

questionText: A 10 kW single-phase load on 400 V operates at 0.707 pf lagging. After a capacitor raises the power factor to 0.9 lagging, the line current falls from about 35.4 A to about:
explanation: I = P/(V cos φ): before, 10 000/(400 × 0.707) ≈ 35.4 A; after, 10 000/(400 × 0.9) ≈ 27.8 A. 25 A would be the current at unity pf.

questionText: A 20 kW load at 0.8 pf lagging has a 25 kVAR capacitor bank connected across it. The resulting power factor is approximately:
explanation: Load Q = 20 × 0.75 = 15 kVAR lagging; net Q = 15 − 25 = −10 kVAR (leading). pf = 20/√(20² + 10²) ≈ 0.894 leading: the bank over-corrects.

questionText: A capacitor bank rated 10 kVAR at 415 V is operated at 380 V with the frequency unchanged. The reactive power it now supplies is approximately:
explanation: Q_C = V²/X_C, so it scales with the square of the voltage: 10 × (380/415)² ≈ 8.38 kVAR. Scaling linearly gives 9.16 kVAR.

questionText: A load has v = 200 sin(314t) V and i = 10 sin(314t − 60°) A. The average power consumed is:
explanation: P = (V_m I_m/2) cos φ = (200 × 10/2) × cos 60° = 1000 × 0.5 = 500 W. Forgetting to convert peak values to rms gives 1000 W.

questionText: A load takes 9 kW at 0.6 pf lagging. Its reactive power is:
explanation: S = P/cos φ = 9/0.6 = 15 kVA, so Q = √(15² − 9²) = 12 kVAR (equivalently P tan φ = 9 × 4/3).

questionText: Which statement about several loads connected to the same AC supply is correct?
options: Their apparent powers always add arithmetically to give the total kVA
Their active powers add, and their reactive powers add algebraically with capacitive VAR taken as negative
Their power factors add to give the overall power factor
Only the active powers add; reactive powers of different loads cannot be combined
explanation: Total P = ΣP and total Q = ΣQ (inductive positive, capacitive negative); the total S = √(P² + Q²) is generally less than the arithmetic sum of the individual kVA.

questionText: For a series RL circuit, which of the following expressions does NOT give the active power?
options: V_R²/R, where V_R is the voltage across R
explanation: Active power is dissipated only in R: P = I²R = VI cos φ = V_R²/R. I²Z = VI is the apparent power in VA.

questionText: Reactive power in an AC circuit represents:
options: Energy converted into heat in the resistance
Power lost permanently in the magnetic core
The peak value of the active power
Energy that flows back and forth between the source and the fields of L and C, with zero average value
explanation: Reactive power measures the rate at which energy is stored and returned by inductors and capacitors each half-cycle; its average over a cycle is zero, so it does no net work.

questionText: A 4-pole alternator runs at 1800 rpm. The frequency of the generated EMF is:
The speed at which a 12-pole alternator must run to generate 50 Hz is:
An alternator driven at 375 rpm generates 50 Hz. The number of poles is:
According to Faraday's law, the EMF induced in a coil is proportional to:
options: The total flux linking the coil
The square of the current in the coil
The rate of change of flux linkage with the coil
explanation: e = −N dΦ/dt: the EMF depends on how fast the flux linkage changes, not on the flux itself.

questionText: Lenz's law is concerned with:
options: The magnitude of the induced EMF
The direction of the induced EMF or current
The force on a current-carrying conductor
explanation: Lenz's law states that the induced EMF opposes the change of flux producing it, fixing its direction; this is the minus sign in Faraday's law.

questionText: In Fleming's right-hand rule for a generator, the middle finger points in the direction of the:
explanation: Thumb gives the motion, forefinger the field (N to S) and middle finger the induced current.

questionText: A straight conductor moves parallel to the lines of a uniform magnetic field. The EMF induced in it is:
explanation: e = Blv sin θ and θ = 0° for motion along the field, so no flux is cut and e = 0.

questionText: A conductor 0.5 m long moves at 10 m/s at right angles to a uniform field of 0.6 T. The induced EMF is:
A conductor 0.4 m long moves at 20 m/s in a uniform field of 1.0 T, its velocity making an angle of 30° with the field lines. The induced EMF is:
explanation: e = Blv sin θ = 1.0 × 0.4 × 20 × sin 30° = 8 × 0.5 = 4 V. Using cos 30° would give 6.93 V.

questionText: In an alternator, the prime mover supplies:
options: Electrical energy to the load directly
Mechanical energy to rotate the rotor
explanation: The prime mover (turbine or engine) provides the mechanical input that the alternator converts into electrical energy; the field is excited separately with DC.

questionText: In most practical large alternators:
options: The armature rotates and the field is stationary
Both field and armature are stationary and the air gap rotates
The field system rotates and the armature winding is stationary
explanation: Large alternators are of the rotating-field type, so the high-voltage armature output is taken from the stator without sliding contacts.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of the stationary-armature, rotating-field construction of alternators?
options: Only the low-voltage DC field current passes through slip rings
The stationary armature winding is easier to insulate for high voltage
The rotor carrying only the field winding is lighter, suiting high speeds
The armature current can be collected through a commutator
explanation: An alternator uses no commutator at all; the armature output is taken from fixed stator terminals. The other three are genuine advantages.

questionText: The field winding of an alternator is supplied with:
explanation: The field poles must have a steady polarity, so they are excited with DC from an exciter or a rectifier, fed in through slip rings.

questionText: An electrical generator converts:
explanation: A generator is driven by a prime mover and delivers electrical output by electromagnetic induction; the reverse conversion is done by a motor.

questionText: Which statement about the EMF in the armature coil of a DC generator is correct?
options: It is alternating; the commutator makes the output at the brushes unidirectional
It is unidirectional because the field is DC
It is unidirectional because the armature rotates in one direction
It is zero until the commutator connects the load
explanation: Every rotating coil in a field generates an alternating EMF; the commutator reverses the coil connections every half cycle so the external output is DC.

questionText: A coil of 100 turns rotating at 1000 rpm in a uniform field generates a peak EMF of 120 V. If the turns are increased to 150 and the speed to 1500 rpm, the field being unchanged, the new peak EMF is:
explanation: Em = NBAω is proportional to both N and speed: Em = 120 × (150/100) × (1500/1000) = 120 × 1.5 × 1.5 = 270 V. Scaling by only one factor gives 180 V.

questionText: The speed of a simple alternator is doubled and at the same time its field flux is halved. Compared with before:
options: The peak EMF and the frequency are both doubled
The peak EMF is unchanged and the frequency is doubled
The peak EMF is halved and the frequency is unchanged
The peak EMF and the frequency are both unchanged
explanation: Em = NΦmω ∝ Φm × speed, so (1/2) × 2 = 1 leaves Em unchanged, while f = PN/120 depends only on speed and doubles.

questionText: A coil generates a peak EMF of 250 V. The EMF when the coil has turned 60° from the position of maximum flux linkage is:
explanation: e = Em sin θ = 250 × sin 60° = 216.5 V; 125 V would result from using cos 60°.

questionText: A coil rotating in a uniform field has a peak EMF of 200 V. At the instant its plane makes an angle of 30° with the field lines, the EMF is:
explanation: A plane parallel to the field is the maximum-EMF position, so 30° from it is θ = 90° − 30° = 60° from the maximum-flux position: e = 200 sin 60° = 173.2 V.

questionText: A coil of 300 turns links a maximum flux of 5 mWb varying sinusoidally at 50 Hz. The RMS value of the induced EMF is:
explanation: E = 4.44 f N Φm = 4.44 × 50 × 300 × 0.005 = 333 V; 471 V is the peak value 2πfNΦm.

questionText: The rotor of a 4-pole alternator makes 25 revolutions per second. The frequency of the generated EMF is:
explanation: With p = 2 pole pairs, f = p × n = 2 × 25 = 50 Hz (equivalently PN/120 = 4 × 1500/120).

questionText: In an 8-pole machine, a mechanical rotation of 45° corresponds to an electrical angle of:
In a 6-pole alternator, one cycle of EMF is generated for every mechanical rotation of:
explanation: One cycle = 360 electrical degrees = 360°/(P/2) = 360°/3 = 120° mechanical.

questionText: The flux linking a coil of 400 turns changes uniformly from 2 mWb to 7 mWb in 0.1 s. The average EMF induced is:
explanation: e = N ΔΦ/Δt = 400 × (7 − 2) × 10⁻³/0.1 = 20 V. Using the sum 9 mWb instead of the change gives 36 V.

questionText: A coil of 100 turns in a 2-pole field links a maximum flux of 10 mWb and rotates at 3000 rpm. The average EMF over a half revolution, from +Φm to −Φm, is:
explanation: In half a revolution the flux linkage changes by 2NΦm in T/2 = 10 ms: E(avg) = 2 × 100 × 0.01/0.01 = 200 V, i.e. 4fNΦm. The peak value would be 314 V.

questionText: A 100-turn coil of area 0.02 m² rotates in a uniform field of 0.5 T. The speed needed for a peak EMF of 157 V is approximately:
A rectangular coil of 40 turns, 0.3 m long and 0.2 m wide, rotates at 3000 rpm in a uniform field of 0.5 T. Its peak EMF is approximately:
explanation: A = 0.3 × 0.2 = 0.06 m² and ω = 2π × 3000/60 = 314.16 rad/s, so Em = NBAω = 40 × 0.5 × 0.06 × 314.16 = 377 V. Counting only one coil side gives 188.5 V.

questionText: A 4-pole alternator running at 1500 rpm generates a peak EMF of 325 V. Taking t = 0 at zero EMF, its instantaneous EMF is:
explanation: f = 4 × 1500/120 = 50 Hz, so the electrical ω = 2π × 50 = 314 rad/s. 157 rad/s is the mechanical speed, not the electrical angular frequency.

questionText: A 2-pole alternator runs at 3000 rpm and its coil has a peak EMF of 300 V. The EMF 3.33 ms after the coil passes the position of maximum flux linkage is approximately:
If the slip rings of an elementary single-loop alternator are replaced by a split-ring commutator, the voltage across the load becomes:
explanation: The commutator reverses the coil connections every half revolution, so both half cycles appear with the same polarity at the load: a pulsating unidirectional voltage.

questionText: For a coil rotating in a magnetic field to generate a purely sinusoidal EMF, which condition is NOT required?
options: The magnetic field must be uniform
The coil must have a large number of turns
The angular velocity must be constant
The field strength must not vary with time
explanation: The number of turns only scales the amplitude; the sine shape comes from a uniform, steady (time-invariant) field and rotation at constant angular velocity.

questionText: For a coil rotating in a uniform field with Φ = Φm cos ωt, the induced EMF:
options: Is in phase with the flux
Is 180° out of phase with the flux
explanation: e = −N dΦ/dt = NΦmω sin ωt = Em cos(ωt − 90°), so the EMF reaches its peak a quarter cycle after the flux: it lags by 90°.

questionText: If the number of turns of the rotating coil of a simple alternator is doubled, speed and field remaining the same:
options: The peak EMF and the frequency both double
The peak EMF doubles and the frequency is unchanged
The frequency doubles and the peak EMF is unchanged
explanation: Em = NBAω is proportional to N, while the frequency depends only on the speed and the number of poles.

questionText: The frequency of the EMF generated by an alternator depends on:
options: The number of poles and the rotor speed only
The number of poles, the rotor speed and the field current
The rotor speed and the number of armature turns
The flux density and the coil area
explanation: f = PN/120 contains only the pole number and speed; field current, turns, flux density and area change the magnitude of the EMF, not its frequency.

questionText: Alternators driven by water turbines in hydro plants usually have a large number of poles because:
options: Water turbines run at low speed, so many poles are needed to give 50 Hz
More poles increase the terminal voltage without limit
More poles reduce the frequency to 25 Hz
Hydro alternators have no field winding
explanation: From P = 120f/N, a low turbine speed requires many poles for 50 Hz, e.g. 24 poles at 250 rpm.

questionText: An alternator generates 60 Hz when driven at 1200 rpm. The speed at which the same machine must run to generate 50 Hz is:
explanation: P = 120 × 60/1200 = 6 poles; for 50 Hz, N = 120 × 50/6 = 1000 rpm. Running at 1440 rpm would give 72 Hz.

questionText: The N-pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards the face of a closed coil. The face of the coil nearest the magnet becomes:
explanation: By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the approaching N-pole, so the near face becomes a north pole and repels the magnet.

questionText: The EMF induced in the armature winding of an alternator is best described as:
explanation: The EMF results from relative motion between the conductors and the field, which is dynamically (motionally) induced EMF, whichever of the two actually moves.

questionText: A magnetic flux density of 1 tesla is equal to:
explanation: Flux density B is flux per unit area, so 1 T = 1 weber per square metre.

questionText: A coil of 80 turns, each of area 250 cm², rotates at ω = 314.16 rad/s in a uniform field of 0.3 T. The peak EMF is approximately:
explanation: A = 250 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.025 m², so Em = NBAω = 80 × 0.3 × 0.025 × 314.16 = 188.5 V. Converting with 10⁻³ instead of 10⁻⁴ gives the tenfold error 1885 V.

questionText: A 250-turn coil links a maximum flux of 4 mWb in a 50 Hz alternator. The EMF 1/600 s after the coil passes the position of maximum flux linkage is approximately:
In a 60 Hz alternator, the time between the instant of maximum flux linkage in a coil and the next instant of maximum EMF in it is:
explanation: Flux linkage and EMF are 90° apart, i.e. a quarter period: T/4 = (1/60)/4 = 4.17 ms.

questionText: An alternator with constant field excitation produces 240 V at 50 Hz. If its speed is reduced until the frequency is 40 Hz, the EMF becomes:
explanation: With constant flux, E ∝ speed ∝ f, so E = 240 × 40/50 = 192 V.

questionText: A vehicle's steel axle 1.5 m long moves horizontally at 72 km/h where the vertical component of the earth's field is 40 µT. The EMF between the ends of the axle is:
explanation: v = 72/3.6 = 20 m/s, so e = Blv = 40 × 10⁻⁶ × 1.5 × 20 = 1.2 × 10⁻³ V = 1.2 mV. Using 72 without converting gives 4.32 mV.

questionText: Which statement about an elementary 2-pole single-loop alternator is NOT correct?
options: One revolution of the coil produces two cycles of EMF
Each slip ring stays connected to the same end of the coil
The EMF reverses every half revolution
The output frequency in Hz equals the number of revolutions per second
explanation: In a 2-pole machine one revolution gives exactly one cycle (P/2 = 1), so f equals rev/s; two cycles per revolution would need 4 poles.

questionText: The armature core of an alternator is built from thin laminations of silicon steel in order to:
options: Increase the resistance of the armature winding
Allow AC to be converted to DC
explanation: The core carries alternating flux; thin insulated laminations limit eddy currents and silicon steel has a narrow hysteresis loop.

questionText: At what speed must a 6-pole alternator be driven to generate a 50 Hz supply?
A coil rotating at constant speed in a uniform magnetic field has maximum induced EMF when the plane of the coil is:
options: Perpendicular to the field, where the flux linkage is maximum
Parallel to the field, where the flux linkage is zero
explanation: The EMF is −N dΦ/dt. The flux linkage BA cos ωt changes fastest when it passes through zero, i.e. when the coil plane is parallel to the field, so the EMF is maximum there.

questionText: A coil of 50 turns, each of area 0.04 m², rotates at 3000 rpm in a uniform field of 0.2 T. The peak EMF generated is approximately:
In a simple single-loop alternator, the alternating EMF is brought out to the external circuit through:
explanation: Each end of the rotating coil is fixed to its own continuous slip ring on which a stationary brush rests, so the output is delivered unchanged as AC; a commutator would make it unidirectional.

questionText: A sinusoidal current has an RMS value of 5 A. Its peak value is:
The RMS value of an alternating current is defined as the:
options: Arithmetic mean of all instantaneous values over one half cycle
Steady direct current that produces the same heat in a given resistance in the same time
Maximum instantaneous value reached during a cycle
Average of the positive and negative peak values
explanation: The RMS (effective) value is defined by heating equivalence with DC; the half-cycle mean is the average value and the maximum is the peak value.

questionText: A sinusoidal voltage has a peak value of 50 V. Its average value taken over one half cycle is:
The voltage v = 311 sin 314t V is applied to a circuit. Its RMS value and frequency are:
Which instrument indicates the true RMS value of a current regardless of its waveform?
explanation: The moving-iron deflecting torque is proportional to i², so it responds to the mean square; PMMC responds to the average and rectifier meters to the rectified average scaled by 1.11.

questionText: The peak-to-peak value of a 12 V (RMS) sinusoidal voltage is:
A permanent-magnet moving-coil (PMMC) voltmeter without a rectifier is connected across a pure 50 Hz sinusoidal supply of 230 V. It reads:
explanation: A PMMC meter responds to the average value, and the average of a symmetrical sine wave over a full cycle is zero, so the pointer stays at zero.

questionText: An average-responding (rectifier-type) voltmeter whose scale is calibrated to read RMS for sine waves is connected to a symmetrical square wave of amplitude ±100 V. The meter reads:
explanation: The rectified average of the square wave is 100 V; the meter multiplies by the sine form factor 1.11 and shows 111 V, although the true RMS is 100 V.

questionText: An average-responding voltmeter calibrated in RMS for sine waves is used on a symmetrical triangular wave of peak 100 V. The error of its reading relative to the true RMS value is:
explanation: Rectified average = 0.5 × 100 = 50 V, so the meter shows 1.11 × 50 = 55.5 V; true RMS = 100/√3 = 57.7 V; error = (55.5 − 57.7)/57.7 = −3.9 %.

questionText: Crest factor is another name for:
explanation: Crest factor and peak factor both mean peak value divided by RMS value; form factor is RMS divided by average.

questionText: A half-wave rectified sine wave has a peak value of 20 V. Its average value over one complete cycle is:
explanation: For half-wave rectification Vavg = Vm/π = 20/3.1416 = 6.37 V; 12.7 V (2Vm/π) would be the full-wave value.

questionText: The RMS value of a half-wave rectified sine wave of peak value 30 V is:
explanation: Only half of each cycle contributes to the mean square, so Vrms = Vm/2 = 30/2 = 15.0 V.

questionText: For which waveform is the form factor equal to exactly 1?
explanation: A square wave has constant magnitude, so its RMS and average values are both Vm and FF = 1; the others give 1.11, 1.155 and 1.57.

questionText: A full-wave rectified sine wave has a peak value of 100 V. Its average (DC) value is:
explanation: Each half cycle is a positive hump, so Vavg = 2Vm/π = 0.637 × 100 = 63.7 V over the whole cycle.

questionText: Among the following waveforms of equal peak value, which has the highest peak factor?
explanation: Peak factors: triangular 1.732, sine 1.414, full-wave rectified sine 1.414, square 1.0.

questionText: A symmetrical square wave alternating between +10 V and −10 V is applied to a 5 Ω resistor. The average power dissipated is:
explanation: For a square wave Vrms = Vm = 10 V, so P = Vrms²/R = 100/5 = 20 W; the sine factor 0.707 does not apply.

questionText: A symmetrical triangular voltage wave has a peak value of 30 V. Its RMS value is:
explanation: For a triangular wave Vrms = Vm/√3 = 30/1.732 = 17.3 V; 21.2 V would wrongly use the sine factor.

questionText: Which statement about RMS, form factor and peak factor is NOT correct?
options: An average-responding meter calibrated for sine waves reads the true RMS value of a square wave
The form factor of a pure sine wave is 1.11
The RMS value of a steady DC voltage equals the DC voltage itself
The peak factor of a symmetrical square wave is 1
explanation: An average-responding meter multiplies the rectified average by 1.11, so on a square wave it reads 11 % high; the other three statements are true.

questionText: A current i = 3 + 4√2 sin ωt A flows through a 10 Ω resistor. The average power dissipated is:
explanation: DC part 3 A, AC part RMS = 4 A; Irms² = 3² + 4² = 25 A², so P = 25 × 10 = 250 W.

questionText: Alternating voltages and currents are normally specified by their RMS values mainly because:
options: RMS values are always larger than peak values
RMS values are zero over a complete cycle and simplify calculation
RMS values give the same heating and power as the equal DC value, so P = VI and P = I²R stay valid
RMS values do not depend on the waveform shape
explanation: The RMS value is defined by equal heating, so power formulas used for DC hold directly; RMS is smaller than the peak and does depend on waveform shape.

questionText: The current i = 10 sin ωt + 10 sin 3ωt A contains a fundamental and a third harmonic. Its RMS value is:
explanation: Components of different frequency add as squares: Irms = √[(10/√2)² + (10/√2)²] = √(50 + 50) = 10.0 A.

questionText: The exact value of the form factor of a pure sine wave is:
explanation: FF = (Vm/√2)/(2Vm/π) = π/(2√2) = 1.11; π/2 = 1.57 is the half-wave rectified value.

questionText: A sinusoidal current flowing through a 100 Ω resistor dissipates 200 W. The peak value of the current is:
If the peak value of a sinusoidal voltage applied to a fixed resistor is doubled, the power dissipated becomes:
explanation: Vrms doubles with the peak, and P = Vrms²/R, so the power becomes 2² = 4 times.

questionText: A 1 kW, 230 V (RMS) electric heater is operated on a sinusoidal supply. The peak value of the heater current is:
The peak value of a sinusoidal voltage is kept constant while its frequency is raised from 50 Hz to 60 Hz. Its RMS value:
explanation: Vrms = Vm/√2 depends only on the amplitude and waveform shape, not on the frequency.

questionText: An alternating voltage waveform has an RMS value of 50 V, an average value of 40 V and a peak value of 80 V. Its form factor and peak factor are:
explanation: Form factor = RMS/average = 50/40 = 1.25; peak factor = peak/RMS = 80/50 = 1.6.

questionText: The form factor of a half-wave rectified sine wave is:
explanation: FF = Vrms/Vavg = (Vm/2)/(Vm/π) = π/2 = 1.57; 2.0 is its peak factor.

questionText: A capacitor is connected directly across a 240 V (RMS), 50 Hz sinusoidal supply. The maximum instantaneous voltage the capacitor dielectric must withstand is:
explanation: Vm = √2 × 240 = 339 V; the dielectric is stressed by the peak value, not the RMS value.

questionText: The dielectric strength of insulation in an AC system must be chosen on the basis of the:
explanation: Breakdown occurs when the instantaneous stress exceeds the dielectric strength, so the peak (maximum) voltage governs insulation design.

questionText: A 50 Hz sinusoidal voltage of RMS value 100 V passes through zero going positive at t = 0. Its instantaneous value at t = 2.5 ms is:
In deriving the RMS value of a sine wave, the mean value of sin²θ over one complete cycle is:
explanation: sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2 and cos 2θ averages to zero over a cycle, leaving 1/2; hence Vrms = Vm/√2.

questionText: A rectangular pulse train switches between 0 V and 10 V with a duty cycle of 20 %. Its RMS value is:
explanation: Vrms = √D × Vm = √0.2 × 10 = 4.47 V; the average would be D × Vm = 2 V.

questionText: A true-RMS voltmeter and a sine-calibrated average-responding voltmeter both read exactly 10 V on the same AC signal. The signal is most likely:
explanation: The average-responding meter is correct only when the form factor is 1.11, i.e. for a sine wave; it reads high on a square wave (FF = 1) and low on a triangle or a narrow pulse train (FF above 1.11).

questionText: The output of a full-wave rectifier is a rectified sine of peak 12 V. A moving-coil DC voltmeter and a true-RMS voltmeter connected across it read respectively:
explanation: The moving-coil meter reads the average 2Vm/π = 0.637 × 12 = 7.64 V; the RMS of a full-wave rectified sine equals Vm/√2 = 8.49 V.

questionText: When a sine wave is full-wave rectified, its RMS value:
options: Remains the same as that of the original sine
explanation: Rectification only reverses the negative half cycles; v² is unchanged at every instant, so the RMS value stays Vm/√2.

questionText: A half-wave rectified sinusoidal current of peak 10 A flows through a 20 Ω resistor. The average power dissipated is:
explanation: Irms of a half-wave rectified sine = Im/2 = 5 A; P = Irms² R = 25 × 20 = 500 W.

questionText: Compared with a full-wave rectified sine wave of the same peak value, a half-wave rectified sine wave has:
options: Half the average value and half the RMS value
Half the average value and 1/√2 times the RMS value
The same average value and half the RMS value
Half the average value and the same RMS value
explanation: Averages: Vm/π versus 2Vm/π, a ratio of 1/2; RMS: Vm/2 versus Vm/√2, a ratio of 1/√2 because the mean square is halved.

questionText: The voltage v = 30√2 sin ωt + 40√2 sin 2ωt V is applied to a true-RMS voltmeter. The meter reads:
explanation: Component RMS values are 30 V and 40 V at different frequencies, so Vrms = √(30² + 40²) = 50 V, not 30 + 40 = 70 V.

questionText: A sawtooth voltage rises linearly from 0 to 9 V and then drops instantly back to zero, repeating every period. Its RMS value is:
explanation: For a linear ramp from 0 to Vm, mean of v² = Vm²/3, so Vrms = Vm/√3 = 9/1.732 = 5.20 V; 4.50 V is the average.

questionText: The RMS value of an alternating quantity is also called its:
explanation: RMS, effective and virtual value are synonyms; mean is the average and crest is the peak.

questionText: For the voltage v = 5 + 10 sin ωt V, the average value over one complete cycle and the RMS value are respectively:
explanation: Full-cycle average = DC part = 5 V; Vrms = √(5² + (10/√2)²) = √(25 + 50) = 8.66 V.

questionText: A sinusoidal voltage of peak 10 V is applied across a 10 Ω resistor for one minute. The heat energy produced is:
explanation: Vrms = 7.07 V, P = Vrms²/R = 50/10 = 5 W; energy = 5 × 60 = 300 J.

questionText: A balanced star-connected load is supplied from a 400 V (line) three-phase system. The voltage across each phase of the load is:
To reverse the direction of rotation of a three-phase induction motor, one should:
options: Shift all three supply lines one place round (R to Y, Y to B, B to R)
Reverse the connection of the neutral wire
Interchange any two of the three supply lines
explanation: Swapping any two lines reverses the phase sequence and hence the rotating field; a cyclic shift keeps the same sequence.

questionText: In a balanced delta-connected load the line current is 17.32 A. The current in each phase of the load is:
In a balanced three-phase, four-wire star system, the current in the neutral wire is:
explanation: The three balanced line currents are equal and 120° apart, so their phasor sum, the neutral current, is zero.

questionText: In a balanced star-connected load each phase carries 15 A. The line current is:
explanation: In star each line is in series with its phase, so I_L = I_ph = 15 A.

questionText: For positive phase sequence RYB in a star-connected system, the line voltage V_RY, compared with the phase voltage V_R:
explanation: V_RY = V_R − V_Y = √3 V_ph∠30°, so the line voltage leads the corresponding phase voltage by 30°.

questionText: A balanced delta-connected load is fed from a 400 V three-phase supply. The voltage across each phase of the load is:
explanation: In delta each phase is connected directly between two lines, so V_ph = V_L = 400 V.

questionText: A three-phase, four-wire supply providing both 400 V and 230 V requires the source windings to be connected in:
options: Star, with the neutral brought out
explanation: Only a star connection has a neutral point; line-to-line gives 400 V and line-to-neutral gives 400/√3 = 230 V.

questionText: A balanced three-phase load takes a line current of 10 A from a 400 V supply at a power factor of 0.8 lagging. The total active power is:
The total instantaneous power delivered to a balanced three-phase load is:
options: Pulsating at twice the supply frequency
Pulsating at three times the supply frequency
explanation: The double-frequency pulsations of the three phases are 120° apart and cancel, leaving a constant 3 V_ph I_ph cos φ.

questionText: A balanced three-phase load draws 50 A from a 400 V supply at a power factor of 0.6 lagging. The total reactive power is:
In the expression P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ for a balanced load, φ is the phase angle between:
explanation: φ is the load impedance angle, the angle between each phase voltage and its phase current; the angle between line voltage and line current is (30° ± φ).

questionText: A balanced three-phase motor takes 10 kW from a 400 V supply at a power factor of 0.85 lagging. The line current is:
In the two-wattmeter method on a balanced load, one wattmeter gives a negative (reversed) reading. This shows that the load power factor is:
explanation: W2 = V_L I_L cos(30° + φ) becomes negative when φ exceeds 60°, i.e. when cos φ < 0.5.

questionText: Three identical 10 Ω resistors are connected in star across a 400 V, three-phase supply. The total power consumed is:
explanation: V_ph = 400/√3 = 231 V; P = 3 × V_ph²/R = 3 × 231²/10 = 16.0 kW (equivalently V_L²/R).

questionText: Three identical 10 Ω resistors are connected in delta across a 400 V, three-phase supply. The line current is:
Two wattmeters measure the power of a balanced, purely inductive three-phase load. Their readings will be:
options: Equal in magnitude but opposite in sign
One zero and the other positive
explanation: With φ = 90°: W1 = V_L I_L cos(−60°) = +0.5 V_L I_L and W2 = V_L I_L cos 120° = −0.5 V_L I_L, so the total is zero.

questionText: A balanced star load with Z = 6 + j8 Ω per phase is connected to a 400 V, three-phase supply. The total active power is:
A balanced delta load with Z = 8 + j6 Ω per phase is connected to a 400 V, three-phase supply. The line current and the power factor are:
Which of the following is NOT an advantage of a three-phase system over a single-phase system?
options: Power delivered to a balanced load is constant rather than pulsating
Less conductor material is needed to transmit the same power
Two different voltages can be obtained from one four-wire supply
Three-phase induction motors need a separate auxiliary winding to start
explanation: Three-phase windings produce a rotating field, so three-phase induction motors are self-starting; an auxiliary starting winding is needed by single-phase motors.

questionText: Two wattmeters connected to measure the power of a balanced three-phase load read 3 kW and 1 kW. The power factor of the load is:
In the two-wattmeter method the readings are W1 = 6 kW and W2 = −1 kW (the second meter had to be reversed). The total power is:
explanation: P = W1 + W2 = 6 + (−1) = 5 kW; a reversed reading must be subtracted.

questionText: A balanced delta-connected resistive load is supplied at constant line voltage. If one phase resistor goes open-circuit, the total power becomes:
explanation: The other two resistors still each see the full line voltage and draw their original power, so 2 of the 3 equal phase powers remain.

questionText: A balanced load of power factor 0.5 lagging takes a total of 8 kW, measured by the two-wattmeter method. The two wattmeter readings are:
explanation: At cos φ = 0.5, φ = 60°: W2 = V_L I_L cos 90° = 0, so W1 carries the whole 8 kW.

questionText: A balanced load with power factor 0.866 lagging takes a total of 9 kW, measured by two wattmeters. The individual readings are:
explanation: φ = 30°: W1 = V_L I_L cos 0° and W2 = V_L I_L cos 60° = W1/2; W1 + W2 = 1.5 W1 = 9 kW gives W1 = 6 kW, W2 = 3 kW.

questionText: A three-phase, three-wire supply feeds an unbalanced star-connected load with no neutral wire. Which statement is correct?
options: The star point of the load shifts from the supply neutral, so the three phase voltages become unequal
The three phase voltages stay equal to V_L/√3 because the line voltages are balanced
The line currents are still equal, only their phase angles change
The load draws no current until a neutral wire is connected
explanation: Without a neutral, unequal impedances move the load star point (neutral shift); the line voltages stay balanced but the phase voltages and currents become unequal.

questionText: A star-connected three-phase system has a line voltage of 11 kV. The phase (line-to-neutral) voltage is:
A delta-connected induction motor takes a starting line current of 60 A when switched direct-on-line. If a star-delta starter is used on the same supply, the starting line current is:
explanation: In star each winding gets V_L/√3, so I_ph falls by √3 and I_L = I_ph (not √3 I_ph); overall the line current is one third: 60/3 = 20 A.

questionText: The minimum number of wattmeters needed to measure the total power of an unbalanced three-phase, four-wire load is:
explanation: By Blondel's theorem the number needed is one fewer than the number of wires: 4 − 1 = 3.

questionText: A balanced delta-connected heater load takes 15 kW from a 400 V, three-phase supply at unity power factor. The current in each phase of the heater is:
explanation: Power per phase = 15/3 = 5 kW; V_ph = V_L = 400 V; I_ph = 5000/400 = 12.5 A (the line current would be √3 × 12.5 = 21.7 A).

questionText: The phasor sum of the three phase voltages of a balanced three-phase supply is:
explanation: Three equal phasors 120° apart form a closed triangle, so their sum is zero at every instant.

questionText: A balanced star-connected load takes 20 kW from a 400 V, three-phase supply at 0.8 power factor lagging. The magnitude of the impedance of each phase is:
A delta-connected induction motor is started with a star-delta starter. Compared with direct-on-line starting in delta, the starting torque is:
explanation: Torque is proportional to the square of the winding voltage; in star it is V_L/√3, so torque falls to (1/√3)² = 1/3.

questionText: A 400 V, three-phase, four-wire system supplies unity power factor loads in star drawing 20 A, 20 A and 10 A in lines R, Y and B respectively. The neutral current is:
explanation: Phasor sum: 20∠0° + 20∠−120° + 10∠120° = (balanced 20 A set, sum 0) − 10∠120°, whose magnitude is 10 A.

questionText: Which statement about a balanced delta connection is NOT correct?
options: The line voltage equals the phase voltage
The line current is √3 times the phase current
Each line current leads the corresponding phase current by 30°
explanation: In a delta connection each line current lags (not leads) the corresponding phase current by 30°; the other three statements are true.

questionText: At a certain instant in a balanced three-phase, three-wire system, i_R = 10 A and i_Y = −4 A. The instantaneous current i_B at that instant is:
explanation: The three instantaneous line currents of a 3-wire system sum to zero: i_B = −(10 − 4) = −6 A.

questionText: Two wattmeters measuring a balanced three-phase load read 5 kW and 3 kW. The total reactive power of the load is:
For the same power, distance, voltage between lines and line loss, a three-phase three-wire line needs, compared with a single-phase two-wire line:
explanation: Three-phase transmission needs only about three quarters of the copper of a single-phase line for the same power and losses.

questionText: Three identical 20 Ω resistors are connected in star (no neutral) across a 400 V, three-phase supply. If one resistor goes open-circuit, the total power consumed becomes:
explanation: The remaining two resistors are in series across the 400 V line: P = V_L²/(2R) = 400²/40 = 4.00 kW, half of the original 8 kW.

questionText: A three-phase, 100 kVA transformer has a secondary line voltage of 400 V. Its full-load secondary line current is:
With the phase sequence RYB and V_R taken as V∠0°, the phase voltage V_B is:
explanation: V_Y lags V_R by 120° and V_B lags by 240°, which is the same as leading by 120°, so V_B = V∠+120°.

questionText: A balanced delta-connected load on a 400 V, three-phase supply carries 10 A in each phase at a power factor of 0.7 lagging. The total active power is:
explanation: P = 3 V_ph I_ph cos φ = 3 × 400 × 10 × 0.7 = 8.40 kW (V_ph = V_L in delta).

questionText: A balanced three-phase load on a 400 V supply gives two-wattmeter readings of 4 kW and 2 kW. The line current is:
Each phase of a balanced three-phase load takes 2 kW and 1.5 kVAR. The total apparent power of the load is:
explanation: Per phase S = √(2² + 1.5²) = 2.5 kVA; total S = 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 kVA (total P = 6 kW, Q = 4.5 kVAR).

questionText: In a 50 Hz three-phase system, the time interval between the positive peaks of two successive phase voltages is:
explanation: The phases are 120° = one third of a cycle apart: T/3 = (1/50)/3 = 6.67 ms.

questionText: The phase sequence of a three-phase supply is the:
options: Angle of 120° between any two phase voltages
Order in which the three phase voltages reach their positive maximum values
Ratio of line voltage to phase voltage
Order in which the phase windings are placed round the alternator stator
explanation: Phase sequence (normally RYB) is the order in which the phase voltages attain their positive peaks; 120° is the phase displacement, not the sequence.

questionText: Which impurity, when added to pure silicon, produces an n-type semiconductor?
explanation: Arsenic is pentavalent and donates its fifth valence electron to the conduction band. Boron, gallium and aluminium are trivalent acceptors that give p-type material.

questionText: Silicon is doped with 5 × 10^16 acceptor atoms per cm³. Taking n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³, the equilibrium electron concentration is:
explanation: p ≈ N_A = 5 × 10^16 per cm³, so n = n_i²/p = 2.25 × 10^20/(5 × 10^16) = 4.5 × 10^3 per cm³. Using n_i instead of n_i² gives the absurd 3 × 10^-7.

questionText: In a semiconductor, a hole is best described as:
options: A vacancy left in a covalent bond, which behaves as a mobile positive charge
A positively charged nucleus that has lost all its electrons
A free proton moving through the crystal
A missing atom in the crystal lattice
explanation: When a valence electron leaves a bond, the vacancy can be filled by a neighbouring bond electron, so the vacancy moves through the crystal and acts as a carrier of charge +q. No atom or proton moves.

questionText: Using q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C, n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³, μ_n = 1350 cm²/V·s and μ_p = 480 cm²/V·s, the resistivity of intrinsic silicon is about:
An n-type silicon sample has far more free electrons than holes. Its net electric charge is:
options: Negative, because electrons are the majority carriers
Zero, because the fixed positive donor ions balance the free electrons
Positive, because each donor atom has lost an electron
Negative at low temperature and positive at high temperature
explanation: Every free electron from a donor leaves behind a fixed positive donor ion, and thermally generated pairs are also neutral, so the sample as a whole is neutral.

questionText: n-type silicon has N_D = 10^16 per cm³. With q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C and μ_n = 1350 cm²/V·s (ignore the holes), its resistivity is about:
explanation: σ = q N_D μ_n = 1.6 × 10^-19 × 10^16 × 1350 = 2.16 S/cm, so ρ = 1/2.16 = 0.463 Ω·cm. The value 2.16 is σ, not ρ; using μ_p gives 1.30 Ω·cm.

questionText: Arranged in order of increasing band gap at 300 K, the semiconductors germanium, silicon and gallium arsenide are:
explanation: The band gaps are about 0.72 eV (Ge), 1.1 eV (Si) and 1.42 eV (GaAs).

questionText: A bar of n-type silicon is 2 mm long with a 1 mm × 1 mm cross-section and N_D = 10^15 per cm³. With q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C and μ_n = 1350 cm²/V·s, its resistance is about:
In an n-type semiconductor, the minority carriers (holes) arise mainly from:
options: Holes injected from the metal contacts
Ionisation of the donor atoms by the applied field
explanation: Donors supply only electrons; every hole in n-type material comes from a thermally broken bond, which is why the minority concentration rises steeply with temperature.

questionText: Electrons in silicon (μ_n = 1350 cm²/V·s) are subjected to an electric field of 100 V/cm. Their drift velocity is:
explanation: v_d = μE = 1350 × 100 = 1.35 × 10^5 cm/s = 1.35 × 10^3 m/s. Quoting 1.35 × 10^5 in m/s forgets the cm-to-m conversion; 4.8 × 10^2 m/s would be the hole value.

questionText: Silicon has 5 × 10^22 atoms per cm³. It is doped with one donor atom per 10^8 silicon atoms. With n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³, the hole concentration is:
explanation: N_D = 5 × 10^22/10^8 = 5 × 10^14 per cm³ ≈ n, so p = n_i²/n = 2.25 × 10^20/(5 × 10^14) = 4.5 × 10^5 per cm³. The value 5 × 10^14 is the electron concentration.

questionText: An n-type silicon sample with N_D = 10^16 per cm³ is warmed from 300 K to 350 K, still well within the extrinsic range. Which statement is correct?
options: The hole concentration rises greatly while the electron concentration stays almost equal to N_D
Both carrier concentrations stay exactly constant
The electron concentration doubles and the hole concentration halves
explanation: n_i rises steeply with temperature, so the minority concentration p = n_i²/N_D increases by orders of magnitude. The majority concentration is fixed by the fully ionised donors as long as n_i remains much smaller than N_D.

questionText: Silicon (n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³) is doped with N_D = 10^17 per cm³. By what factor is the hole concentration reduced below its intrinsic value?
Which statement about the mass-action law n·p = n_i² is NOT correct?
options: It applies only to intrinsic semiconductors
It holds in thermal equilibrium for both intrinsic and extrinsic material
Because n_i depends on temperature, the product n·p changes with temperature
Increasing the donor density lowers the hole density
explanation: The law holds for any non-degenerate semiconductor in thermal equilibrium, doped or not; that is exactly what lets us find minority concentrations in extrinsic material.

questionText: A silicon sample contains N_D = 3 × 10^16 donors and N_A = 10^16 acceptors per cm³. With n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³, the type of the material and its hole concentration are:
explanation: Net doping N_D − N_A = 2 × 10^16 per cm³ of donors, so it is n-type with n = 2 × 10^16 and p = 2.25 × 10^20/(2 × 10^16) ≈ 1.1 × 10^4 per cm³. Ignoring the acceptors gives 7.5 × 10^3.

questionText: Diffusion current in a semiconductor is caused by:
options: Collisions of carriers with impurity ions
explanation: Carriers move from regions of high concentration to low concentration by random thermal motion, even with no field. Current driven by an electric field is drift current.

questionText: By what factor does the conductivity of silicon increase when it is doped with N_D = 10^16 per cm³, compared with intrinsic silicon? Use n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³, μ_n = 1350 and μ_p = 480 cm²/V·s, and neglect holes in the doped sample.
explanation: σ_doped/σ_i = N_D μ_n/[n_i(μ_n + μ_p)] = (10^16 × 1350)/(1.5 × 10^10 × 1830) ≈ 4.9 × 10^5. The ratio N_D/n_i = 6.7 × 10^5 alone ignores the mobilities.

questionText: In silicon the electron mobility (about 1350 cm²/V·s) is greater than the hole mobility (about 480 cm²/V·s) mainly because:
options: Electrons carry a larger charge than holes
There are always more electrons than holes
Conduction-band electrons have a smaller effective mass and move more freely than holes, whose motion is a chain of valence-bond transfers
The applied field acts only on electrons
explanation: Mobility depends on effective mass and scattering, not on concentration. Electrons and holes carry equal and opposite charge, and the field acts on both.

questionText: What donor concentration gives n-type silicon a resistivity of 1 Ω·cm? Use q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C and μ_n = 1350 cm²/V·s.
Which change would INCREASE the electron mobility in a silicon sample?
options: Reducing the doping concentration at the same temperature
explanation: Mobility is limited by lattice scattering, which grows with temperature, and by impurity scattering, which grows with doping. Lighter doping therefore raises mobility; the applied voltage changes the drift velocity, not the mobility (at high fields mobility actually falls).

questionText: At 300 K (V_T = kT/q = 26 mV), the diffusion constant of electrons in silicon with μ_n = 1350 cm²/V·s is about:
explanation: Einstein relation: D_n = μ_n V_T = 1350 × 0.026 = 35.1 cm²/s. Dividing μ by V_T gives 5.2 × 10^4; using μ_p = 480 gives 12.5 cm²/s.

questionText: In an intrinsic semiconductor the Fermi level lies:
options: Very close to the middle of the band gap
explanation: With equal electron and hole concentrations the Fermi level sits almost at mid-gap (exactly at mid-gap if the effective masses were equal). Donor doping moves it up towards the conduction band, acceptor doping down towards the valence band.

questionText: The electron concentration in a silicon region falls linearly from 10^15 per cm³ to zero over a distance of 10 µm. With D_n = 35 cm²/s and q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C, the magnitude of the electron diffusion current density is:
explanation: dn/dx = 10^15/(10 × 10^-4 cm) = 10^18 per cm⁴; J = q D_n dn/dx = 1.6 × 10^-19 × 35 × 10^18 = 5.6 A/cm². Converting 10 µm wrongly as 10^-2 cm gives 0.56 A/cm².

questionText: In n-type silicon, the donor energy level lies:
options: Slightly above the top of the valence band
Slightly below the bottom of the conduction band (roughly 0.05 eV)
Exactly at the middle of the band gap
explanation: The fifth electron of a donor is so weakly bound that only a few hundredths of an electronvolt lift it into the conduction band, so donors are fully ionised at room temperature. Acceptor levels lie just above the valence band.

questionText: For silicon (E_g = 1.1 eV, k = 8.62 × 10^-5 eV/K), using n_i ∝ T^(3/2) e^(−E_g/2kT), the ratio n_i(310 K)/n_i(300 K) is about:
explanation: Ratio = (310/300)^1.5 × exp[(1.1/(2 × 8.62 × 10^-5)) × (1/300 − 1/310)] = 1.05 × e^0.686 ≈ 1.05 × 1.99 ≈ 2.1. Omitting the 2 in 2kT gives about 4.1; the temperature factor alone is only 1.05.

questionText: Silicon has atomic number 14. The number of valence electrons in each silicon atom is:
explanation: The configuration is 2, 8, 4, so silicon is tetravalent and forms four covalent bonds with its neighbours.

questionText: Silicon's band gap is 1.1 eV. Expressed in joules (1 eV = 1.6 × 10^-19 J), this is:
explanation: E = 1.1 × 1.6 × 10^-19 = 1.76 × 10^-19 J. Dividing instead of multiplying gives 6.9 × 10^18, which is absurdly large.

questionText: Silicon is a poor light emitter, whereas GaAs is used in LEDs and laser diodes. The reason is that:
options: Silicon has an indirect band gap, while GaAs has a direct band gap
Silicon has a larger band gap than GaAs
GaAs cannot be doped n-type or p-type
Silicon has no holes at room temperature
explanation: In a direct-gap material an electron can drop into a hole and emit a photon directly; in indirect-gap silicon the transition needs a lattice vibration as well, so recombination mostly produces heat. GaAs (1.42 eV) actually has the larger gap.

questionText: The longest wavelength of light that can create electron-hole pairs in germanium (E_g = 0.72 eV) is about (use λ in µm ≈ 1.24/E_g in eV):
explanation: λ_c = 1.24/0.72 = 1.72 µm; longer wavelengths carry photons of less than 0.72 eV. The value 1.13 µm is the silicon cut-off and 0.58 comes from inverting the ratio.

questionText: The carrier lifetime in a semiconductor is the:
options: Average time an excess minority carrier exists before recombining
Time taken for a carrier to cross the whole device
Time needed to dope the crystal
Time after which the crystal becomes intrinsic
explanation: Excess minority carriers recombine with majority carriers; their average survival time τ is the lifetime, and together with the diffusion constant it sets the diffusion length L = √(Dτ).

questionText: Intrinsic silicon at 300 K has n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³. The total concentration of free carriers (electrons plus holes) is:
explanation: In intrinsic material n = p = n_i, so n + p = 2 × 1.5 × 10^10 = 3 × 10^10 per cm³. 2.25 × 10^20 is the product n·p, not the sum.

questionText: The Einstein relation connects which two carrier properties?
options: The conductivity and the resistivity: σ = 1/ρ
The diffusion constant and the mobility: D/μ = kT/q
The drift velocity and the field: v_d = μE
The electron and hole concentrations: n·p = n_i²
explanation: Diffusion and drift are both limited by the same scattering processes, so D/μ equals the thermal voltage kT/q, about 26 mV at 300 K.

questionText: Silicon contains 5 × 10^22 atoms per cm³. If it is doped with 10^16 donor atoms per cm³, there is one donor atom for every:
explanation: 5 × 10^22/10^16 = 5 × 10^6, so one donor per five million silicon atoms. The inverse, 2 × 10^-7, is the fractional impurity content.

questionText: A silicon sample is doped with N_D = N_A = 10^16 per cm³. Compared with pure silicon at the same temperature, this fully compensated sample has:
options: Electron and hole concentrations of 10^16 per cm³ each
About the same electron and hole concentrations (n ≈ p ≈ n_i), but lower mobility because of the ionised impurities
An electron concentration of 2 × 10^16 per cm³
explanation: The acceptors capture all the donor electrons, so the net doping is zero and the mass-action law with neutrality gives n = p = n_i. The 2 × 10^16 ionised impurities still scatter carriers, lowering the mobility.

questionText: Carriers in a semiconductor move with an average drift velocity of 2 × 10^4 cm/s in a field of 50 V/cm. Their mobility is:
explanation: μ = v_d/E = 2 × 10^4/50 = 400 cm²/V·s. Multiplying gives 10^6 and inverting gives 2.5 × 10^-3.

questionText: In an intrinsic semiconductor at room temperature:
options: There are more holes than free electrons
There are no holes, only free electrons
The free-electron concentration equals the hole concentration
explanation: Each broken bond creates one free electron and one hole, so n = p = n_i. The conductivity is small but not zero at room temperature.

questionText: p-type silicon has N_A = 2 × 10^16 per cm³ and μ_p = 480 cm²/V·s. With q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C and ignoring electrons, its conductivity is about:
explanation: σ = q N_A μ_p = 1.6 × 10^-19 × 2 × 10^16 × 480 = 1.54 S/cm. Using μ_n = 1350 gives 4.32 S/cm, and 0.65 is the resistivity in Ω·cm.

questionText: When an electric field is applied to a semiconductor, holes drift:
options: Opposite to the field, so their current cancels the electron current
In the direction of the field, but their current opposes the electron current
Not at all, because holes are fixed in the lattice
In the direction of the field, and their current adds to the electron current
explanation: Holes are positive and move along the field, electrons move against it; because the charges are opposite, both motions give conventional current in the field direction, so σ = q(nμ_n + pμ_p).

questionText: An intrinsic germanium bar (n_i = 2.5 × 10^13 per cm³, μ_n = 3900 cm²/V·s, μ_p = 1900 cm²/V·s, q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C) has a field of 10 V/cm applied. The total drift current density is about:
explanation: J = q n_i (μ_n + μ_p) E = 1.6 × 10^-19 × 2.5 × 10^13 × 5800 × 10 = 0.232 A/cm². Only the electron term gives 0.156 A/cm²; subtracting the mobilities gives 0.080 A/cm².

questionText: If an extrinsic silicon sample is heated to a very high temperature (several hundred °C), it:
options: Behaves like intrinsic material, because thermally generated carriers far outnumber the dopant carriers
Changes permanently from n-type to p-type
Keeps its carrier concentration fixed at the doping level
explanation: n_i grows exponentially with temperature; once it greatly exceeds the doping, n ≈ p ≈ n_i and the doping no longer controls conduction. This sets the upper temperature limit of devices.

questionText: Using n_i = 2.5 × 10^13 per cm³ for Ge and 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³ for Si, and μ_n + μ_p = 5800 cm²/V·s for Ge and 1830 cm²/V·s for Si, the ratio of the intrinsic conductivity of germanium to that of silicon is about:
explanation: σ_Ge/σ_Si = (2.5 × 10^13 × 5800)/(1.5 × 10^10 × 1830) ≈ 5.3 × 10^3. The n_i ratio alone is 1.7 × 10^3 and the mobility ratio alone is 3.2.

questionText: The SI unit of carrier mobility μ is:
explanation: Mobility is drift velocity per unit field, μ = v_d/E, so its unit is (m/s)/(V/m) = m²/(V·s). In practice it is usually quoted in cm²/(V·s), where 1 m²/(V·s) = 10^4 cm²/(V·s).

questionText: Which of the following is NOT a semiconductor?
explanation: Copper is a metal whose conduction and valence bands overlap. Germanium, gallium arsenide and silicon carbide all have band gaps (about 0.72, 1.42 and 3.3 eV).

questionText: In a silicon sample at 300 K (n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³) the measured hole concentration is 4 × 10^5 per cm³. The sample is:
options: p-type, with holes as majority carriers at 4 × 10^5 per cm³
explanation: p is far below n_i, so holes are the minority carriers and the sample is n-type: n = n_i²/p = 2.25 × 10^20/(4 × 10^5) ≈ 5.6 × 10^14 per cm³.

questionText: For n-type silicon with N_D = 10^16 per cm³ at 300 K (kT = 0.026 eV, n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³), how far above the intrinsic level E_i does the Fermi level lie? Use E_F − E_i = kT ln(N_D/n_i).
Excess electrons in p-type silicon have D_n = 35 cm²/s and lifetime τ_n = 1 µs. Their diffusion length L_n = √(D_n τ_n) is about:
explanation: L_n = √(35 × 10^-6) cm = 5.92 × 10^-3 cm = 59 µm. Slipping a factor of 10 in the cm-to-µm conversion gives 5.9 or 590 µm.

questionText: At absolute zero temperature, a pure silicon crystal behaves as:
explanation: At 0 K every valence electron is locked in a covalent bond and the conduction band is empty, so no carriers are available and pure silicon acts as an insulator. Carriers appear only when thermal energy breaks bonds.

questionText: Silicon is doped with 10^15 donor atoms per cm³. Taking n_i = 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³, the equilibrium hole concentration is approximately:
explanation: With n ≈ N_D = 10^15 per cm³, the mass-action law gives p = n_i²/n = (1.5 × 10^10)²/10^15 = 2.25 × 10^20/10^15 = 2.25 × 10^5 per cm³.

questionText: The depletion region of an unbiased pn junction consists mainly of:
options: A high concentration of free electrons and holes
Immobile ionised donor and acceptor atoms with almost no free carriers
Only free electrons that have diffused from the n side
Neutral atoms of the intrinsic semiconductor
explanation: Majority carriers diffuse across and recombine, leaving uncovered positive donor ions on the n side and negative acceptor ions on the p side; the region is depleted of mobile carriers.

questionText: When the forward bias applied to a pn junction is increased, the width of the depletion region:
explanation: Forward bias opposes the built-in potential, pushing majority carriers towards the junction and narrowing the depletion layer.

questionText: For a silicon diode carrying a constant forward current, a rise in junction temperature causes its forward voltage to:
explanation: Because I_S rises steeply with temperature, less voltage is needed for the same current; the forward drop has a temperature coefficient of about −2 mV/°C.

questionText: A silicon diode (practical model, V_D = 0.7 V) is connected in forward bias in series with a 1 kΩ resistor across a 5 V DC supply. The diode current is:
explanation: I = (5 − 0.7)/1 kΩ = 4.3 mA. Ignoring the drop gives 5 mA; using 0.3 V (germanium) gives 4.7 mA.

questionText: A silicon diode has I_S = 1 × 10^-13 A and n = 1. Taking V_T = 26 mV, the forward current at V_D = 0.60 V is about:
For a diode with ideality factor n = 2 at V_T = 26 mV, the increase in forward voltage needed to raise the current tenfold is about:
explanation: ΔV = nV_T ln(10) = 2 × 26 mV × 2.303 ≈ 120 mV. With n = 1 it would be about 60 mV.

questionText: A diode (n = 1, V_T = 26 mV) has a forward drop of 0.650 V at 1 mA. Using the Shockley equation, its forward voltage at 20 mA is about:
The dynamic (AC) resistance of a forward-biased diode with n = 1 at I_D = 2 mA and V_T = 26 mV is:
explanation: r_d = nV_T/I_D = 26 mV / 2 mA = 13 Ω.

questionText: A silicon diode has a forward voltage of 0.65 V when it carries 5 mA. Its static (DC) resistance at this point is:
explanation: R_D = V_D/I_D = 0.65 V / 5 mA = 130 Ω. The 5.2 Ω value is the dynamic resistance 26 mV/5 mA, which is a different quantity.

questionText: Which statement about the dynamic resistance r_d of a forward-biased diode is correct?
options: It is equal to V_D/I_D at the operating point
It is inversely proportional to the DC current through the diode
It increases as the forward current increases
It is independent of the operating point
explanation: r_d = nV_T/I_D is the slope of the V-I curve at the Q-point; doubling I_D halves r_d. V_D/I_D is the static resistance.

questionText: A diode biased at I_D = 0.5 mA (n = 1, V_T = 25 mV) is fed a 10 mV peak AC signal through a 950 Ω series resistor, with the DC bias path having no effect on the AC signal. The peak AC voltage across the diode is:
explanation: r_d = 25 mV / 0.5 mA = 50 Ω. By voltage division v_d = 10 mV × 50/(950 + 50) = 0.5 mV.

questionText: A silicon diode (0.7 V) and a germanium diode (0.3 V) are connected in series, both forward biased, with a 2.2 kΩ resistor across a 12 V DC supply. The circuit current is:
A silicon diode is connected in reverse bias in series with a 1 kΩ resistor across a 10 V DC supply. Using the practical model, the voltage across the resistor is about:
explanation: A reverse-biased diode behaves as an open circuit, so almost no current flows; the resistor drop is about 0 V and nearly all 10 V appears across the diode.

questionText: A silicon diode (0.7 V) and a germanium diode (0.3 V) are connected in parallel, both forward biased, and fed from a 10 V DC supply through a 1 kΩ resistor. The current through the silicon diode is about:
explanation: The germanium diode turns on first and holds the parallel voltage at 0.3 V, below the 0.7 V the silicon diode needs, so the silicon diode carries practically no current; the germanium diode carries (10 − 0.3)/1 k = 9.7 mA.

questionText: Two identical silicon diodes (0.7 V) are connected in parallel and fed from a 5 V DC supply through a 430 Ω resistor. Assuming they share current equally, the current in each diode is:
explanation: Total current = (5 − 0.7)/430 = 10 mA; shared equally, each diode carries 5.0 mA.

questionText: A half-wave rectifier with an ideal diode is fed a sinusoidal voltage of 20 V peak. The average (DC) output voltage across a resistive load is:
explanation: V_dc = V_m/π = 20/π = 6.37 V. The value 2V_m/π = 12.7 V applies to a full-wave rectifier.

questionText: A bridge rectifier using silicon diodes (0.7 V each) is fed from a transformer secondary of 12 V rms and drives a resistive load with no filter. The average output voltage is about:
explanation: V_m = 12√2 = 16.97 V; two diodes conduct, so the output peak is 16.97 − 1.4 = 15.57 V and V_dc = 2 × 15.57/π = 9.91 V.

questionText: In a centre-tapped full-wave rectifier each half of the secondary delivers 15 V peak. With ideal diodes, the peak inverse voltage across each diode is:
explanation: When one diode conducts, the non-conducting diode sees the full secondary: PIV = 2V_m = 2 × 15 = 30 V.

questionText: For the same peak secondary voltage V_m per diode path, which rectifier requires diodes with a peak inverse voltage rating of 2V_m?
options: None; every rectifier requires only V_m
explanation: In the centre-tapped circuit the reverse-biased diode sees the voltage of both halves of the secondary, 2V_m; in the bridge each diode sees only V_m.

questionText: A full-wave rectifier is supplied from 50 Hz mains. The fundamental frequency of the ripple in its output is:
explanation: A full-wave rectifier produces two output pulses per input cycle, so the ripple frequency is 2 × 50 = 100 Hz.

questionText: The ripple factor of an unfiltered full-wave rectifier with a resistive load is about:
explanation: γ = √((V_rms/V_dc)² − 1) with V_rms = V_m/√2 and V_dc = 2V_m/π gives √(π²/8 − 1) ≈ 0.48; the half-wave value is 1.21.

questionText: The maximum theoretical rectification efficiency (DC load power divided by AC input power) of a half-wave rectifier is:
explanation: η = P_dc/P_ac = (V_m/π)²/(V_m/2)² = 4/π² = 0.405, i.e. 40.5 %; a full-wave rectifier reaches 8/π² = 81.1 %.

questionText: A full-wave rectifier on 50 Hz mains feeds a 100 mA load through a 1000 µF reservoir capacitor. The approximate peak-to-peak ripple voltage is:
explanation: V_r(pp) = I/(f_r C) with f_r = 2 × 50 = 100 Hz: 0.1/(100 × 1000 × 10^-6) = 1.0 V. Using 50 Hz gives the half-wave value, 2.0 V.

questionText: A half-wave rectifier with a silicon diode (0.7 V) is fed a 10 V peak sine wave and drives a 1 kΩ resistive load. The average load current is about:
