explanation: Class C places the Q-point beyond cut-off, so the input must first overcome the reverse bias and V_BE before any collector current flows, giving conduction for less than 180°.

questionText: The low-pass LC filter at the output of a class D amplifier is needed to:
options: Remove the high-frequency switching component and leave the amplified audio signal
Generate the triangle carrier for the modulator
Bias the MOSFETs at the edge of conduction
Store energy between current pulses at the signal frequency, as in a class C tank
explanation: The switches produce a full-amplitude PWM square wave; the filter passes its slowly varying average (the audio) and rejects the switching frequency and its harmonics.

questionText: Crossover distortion in an unbiased complementary class B stage is caused by:
options: Both transistors conducting simultaneously near the zero crossing
Saturation of the transistors at the signal peaks
Neither transistor conducting while the input is below about ±0.7 V
The output coupling capacitor blocking low frequencies
explanation: Each base-emitter junction needs about 0.7 V to turn on, so for small input levels around zero both transistors are off and the output stays at zero, producing a step at each crossing.

questionText: An unbiased complementary class B emitter-follower stage uses silicon transistors (V_BE(on) = 0.7 V). The input is a sine wave of 5 V peak. Ignoring other losses, the peak output voltage is:
explanation: The output follows the input minus one V_BE drop: 5 − 0.7 = 4.3 V. Subtracting 2V_BE (3.6 V) confuses it with the voltage between the two bases.

questionText: An unbiased complementary class B stage has V_BE(on) = 0.7 V for each transistor and is driven by a 1.4 V peak sine wave. For how many degrees of each cycle does each transistor conduct?
explanation: Conduction starts when 1.4 sin θ = 0.7, i.e. θ = 30°, and ends at 150°, so each device conducts for 150° − 30° = 120° instead of the ideal 180°.

questionText: An emitter follower is widely used as a power output stage mainly because it:
options: Conducts for less than 180° and is therefore very efficient
Inverts the signal, cancelling even harmonics
Has a low output resistance and so can drive a low-resistance load without losing gain
explanation: The follower's output resistance is only about r_e plus the source resistance divided by β, so a loudspeaker of a few ohms receives almost the full voltage; its voltage gain is just below 1.

questionText: A class A emitter-follower output stage runs from ±12 V, drives R_L = 100 Ω and is biased by a 120 mA constant current source. Ignoring saturation voltages, its efficiency at the largest undistorted output is:
A series-fed class A amplifier with V_CC = 20 V and a collector load of 20 Ω is biased at the centre of its load line. The maximum AC power it can deliver to the load is:
explanation: Peak voltage = V_CC/2 = 10 V and peak current = I_CQ = 0.5 A, so P_ac = (10 × 0.5)/2 = 2.5 W, i.e. V_CC²/(8R_L). The 10 W figure is the DC input power.

questionText: A series-fed class A stage with V_CC = 24 V and R_C = 24 Ω is biased at I_CQ = 0.5 A. A signal produces a sinusoidal collector current of 0.3 A peak. Its efficiency is:
explanation: P_ac = I_p² R_C/2 = 0.09 × 24/2 = 1.08 W; P_dc = V_CC I_CQ = 12 W; η = 1.08/12 = 9 %. Forgetting the 1/2 of the rms conversion gives 18 %.

questionText: A transformer-coupled class A amplifier operates from V_CC = 12 V with a quiescent collector current of 250 mA. The maximum AC power it can deliver to the load (ideal transformer) is:
explanation: P_dc = 12 × 0.25 = 3 W, and the theoretical maximum efficiency of transformer-coupled class A is 50 %, so P_ac(max) = 1.5 W. The 0.75 W figure uses the 25 % series-fed limit.

questionText: In a transformer-coupled class A amplifier with V_CC = 10 V, the collector voltage swings between 4 V and 16 V. Using η = 50 % × [(V_max − V_min)/(V_max + V_min)]², its efficiency is:
A class B push-pull stage with V_CC = 20 V delivers a sine output of 10 V peak. Its efficiency is approximately:
explanation: η = (π/4)(V_m/V_CC) = 0.785 × 10/20 = 39.3 %. The 78.5 % limit applies only at full swing V_m = V_CC.

questionText: A complementary class B stage runs from ±15 V and drives an 8 Ω load with an output of 12 V peak. The total DC power drawn from the two supplies is approximately:
explanation: I_m = 12/8 = 1.5 A; each supply provides an average of I_m/π, so P_S = 2V_CC I_m/π = 2 × 15 × 1.5/π = 14.3 W. The 9 W figure is the load power.

questionText: A complementary class B stage with supplies of ±20 V drives an 8 Ω load with 16 V peak output. The power dissipated in each output transistor is approximately:
explanation: I_m = 2 A; P_S = 2 × 20 × 2/π = 25.46 W; P_L = 16²/(2 × 8) = 16 W; P_D = 9.46 W for the pair, so 4.73 W per transistor.

questionText: A complementary class B amplifier uses ±12 V supplies and an 8 Ω load. The maximum power that each transistor may have to dissipate, over all signal levels, is approximately:
explanation: Worst-case dissipation occurs at V_m = 2V_CC/π and totals 2V_CC²/(π²R_L) = 2 × 144/(9.87 × 8) = 3.65 W, which is 1.82 W per transistor.

questionText: Ignoring saturation voltages, the maximum sine-wave power a complementary class B stage with ±15 V supplies can deliver into an 8 Ω load is:
explanation: At full swing V_m = V_CC = 15 V: P_L = V_m²/(2R_L) = 225/16 = 14.1 W. Using V_m²/R_L gives 28.1 W.

questionText: A class B complementary stage is designed for a maximum sine output of 20 W. The worst-case dissipation for which each output transistor must be rated is approximately:
explanation: Per-transistor worst case V_CC²/(π²R_L) divided by P_L(max) = V_CC²/(2R_L) is 2/π² = 0.203, so each device needs about 0.203 × 20 = 4.05 W; 8.1 W is for the pair.

questionText: In a class B push-pull stage with V_CC = 18 V, the transistor dissipation is greatest when the peak output voltage is approximately:
explanation: Dissipation peaks at V_m = 2V_CC/π = 36/π = 11.5 V, not at full output.

questionText: A series-fed class A stage has V_CC = 12 V, R_C = 6 Ω and a quiescent current of 1 A. With no input signal, the power dissipated in the transistor is:
explanation: V_CEQ = 12 − 1 × 6 = 6 V, so P_D = V_CEQ × I_CQ = 6 W. The supply delivers 12 W, of which the other 6 W heats R_C.

questionText: In a class A power amplifier, the power dissipated in the transistor is greatest when:
options: The output is at its maximum undistorted swing
The output swing is 63.7 % of V_CC
The load is open-circuited during full swing
explanation: The DC input power of class A is constant; P_D = P_dc − P_ac, so the transistor dissipates most when P_ac = 0, i.e. at idle.

questionText: Which statement about power dissipation in a class B push-pull stage is correct?
options: It is greatest with no signal, as in class A
It rises continuously and is greatest at full output swing
It is independent of the signal level
It is zero with no signal and reaches its maximum at a peak output of about 0.64 V_CC
explanation: With zero quiescent current there is no idle loss; P_D = P_S − P_L rises and then falls with swing, peaking at V_m = 2V_CC/π ≈ 0.637 V_CC.

questionText: A class AB complementary output stage runs from ±15 V and is biased at a quiescent current of 20 mA. The power drawn from the supplies with no signal is:
explanation: The quiescent current flows from +15 V through both transistors to −15 V, a total of 30 V: P = 30 × 0.02 = 0.6 W. Zero would be true only for pure class B.

questionText: The output of an unbiased class B stage driven by a small sine wave shows a flat step each time the waveform passes through zero. This defect is called:
explanation: The flat step around the zero crossing, where neither transistor conducts, is crossover distortion; clipping occurs at the peaks.

questionText: A class C amplifier is driven at 10 MHz and its collector tank is tuned to 30 MHz. The output frequency is:
explanation: The pulsed collector current is rich in harmonics; a tank tuned to the third harmonic selects 3 × 10 = 30 MHz, so the stage acts as a frequency tripler.

questionText: In a class C stage the transistor begins to conduct only when the input exceeds 2.0 V (reverse bias plus V_BE). If the input is a sine wave of 2.83 V peak, the conduction angle is approximately:
explanation: Conduction begins where 2.83 sin θ = 2.0, i.e. θ ≈ 45°, and ends at 135°, so θ_c = 135° − 45° = 90° (equivalently 2 arccos(2.0/2.83)).

questionText: A class C stage cannot be used as a wide-band audio amplifier because:
options: Its efficiency is too low for audio power levels
It requires a complementary npn-pnp pair
Its collector current is a train of narrow pulses, and a sine output is restored only by a load tuned to one frequency
explanation: Without a tuned tank the output would be the distorted pulse train itself; the tank works at a single frequency, which is unsuitable for a broadband audio signal.

questionText: A class D half-bridge switches its output between 0 V and 24 V. When the duty cycle is 0.6, the average (filtered) output voltage is:
explanation: V_o(avg) = D × V_DD = 0.6 × 24 = 14.4 V; 9.6 V would be the result of using the off-time fraction.

questionText: In a class D stage only one MOSFET conducts at a time, each having an on-resistance of 0.1 Ω, and the load is 8 Ω. Neglecting switching and filter losses, the efficiency is approximately:
explanation: The on-switch is in series with the load, so η = R_L/(R_L + R_on) = 8/8.1 = 98.8 %. 1.2 % is the fraction lost, not the efficiency.

questionText: In a class D amplifier the pulse-width-modulated drive signal is usually generated by:
options: Passing the input through a tuned LC tank
Comparing the input signal with a high-frequency triangle wave in a comparator
Rectifying the input with a bridge rectifier
Biasing the output transistors slightly above cut-off
explanation: The comparator output is high whenever the input exceeds the triangle, so the pulse width follows the instantaneous input level.

questionText: The output transistors of a class D amplifier dissipate very little power because:
options: When on their voltage is almost zero and when off their current is almost zero, so the V × I product stays small
They conduct for exactly 180° of each cycle
Their quiescent current is set just above cut-off
The output filter absorbs the heat
explanation: Dissipation is the product of device voltage and current; a switch that is fully on or fully off keeps one of them near zero except during the brief transitions.

questionText: A class D audio amplifier must reproduce signals up to 20 kHz. Which switching frequency is the most suitable?
explanation: The switching frequency must be many times the highest audio frequency so the output filter can remove it without affecting the audio band; 400 kHz is 20 times 20 kHz.

questionText: In a complementary-symmetry class B output stage, during the positive half-cycle of the input:
options: The pnp transistor conducts and the npn transistor is cut off
The npn transistor conducts and the pnp transistor is cut off
explanation: A positive input forward-biases the npn base-emitter junction and reverse-biases the pnp one, so the npn device sources current into the load; the roles reverse on the negative half-cycle.

questionText: Which statement about a complementary-symmetry push-pull output stage is correct?
options: It requires both transistors to be of the same polarity (both npn)
It needs a phase-splitter to produce two antiphase drive signals
It needs no centre-tapped transformer, because the joined emitters of the npn and pnp devices drive the load directly
It cannot be operated from a single supply
explanation: The opposite polarities of the npn and pnp devices mean one input signal turns on one device per half-cycle, so no phase splitter or transformer is needed; a single supply with an output capacitor also works.

questionText: A complementary class B stage is powered from a single 24 V supply, with the midpoint coupled to an 8 Ω load through a large capacitor. Ignoring saturation voltages, the maximum sine output power is:
explanation: The midpoint sits at 12 V, so the peak swing is V_CC/2 = 12 V and P = 12²/(2 × 8) = 9 W. Using the full 24 V gives 36 W.

questionText: A complementary class B amplifier must deliver 25 W of sine power into an 8 Ω load. If each transistor has V_CE(sat) = 2 V, the minimum symmetrical supply voltage is:
explanation: V_m = √(2 P R_L) = √(2 × 25 × 8) = 20 V peak; allowing 2 V saturation, V_CC = 20 + 2 = 22 V on each rail. 14.1 V is the rms output.

questionText: In a transformer-coupled class B push-pull amplifier each transistor carries half-sine pulses of 3 A peak. The average current drawn from the single supply is approximately:
explanation: Each transistor averages I_m/π = 0.955 A and both draw from the same supply, so I_dc = 2I_m/π = 1.91 A. 2.12 A is the rms value of a 3 A sine.

questionText: In a class B push-pull stage, reducing the peak output voltage to half its previous value changes the efficiency to:
options: One quarter of its previous value
explanation: η = (π/4)(V_m/V_CC) is directly proportional to V_m, so halving the swing halves the efficiency. In class A, where η is proportional to V_m², it would fall to one quarter.

questionText: A series-fed class A amplifier with V_CC = 24 V is biased at the centre of its load line. When the peak output voltage is 6 V, its efficiency is:
explanation: At centre bias P_dc = V_CC²/(2R_C) and P_ac = V_m²/(2R_C), so η = (V_m/V_CC)² = (6/24)² = 6.25 %. Class A efficiency falls with the square of the swing.

questionText: A series-fed (resistive-load) class A stage is limited to 25 % efficiency, whereas a transformer-coupled one can reach 50 %, because:
options: The transformer-coupled stage conducts for only 180°
The transformer adds energy to the signal
The series-fed stage has a higher quiescent current for the same load
In the series-fed stage the DC collector current also flows in the load resistor, wasting power and limiting the swing to V_CC/2
explanation: With a transformer the load carries no DC and the collector can swing from nearly 0 to 2V_CC, doubling the AC output for the same DC input power.

questionText: The theoretical maximum efficiency π/4 of a class B push-pull stage is reached when:
options: The peak output voltage equals the supply voltage V_CC
The quiescent current is set at a few milliamperes
explanation: η = (π/4)(V_m/V_CC) reaches its maximum of 78.5 % only when V_m = V_CC; at 2V_CC/π the transistor dissipation is maximum instead.

questionText: Which statement about output-stage classes is NOT correct?
options: A class A transistor conducts for the whole cycle
Each class B transistor conducts for half of each cycle
A class C transistor conducts for more than 180° of each cycle
Class D output transistors operate as switches
explanation: Class C conducts for less than 180°, which is why it needs a tuned load; the other three statements are the standard definitions.

questionText: A class A emitter-follower output stage uses ±15 V supplies, a 0.2 A constant current source as its emitter bias, and a 50 Ω load. Ignoring saturation voltages, the largest symmetrical (undistorted) peak output voltage is:
explanation: The output can rise to about +15 V but can fall only to −I R_L = −0.2 × 50 = −10 V before the transistor cuts off, so the symmetrical limit is 10 V peak.

questionText: A class A emitter-follower output stage with ±15 V supplies, 0.2 A constant-current emitter bias and a 50 Ω load delivers a 10 V peak sine output. Its efficiency is approximately:
explanation: P_L = 10²/(2 × 50) = 1 W; the supplies deliver 2 × 15 × 0.2 = 6 W regardless of signal; η = 1/6 = 16.7 %. Counting only one supply gives 33.3 %.

questionText: In a class C amplifier the collector current flows in short pulses, yet the output voltage is nearly sinusoidal because:
options: The load is an LC tank tuned to the signal frequency, which rings between pulses
The transistor is biased at the centre of the load line
Two transistors are used in push-pull
explanation: The tuned tank stores energy and oscillates at its resonant frequency; each current pulse merely replaces the energy lost, so the tank voltage is a sine wave (flywheel effect).

questionText: The Q-point of each transistor in a class B push-pull stage is located:
options: At the centre of the DC load line
Slightly above cut-off with a small quiescent current
At cut-off, with essentially zero quiescent collector current
explanation: Class B biases each device at cut-off so it conducts only for the half-cycle that drives it on; the centre of the load line is class A and slightly above cut-off is class AB.

questionText: Classes A, B and C arranged in increasing order of conduction angle are:
options: Class C, class B, class A
Class A, class B, class C
Class B, class C, class A
Class C, class A, class B
explanation: Class C conducts for less than 180°, class B for 180° and class A for the full 360°.

questionText: Which class of amplifier draws the same average current from the supply whether or not a signal is present?
explanation: In class A the transistor is biased at the centre of the load line, so the supply delivers a steady V_CC I_CQ at all signal levels. Classes B, C and D draw current that rises with the signal.

questionText: Which ordering of the maximum theoretical efficiency is correct?
options: Class B < class A < class C
Class C < class B < class A
Class A < class B < class C
Class A < class C < class B
explanation: Efficiency rises as the conduction angle falls: class A at most 50 %, class B 78.5 %, class C about 90 % or more.

questionText: The figure of merit P_D(max)/P_L(max) of a power amplifier compares:
options: The output power with the power taken from the supply
The load power with the input signal power
The peak collector current with the quiescent collector current
The largest power the output transistor must dissipate with the largest power delivered to the load
explanation: The figure of merit sets the transistor dissipation rating needed for a given output; output/supply power is the efficiency and load/input power is the power gain.

questionText: A transistor rated for 20 W maximum dissipation is used in an ideal transformer-coupled class A amplifier. The largest output power it can deliver without exceeding its rating is:
explanation: The figure of merit of transformer-coupled class A is 2: P_D(max) = V_CC I_CQ at idle and P_L(max) = V_CC I_CQ/2, so P_L(max) = 20/2 = 10 W.

questionText: In an ideal class B push-pull amplifier, the maximum dissipation of EACH transistor, as a fraction of the maximum load power, is about:
explanation: Each transistor dissipates at most V_CC²/(π²R_L) while P_L(max) = V_CC²/(2R_L); the ratio is 2/π² = 0.203. The 0.4 figure is for both transistors together.

questionText: An ideal class B push-pull stage must deliver a maximum of 25 W to its load. The minimum dissipation rating needed for each output transistor is about:
explanation: Each device dissipates at most (2/π²)P_L(max) = 0.203 × 25 = 5.07 W. 10 W is the total for both devices and 50 W would be needed by a class A stage.

questionText: Power transistors rated for 15 W dissipation each are available. Ideally, what maximum output power can one of them give as a transformer-coupled class A stage, and two of them as a class B push-pull pair?
options: 30 W in class A and about 37 W in class B
7.5 W in class A and about 74 W in class B
7.5 W in class A and about 37 W in class B
15 W in class A and about 74 W in class B
explanation: Class A: P_L(max) = P_D(max)/2 = 7.5 W. Class B: each device dissipates at most 0.203 P_L(max), so P_L(max) = 15/0.203 = 74 W.

questionText: A transformer-coupled class A amplifier runs from V_CC = 12 V with I_CQ = 0.5 A. Assuming ideal operation, the transistor dissipation with no signal and at maximum output is:
options: 3 W with no signal and 6 W at maximum output
0 W with no signal and 3 W at maximum output
6 W with no signal and 6 W at maximum output
6 W with no signal and 3 W at maximum output
explanation: P_dc = 12 × 0.5 = 6 W at all times. With no signal all of it is dissipated; at maximum output P_ac = 6/2 = 3 W goes to the load, leaving P_D = 6 − 3 = 3 W.

questionText: Which statement about output-transistor dissipation versus signal level is correct?
options: Both class A and class B dissipate most at full output
Class A dissipation rises with signal while class B dissipation falls with signal
Class A dissipation is greatest with no signal, while class B dissipation is zero with no signal and peaks below full output
Neither class A nor class B dissipates power with no signal
explanation: Class A takes constant supply power, so the more goes to the load the less heats the transistor. Class B dissipates nothing at idle and most at a swing of about 0.637 V_CC.

questionText: A transformer-coupled class A stage and a class B push-pull stage are each operated with their peak output swing reduced to half the maximum possible. Their ideal efficiencies are:
options: 25 % for class A and 39.3 % for class B
12.5 % for class A and 39.3 % for class B
25 % for class A and 78.5 % for class B
12.5 % for class A and 19.6 % for class B

questionText: An ideal class B amplifier is delivering one tenth of its maximum output power. Its efficiency is about:
explanation: Power scales as V_m², so V_m/V_CC = √0.1 = 0.316 and η = 78.5 % × 0.316 = 24.8 %. Scaling by 0.1 directly (7.85 %) is the class A rule, not class B.

questionText: With speech or music, whose average level is far below full output, a class B or AB stage wastes much less power than a class A stage because:
options: Class A draws its full supply power all the time, whereas the class B supply current falls with the signal amplitude
Class B has a higher voltage gain than class A
Class A transistors have a lower current rating
Class B uses an output transformer that stores the unused energy
explanation: The class A supply power V_CC I_CQ is constant, so at low output nearly all of it becomes heat. The class B supply current 2I_m/π is proportional to the signal peak.

questionText: An amplifier must deliver 10 W at full output. Ideally, the power taken from the supply by a transformer-coupled class A stage and by a class B push-pull stage is:
options: 40 W for class A and 12.7 W for class B
12.7 W for class A and 20 W for class B
20 W for class A and 7.85 W for class B
20 W for class A and 12.7 W for class B
explanation: P_dc = P_L/η: class A 10/0.5 = 20 W; class B 10/0.785 = 12.7 W. Multiplying by the efficiency (7.85 W) is the common slip.

questionText: A 100 W audio amplifier can be built as class AB with 70 % efficiency or as class D with 92 % efficiency at full output. The heat to be removed at full output in each case is:
options: 30 W for class AB and 8 W for class D
42.9 W for class AB and 8.7 W for class D
142.9 W for class AB and 108.7 W for class D
70 W for class AB and 92 W for class D
explanation: Heat = P_L/η − P_L: class AB 100/0.70 − 100 = 42.9 W; class D 100/0.92 − 100 = 8.7 W. Taking (1 − η) × P_L gives the wrong 30 W and 8 W.

questionText: A portable speaker has a 12 V, 7.2 Ah battery (assume all 86.4 Wh are usable) and delivers a steady 20 W average output. The playing time with a class AB stage of 60 % efficiency and with a class D stage of 90 % efficiency is:
options: 7.2 h for class AB and 4.8 h for class D
2.59 h for class AB and 3.89 h for class D
3.89 h for class AB and 2.59 h for class D
explanation: Input power = 20/0.6 = 33.3 W and 20/0.9 = 22.2 W; time = 86.4 Wh / 33.3 W = 2.59 h and 86.4/22.2 = 3.89 h. Ignoring efficiency gives 86.4/20 = 4.32 h for both.

questionText: A class D amplifier with 92 % efficiency delivers 46 W to a loudspeaker. The power drawn from the supply and the power lost as heat are:
explanation: P_dc = 46/0.92 = 50 W and the loss is 50 − 46 = 4 W.

questionText: A class D half-bridge delivers 50 W of sine-wave power into 8 Ω. Its MOSFETs each have R_DS(on) = 0.1 Ω and one of them always carries the load current. The conduction loss in the switches is:
explanation: I_rms = √(P/R) = √(50/8) = 2.5 A; conduction loss = I_rms² × R_DS(on) = 6.25 × 0.1 = 0.625 W. Using the peak current gives 1.25 W.

questionText: A 30 W (full-output) amplifier is redesigned from class AB at 65 % efficiency to class D at 90 % efficiency. The reduction in supply power at full output is about:
An audio power amplifier driving a loudspeaker is measured to have 85 % efficiency at full output. Which class is it most likely to be?
explanation: Linear classes cannot exceed the class B limit of 78.5 %, and class C cannot reproduce a wideband audio signal, so an 85 % audio amplifier must be a switching (class D) design.

questionText: An ideal class B push-pull stage dissipates the most heat when its output power is about what fraction of its maximum output power?
explanation: Maximum dissipation occurs at V_m = 2V_CC/π = 0.637 V_CC; power goes as V_m², so P_L/P_L(max) = (2/π)² = 0.405. The 63.7 % figure is the voltage ratio, not the power ratio.

questionText: A class B complementary stage runs from ±20 V into an 8 Ω load. The worst-case dissipation of each transistor is:
explanation: P_D(max) per transistor = V_CC²/(π²R_L) = 400/(9.87 × 8) = 5.07 W; 10.1 W is the total for both, and 25 W is the maximum load power.

questionText: For the same maximum load power of 25 W, a transformer-coupled class A design needs a transistor rated for 50 W, whereas a class B design needs two transistors each rated for about 5.07 W. The ratio of the class A rating to each class B rating is about:
explanation: 50/5.07 = 9.9, about 10, which is the ratio of the figures of merit 2/(2/π²) = π².

questionText: An ideal class B stage at full output (78.5 % efficiency) produces how much heat for every watt delivered to the load?
explanation: Heat per watt = 1/η − 1 = 4/π − 1 = 1.273 − 1 = 0.273 W. The figure 1 − 0.785 = 0.215 W is heat per watt of supply power, not per watt of output.

questionText: Class C amplifiers are not used as audio power amplifiers because:
options: Their efficiency is too low for audio
They need two transistors in push-pull
The collector current is a train of pulses rich in harmonics, and a tuned tank can restore only one frequency, not a whole audio band
They cannot be operated from a DC supply
explanation: A class C stage relies on a resonant tank to rebuild a sine wave at one frequency; a wideband signal such as audio would be severely distorted. Its efficiency is actually the highest of the bias classes A, B, AB and C.

questionText: For the highest efficiency in the final power stage of an FM broadcast transmitter, whose signal has constant amplitude, the preferred class is:
explanation: An FM carrier has a constant envelope and a single narrow band, so a class C stage with a tuned tank gives the best efficiency without losing information.

questionText: A power amplifier must amplify an amplitude-modulated signal whose envelope carries the information, without distorting that envelope. Which choice is suitable?
options: A class C stage with a tuned tank
A class C stage biased further below cut-off
explanation: The output of a class C stage does not follow the input amplitude linearly, so it distorts the envelope; a linear class (A or AB) must be used to amplify an already-modulated signal.

questionText: A transmitter must convert a 30 MHz oscillator signal into a 90 MHz signal efficiently. The usual choice is:
options: A class B push-pull stage with its tank tuned to 30 MHz
A class C stage with its tank tuned to 90 MHz
explanation: The narrow class C current pulses are rich in harmonics; tuning the tank to the third harmonic selects 90 MHz (a frequency multiplier).

questionText: The best class for the output stage of a battery-powered portable Bluetooth speaker, where battery life and small size matter most, is:
options: Class B with a large heat sink
explanation: Class D switching stages exceed 90 % efficiency, giving the longest battery life and needing little or no heat sink.

questionText: A microphone preamplifier handles signals of a few millivolts and delivers well under a milliwatt. Its amplifying stage is normally operated in:
explanation: At such small power levels efficiency does not matter, and class A, which never switches off, gives the most faithful small-signal amplification.

questionText: Class A operation is still used in small-signal stages despite its low efficiency because:
options: Class A has the highest efficiency at low signal levels
Class A needs no DC bias
The power involved is tiny, so the wasted power is negligible while the linearity is the best of all classes
explanation: At milliwatt levels a few milliwatts of heat are unimportant, so linearity decides the choice. Class A efficiency is actually lowest at small signals.

questionText: Which statement about amplifier classes is NOT correct?
options: A class A output transistor runs cooler at full output than with no signal
A class C stage can amplify audio if a large coupling capacitor is used
The transistors of a class D stage dissipate little because they are either fully on or fully off
A class B stage needs two transistors to reproduce the whole cycle
explanation: Class C needs a tuned load and cannot reproduce a wideband audio signal whatever the coupling. The other three statements are correct.

questionText: Compared with a class AB stage, a disadvantage of a class D audio amplifier is:
options: It needs an LC output filter and its fast switching edges can cause electromagnetic interference
It has a much lower efficiency
It needs a much larger heat sink
It cannot be made with MOSFETs
explanation: Class D switches at a high frequency; an output filter must remove the switching component and careful layout is needed to limit EMI. Its efficiency and heat-sink needs are better than class AB.

questionText: The switching frequency of a class D audio amplifier is chosen to be:
options: Well above the audio band, typically a few hundred kilohertz
Equal to the highest audio frequency, 20 kHz
Below 20 Hz so that it is inaudible
explanation: The carrier must be far above 20 kHz so that the LC low-pass filter can remove it while passing the whole audio band; typical values are 250 kHz to 1 MHz.

questionText: The output stage of an integrated-circuit op-amp is normally biased in class AB because:
options: It gives the highest possible efficiency of any class
It needs a tuned load that is easy to integrate
It allows the output transistors to operate as switches
It combines a small idle current with freedom from crossover distortion
explanation: Class A would waste too much standby power and pure class B would add crossover distortion; class AB keeps the quiescent current small while both devices conduct near zero output.

questionText: As the conduction angle of a class C stage is reduced from 180° towards very small values (same peak collector current), which is true?
options: Efficiency and output power both rise
Efficiency falls but output power rises
Efficiency rises towards 100 % but the output power falls
Efficiency stays at 78.5 % and output power is unchanged
explanation: Shorter pulses flow only near the minimum collector voltage, so less is dissipated, but they contain less fundamental power; practical stages use about 120° to 150°.

questionText: An oscilloscope shows the output sine wave of a power amplifier flattened at both positive and negative peaks, while the zero-crossing region is clean. The most likely cause is:
options: Crossover distortion of an unbiased class B stage
The input is driving the stage into saturation and cut-off (clipping)
Cancellation of even harmonics in the push-pull stage
explanation: Flat tops at the peaks mean the output has reached the supply limits; crossover distortion would appear as a step near zero, not at the peaks.

questionText: Crossover distortion in a class B stage is more objectionable at low volume than at high volume because:
options: The dead band of about 1.4 V is fixed, so it forms a larger fraction of a small signal
The transistors' gain falls at high volume
Crossover distortion only occurs when the output is below 1 W
The load impedance rises at low volume
explanation: The step at the zero crossing is set by the two base-emitter drops, so its relative size, and therefore the percentage distortion, grows as the signal becomes smaller.

questionText: For the same rated output power, which class needs the largest heat sink?
explanation: A class A stage must dissipate its full quiescent power, twice the maximum output, continuously; the other classes dissipate far less.

questionText: The maximum efficiency of a class AB push-pull stage lies:
options: Between the class A and class B values, roughly 50 % to 78.5 %
explanation: The small quiescent current adds to the supply power, so class AB is slightly less efficient than ideal class B but far better than class A.

questionText: Which class can reproduce the whole input cycle using only a single transistor?
explanation: Only class A conducts for the full 360°. Classes B and AB need a push-pull pair, and class C conducts for less than half a cycle.

questionText: Which loss mechanism in a class D stage increases in proportion to the switching frequency?
options: Switching loss during the on-off transitions of the transistors
Conduction loss in the on-resistance R_DS(on)
Power delivered to the load resistance
Quiescent bias loss of the output pair
explanation: Each transition briefly has both voltage across and current through the switch, so the energy lost per transition is multiplied by the number of transitions per second. Conduction loss depends on I_rms² R_DS(on), not on frequency.

questionText: Using the ideal efficiency relation η = (θ − sin θ)/(4[sin(θ/2) − (θ/2)cos(θ/2)]), a class C stage with a conduction angle of 120° has a maximum efficiency of about:
A 6 W output is needed. Ideally, the supply power required by a series-fed (resistive-load) class A stage and by a class B push-pull stage, both at their maximum efficiency, is:
options: 24 W for class A and 7.64 W for class B
12 W for class A and 7.64 W for class B
24 W for class A and 4.71 W for class B
6 W for class A and 7.64 W for class B
explanation: Series-fed class A: 6/0.25 = 24 W; class B: 6/0.785 = 7.64 W. 12 W would apply to a transformer-coupled class A stage.

questionText: Which statement correctly describes the trend from class A through class B to class C?
options: Conduction angle rises while efficiency falls
Efficiency rises while the conduction angle and linearity fall
explanation: Class A conducts 360° with the best linearity and lowest efficiency; class C conducts least, is least linear and most efficient.

questionText: An unbiased complementary emitter-follower (class B) stage with silicon transistors (V_BE = 0.7 V) is driven by a 2 V peak sine wave. The peak output voltage is about:
explanation: Each transistor conducts only after its base-emitter drop is overcome, so the output peak is 2.0 − 0.7 = 1.3 V. Subtracting the full 1.4 V dead band (0.6 V) is the usual slip.

questionText: A complementary emitter-follower stage with silicon transistors, correctly biased into class AB, is driven by a 2 V peak sine wave into its load. The peak output voltage is about:
options: 1.3 V, because V_BE is still lost on each half-cycle
2 V, because the biased emitter followers have a gain close to 1 and no dead zone
0.6 V, because both transistors conduct at once
4 V, because the bias adds voltage gain
explanation: The bias network supplies the base-emitter drops, so the output follows the input with the gain of an emitter follower, slightly less than 1.

questionText: An unbiased complementary class B stage (V_BE = 0.7 V for each transistor) is driven by a 1 V peak sine wave. For roughly what fraction of each cycle is neither transistor conducting?
explanation: Neither conducts while |sin ωt| < 0.7, i.e. within 44.4° of each zero crossing. That is 4 × 44.4° = 177.7° of 360°, about 49 % of the cycle.

questionText: With no emitter resistors, the voltage needed between the bases of a complementary silicon output pair to bring both transistors just into conduction is about:
explanation: Each base-emitter junction needs about 0.7 V, and the two junctions are in series between the bases, so about 2V_BE = 1.4 V is required.

questionText: At constant current, the forward voltage of a silicon diode changes with temperature by approximately:
explanation: Both a diode's forward drop and a transistor's V_BE fall by about 2 mV for every °C rise, which is why diodes can track the output transistors.

questionText: A class AB stage uses a Darlington pair on each side of the output (four base-emitter junctions between the two input bases). If simple diode bias is used, the number of diodes required is:
explanation: One diode is needed for each base-emitter junction in the path between the two driving bases: 2 per Darlington, 4 in total, about 2.6 V to 2.8 V.

questionText: The bias transistor of a V_BE multiplier has V_BE = 0.6 V, with 2.2 kΩ between its collector and base and 1 kΩ between its base and emitter. The multiplier holds the two output bases apart by:
explanation: V_bias = V_BE(1 + R1/R2) = 0.6 × (1 + 2.2) = 1.92 V. Forgetting the 1 gives 1.32 V; inverting the ratio gives 0.87 V.

questionText: A V_BE multiplier must produce 1.8 V using a transistor with V_BE = 0.6 V and R2 = 1.2 kΩ (base to emitter). The required R1 (collector to base) is:
explanation: 1 + R1/R2 = 1.8/0.6 = 3, so R1/R2 = 2 and R1 = 2 × 1.2 = 2.4 kΩ. Taking R1/R2 = 3 gives the wrong 3.6 kΩ.

questionText: A V_BE multiplier uses R1 = 2 kΩ and R2 = 1 kΩ, and its transistor's V_BE changes by −2 mV/°C. The temperature coefficient of the bias voltage is:
explanation: The whole voltage is V_BE(1 + R1/R2) = 3V_BE, so its coefficient is 3 × (−2) = −6 mV/°C.

questionText: A class AB pair with 0.47 Ω emitter resistors must idle at I_Q = 50 mA with V_BE(Q) = 0.6 V for each output transistor. The bias comes from a V_BE multiplier with V_BE = 0.6 V and R2 = 1 kΩ. The required R1 is about:
explanation: V_bias = 2(0.6) + 2(0.05)(0.47) = 1.247 V; R1/R2 = 1.247/0.6 − 1 = 1.078, so R1 = 1.08 kΩ. Ignoring the emitter-resistor drop gives 1.00 kΩ.

questionText: A class AB stage has V_bias = 1.4 V between the bases, V_BE(Q) = 0.62 V for each output transistor and 0.47 Ω emitter resistors. The quiescent current is about:
explanation: I_Q = (V_bias − 2V_BE(Q))/(2R_E) = (1.4 − 1.24)/(0.94) = 0.170 A. Using a single R_E gives 340 mA.

questionText: A class AB stage has fixed resistor-divider bias V_bias = 1.4 V (no thermal tracking), R_E = 0.5 Ω in each emitter and V_BE(Q) = 0.65 V at 25 °C. If the output transistors warm by 20 °C and each V_BE(Q) falls at 2 mV/°C, the quiescent current changes from 100 mA to about:
explanation: New V_BE(Q) = 0.65 − 0.04 = 0.61 V; I_Q = (1.4 − 1.22)/(2 × 0.5) = 0.18 A. Changing only one transistor's V_BE gives 140 mA.

questionText: An output transistor with no emitter resistor is held at a fixed base-emitter voltage while it warms by 25 °C. Taking dV_BE/dT = −2 mV/°C and V_T = 26 mV, its collector current increases by a factor of about:
explanation: The 50 mV reduction in the required V_BE acts like 50 mV extra drive: I_C2/I_C1 = e^(50/26) = e^1.92 = 6.8. The linear ratio 50/26 = 1.9 is a common slip.

questionText: Taking V_T = 26 mV, by how much must a transistor's base-emitter voltage increase to double its collector current?
explanation: I_C ∝ e^(V_BE/V_T), so doubling needs ΔV_BE = V_T ln 2 = 26 × 0.693 = 18 mV. About 60 mV gives a tenfold increase.

questionText: A class AB stage running from ±25 V supplies has a quiescent current of 40 mA. Its total standby dissipation is:
explanation: P_standby = 2V_CC I_Q = 2 × 25 × 0.04 = 2 W, shared equally (1 W per transistor). Using one rail only gives 1 W.

questionText: A complementary stage on ±20 V drives an 8 Ω load with a full 20 V peak swing (ideal). Pure class B would then have 78.5 % efficiency. If it is biased into class AB with I_Q = 100 mA and the supply is assumed to draw the class B current plus I_Q, the efficiency becomes about:
explanation: P_L = 20²/(2 × 8) = 25 W; class B P_dc = 2 × 20 × 2.5/π = 31.8 W; standby adds 2 × 20 × 0.1 = 4 W; η = 25/35.8 = 69.8 %. Counting only one rail's 2 W gives 73.9 %.

questionText: Two bias diodes (0.7 V each) and two 2.2 kΩ resistors are connected in series from +15 V to −15 V, with the diodes between the output bases. Neglecting base currents, the diode current is about:
explanation: I = (30 − 1.4)/(2 × 2.2 kΩ) = 28.6/4.4 kΩ = 6.5 mA. Taking only half the 28.6 V drop gives about 3.3 mA; using one resistor gives 13 mA.

questionText: In a diode-biased class AB stage the peak load current is 2 A and the output transistors have β = 50. The current supplied to the bias chain must be at least about:
explanation: At the signal peak the conducting output transistor needs I_B = 2/50 = 40 mA from the bias chain; if the chain current were smaller, the peak would be clipped.

questionText: In an IC output stage the bias diodes are diode-connected transistors matched to the output transistors, which have four times their emitter area. With 2 mA through the diodes and no emitter resistors, the quiescent current is:
explanation: Matched junctions at the same V_BE form a current mirror; current scales with emitter area, so I_Q = 4 × 2 mA = 8 mA.

questionText: A single-supply complementary class AB stage runs from V_CC = 24 V, with the loudspeaker connected through a coupling capacitor. With no signal, the DC voltage at the joined emitters should be:
explanation: With one supply the output node rests at V_CC/2 = 12 V so that it can swing equally up and down; the coupling capacitor blocks this DC from the load.

questionText: A class AB emitter-follower output stage has R_E = 0.5 Ω in series with each emitter and drives an 8 Ω load. Neglecting the transistors' internal emitter resistance, its voltage gain is about:
explanation: The conducting half is a follower whose output divides between R_E and R_L: A_v = R_L/(R_L + R_E) = 8/8.5 = 0.941.

questionText: A class AB stage delivers a sine wave of 3 A peak to its load; each emitter resistor is 0.33 Ω and carries the current of its own half-cycle only. Neglecting I_Q, the average power dissipated in EACH emitter resistor is about:
explanation: A half-wave sine current of peak I_p has mean-square value I_p²/4, so P = 9 × 0.33/4 = 0.74 W. Assuming a full sine wave (I_p²/2) gives 1.49 W.

questionText: A class AB stage delivers 3 A peak to its load and has R_E = 0.33 Ω in each emitter. The peak voltage lost across the conducting emitter resistor, which reduces the available output swing, is about:
explanation: V = I_p × R_E = 3 × 0.33 = 0.99 V; only one emitter resistor carries the load current at a time.

questionText: A class AB pair is biased by two diodes giving V_bias = 1.3 V, and each output transistor has V_BE(Q) = 0.6 V. To obtain I_Q = 50 mA, each emitter resistor must be:
explanation: 2R_E = (V_bias − 2V_BE(Q))/I_Q = (1.3 − 1.2)/0.05 = 2 Ω, so R_E = 1 Ω each. Stopping at 2 Ω forgets that there are two resistors in series.

questionText: A V_BE multiplier with R2 = 600 Ω (base to emitter) and V_BE = 0.6 V is fed with a total bias current of 5 mA. Neglecting base current, the collector current of the multiplier transistor is:
explanation: The resistor chain takes V_BE/R2 = 0.6/600 = 1 mA; the transistor carries the rest, 5 − 1 = 4 mA.

questionText: A V_BE multiplier has R2 = 600 Ω from base to emitter, V_BE = 0.6 V, and R1 is a 0 to 2 kΩ trimmer from collector to base. Over the trimmer's full range, the bias voltage can be set anywhere between:
explanation: With R1 = 0 the network is just one V_BE, 0.6 V; with R1 = 2 kΩ it is 0.6 × (1 + 2000/600) = 0.6 × 4.33 = 2.6 V.

questionText: Which sequence correctly describes thermal runaway in a class AB output stage with fixed bias?
options: Temperature rises, the required V_BE falls, collector current rises at the fixed bias, dissipation rises, temperature rises further
Temperature rises, V_BE rises, collector current falls, the transistor cools
Collector current rises, V_BE rises, the bias voltage increases, the transistor cools
Temperature rises, the load resistance falls, the supply voltage collapses
explanation: Because V_BE falls by about 2 mV/°C, a fixed bias voltage drives more current into a warmer transistor, which heats it further: a positive feedback loop.

questionText: In a V_BE multiplier bias circuit, R1 (collector to base) goes open-circuit. What happens?
options: The bias falls to one V_BE and crossover distortion appears
Nothing changes because R2 still sets the voltage
The multiplier transistor turns off, the bias voltage rises, and the quiescent current becomes dangerously large
The output transistors are cut off and the amplifier goes silent
explanation: With R1 open the multiplier gets no base drive and stops conducting, so the whole bias current is forced into the output bases and I_Q soars.

questionText: In a V_BE multiplier bias circuit, R2 (base to emitter) goes open-circuit. The most likely result is:
options: The bias voltage rises and I_Q becomes very large
The bias voltage falls to about one V_BE, so the output pair is cut off at idle and crossover distortion returns
explanation: With R2 open, R1 feeds the base directly from the collector, so the transistor conducts heavily with V_CE only slightly above V_BE, about 0.7 V, which is less than the 2V_BE needed.

questionText: To increase the quiescent current of a class AB stage biased by a V_BE multiplier, the adjustment should be to:
options: Scale R1 and R2 up by the same factor
explanation: V_bias = V_BE(1 + R1/R2) rises when R1/R2 rises. Increasing R2 or shorting R1 lowers the bias; scaling both keeps the ratio and the voltage unchanged.

questionText: In discrete audio amplifiers a V_BE multiplier is usually preferred to a string of bias diodes because:
options: It needs no thermal contact with the output transistors
It carries the full load current
It removes the need for a driver stage
Its voltage can be trimmed to any multiple of V_BE, and a single transistor on the heat sink gives the thermal tracking
explanation: A trimmer in R1 or R2 sets I_Q precisely, whereas diodes give only whole multiples of one diode drop; the multiplier transistor must still be mounted on the heat sink.

questionText: A V_BE multiplier is mounted on the circuit board far from the output heat sink. As the amplifier warms up during use:
options: The quiescent current falls to zero
The quiescent current stays constant because the multiplier is adjustable
The quiescent current creeps up, because the bias voltage does not fall with the output transistors' V_BE
The voltage gain of the stage doubles
explanation: Without thermal coupling the bias stays at its cold value while the output V_BE falls, so the effective drive and I_Q increase, with a risk of thermal runaway.

questionText: Emitter resistors in a class AB power stage are kept to a fraction of an ohm because larger values would:
options: Raise the voltage gain above unity
Waste output power and reduce the voltage swing available to the load
explanation: The full load current flows through the emitter resistor of the conducting device, so a large R_E drops a significant voltage and dissipates power; larger values actually improve thermal stability.

questionText: Which statement about the quiescent current of a class AB stage is NOT correct?
options: Increasing I_Q reduces crossover distortion at small signals
A very large I_Q makes the stage operate in class A
Increasing I_Q raises the standby dissipation
Increasing I_Q always increases the efficiency
explanation: More quiescent current adds 2V_CC I_Q of standby power, lowering efficiency; the other three statements are correct.

questionText: When a complementary stage is correctly biased into class AB, each output transistor conducts for:
options: Slightly more than 180° of each cycle
explanation: The small quiescent current keeps both devices on around the zero crossing, so each conducts a little longer than a half-cycle.

questionText: The main drawback of biasing a class AB pair with a simple resistor between the bases is that:
options: The bias voltage does not fall with temperature, so the quiescent current rises as the transistors warm
It makes the stage a class C amplifier
explanation: A resistor's drop is fixed by the chain current and has no thermal tracking, so it is used only with emitter resistors and at modest power.

questionText: The distortion produced by the dead zone of an unbiased class B stage consists mainly of:
explanation: The notch affects the positive and negative halves identically, giving a half-wave-symmetric waveform whose distortion products are odd harmonics.

questionText: An op-amp with an open-loop gain of 100 000 drives an unbiased complementary pair enclosed in its negative-feedback loop. The input dead zone of about 0.7 V on each side is reduced to about:
explanation: The op-amp output jumps across the dead zone when its input changes by only 0.7 V/A_OL = 0.7/100 000 = 7 µV, so the crossover error is reduced by the open-loop gain.

questionText: A quasi-complementary output stage is one in which:
options: Both output transistors are pnp and no driver is used
Both output power transistors are npn, driven by a complementary pair of smaller transistors
An output transformer replaces the pnp transistor
The output transistors are biased in class C
explanation: Before good pnp power devices were common, two npn power transistors were used, with the lower one driven by a pnp driver so that the pair behaves like a complementary stage.

questionText: The bias diodes of a class AB stage are connected:
options: In series between the two output bases, forward biased by the bias current
In parallel with the emitter resistors
explanation: Forward-biased diodes between the bases hold them about 2V_BE apart; they carry the bias current, not the load current.

questionText: When several output transistors are paralleled to share a large load current, each must have its own emitter resistor because:
options: A shared resistor would raise the voltage gain
Without individual ballast, the device with the lowest V_BE takes most of the current, heats up and takes even more
Individual resistors eliminate crossover distortion completely
Separate resistors increase the output impedance to match the loudspeaker
explanation: Parallel junctions share one V_BE, so a hotter device with a lower V_BE hogs current. An individual R_E adds a drop proportional to each device's own current, which forces current sharing.

questionText: In an integrated-circuit op-amp, the class AB bias of the output pair is usually produced by:
options: A trimmer potentiometer adjusted during manufacture
A large emitter resistor of several kilohms
Diode-connected transistors carrying a reference current, forming current mirrors with the output transistors
explanation: Matched transistors on the same chip track each other in temperature, so diode-connected devices set I_Q through the current-mirror principle without adjustment.

questionText: A technician finds an amplifier's output heat sink hot with no signal and measures I_Q = 500 mA where 50 mA was intended. The most likely cause is:
options: The bias voltage is set too low
The emitter resistors are too large
The bias voltage is set too high, for example R1 of the V_BE multiplier too large
explanation: A small excess of bias above 2V_BE(Q) drives a large rise in I_Q. Too low a bias would give crossover distortion, and larger emitter resistors would reduce I_Q.

questionText: To check the quiescent current, a technician measures 22 mV across the two 0.22 Ω emitter resistors in series (emitter to emitter). The quiescent current is:
explanation: The two resistors total 0.44 Ω, so I_Q = 22 mV/0.44 Ω = 50 mA. Dividing by one 0.22 Ω resistor gives 100 mA.

questionText: A class AB stage has R_E = 0.5 Ω in each emitter. The V_BE multiplier stays at room temperature while the output transistors warm by 30 °C, each V_BE falling by 2 mV/°C. The quiescent current increases by about:
explanation: The two output V_BE values fall by 2 × 30 × 2 mV = 120 mV while V_bias is unchanged; ΔI_Q = 0.12 V/(2 × 0.5 Ω) = 120 mA. Counting only one junction gives 60 mA.

questionText: In a typical discrete audio power amplifier, the V_BE multiplier is connected:
options: Between the bases of the output pair, in the collector circuit of the class A driver (voltage-amplifier) transistor
Between the output node and ground
Across the positive supply rail only
explanation: The driver's collector current flows through the multiplier, which then holds the two output bases a fixed, temperature-tracking voltage apart.

questionText: In a diode-biased class AB output stage the two bias diodes are mounted on the same heat sink as the output transistors so that:
options: Their forward voltage tracks the transistors' V_BE with temperature, holding the quiescent current steady
They can carry the full load current
The stage can operate without any emitter resistors
explanation: A diode drop and a transistor V_BE both fall by about 2 mV per °C. Thermally coupling them makes the bias voltage fall as the transistors warm, which prevents the quiescent current from rising (thermal runaway).

questionText: A V_BE multiplier uses R1 = 1 kΩ (collector to base) and R2 = 1 kΩ (base to emitter). If its transistor's V_BE is 0.65 V, the bias voltage across the network is:
explanation: V_bias = V_BE(1 + R1/R2) = 0.65 × (1 + 1) = 1.30 V, which is the 2V_BE needed to bias a complementary pair into class AB.

questionText: Small resistors of 0.1 Ω to 1 Ω are connected in series with the emitters of a class AB complementary pair mainly to:
options: Increase the voltage gain of the stage
Stabilise the quiescent current against thermal runaway and equalise current sharing
Provide the 1.4 V bias between the bases
Match the loudspeaker impedance to the transistors
explanation: If I_Q rises, the extra drop across R_E reduces the effective base-emitter voltage and limits the current (negative feedback); the resistors also share current evenly between imperfectly matched devices.

questionText: The output impedance of an ideal op-amp is:
explanation: An ideal op-amp behaves as a perfect voltage source at its output, so its output impedance is zero; 75 Ω is the typical value for a real 741.

questionText: An inverting amplifier has R_in = 5 kΩ and R_f = 50 kΩ. For a DC input of 0.2 V the output voltage is:
explanation: V_o = −(R_f/R_in) V_in = −(50/5) × 0.2 = −2 V. The value 2.2 V would come from wrongly using the non-inverting gain 1 + R_f/R_in = 11.

questionText: A non-inverting amplifier uses R_1 = 10 kΩ (inverting input to ground) and R_f = 20 kΩ. With 1.5 V DC at the input the output is:
explanation: Gain = 1 + R_f/R_1 = 1 + 20/10 = 3, so V_o = 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 V, in phase with the input.

questionText: The main use of an op-amp voltage follower is to:
options: Buffer a high-impedance source so it can drive a low-impedance load
Provide a large voltage gain with phase inversion
Integrate the input signal with respect to time
Convert a sine wave into a square wave
explanation: The follower has unity gain, very high input impedance and near-zero output impedance, so it isolates a weak source from a heavy load without loading it.

questionText: An inverting summing amplifier has R_1 = R_2 = R_3 = R_f = 10 kΩ. The inputs are V_1 = 1 V, V_2 = 2 V and V_3 = −0.5 V. The output is:
explanation: V_o = −R_f(V_1/R_1 + V_2/R_2 + V_3/R_3) = −(1 + 2 − 0.5) = −2.5 V. Ignoring the sign of V_3 would give −3.5 V.

questionText: A two-input inverting summing amplifier has R_f = 100 kΩ, R_1 = 50 kΩ and R_2 = 25 kΩ. With V_1 = 0.2 V and V_2 = 0.1 V the output is:
explanation: V_o = −100k(0.2/50k + 0.1/25k) = −(0.4 + 0.4) = −0.8 V. Simply adding the inputs (−0.3 V) ignores the different weights R_f/R_k.

questionText: A difference amplifier uses R_1 = 10 kΩ in both input paths and R_2 = 100 kΩ as the feedback and ground resistors. With V_1 = 1.0 V on the inverting side and V_2 = 1.2 V on the non-inverting side, the output is:
explanation: V_o = (R_2/R_1)(V_2 − V_1) = 10 × (1.2 − 1.0) = 2 V. The common part of the inputs (about 1.1 V) is rejected.

questionText: An op-amp integrator has R = 10 kΩ and C = 0.1 µF, with the capacitor initially uncharged. A constant +1 V is applied to the input. The output 1 ms later is:
explanation: RC = 10 kΩ × 0.1 µF = 1 ms, so V_o = −(1/RC) V_in t = −(1/0.001) × 1 × 0.001 = −1 V (a negative-going ramp).

questionText: An integrator with R = 100 kΩ and C = 1 µF saturates at ±12 V. Starting from 0 V, a constant input of +0.5 V is applied. How long does the output take to reach saturation?
explanation: Slope = V_in/RC = 0.5/0.1 = 5 V/s (negative-going). Time to reach −12 V = 12/5 = 2.4 s.

questionText: An op-amp differentiator has R = 10 kΩ (feedback) and C = 0.01 µF (input). The input is a ramp rising at 1000 V/s. The output is:
explanation: V_o = −RC dV_in/dt = −(10⁴ × 10⁻⁸) × 1000 = −10⁻⁴ × 1000 = −0.1 V, a constant level while the ramp lasts.

questionText: A differentiator with R = 10 kΩ and C = 10 nF is fed with a symmetrical triangular wave of 2 V peak-to-peak at 1 kHz. The output is a square wave of amplitude:
explanation: Each ramp changes 2 V in half a period (0.5 ms), so |dV/dt| = 4000 V/s. |V_o| = RC × 4000 = 10⁻⁴ × 4000 = 0.4 V, i.e. a ±0.4 V square wave.

questionText: The main practical drawback of the basic (uncompensated) op-amp differentiator is that:
options: Its output drifts into saturation because the input offset voltage is integrated
Its input impedance is zero for DC signals
Its gain rises with frequency, so high-frequency noise is strongly amplified
It inverts only signals below a few hertz
explanation: The differentiator gain is ωRC, rising 20 dB per decade, so noise and fast spikes dominate and the circuit tends to be unstable; a small resistor in series with C is added in practice. Output drift from offset is the integrator's problem.

questionText: In a practical integrator a large resistor is connected in parallel with the feedback capacitor. Its purpose is to:
options: Limit the DC gain so input offset and bias currents cannot slowly drive the output into saturation
Increase the slope of the output ramp
Make the circuit behave as a differentiator at high frequencies
Reduce the input impedance to match the source
explanation: At DC the ideal capacitor gives infinite gain, so even a few millivolts of offset ramp the output to a rail. The shunt resistor R_F sets the DC gain to −R_F/R while the circuit still integrates above f = 1/(2πR_F C).

questionText: An op-amp has a differential gain of 2 × 10⁵ and a common-mode gain of 2. Its CMRR is:
explanation: CMRR = A_d/A_cm = 2 × 10⁵/2 = 10⁵, and 20 log₁₀(10⁵) = 100 dB. Using 10 log gives the wrong value of 50 dB.

questionText: A differential amplifier has differential gain A_d = 1000 and CMRR = 80 dB. The inputs are V_1 = 1.0005 V and V_2 = 0.9995 V. Taking the differential and common-mode contributions as adding, the output magnitude is:
The common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR) of an op-amp is defined as the ratio of:
explanation: CMRR = A_d/A_cm; a large value means the amplifier responds to the difference between its inputs and ignores what is common to both. Ideally it is infinite.

questionText: The slew rate of an op-amp is:
options: The frequency at which its open-loop gain falls to unity
The DC voltage needed between its inputs to make the output zero
The ratio of output voltage change to supply voltage change
The maximum rate of change of its output voltage, usually given in V/µs
explanation: Slew rate is the fastest the output can change (0.5 V/µs for a 741), set by the current available to charge the internal compensation capacitor. The first option describes the unity-gain frequency (numerically equal to the GBW), and the second the input offset voltage.

questionText: An audio amplifier must deliver a 20 V peak sine wave at 20 kHz. The minimum slew rate required of its op-amp is about:
explanation: SR ≥ 2π f V_p = 2π × 20 000 × 20 = 2.51 × 10⁶ V/s = 2.51 V/µs. Using the peak-to-peak value 40 V would double this to 5.03 V/µs.

questionText: A 741 (GBW = 1 MHz, SR = 0.5 V/µs) is used as a non-inverting amplifier with gain 20 to produce a 5 V peak sine output. The highest frequency at which the output is undistorted is about:
options: 50 kHz, set by the gain-bandwidth product
15.9 kHz, set by the slew rate
1 MHz, set by the unity-gain frequency
7.96 kHz, set by the slew rate
explanation: Small-signal BW = 1 MHz/20 = 50 kHz, but the full-power limit is SR/(2π V_p) = 0.5 × 10⁶/(2π × 5) = 15.9 kHz. The lower of the two limits applies.

questionText: An op-amp with a gain-bandwidth product of 1 MHz is used in a non-inverting amplifier of gain 50. The closed-loop bandwidth is:
explanation: Gain × bandwidth is constant: BW = GBW/A_CL = 1 MHz/50 = 20 kHz.

questionText: A non-inverting amplifier with a gain of 40 dB is to be built with R_1 = 1 kΩ using an op-amp of GBW = 1 MHz. The required R_f and the resulting bandwidth are:
explanation: 40 dB = 20 log A gives A = 100, so 1 + R_f/1 kΩ = 100 and R_f = 99 kΩ. BW = 1 MHz/100 = 10 kHz. Treating 40 dB as a gain of 40 gives the 39 kΩ and 25 kHz distractors.

questionText: An inverting amplifier has R_f = 10 kΩ and R_in = 1 kΩ. Its op-amp has an input offset voltage of 2 mV. With the signal input grounded, the DC error at the output is about:
explanation: The offset voltage appears between the inputs, so it is amplified by the noise gain 1 + R_f/R_in = 11, not by the signal gain 10: error = 2 mV × 11 = 22 mV.

questionText: The input offset voltage of an op-amp is the:
options: Voltage at the output when both inputs are connected to the positive supply
Maximum differential voltage the inputs can withstand
Average of the voltages at the two input terminals
DC voltage that must be applied between the inputs to make the output exactly zero
explanation: Because the input transistors are never perfectly matched, a small differential DC voltage (1 to 6 mV for a 741) is needed to null the output. The third option (average of the two input voltages) describes the common-mode voltage.

questionText: An op-amp used as a comparator saturates at ±10.5 V. A 2 V reference is connected to its inverting input and 1.5 V to its non-inverting input. The output is:
explanation: With no feedback the output is A_OL(V+ − V−) limited by saturation. V+ − V− = −0.5 V, so the output sits at −V_sat = −10.5 V.

questionText: A sine wave is applied to the non-inverting input of an open-loop op-amp whose inverting input is grounded. The output is:
options: A sine wave amplified by the open-loop gain
A square wave that switches between ±V_sat at the zero crossings, in phase with the input
A triangular wave of the same frequency
A steady 0 V because the inputs form a virtual short
explanation: This is a zero-crossing detector. The huge open-loop gain drives the output to +V_sat whenever the input is positive and to −V_sat when it is negative, producing a square wave.

questionText: A three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier has 10 kΩ feedback resistors in each input-stage op-amp, a gain-setting resistor R_G = 1 kΩ between them, and a difference stage with R_2/R_1 = 2. For a differential input of 20 mV, the output voltage is:
explanation: Input stage gain = 1 + 2R/R_G = 1 + 20 = 21, difference stage gain = 2, so A = 42 and V_o = 42 × 20 mV = 0.84 V. Forgetting the difference stage gives 0.42 V; using 1 + R/R_G gives 0.44 V.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT a property of an ideal op-amp?
explanation: The ideal op-amp has zero output impedance so that its output voltage does not depend on the load. Infinite gain and CMRR and zero offset are all ideal properties.

questionText: In an inverting amplifier the non-inverting input is often returned to ground through a resistor equal to R_in ∥ R_f instead of directly. This is done to:
options: Raise the input impedance seen by the source
Improve the slew rate of the op-amp
Cancel the output error produced by the input bias currents
explanation: Equal bias currents flowing through equal resistances at both inputs produce equal voltage drops, so their effects cancel at the output. The resistor has no effect on the signal gain or slew rate.

questionText: An inverting amplifier uses R_in = 4.7 kΩ and R_f = 47 kΩ. The input resistance seen by the signal source is:
options: Very high, equal to the op-amp's own input resistance
explanation: The inverting input is a virtual ground, so the source sees only R_in between its terminal and 0 V: R_i = V_in/I_in = R_in = 4.7 kΩ.

questionText: An inverting amplifier of gain −20 runs from ±15 V supplies and its output saturates at ±13 V. A 1 V peak sine wave is applied. The peak output voltage is:
options: 15 V, clipped at the supply rails
explanation: The ideal output would be 20 V peak, but the output cannot exceed the saturation level, so it is clipped at about 13 V (below the 15 V rails).

questionText: An op-amp has an open-loop gain of 2 × 10⁵ and no feedback. If V+ − V− = 20 µV (and the output is not saturated), the output voltage is:
explanation: V_o = A_OL(V+ − V−) = 2 × 10⁵ × 20 × 10⁻⁶ = 4 V. This shows why a few tens of microvolts between the inputs is all a linear op-amp circuit needs.

questionText: A non-inverting amplifier is designed for an ideal gain of 100 (feedback fraction β = 0.01), but the op-amp's open-loop gain is only 1000. The actual closed-loop gain is about:
explanation: A_CL = A_OL/(1 + A_OL β) = 1000/(1 + 10) = 90.9. The ideal result 1/β = 100 is only accurate when the loop gain A_OL β is much greater than 1.

questionText: A 5 V source with an internal resistance of 10 kΩ must drive a 100 Ω load. With an ideal voltage follower inserted between them, the load voltage is:
explanation: The follower draws no input current, so no voltage is lost in the 10 kΩ source resistance, and its zero output impedance delivers the full 5 V to the load. Direct connection would give only 5 × 100/10 100 ≈ 0.05 V.

questionText: A summing amplifier has three 30 kΩ input resistors and R_f = 10 kΩ. The inputs are 3 V, 6 V and 9 V. The output is:
explanation: V_o = −(10/30)(3 + 6 + 9) = −18/3 = −6 V. With R_f = R/n the circuit is an inverting averager: the output is minus the average of the inputs.

questionText: An op-amp has R_1 = 10 kΩ from input V_1 to the inverting terminal and R_f = 40 kΩ from output to the inverting terminal. Input V_2 is applied directly to the non-inverting terminal. With V_1 = 0.5 V and V_2 = 1 V, the output is:
explanation: By superposition: V_1 alone gives −(40/10) × 0.5 = −2 V; V_2 alone gives (1 + 40/10) × 1 = 5 V. V_o = 5 − 2 = 3 V. The 2 V distractor assumes a balanced difference amplifier, which needs a divider in front of the + input.

questionText: A general-purpose op-amp such as the 741 contains a small internal capacitor (about 30 pF) for frequency compensation. Its purpose is to:
options: Increase the slew rate of the op-amp
Make the op-amp stable with negative feedback by creating a single dominant pole
Raise the open-loop gain at high frequencies
Block DC from reaching the output stage
explanation: The compensation capacitor makes the open-loop gain roll off at 20 dB/decade from a low dominant-pole frequency, so the loop gain falls below 1 before the phase shift can cause oscillation. It actually limits the slew rate rather than increasing it.

questionText: An integrator uses R = 10 kΩ and C = 0.1 µF. The frequency at which the magnitude of its gain equals 1 is about:
explanation: |A| = 1/(ωRC) = 1 when f = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 10⁻³) = 159 Hz. Below this frequency the integrator amplifies; above it, it attenuates.

questionText: The input stage of a general-purpose op-amp such as the 741 is a:
explanation: The two inputs drive a differential pair, which amplifies V+ − V− and rejects common-mode signals; later stages add gain and a push-pull output.

questionText: Which statement about the virtual short between the inputs of an op-amp is correct?
options: It means the two input terminals are physically connected together
It holds only while negative feedback keeps the output within its linear range
It also holds for an open-loop comparator
It allows a large current to flow from one input to the other
explanation: The inputs are at almost the same voltage because the feedback forces the output to a value that makes V+ − V− ≈ 0; no current flows between them. In saturation or without feedback the rule fails.

questionText: An op-amp with a slew rate of 13 V/µs must give a 10 V peak sine output. Its full-power bandwidth is about:
explanation: f = SR/(2π V_p) = 13 × 10⁶/(2π × 10) ≈ 207 kHz. Faster-slewing FET-input op-amps are chosen when large high-frequency swings are needed.

questionText: The output of a voltage follower must step from −5 V to +5 V. If its slew rate is 0.5 V/µs, the transition takes at least:
explanation: The output must change by 10 V at no more than 0.5 V/µs: t = 10/0.5 = 20 µs. Using only 5 V of change gives the 10 µs error.

questionText: A 3-bit weighted-resistor DAC uses an inverting summing amplifier with R_f = 10 kΩ and input resistors of 10 kΩ (MSB), 20 kΩ and 40 kΩ (LSB). Logic 1 is 5 V and logic 0 is 0 V. For the input code 101 the output is:
An op-amp has a differential gain of 10⁵ and a CMRR of 90 dB. Its common-mode gain is about:
explanation: CMRR = 10^(90/20) = 31 623, so A_cm = A_d/CMRR = 10⁵/31 623 ≈ 3.16. Dividing by 90 directly (1111) ignores the decibel scale.

questionText: A constant positive DC voltage is applied to an ideal op-amp integrator whose capacitor is initially uncharged. The output is:
options: A ramp going negative at a constant rate until the op-amp saturates
A ramp going positive until it saturates
A decaying exponential that settles at 0 V
explanation: V_o = −(1/RC)∫V_in dt, so a constant positive input gives a linearly falling output of slope −V_in/RC, ending at −V_sat.

questionText: Which statement comparing the inverting and non-inverting amplifiers is correct?
options: The inverting amplifier cannot have a gain magnitude greater than 1
The non-inverting amplifier's output is 180° out of phase with its input
The non-inverting amplifier has a much higher input impedance than the inverting amplifier
Both have an input impedance equal to R_in
explanation: The non-inverting input draws almost no current, so its input impedance is essentially that of the op-amp, whereas the inverting amplifier's is only R_in. The inverting amplifier can have any gain magnitude, and the non-inverting output is in phase.

questionText: A non-inverting amplifier of gain 11 uses an op-amp with SR = 0.5 V/µs. A 1 V peak, 20 kHz sine is applied. The largest output peak that can be delivered at this frequency without slew distortion is about:
options: 25 V, so the 11 V peak output is undistorted
3.98 V, so the 11 V peak output is slew-limited
7.96 V, so the output is slightly distorted
explanation: The ideal output needs 2π × 20 000 × 11 = 1.38 V/µs, more than 0.5 V/µs. The largest clean peak is SR/(2π f) = 0.5 × 10⁶/(2π × 20 000) = 3.98 V, so the output becomes triangular. Forgetting the 2π gives 0.5 × 10⁶/20 000 = 25 V, which wrongly suggests no distortion.

questionText: A non-inverting op-amp amplifier uses R_f = 47 kΩ and R_1 = 4.7 kΩ. Its closed-loop voltage gain is:
explanation: For the non-inverting configuration A_v = 1 + R_f / R_1 = 1 + 47 / 4.7 = 11, with no phase inversion. A gain of −10 would be the inverting configuration with the same resistors.

questionText: In an inverting amplifier with negative feedback, the inverting input terminal is called a virtual ground because:
options: The input resistor is very large, so almost no voltage appears across it
The output is saturated at the negative supply rail
The op-amp draws a large current from that node to ground
The huge open-loop gain forces V− to equal the grounded V+ while no current flows into it
explanation: With negative feedback the output adjusts until V+ − V− ≈ 0. Since V+ is tied to ground, V− sits at 0 V without being connected to ground, and the infinite input impedance means it sinks no current.

questionText: An op-amp has a slew rate of 0.5 V/µs. The highest frequency at which it can deliver a 10 V peak sinusoidal output without slew-rate distortion is approximately:
explanation: f_max = SR / (2π V_p) = 0.5 × 10⁶ / (2π × 10) ≈ 7.96 kHz. Above this the required dV/dt exceeds the slew rate and the output becomes triangular even though the 1 MHz GBW would allow more.

questionText: A power transistor has T_J(max) = 150 °C and a total junction-to-ambient thermal resistance of 2.5 °C/W. At an ambient temperature of 25 °C the maximum power it may dissipate is:
explanation: P_D(max) = (T_J(max) − T_A)/θ_JA = (150 − 25)/2.5 = 50 W. Dividing 150 alone by 2.5 (60 W) forgets the ambient temperature.

questionText: A transistor dissipating 15 W has θ_JC = 1.5 °C/W, θ_CS = 0.5 °C/W and a heat sink with θ_SA = 3 °C/W. At T_A = 40 °C its junction temperature is:
explanation: θ_JA = 1.5 + 0.5 + 3 = 5 °C/W, so T_J = 40 + 15 × 5 = 115 °C. Using only one of the resistances gives the lower distractors.

questionText: A transistor must dissipate 20 W at an ambient of 50 °C without its junction exceeding 150 °C. Given θ_JC = 2 °C/W and θ_CS = 0.5 °C/W, the largest acceptable heat-sink thermal resistance θ_SA is:
explanation: θ_JA(max) = (150 − 50)/20 = 5 °C/W, so θ_SA = 5 − 2 − 0.5 = 2.5 °C/W. Forgetting θ_CS gives 3 °C/W; stopping at θ_JA gives 5 °C/W.

questionText: A power transistor is rated 40 W at a case temperature of 25 °C, with T_J(max) = 150 °C. Its allowable dissipation when the case is at 75 °C is:
A data sheet rates a transistor at 25 W for a case temperature of 25 °C and gives T_J(max) = 150 °C. The power derating factor is:
explanation: Derating factor = P_D(25)/(T_J(max) − 25) = 25/125 = 0.2 W/°C, which is 1/θ_JC with θ_JC = 5 °C/W. Dividing by 150 instead of 125 gives 0.167 W/°C.

questionText: A heat sink allows a power transistor to dissipate more power because it:
options: Lowers the thermal resistance from the case to the surrounding air
Raises the maximum junction temperature of the device
Reduces the collector current at a given base current
Increases the thermal resistance from junction to case
explanation: P_D(max) = (T_J(max) − T_A)/θ_JA. The sink cannot change T_J(max) or θ_JC, but it replaces the large case-to-air resistance with a much smaller θ_CS + θ_SA.

questionText: Thermal resistance is normally expressed in:
explanation: Thermal resistance is the temperature rise per watt of heat flow, °C/W (or K/W). W/°C is the unit of the derating factor, which is its reciprocal.

questionText: A thin mica washer coated with thermal grease is placed between a TO-3 transistor and its heat sink in order to:
options: Raise the thermal resistance so the heat sink stays cool
Increase the breakdown voltage V_CEO of the transistor
Act as a fuse that opens if the junction overheats
Insulate the case electrically from the sink while keeping the case-to-sink thermal resistance low
explanation: The case is usually the collector, so it must often be isolated from a grounded chassis. Mica is a good electrical insulator, and the grease fills air gaps so θ_CS stays around 0.3 to 0.5 °C/W.

questionText: In most power BJT packages (TO-3, TO-220) the metal case or mounting tab is electrically connected to the:
explanation: Most of the heat is produced at the collector-base junction, so the collector is bonded directly to the metal to give the shortest thermal path to the heat sink.

questionText: The safe operating area of a power BJT is bounded by several limits. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
options: The maximum power dissipation hyperbola V_CE I_C = P_D(max)
The second-breakdown limit at high V_CE
explanation: The SOA is set by I_C(max), P_D(max), second breakdown and V_CEO. Current gain varies with operating point but does not define a safe-operating boundary.

questionText: A power transistor has P_D(max) = 30 W at the operating case temperature. At V_CE = 20 V, the largest collector current allowed by the power limit of its SOA is:
explanation: On the constant-power boundary I_C = P_D(max)/V_CE = 30/20 = 1.5 A. The inverted ratio 20/30 gives the 0.67 A slip.

questionText: A transformer-coupled class A amplifier runs from V_CC = 12 V and drives an 8 Ω loudspeaker through a 5 : 1 transformer. With ideal full swing, the maximum AC output power is:
explanation: R' = 5² × 8 = 200 Ω. P_o(max) = V_CC²/(2R') = 144/400 = 0.36 W. 0.72 W is the DC supply power V_CC²/R', and 9 W wrongly uses the 8 Ω speaker directly.

questionText: A loudspeaker of 8 Ω is connected to the secondary of a transformer with a 10 : 1 primary-to-secondary turns ratio. The resistance seen at the primary is:
explanation: R' = (N_1/N_2)² R_L = 10² × 8 = 800 Ω. Forgetting to square the ratio gives 80 Ω.

questionText: A transistor stage works best into a 1.8 kΩ collector load but must drive an 8 Ω loudspeaker. The required primary-to-secondary turns ratio of the output transformer is:
explanation: (N_1/N_2)² = R'/R_L = 1800/8 = 225, so N_1/N_2 = √225 = 15. 225 : 1 is the impedance ratio, not the turns ratio.

questionText: Replacing the collector resistor of a series-fed class A stage by the primary of an output transformer raises the maximum theoretical efficiency from:
explanation: The resistor wastes half the supply power in the series-fed stage (25 % ceiling). The winding has negligible DC resistance and lets the collector swing to 2V_CC, so the ceiling doubles to 50 %. 78.5 % needs class B.

questionText: Why can the collector of a transformer-coupled class A stage swing well above the supply voltage V_CC?
options: The transformer steps up the supply voltage on the primary side
The transistor enters avalanche breakdown on every cycle
The primary inductance stores energy and its induced voltage adds to V_CC on the half-cycle when the collector current falls
The load resistance appears in parallel with the supply
explanation: V_CEQ ≈ V_CC because the winding drops no DC voltage. When the current falls below I_CQ the inductance opposes the change and its EMF adds to V_CC, so v_CE can reach nearly 2V_CC.

questionText: In an ideal transformer-coupled class A amplifier supplied from V_CC = 10 V and driven to full swing, the collector-emitter voltage reaches a peak of about:
explanation: With V_CEQ ≈ V_CC = 10 V and a full symmetrical swing of ±V_CC, v_CE swings from about 0 to 2V_CC = 20 V, so the transistor must be rated for at least twice the supply.

questionText: A transformer-coupled class A stage has V_CC = 20 V and I_CQ = 0.5 A. With signal, v_CE swings between 5 V and 35 V. The efficiency is about:

A transformer-coupled class A amplifier with V_CC = 12 V drives a 16 Ω load through a 3 : 1 transformer. The collector voltage swings 10 V peak. The power delivered to the load (ideal transformer) is:
explanation: R' = 3² × 16 = 144 Ω. P_o = V_p²/(2R') = 100/288 = 0.347 W. Leaving out the square gives 1.04 W; leaving out the 2 for RMS gives 0.694 W.

questionText: A drawback of the single-ended transformer-coupled class A stage that the push-pull stage avoids is:
options: The need for two transistors of opposite type
DC magnetisation of the output transformer core by the quiescent collector current
Inability to match a low-impedance load
