questionText: A processor runs at 200 MHz with an average of 4 clock cycles per instruction (CPI). Its MIPS rating is:
An 8-bit processor runs at 3 MHz and its instructions take 5 T-states on average. Its speed in MIPS is:
explanation: MIPS = f / (CPI × 10^6) = 3 × 10^6 / (5 × 10^6) = 0.6. 15 multiplies instead of dividing.

questionText: A program of 2 × 10^6 instructions runs on a 500 MHz processor with an average CPI of 2.5. The CPU execution time is:
explanation: CPU time = instruction count × CPI / f = 2 × 10^6 × 2.5 / (500 × 10^6) = 0.01 s = 10 ms. Ignoring CPI gives 4 ms; dividing by CPI gives 1.6 ms.

questionText: A program mix is 50% ALU instructions (CPI 1), 30% load/store (CPI 3) and 20% branches (CPI 2). On a 900 MHz processor the MIPS rating is:
explanation: Average CPI = 0.5×1 + 0.3×3 + 0.2×2 = 0.5 + 0.9 + 0.4 = 1.8. MIPS = 900 / 1.8 = 500. 1620 multiplies by CPI; 450 uses a CPI of 2.

questionText: A system bus is 16 bits wide and one bus cycle takes 4 clock periods at 8 MHz. The maximum data transfer rate is:
explanation: Bus cycles per second = 8 × 10^6 / 4 = 2 × 10^6; each moves 2 bytes, so rate = 2 × 10^6 × 2 = 4 × 10^6 bytes/s = 4 MB/s (decimal megabytes). Forgetting the 2 bytes gives 2 MB/s.

questionText: An ideal 5-stage instruction pipeline (one clock per stage, no stalls) executes 100 instructions. The number of clock cycles required is:
explanation: Cycles = k + (n − 1) = 5 + 99 = 104: the first instruction needs 5 cycles to fill the pipeline, then one instruction completes every cycle. 500 is the unpipelined count.

questionText: Which of the following devices integrates a CPU, RAM, ROM, timers and I/O ports on a single chip?
explanation: The 8051 is a microcontroller with on-chip memory, timers, serial port and I/O ports. The 8085, 8086 and 80386 are microprocessors that need external memory and I/O chips.

questionText: Which statement about microprocessors and microcontrollers is NOT correct?
options: A microprocessor needs external memory and I/O chips to form a working system
A microcontroller has on-chip memory, timers and I/O ports
A microcontroller is preferred for general-purpose personal computers because of its large external memory
Microcontrollers are preferred in embedded products where cost, size and power matter
explanation: General-purpose computers use microprocessors with large external memory; microcontrollers are built for dedicated embedded control with limited on-chip memory.

questionText: Which bus of a microprocessor system is bidirectional?
explanation: The data bus carries data from memory/I/O to the processor during a read and from the processor to them during a write, so it is bidirectional. The address bus is driven only by the processor.

questionText: Why is the address bus of a simple microprocessor system called unidirectional?
options: It carries data in one direction during reads and the other during writes
Only the processor places addresses on it; memory and I/O only receive them
It can address only one memory chip at a time
It is used only for the instruction fetch operation
explanation: The processor alone generates the address of the memory location or port it wants; memory and I/O devices decode it but never drive it (DMA controllers aside, which take over the bus only after the processor releases it).

questionText: The word length of a microprocessor refers to:
options: the number of bits it can process in one operation, set by its ALU and data-bus width
the number of address lines it provides
the number of instructions in its instruction set
the number of bytes in its longest instruction
explanation: Word length is the size of the data the processor handles at once; an 8085 is an 8-bit processor even though it has 16 address lines.

questionText: If a microprocessor's data bus is widened from 8 to 16 bits while its address bus stays at 16 bits, what changes?
options: The number of addressable locations doubles to 2^17
The number of addressable locations halves
Neither the transfer width nor the number of locations changes
The number of bits moved per bus transfer doubles; the number of addressable locations stays 2^16
explanation: Address lines alone fix the number of locations (2^n); data lines fix how many bits move per transfer.

questionText: In the fetch–decode–execute cycle, which step immediately follows fetching the opcode into the instruction register?
options: Decoding the opcode in the control unit
explanation: After the opcode is fetched it must be decoded so the control unit knows which operation and which further machine cycles are required; execution comes after decoding.

questionText: During the fetch phase of an instruction, which sequence of events is correct?
options: The PC is placed on the address bus, the opcode is read into the IR and the PC is incremented
The SP is placed on the address bus, the opcode is read into the accumulator and the SP is decremented
The IR is placed on the address bus, the opcode is read into the PC and the PC is decremented
The accumulator is placed on the address bus and the opcode is written to memory
explanation: The program counter supplies the address of the next instruction, the memory returns the opcode on the data bus into the instruction register, and the PC is incremented to point to the next byte.

questionText: Which register holds the opcode of the current instruction while it is being decoded?
explanation: The fetched opcode is latched into the instruction register (IR), whose output feeds the instruction decoder. The PC already points to the next byte.

questionText: The program counter of a microprocessor holds:
options: the address of the next instruction byte to be fetched
the opcode of the instruction being executed
the number of instructions executed since reset
the address of the top of the stack
explanation: The PC is a 16-bit pointer (in the 8085) that always addresses the next byte of the program; it is incremented after each fetch and reloaded by jumps, calls and returns.

questionText: What does the flag (status) register of a microprocessor record?
options: The address of the next instruction
The operand of the current instruction
Conditions of the result of the last arithmetic or logic operation, such as zero, sign and carry
explanation: Flag bits are set or reset by the ALU to describe the result (zero, negative, carry, parity and so on); conditional jumps test them.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT a function of the ALU?
options: Decoding the opcode of the fetched instruction
Shifting or rotating a data byte
explanation: Opcode decoding is done by the instruction decoder in the control unit. The ALU performs arithmetic, logic, shift and rotate operations on data.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT a control-bus signal of a microprocessor system?
explanation: RD, WR and ALE are control/timing signals. AD7 is a multiplexed address/data line, part of the address and data buses.

questionText: Why are bus lines driven through tri-state buffers in a microprocessor system?
options: To increase the clock frequency of the processor
To convert the data bus into an address bus
So that a device can electrically disconnect itself (high impedance) and let another device drive the shared bus
To store data when the power fails
explanation: Tri-state outputs have 0, 1 and high-impedance states; only one device drives a shared line at a time while the others float, which also lets a DMA controller take over the bus.

questionText: One T-state of a microprocessor is:
options: one period of the processor clock
the time for one complete bus operation
the time to fetch and execute one instruction
the time for one memory write
explanation: A T-state is the basic timing unit, equal to one clock period (1/f). A machine cycle is one bus operation and an instruction cycle is the complete fetch and execute of one instruction.

questionText: Which ordering of timing units, from shortest to longest, is correct?
explanation: A machine cycle is made of several T-states, and an instruction cycle is made of one or more machine cycles.

questionText: A machine cycle is best defined as:
options: one period of the system clock
the time needed to execute the longest instruction
the time required to complete one operation of accessing memory or an I/O device
explanation: Each machine cycle (opcode fetch, memory read, memory write, I/O read, I/O write, interrupt acknowledge) is one bus operation lasting several T-states.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a RISC processor?
options: Fixed-length instructions that are easy to pipeline
Many variable-length instructions with complex memory addressing modes
Only load and store instructions access memory
A large set of general-purpose registers
explanation: Variable-length instructions with rich memory addressing modes are the hallmark of CISC designs such as the x86. RISC keeps instructions simple, fixed-length and register-to-register.

questionText: The control unit of a typical CISC processor is implemented as ___, while a typical RISC processor uses ___.
explanation: Complex, variable instructions are easier to implement as microcode sequences stored in a control ROM; simple RISC instructions are decoded by fast hardwired logic.

questionText: Why are RISC processors particularly well suited to pipelining?
options: Their instructions are of uniform length and similar execution time, so each stage takes about one clock
They have fewer registers, so less data has to be saved
They allow memory operands in every instruction
They use microcode for every instruction
explanation: Uniform, simple instructions let fetch, decode, execute and write-back be divided into equal stages; variable-length CISC instructions make stage timing irregular.

questionText: The "von Neumann bottleneck" refers to:
options: the small number of registers in RISC processors
the delay caused by interrupt handling
the heat generated by high clock speeds
the limit on throughput because instructions and data share one memory and one bus
explanation: In a von Neumann machine an instruction fetch and a data access cannot use the single bus at the same time, so the bus limits performance; Harvard architecture removes this by using separate buses.

questionText: Which statement about von Neumann and Harvard architectures is correct?
options: The 8085 follows the Harvard model because it has separate RD and WR lines
A Harvard processor cannot store constant data in program memory in any form
Von Neumann processors always have separate instruction and data caches
The 8085 and 8086 follow the von Neumann model, whereas many DSPs and the 8051 follow the Harvard model
explanation: The 8085/8086 fetch instructions and data from one memory over one bus. Separate RD and WR strobes do not make separate memories; DSPs and the 8051 have separate program and data spaces.

questionText: The first commercial microprocessor, the Intel 4004, was a ___ processor.
explanation: The 4004 (1971) had a 4-bit data path and a 12-bit address range; the 8008/8080/8085 were 8-bit and the 8086 16-bit.

questionText: A microprocessor with a 24-bit address bus and an 8-bit data bus can directly address a maximum memory of:
explanation: Capacity = 2^24 locations = 16,777,216 bytes = 16 MB. The data bus width does not change the number of addressable locations.

questionText: An 8085 operates from a 3 MHz internal clock. The duration of one T-state is approximately:
explanation: One T-state is one clock period: T = 1 / (3 × 10^6) = 333 ns. An opcode fetch of 4 T-states therefore takes about 1.33 μs.

questionText: A Harvard architecture processor differs from a Von Neumann processor in that it:
options: uses a single memory for program and data
has no need for a control unit
keeps program and data in separate memories with separate buses
explanation: Harvard architecture provides separate program and data memories and buses so instruction fetch and data access can overlap; Von Neumann machines such as the 8085 share one memory and bus for both.

questionText: Which block of a microprocessor decodes the opcode and generates the timing and control signals for the rest of the chip?
explanation: The control unit interprets the fetched opcode and produces the sequence of internal and external control signals; the ALU only performs the arithmetic and logic operations it is told to perform.

questionText: A 16K × 8 memory chip needs how many address lines?
explanation: 16K = 16 × 1024 = 16384 = 2^14 locations, so n = log2(16384) = 14 address lines (A0 to A13). The 8 is the number of data lines, not address lines.

questionText: A 2K × 8 static RAM has address pins, data pins, three control pins (CS, OE, WE) and two power pins (VCC, GND). What is its minimum pin count?
explanation: Address pins = log2(2048) = 11, data pins = 8, so 11 + 8 + 3 + 2 = 24 pins; this is why the 6116 comes in a 24-pin package.

questionText: How many 4K × 8 memory chips are needed to build 32 KB of memory for an 8-bit microprocessor?
explanation: The chip is already 8 bits wide, so each bank is a single chip and chips = 32 KB / 4 KB = 8, selected one at a time by a 3-to-8 decoder.

questionText: A 16K × 8 memory is to be built from 1K × 4 RAM chips. How many chips are required?
explanation: Depth: 16K / 1K = 16 rows; width: 8 / 4 = 2 chips per row; total = 16 × 2 = 32. Forgetting the width factor gives 16.

questionText: How many 16K × 4 chips are needed to build a 64K × 16 memory?
explanation: (64K × 16) / (16K × 4) = (64/16) × (16/4) = 4 × 4 = 16 chips: four banks, each four chips wide.

questionText: An 8085 system needs 4 KB of RAM built from 1K × 1 chips. How many chips are required?
explanation: 4 KB = 4K × 8. Each row needs 8 one-bit chips to make a byte, and 4K / 1K = 4 rows, so 4 × 8 = 32 chips.

questionText: The 2764 EPROM is a 64 Kbit device organised as 8K × 8. How many 2764 chips are needed for 32 KB of program memory?
explanation: Each 2764 holds 64 Kbit / 8 = 8 KB, so 32 KB / 8 KB = 4 chips. Dividing 32 KB by 64 Kbit without converting bits to bytes gives a wrong answer.

questionText: Eight 4K × 8 chips form 32 KB of memory at 0000H–7FFFH in an 8085 system. Which decoding arrangement selects the chips correctly (full decoding)?
options: A 3-to-8 decoder driven by A13, A14, A15
A 3-to-8 decoder driven by A12, A13, A14 and enabled only when A15 = 0
A 2-to-4 decoder driven by A12, A13 and enabled when A14 = 0
A 3-to-8 decoder driven by A12, A13, A14, with A15 not connected
explanation: A 4K chip uses A0 to A11 (2^12 = 4096), so the next three lines A12 to A14 pick one of 8 chips, and A15 = 0 is required so the block stays in 0000H–7FFFH. Leaving A15 unconnected is partial decoding: every chip would appear again in 8000H–FFFFH. A13–A15 would suit 8K chips instead, and a 2-to-4 decoder can select only four chips.

questionText: A 4K × 8 RAM in an 8085 system is selected only when A15 A14 A13 A12 = 0 1 0 1 (full decoding). Its address range is:
explanation: The 4K chip uses A0 to A11. The fixed nibble 0101 followed by twelve 0s gives 5000H, and with twelve 1s gives 5FFFH. Reading the pattern in reverse bit order gives A000H.

questionText: An 8K × 8 EPROM is enabled when A15 A14 A13 = 1 1 0, with all other high-order lines used by the chip itself. Its address range is:
explanation: 8K = 2^13, so A0 to A12 go to the chip. 110 followed by thirteen 0s = 1100 0000 0000 0000 = C000H; with thirteen 1s = 1101 1111 1111 1111 = DFFFH.

questionText: A 2K × 8 RAM begins at address 3800H. What is its last address?
explanation: 2K = 2048 = 800H locations, so last = 3800H + 800H − 1 = 3FFFH. 4000H is one past the end (off-by-one), and adding 2000H treats 2K as a hex number.

questionText: A memory chip occupies the address range 2000H to 27FFH with full decoding. What is its capacity?
explanation: Size = 27FFH − 2000H + 1 = 800H = 2048 bytes = 2 KB.

questionText: A fully decoded memory chip occupies F000H to FFFFH in an 8085 system. How many of the processor address lines connect directly to the chip's address pins?
explanation: Size = FFFFH − F000H + 1 = 1000H = 4096 = 2^12, so A0 to A11 (12 lines) go to the chip and the remaining 4 lines (A15–A12 = 1111) drive the chip select.

questionText: In an 8086 system (20 address lines) a 64 KB EPROM is placed at the very top of memory so that it contains the reset address FFFF0H. Its address range is:
explanation: The top of a 1 MB space is FFFFFH. 64 KB = 10000H bytes, so the start is 100000H − 10000H = F0000H and the range is F0000H to FFFFFH.

questionText: An 8085 memory map starts with an 8 KB ROM at 0000H, followed immediately by three 4K × 8 RAM chips placed one after another. What is the last address of the third RAM?
explanation: ROM ends at 1FFFH, so RAM starts at 2000H; three 4 KB chips span 3 × 1000H = 3000H bytes, ending at 2000H + 3000H − 1 = 4FFFH.

questionText: A 2K × 8 RAM uses A0–A10 and its chip select is driven by A15-bar · A14 only; A13, A12 and A11 are not connected. At how many different addresses does each RAM byte respond?
explanation: Each unused line doubles the number of addresses at which a byte responds: 2^3 = 8. The chip therefore fills 4000H–7FFFH (16 KB) with eight copies of the same 2 KB.

questionText: A 4K × 8 RAM uses A0–A11. Its chip select is active when A15 = 1 and A13 = 0; A14 and A12 are not decoded. Which address blocks does the RAM respond to?
explanation: With A15 = 1 and A13 = 0 fixed, A14 A12 take all four values 00, 01, 10, 11, giving blocks starting at 8000H, 9000H, C000H and D000H (overall 8000H–9FFFH, C000H–DFFFH). Treating A13 as free instead of A12 gives the A000H/E000H list.

questionText: A 4K × 8 EPROM (A0–A11) is selected by A15-bar · A14, with A13 and A12 left undecoded. Its first image is 4000H–4FFFH. Which of these addresses also selects the EPROM?
explanation: 6ABCH = 0110 1010 1011 1100: A15 = 0 and A14 = 1, so the chip is selected (A13 A12 = 10 are ignored). 8ABCH and CABCH have A15 = 1, and 2ABCH has A14 = 0.

questionText: A 74138 decoder in an 8085 system has C = A15, B = A14, A = A13 (A is the LSB input) and its enables asserted for memory cycles. Which output goes low when the CPU reads address 9A34H?
explanation: 9A34H = 1001 1010 0011 0100, so A15 A14 A13 = 100 = 4, and output Y4 is selected. Taking the bits in reverse order (001) would wrongly give Y1.

questionText: In an 8085 board, all memory-mapped I/O devices are selected when A15 = 1 and memory is selected only when A15 = 0. What is the maximum memory the system can have?
explanation: Memory uses only addresses with A15 = 0, i.e. 0000H–7FFFH = 2^15 bytes = 32 KB; the other half of the map is given to I/O.

questionText: A 64K × 1 DRAM uses address multiplexing with RAS and CAS strobes. How many address pins does the chip need?
explanation: 64K = 2^16 locations need 16 address bits, sent in two halves (row, then column) over the same pins: 16 / 2 = 8 pins.

questionText: A 1 Mbit memory chip is organised as 256K × 4 and does NOT multiplex its address. How many address lines does it need?
explanation: Locations = 256K = 2^18, so 18 address lines. 20 lines would be right only for 1M × 1 organisation.

questionText: A processor with a 100 ns clock period allows 300 ns for a memory to respond when no wait states are used, and each wait state adds one clock period. A memory with a 450 ns access time needs how many wait states?
explanation: Shortfall = 450 − 300 = 150 ns; wait states = ceil(150 / 100) = ceil(1.5) = 2. One wait state gives only 400 ns, which is still too short.

questionText: A cache has a hit ratio of 0.95 and an access time of 5 ns; main memory has an access time of 80 ns. Using T_eff = h·t_c + (1 − h)·t_m, the effective access time is:
explanation: T_eff = 0.95 × 5 + 0.05 × 80 = 4.75 + 4.00 = 8.75 ns. Swapping h and (1 − h) gives 76.25 ns, and a plain average of 5 and 80 gives 42.5 ns.

questionText: Cache access time is 10 ns and main memory access time is 100 ns. Using T_eff = h·t_c + (1 − h)·t_m, what hit ratio h gives an effective access time of 19 ns?
explanation: 19 = 10h + 100(1 − h) = 100 − 90h, so h = 81 / 90 = 0.90. 0.81 comes from forgetting to divide by (t_m − t_c) = 90.

questionText: A DRAM has 256 rows, every row must be refreshed once every 4 ms, and one row refresh takes 200 ns. What percentage of memory time is used for refresh?
explanation: Refresh time per period = 256 × 200 ns = 51.2 µs; 51.2 µs / 4 ms = 0.0128 = 1.28 %. Forgetting the 256 rows gives 200 ns / 4 ms = 0.005 %, and misplacing the decimal point gives 12.8 %.

questionText: A 16 KB memory for an 8085 is built from 2K × 4 chips. How many chips are needed, and how many high-order address lines must be decoded to select a bank (row) of chips?
options: 8 chips; 3 address lines to the bank decoder
16 chips; 3 address lines to the bank decoder
16 chips; 4 address lines to the bank decoder
32 chips; 4 address lines to the bank decoder
explanation: Width 8 / 4 = 2 chips per bank, depth 16K / 2K = 8 banks, so 16 chips. The 2K chips use A0–A10, and 8 banks need log2(8) = 3 select lines (A11–A13).

questionText: Using variable port addressing (port number in DX), how many different 8-bit I/O ports can the 8086 address?
explanation: DX is a 16-bit register, so port numbers run from 0000H to FFFFH: 2^16 = 65,536 ports. 256 is the limit for the fixed 8-bit port form.

questionText: In a static RAM (SRAM) cell, one bit is stored in:
options: A charged capacitor with one access transistor
A bistable latch (flip-flop) of about six transistors
explanation: SRAM keeps each bit in a cross-coupled latch, so it holds data without refresh while powered. The capacitor cell is DRAM, the floating gate is EPROM/flash, and fuses are PROM.

questionText: Why must dynamic RAM be refreshed periodically?
options: The charge on each cell capacitor leaks away within milliseconds
Its flip-flops lose state when the clock stops
Reading a cell sets it to all ones
Refresh is needed to erase the chip before writing
explanation: A DRAM bit is charge on a tiny capacitor that leaks, so every row is read and rewritten every few milliseconds. DRAM does not use flip-flops, and refresh is not an erase operation.

questionText: How is a conventional EPROM erased?
options: By applying an electrical pulse to one byte at a time
By exposing the chip to ultraviolet light through its quartz window
explanation: UV light gives the trapped floating-gate electrons enough energy to escape, erasing the whole chip. Byte-wise electrical erase describes EEPROM, and fuses are used in PROM.

questionText: Which of the following memories keeps its contents when power is switched off?
explanation: Flash stores charge on an insulated floating gate, so it is non-volatile. SRAM, DRAM and registers are all volatile and lose their data without power.

questionText: What is the main practical difference between EEPROM and flash memory?
options: EEPROM can be erased and rewritten byte by byte, while flash is erased a whole block (sector) at a time
EEPROM is volatile, while flash is non-volatile
Flash is erased by ultraviolet light, while EEPROM is erased electrically
EEPROM can be programmed only once, while flash can be reprogrammed
explanation: Both are electrically erasable floating-gate memories. Block erasure makes flash denser and cheaper, which is why it is used for SSDs and firmware, while EEPROM suits small configuration data.

questionText: A PROM is programmed by:
options: The manufacturer, using a mask during fabrication
The user, repeatedly, with ultraviolet erasure between programs
The user, once, by blowing selected fusible links
The CPU during normal operation, like RAM
explanation: A PROM leaves the factory blank and is programmed once by the user; a blown fuse cannot be restored. Mask programming describes mask ROM and UV erasure describes EPROM.

questionText: A mask ROM is best suited for:
options: Firmware that is still being developed and changed often
Very large production runs of firmware that will never change
Storing user settings that change during operation
explanation: The data is fixed by a photomask at manufacture, which is cheap per chip only in large volumes and cannot be altered. Development work uses EPROM or flash, and changing settings need EEPROM.

questionText: A loop body executes the same instructions again and again. Which property of programs does this illustrate, allowing a cache to be effective?
explanation: Temporal locality means an item used now is likely to be used again soon, as the loop instructions are. Spatial locality refers to nearby addresses, such as the next array element.

questionText: Which statement about the memory hierarchy is NOT correct?
options: Access time increases as we move from registers towards secondary storage
Capacity increases as we move from cache towards secondary storage
Cost per bit rises as we move from cache towards secondary storage
The hierarchy works because programs show locality of reference
explanation: Moving down the hierarchy, each level is slower, larger and cheaper per bit, so cost per bit falls rather than rises. The other three statements are correct.

questionText: Which statement comparing full and partial address decoding is correct?
options: Partial decoding needs fewer gates but makes each location appear at more than one address
Full decoding makes each location appear at several addresses (foldback)
Partial decoding increases the usable capacity of each memory chip
Full decoding ignores some of the high-order address lines
explanation: In partial decoding some address lines are left out, which saves logic but creates mirror images and wastes address space. Full decoding uses every line so each location has a unique address, and neither scheme changes chip capacity.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of memory-mapped I/O in an 8085 system?
options: Any memory-reference instruction can be used to access a port
Data can be moved between a port and any register, not only the accumulator
Arithmetic and logic can be done directly on a port location
It leaves the complete 64 KB address space available for memory
explanation: Memory-mapped ports occupy memory addresses, so they reduce the space left for memory; keeping the full 64 KB is an advantage of I/O-mapped (isolated) I/O. The other three are genuine advantages.

questionText: In the 8085, during which T-state of a memory read machine cycle is the READY input first sampled to decide whether wait states are needed?
explanation: The 8085 checks READY during T2. If READY is low it inserts wait states (Tw) between T2 and T3 until READY goes high, then continues with T3.

questionText: In an 8085 system, which combination of signals indicates a memory read operation?
explanation: IO/M low selects memory and an active-low RD means read, so together they form MEMR. IO/M = 1 with RD = 0 is an I/O read (IOR), and WR = 0 means a write.

questionText: Why do DRAM chips multiplex their address pins using RAS and CAS?
options: To double the data transfer rate
To avoid the need for refresh
To halve the number of address pins, keeping the package small for large capacities
To allow the chip to be erased electrically
explanation: The row address and column address are sent one after another on the same pins, latched by RAS and CAS, so a 2^16-location chip needs 8 pins instead of 16. It does not remove refresh or change the data rate.

questionText: Which statement about the buses of an 8085 microprocessor system is correct?
options: The address bus is bidirectional and the data bus is unidirectional
The address bus is unidirectional (from the CPU) and the data bus is bidirectional
Both the address bus and the data bus are unidirectional
The control bus carries the data being written to memory
explanation: Only the CPU places addresses on the address bus, while data travels both ways, to memory on writes and to the CPU on reads. The control bus carries timing and command signals such as RD, WR and IO/M.

questionText: Which statement comparing SRAM with DRAM is NOT correct?
options: DRAM stores more bits per chip area than SRAM
SRAM costs more per bit than DRAM
SRAM must be refreshed periodically, while DRAM keeps its data without refresh
explanation: It is DRAM that needs refresh, because its capacitor cells leak; SRAM latches hold data while powered. SRAM is faster but larger and dearer per bit, which is why DRAM is used for main memory.

questionText: The access time of a memory chip is defined as the time from:
options: Power-on until the chip is ready for its first read
One read operation starting until the next read can start
A stable address being applied to valid data appearing at the outputs
The write strobe until the data is permanently stored
explanation: Access time measures how long the chip takes to deliver data after the address is valid. The minimum time between successive starts of operations is the cycle time, which is at least as long.

questionText: In a microcomputer, which memory is accessed directly by the CPU through its address bus, rather than through I/O transfers?
explanation: Main memory (RAM and ROM) sits on the processor buses and is addressed directly by instructions. Disks, tapes and optical media are secondary or tertiary storage reached through I/O controllers.

questionText: A 2K x 8 memory chip in an 8085 system is selected only when A15 A14 A13 A12 A11 = 1 0 1 1 0 (full decoding). What address range does the chip occupy?
explanation: 2K = 2^11 locations use A0 to A10, so A11 to A15 select the chip. The fixed pattern 10110 followed by eleven 0s is 1011 0000 0000 0000 = B000H, and with eleven 1s it is 1011 0111 1111 1111 = B7FFH.

questionText: In polling (programmed) I/O, how does the CPU find out that a device needs service?
options: The device drives an interrupt pin and the CPU jumps to a vector address
The device takes over the system bus and writes directly into memory
The CPU executes a software interrupt instruction that asks the device for its status
It repeatedly reads the device status register in a loop until the ready bit is set
explanation: Polling is CPU-initiated: the program keeps testing a status bit. An interrupt pin is interrupt-driven I/O and taking over the bus is DMA.

questionText: Which 8085 interrupt input is non-vectored?
explanation: TRAP and RST 7.5/6.5/5.5 branch to fixed internal addresses. For INTR the external logic must supply an RST n or CALL instruction on the data bus during INTA.

questionText: Which 8085 interrupt input is purely edge-triggered, with the request stored in an internal flip-flop?
explanation: RST 7.5 responds to a rising edge and latches it. RST 6.5, RST 5.5 and INTR are level-sensitive; TRAP needs both an edge and a sustained high level.

questionText: Which of the following is a software interrupt in the 8085?
options: A rising edge on the RST 7.5 pin
A high level on the TRAP pin
A request on INTR answered with INTA
explanation: A software interrupt is caused by an instruction in the program; RST 3 is an instruction that pushes PC and branches to 0018H. The other three are hardware requests arriving on pins.

questionText: What does the 8085 instruction EI do?
options: Enables TRAP, which is disabled after every reset
Sets the interrupt-enable flip-flop so that the maskable interrupts can be accepted
Clears the RST 7.5, 6.5 and 5.5 mask bits
explanation: EI only sets the global interrupt-enable flip-flop. The individual mask bits are changed only by SIM, and TRAP is never disabled, so it needs no enabling.

questionText: Which 8085 instruction disables all maskable interrupts in one step?
explanation: DI resets the interrupt-enable flip-flop, blocking RST 7.5, 6.5, 5.5 and INTR (TRAP is unaffected). CLI is the 8086 equivalent and does not exist in the 8085 instruction set.

questionText: The 8085 software instruction RST 5 transfers control to address:
explanation: RST n branches to 8 × n: 8 × 5 = 40 = 0028H. 002CH is the hardware RST 5.5 vector, and 0050H results from multiplying by 16 instead of 8.

questionText: An 8085 interrupt service routine that must allow later maskable interrupts to be accepted should normally end with:
explanation: The 8085 disables interrupts automatically when it accepts one, so the ISR must re-enable them with EI and then return with an ordinary RET. The 8085 has no IRET instruction.

questionText: An interrupt is described as maskable when:
options: It always has the highest priority in the system
Its service routine starts at a fixed address
It is generated by an instruction rather than by a pin
The program can disable it so that a request on it is ignored
explanation: Maskable means it can be turned off by software (EI/DI, SIM, STI/CLI). A fixed address describes a vectored interrupt and an instruction-generated one is a software interrupt.

questionText: Which 8085 interrupt has the lowest priority?
explanation: The priority order is TRAP > RST 7.5 > RST 6.5 > RST 5.5 > INTR, so INTR is served last when several requests are pending together.

questionText: In the 8086, the instruction STI:
options: Sets TF so that the processor single-steps
Enables the NMI input, which is disabled after reset
Sets IF so that requests on the INTR pin are recognised
Stores the interrupt vector of the current ISR in the vector table
explanation: STI sets the Interrupt Flag; IF affects only the maskable INTR input. NMI cannot be disabled, and TF is the Trap Flag used for single-stepping.

questionText: What does the 8085 instruction RIM do?
options: Writes the accumulator into the interrupt mask register
Loads HL with the vector address of the highest-priority pending interrupt
Returns from an interrupt service routine and re-enables interrupts
Loads the accumulator with the mask bits, pending-interrupt bits, the interrupt-enable status and the SID bit
explanation: RIM (Read Interrupt Mask) is the read side: D7 = SID, D6-D4 = pending 7.5/6.5/5.5, D3 = IE, D2-D0 = masks. Writing the masks is SIM.

questionText: How many interrupt input pins does the 8085 have?
explanation: The inputs are TRAP, RST 7.5, RST 6.5, RST 5.5 and INTR. INTA is an output (acknowledge), not an interrupt input.

questionText: When the 8085 accepts a request on INTR, which signal does it activate so that the external logic can supply an instruction?
explanation: INTA is the interrupt acknowledge output. The device or controller places an RST n or CALL opcode on the data bus while INTA is low. HLDA acknowledges a DMA HOLD request.

questionText: An 8085 program must unmask RST 7.5, mask RST 6.5 and RST 5.5, leave the RST 7.5 latch alone and not use SOD. The byte loaded into A before SIM is:
explanation: SIM bits: D3 MSE = 1 to make the masks valid, D2 M7.5 = 0, D1 M6.5 = 1, D0 M5.5 = 1, all others 0: 0000 1011 = 0BH. 03H forgets MSE, so the masks would not change.

questionText: An 8085 executes MVI A,0DH followed by SIM. Which of RST 7.5, RST 6.5 and RST 5.5 are now unmasked?
explanation: 0DH = 0000 1101: MSE (D3) = 1 so the masks load; M7.5 = 1, M6.5 = 0, M5.5 = 1. A 1 means masked, so only RST 6.5 is unmasked.

questionText: What is the effect of MVI A,1FH followed by SIM in an 8085?
options: RST 7.5, 6.5 and 5.5 are all masked and any pending RST 7.5 request is cleared
RST 7.5, 6.5 and 5.5 are all unmasked and any pending RST 7.5 request is cleared
RST 7.5, 6.5 and 5.5 are all masked and SOD is set to 1
Nothing changes, because the mask-set-enable bit is 0
explanation: 1FH = 0001 1111: D4 = 1 resets the RST 7.5 flip-flop, D3 MSE = 1 enables loading, and D2-D0 = 111 mask all three. D6 SDE = 0, so SOD is not affected.

questionText: An 8085 has RST 6.5 masked. The program executes MVI A,05H then SIM, intending to unmask RST 6.5. What happens?
options: RST 6.5 is unmasked and RST 7.5 and RST 5.5 are masked
All three RST inputs are unmasked
RST 6.5 is unmasked and SOD outputs 1
The masks do not change, because bit D3 (MSE) of 05H is 0
explanation: 05H = 0000 0101 has MSE = 0, so SIM ignores D2-D0 and the old masks remain. The correct byte would be 0DH (MSE = 1, M7.5 = 1, M6.5 = 0, M5.5 = 1).

questionText: In an 8085, RIM returns A = 62H. Which statement is correct?
options: RST 7.5 and RST 6.5 are pending and the interrupt system is disabled
RST 6.5 and RST 5.5 are pending and the interrupt system is enabled
RST 7.5 and RST 6.5 are pending and the interrupt system is enabled
Only RST 6.5 is pending and RST 5.5 is masked

questionText: Which byte, used with SIM, sends a logic 1 out of the 8085 SOD pin without changing the interrupt masks?
explanation: SOD = D7 = 1 and SDE = D6 = 1 (serial data enable), with MSE = D3 = 0 so the masks are untouched: 1100 0000 = C0H. 80H lacks SDE, 40H outputs 0, and C8H would also load the masks (all unmasked).

questionText: The one-byte opcode of the 8085 instruction RST 5 is:
explanation: RST n is encoded 11 NNN 111. For n = 5 (101): 1110 1111 = EFH. E7H is RST 4, 28H is the vector address rather than the opcode, and F5H is PUSH PSW.

questionText: When an 8085 acknowledges an INTR request, what must the external hardware place on the data bus?
options: An 8-bit type number that the CPU multiplies by 4
An RST n opcode or the three bytes of a CALL instruction
The 16-bit ISR address alone, with no opcode
Nothing, because the CPU then jumps to 0024H
explanation: INTR is non-vectored, so during INTA the CPU fetches an instruction from the data bus: a one-byte RST n or a CALL (with further INTA cycles for its two address bytes). The type-number method belongs to the 8086.

questionText: Which statement about the 8085 TRAP interrupt is correct?
options: It is both edge- and level-sensitive and cannot be disabled by DI or SIM
It can be masked by setting bit D3 of the SIM byte
It is non-vectored, so the device supplies the ISR address
It has the lowest priority of the five interrupt inputs
explanation: TRAP needs a rising edge followed by a sustained high level, which protects it against noise. It is non-maskable, vectored to 0024H and has the highest priority.

questionText: An interrupt is called vectored when:
options: The interrupting device must supply the ISR address or an opcode on the data bus
The processor itself knows the starting address of its service routine
It can be disabled by the program
It is triggered by an edge rather than a level
explanation: For a vectored interrupt the ISR address is fixed or looked up internally (8085 TRAP, RST 7.5/6.5/5.5; every 8086 type through the IVT). If the device must supply it, the interrupt is non-vectored, like 8085 INTR.

questionText: Which list gives the 8085 hardware interrupts in decreasing order of priority?
explanation: TRAP is highest, then RST 7.5, RST 6.5, RST 5.5, and INTR is lowest. Among the three RST inputs, the higher the RST number (and vector address), the higher the priority; TRAP is the exception, with the lowest vector (0024H) but the highest priority.

questionText: The RST 5.5 vector is 002CH and the next restart vector, RST 6, is at 0030H. How many bytes are available at 002CH before RST 6 begins?
explanation: 0030H − 002CH = 4 bytes. That is too small for a real ISR, so the location normally holds a 3-byte JMP to the routine elsewhere in memory.

questionText: An 8085 ISR modifies the accumulator and the flags. Which instruction at the start of the ISR preserves both?
explanation: PUSH PSW saves the accumulator and the flag register as one 16-bit pair. PUSH A does not exist, PUSHF is an 8086 instruction and SPHL copies HL into SP.

questionText: Interrupt latency is best defined as:
options: The time from the interrupt request until the first instruction of the ISR begins
The total time spent executing the ISR
The time from the end of the ISR until the main program resumes
The number of interrupts the CPU can service per second
explanation: Latency covers finishing the current instruction, saving the return state and fetching the vector. The ISR execution time is a separate figure, the service time.

questionText: Which statement about software interrupts is correct?
options: In the 8086 they are blocked by CLI
They occur exactly where the interrupt instruction is placed, so they are synchronous with the program
They need an interrupt acknowledge bus cycle to obtain the type
They are triggered by a signal from an external device
explanation: INT n (8086) and RST n (8085) are instructions, so they happen at a predictable point. The type is in the instruction, no INTA cycle is needed, and IF does not block them.

questionText: An 8085 ISR ends with EI immediately followed by RET, and another interrupt is already pending. Why is the ISR not interrupted before RET executes?
options: RET cannot be interrupted because it is a privileged instruction
The pending request is discarded when EI is executed
EI takes effect only after two further instructions have been executed
EI takes effect only after the instruction that follows it has been executed
explanation: The 8085 delays the enable by one instruction, so RET completes and the stack is unwound before the next interrupt is accepted. This keeps the stack from growing with every back-to-back request.

questionText: An 8085 ISR for RST 6.5 ends with RET but the programmer forgot EI. What is the result?
options: Later RST 7.5, 6.5, 5.5 and INTR requests are ignored, but TRAP is still accepted
All interrupts including TRAP are ignored
The next RST 6.5 request re-enables interrupts automatically
The RET fails and the program restarts at 0000H
explanation: Accepting an interrupt resets the interrupt-enable flip-flop. Without EI it stays reset, so every maskable request is ignored; only the non-maskable TRAP still gets through.

questionText: An 8085 executes HLT with interrupts enabled. How can it continue executing instructions?
options: Only through RESET, because interrupts are not sampled in the halt state
Only through TRAP, because maskable interrupts are disabled by HLT
Through an enabled interrupt (or TRAP), or through RESET
Only through a HOLD request, which restarts the program after the DMA transfer
explanation: In the halt state the 8085 still samples its interrupt pins; a valid interrupt pushes PC and enters the ISR, returning to the instruction after HLT. RESET also ends the halt. HOLD only lends the bus and the CPU stays halted.

questionText: A CPU polls a device every 100 µs and each poll takes 4 µs, whether or not the device is ready. What fraction of CPU time is spent polling?
explanation: Fraction = poll time / polling period = 4 µs / 100 µs = 0.04 = 4%. This time is lost even when the device has nothing to transfer.

questionText: Which of the following increases the worst-case interrupt latency of a system?
options: Using a vectored interrupt instead of a non-vectored one
Making the ISR of that interrupt shorter
Long sections of code that run with interrupts disabled
Giving the interrupt a higher priority
explanation: A request that arrives while interrupts are disabled must wait for the matching EI/STI, so disabled sections add directly to latency. The other three either reduce latency or do not affect it.

questionText: What is the effect of MVI A,18H followed by SIM in an 8085?
options: Any pending RST 7.5 request is cleared and RST 7.5, 6.5 and 5.5 are all unmasked
Only RST 7.5 is unmasked and its latch is cleared
All three are masked and the pending RST 7.5 request is cleared
SOD outputs 1 and the masks stay as they were
explanation: 18H = 0001 1000: D4 = 1 resets the RST 7.5 flip-flop, D3 MSE = 1 loads the masks, and D2-D0 = 000 unmask all three. D7 and D6 are 0, so SOD is unaffected.

questionText: The TRAP vector 0024H is sometimes called "RST 4.5". Using the rule vector = 8 × n, what value of n gives 0024H?
explanation: 0024H = 36 decimal, and 36 / 8 = 4.5. Reading 24 as decimal gives 3, and dividing 24H by 16 gives 2.25. The same reasoning gives 5.5, 6.5 and 7.5 for 002CH, 0034H and 003CH.

questionText: Which 8085 interrupts are controlled by the mask bits written with SIM?
explanation: SIM has mask bits only for the three RST inputs. INTR is controlled only by EI/DI, and TRAP cannot be masked at all.

questionText: An 8085 main loop executes RIM and gets A = 2BH. RST 6.5 is being requested but is not being serviced. Why?
options: A pending RST 7.5 request of higher priority is being served first
RST 6.5 is edge-triggered and the edge was missed
explanation: 2BH = 0010 1011: D5 I6.5 = 1 (pending), D3 IE = 1 (enabled), D6 I7.5 = 0, and D1 M6.5 = 1, so the request is masked. RST 6.5 is level-triggered.

questionText: In an 8085, RST 7.5 and RST 5.5 are both unmasked but interrupts are disabled with DI. A 1 µs pulse arrives on each pin, after which both pins stay low. The program later executes EI. Which interrupt is serviced?
options: Both, RST 7.5 first and then RST 5.5
Neither, because both requests arrived while interrupts were disabled
explanation: The rising edge on RST 7.5 sets its internal flip-flop, which holds the request until it is served. RST 5.5 is level-sensitive and not latched, so its request vanished when the pin went low.

questionText: A keyboard is pressed 10 times per second. Polling checks it 500 times per second at 20 µs per check. With interrupts, each key press costs 50 µs (entry, service and return). How many times more CPU time does polling use than the interrupt method?
explanation: Polling: 500 × 20 µs = 10000 µs per second. Interrupts: 10 × 50 µs = 500 µs per second. Ratio = 10000 / 500 = 20.

questionText: An 8085 runs at a 3 MHz clock. A RST 7.5 request arrives just as an 18 T-state CALL instruction begins, and the CPU then needs 12 T-states to save PC and branch to 003CH. What is the worst-case latency until the vector location is fetched?
explanation: T = 1 / 3 MHz = 0.333 µs. Latency = (18 + 12) T-states × 0.333 µs = 30 / 3 = 10 µs. Counting only the CALL gives 6 µs and only the response 4 µs.

questionText: An 8085 executes MVI A,0EH, SIM, EI. Then a rising edge arrives on RST 7.5 while RST 6.5 and RST 5.5 are both held high. Which interrupt is serviced first, and at which vector?
options: None, because all three are masked
explanation: 0EH = 0000 1110: MSE = 1, M7.5 = 1, M6.5 = 1, M5.5 = 0. RST 7.5 and RST 6.5 are masked despite their higher priority, so RST 5.5 is the only one accepted, at 002CH.

questionText: During INTA, the interrupting device places DFH on the 8085 data bus. Where does the processor transfer control?
explanation: DFH = 11 011 111, the RST n pattern 11 NNN 111 with NNN = 011, so it is RST 3. The vector is 8 × 3 = 24 = 0018H. 0030H results from multiplying by 16.

questionText: An 8085 has SP = 2000H. The 3-byte instruction LXI H,3000H occupies 2050H-2052H, and a RST 6.5 request is accepted at its end. After the return address is pushed, what do locations 1FFFH and 1FFEH contain?
explanation: The return address is the next instruction, 2050H + 3 = 2053H. A push decrements SP and stores the high byte first: 20H goes to 1FFFH and 53H to 1FFEH, leaving SP = 1FFEH.

questionText: An 8085 program runs RIM, ANI x, CPI x and JZ to jump only when RST 7.5 is pending AND the interrupt system is enabled. What is x?
explanation: In the RIM byte, D6 = RST 7.5 pending and D3 = IE, so x = 0100 1000 = 48H. 44H picks D2 (the RST 7.5 mask) instead of IE, and 84H picks the SID bit.

questionText: With a single SIM, an 8085 must mask RST 7.5 and RST 5.5, unmask RST 6.5, clear the RST 7.5 latch and output 0 on SOD. The byte in A is:
explanation: SOD = 0, SDE = 1, D5 = 0, R7.5 = 1, MSE = 1, M7.5 = 1, M6.5 = 0, M5.5 = 1: 0101 1101 = 5DH. 1DH leaves SDE = 0 so SOD is not driven, DDH outputs 1, and 5AH inverts the mask bits.

questionText: The vector address of the 8085 interrupt RST 6.5 is:
explanation: The vectored 8085 interrupts are 8 bytes apart: TRAP 0024H, RST 5.5 002CH, RST 6.5 0034H and RST 7.5 003CH. RST 6.5 lies midway between RST 6 (0030H) and RST 7 (0038H), that is 6.5 × 8 = 52 = 0034H.

questionText: What is the output?
explanation: 5 and 2 are both ints, so 5/2 performs integer division = 2. Use 5.0/2 for 2.5.

questionText: On a typical 32/64-bit compiler, sizeof(char) is:
explanation: The C standard guarantees sizeof(char) == 1 byte, always.

questionText: What is the value of b?
explanation: Post-increment uses the value first: b gets 5, then y becomes 6.

questionText: The result of 12 % 5 is:
explanation: The modulus operator gives the integer remainder: 12 = 2×5 + 2.

questionText: Which expression is TRUE (non-zero)?
A switch statement in C/C++ can switch on which type?
explanation: switch requires an integral type (int, char, enum). Floating-point and strings are not allowed.

questionText: What prints if the break statements are omitted from matching cases below case 1?
explanation: Without break, control falls through every following case, printing one two three.

questionText: How many times does this loop body execute?
explanation: do-while checks the condition AFTER the body, so it always runs at least once even though 10 < 5 is false.

questionText: What is the output?
explanation: continue skips the print when i == 3, so 3 is missing but the loop continues to 4.

questionText: What does this function return for factorial(4)?
explanation: 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24; the base case n <= 1 stops the recursion.

questionText: In C, arguments are passed to functions by default:
explanation: C passes copies of arguments. To let a function modify the caller's variable you must pass its address (a pointer).

questionText: What is x after calling swap(x, y)?
explanation: swap receives copies (pass by value); the originals are untouched, so x is still 10.

questionText: Valid indices of int arr[10] run from:
explanation: C arrays are zero-based: arr[0] through arr[9]. arr[10] is out of bounds (undefined behaviour).

questionText: strlen("EXAM") and sizeof("EXAM") are respectively:
explanation: strlen counts characters before '\0' (4); sizeof includes the terminator (5).

questionText: What is the output?
explanation: *p = 10 writes through the pointer into x, so printing x gives 10.

questionText: If int *q points to a[0], what does *(q + 2) evaluate to?
explanation: Pointer arithmetic moves in element units: q + 2 points to a[2] = 30, and * dereferences it.

questionText: Memory allocated with new[] must be released with:
explanation: Array new pairs with delete[]. Mismatching allocation/deallocation families is undefined behaviour.

questionText: A pointer that references memory which has already been freed is called a:
explanation: Dangling pointers point at dead memory; dereferencing them is undefined behaviour.

questionText: Given struct Point *ptr, the correct way to access member x is:
explanation: Pointers use the arrow operator: ptr->x, equivalent to (*ptr).x. The dot alone works only on objects.

questionText: If a union contains an int (4 bytes) and a double (8 bytes), sizeof the union is:
explanation: Union members share storage; its size equals the largest member — 8 bytes.

questionText: The default access specifier for members of a C++ class is:
explanation: Members of a class are private by default, while members of a struct are public by default. The same default applies to base classes (class D : B means private inheritance, struct D : B public inheritance); these defaults are the only difference between class and struct.

questionText: Bundling data with the methods that operate on it, while hiding internals, is called:
explanation: Encapsulation is data + methods in one unit with restricted access — enforced via private/protected specifiers.

questionText: Which statement invokes the copy constructor?
explanation: Initialization from an existing object calls the copy constructor. b = a on an EXISTING object is the assignment operator instead.

questionText: A destructor in C++:
options: Has no parameters and cannot be overloaded
explanation: A class has exactly one destructor: ~Name(), no parameters, no return type.

questionText: What is the output?
explanation: show() is virtual, so the call through a Base pointer dispatches at runtime to Derived::show().

questionText: A class containing a pure virtual function is called:
explanation: A pure virtual function (= 0) makes the class abstract: it cannot be instantiated, and a derived class must override the function to become instantiable (otherwise it is abstract too).
Both operands are int, so 17 / 5 = 3.4 is truncated to 3. The remainder is 17 % 5 = 17 - 3 × 5 = 2.

C99 and C11 truncate the quotient toward zero (C89 left this implementation-defined), so -17 / 5 = -3.4 -> -3 (not -4). The remainder follows a % b = a - (a / b) × b: -17 - (-3 × 5) = -2 and 17 - (-3 × -5) = 2, so it takes the sign of the dividend.

questionText: Which of the following expressions causes a compile error in C?
explanation: The % operator requires integer operands; a floating-point remainder needs fmod() from <math.h>. The other three are legal and give 1, -1 and 3.5.
a / b * b groups left to right in int arithmetic: 9 / 4 = 2, then 2 × 4 = 8. The cast binds tighter than /, so (double)a / b = 9.0 / 4 = 2.25. r = 8 + 2.25 = 10.25.
* / % share one precedence level and group left to right: n % 10 = 9, n / 10 % 10 = 472 % 10 = 2 and n / 100 % 10 = 47 % 10 = 7. s = 9 + 2 + 7 = 18.
Relational, equality and logical operators produce an int: 1 for true and 0 for false. 5 > 3 is 1, 5 == 3 is 0 and !(5 < 3) is !0 = 1.
== groups left to right and yields 0 or 1: a == b == c is (a == b) == c = 1 == 5 = 0, while a == b == 1 is (5 == 5) == 1 = 1 == 1 = 1. C never reads a chain of comparisons the mathematical way.
i++ > 0 compares the old value 0, so it is false, and i becomes 1. Because the left side of || is false, the right side must be evaluated: j becomes 6 and 6 > 5 is true, so r = 1.

&& binds tighter than ||, so r = (a-- && b++) || ++c. a-- yields 1 (a becomes 0), so b++ is evaluated: it yields 0 (b becomes 1) and the && is false. The || therefore evaluates ++c, giving c = 6 (true), so r = 1.
&& has higher precedence, so the expression is x || (++y && ++y). x = 4 is true, so || stops at once: neither ++y runs, y stays 0, and z = 1 because logical operators produce 1, not the value 4.

questionText: In C, what does a relational or logical expression such as a < b or a && b evaluate to?
options: A bool whose value is true or false
An int that may be any non-zero value when true
An int whose value is 1 (true) or 0 (false)
explanation: C operators such as <, ==, && and ! give an int that is exactly 1 or 0. Any non-zero value counts as true when it is tested, but these operators always produce 1 for true.
12 = 1100 and 10 = 1010 in binary. AND keeps the common 1s: 1000 = 8; OR keeps every 1: 1110 = 14; XOR keeps the bits that differ: 0110 = 6.
x << n multiplies by 2^n: 3 × 2^4 = 48. x >> n divides a non-negative value by 2^n and drops the remainder: 100 / 8 = 12.5 -> 12.
In two's complement ~x = -x - 1, so ~12 = -12 - 1 = -13 and ~(-12) = 12 - 1 = 11. Flipping only the four bits of 1100 to get 0011 = 3 forgets that an int has 32 bits.
== has higher precedence than &, so the condition is x & (2 == 2) = 6 & 1 = 110 & 001 = 0, which is false. Writing (x & 2) == 2 would print yes.
Additive operators bind tighter than shifts, so the expression is 1 << (2 + 3) = 1 << 5 = 32, not (1 << 2) + 3 = 7.
0x5A = 0101 1010. f |= 1 sets bit 0: 0101 1011 (0x5B). f &= ~(1u << 4) clears bit 4: 0100 1011 (0x4B). f ^= 1u << 7 flips bit 7 from 0 to 1: 1100 1011 = 0xCB, printed by %X as CB.
Step by step: 10 + 5 = 15, 15 × 2 = 30, 30 - 4 = 26, and 26 / 3 = 8 because both operands are int.
A compound assignment evaluates its whole right side first: a *= 2 + 3 means a = a * (2 + 3) = 4 × 5 = 20, not a * 2 + 3 = 11.
x = 5 is an assignment, not a comparison: it stores 5 in x and the value of the expression, 5, is non-zero (true), so the if branch prints A 5.

questionText: Given int x = 1, y = 2; which of the following statements causes a compile error?
explanation: The left operand of an assignment must be a modifiable lvalue such as a variable. x + 1 is a computed value with no storage, so it cannot be assigned to. The others are a chained assignment, a chained compound assignment and a comma expression.
Assignment operators group right to left: a += (b *= (c -= 1)). First c = 4 - 1 = 3, then b = 3 × 3 = 9, then a = 2 + 9 = 11.
Post-decrement hands the old value 8 to the expression, so n = 8 - 3 = 5; afterwards m is 7.
++i increments first and yields 4; j-- yields the old value 3 and then j becomes 2. k = 4 × 3 = 12.
Each test uses the old i and then increments it. The tests 0, 1, 2 and 3 < 4 succeed and add the new values 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. The failing test 4 < 4 still increments i, so i ends at 5.
The compiler always takes the longest possible token (maximal munch), so x+++y is read as (x++) + y: z = 5 + 2 = 7, x then becomes 6 and y is unchanged.

questionText: When i++; and ++i; are each used as a complete statement on its own, how do they differ?
options: They have the same effect: each adds 1 to i
i++; leaves i unchanged and only ++i; increments it
++i; is not allowed as a stand-alone statement
They differ only when i is a float
explanation: The difference between pre- and post-increment is only in the value the expression yields. When that value is not used, both simply add 1 to i.

options: The behaviour is undefined, because i is modified more than once without sequencing
explanation: ++i, i++ and the assignment all modify i with no sequence point between them, so the behaviour is undefined and different compilers may print different values. Only output questions that modify each variable once per expression have a defined answer.
7 % 2 is 1, which is non-zero (true), so the conditional operator selects its second operand, the string "odd".
?: groups right to left, so the chain works like an else-if ladder: 65 >= 80 is false, 65 >= 60 is true, so g = 'B' and the remaining tests are never evaluated.
3 > 7 is false, so only the third operand b-- is evaluated: c receives the old value 7 and b becomes 6. The a++ in the unchosen branch never runs, so a stays 3.
?: has lower precedence than +, so y = x > 3 ? 10 : (20 + 1) = 10. In z the parentheses finish the conditional first, giving 10 + 1 = 11.
The comma operator evaluates left to right and yields its last operand: a += 3 makes a = 5, a * 2 is computed and thrown away, and a - 1 = 4 is stored in b.

Assignment binds more tightly than the comma operator, so x = a++, b + a; means (x = a++), (b + a): x gets 2, a becomes 3 and the value of b + a is thrown away. In y = (a++, b + a) the parentheses make the whole comma expression the value assigned; a becomes 4 before b + a is evaluated, so y = 5 + 4 = 9.
In c + 1 the char is promoted to int, so the size is 4. c = 'B' has the type of c (char, size 1), but sizeof never evaluates its operand, so the assignment never happens and c is still 'A'.

questionText: Which statement about sizeof in C is correct?
options: It is a library function declared in <stdlib.h>
It is a preprocessor directive like #define
It returns the number of elements of any array passed to a function
It is a unary operator, normally worked out at compile time, that gives a size in bytes
explanation: sizeof is a keyword operator that the compiler evaluates from the type of its operand (only variable-length arrays need run time), and its result has type size_t. Parentheses are required only around a type name, as in sizeof(int).

options: Compile error: signed and unsigned cannot be compared
explanation: When an int meets an unsigned int, the int is converted to unsigned: -5 becomes 2^32 - 5 = 4,294,967,291, which is not less than 3, so the else branch runs.
Integer promotion converts both char operands to int before the addition, so 100 + 100 = 200 is computed in int and stored in the int s without any overflow.
Converting a floating value to int discards the fraction (truncation toward zero, not rounding down): (int)-3.7 = -3, (int)3.7 = 3 and (int)-0.5 = 0, so the second value is 3 + 0 = 3.
In u + i the int -3 is converted to unsigned, and the sum is taken modulo 2^32: 2 - 3 = -1 -> 4,294,967,295. That unsigned value is greater than 5, so the comparison gives 1.

questionText: Given the declarations int i; float f; double d;, what is the type of the expression i * f + d?
explanation: By the usual arithmetic conversions, i * f is computed as float, and float + double is computed as double, so the whole expression has type double.
* / % have equal precedence and group left to right: 3 * 4 = 12, 12 % 5 = 2 and 6 / 4 = 1 in integer division. Then 2 + 2 - 1 = 3.
From high to low the levels used are +, <<, &, |. So 1 + 2 = 3, 3 << 1 = 6, 6 & 7 = 6, and finally 8 | 6 = 1000 | 0110 = 1110 = 14. Reading strictly left to right would give 6.

questionText: Which group of C operators associates from right to left?
options: Unary operators, the conditional operator ?: and the assignment operators
The logical operators && and || and the comma operator
explanation: Unary operators (such as !, ~, prefix ++ and casts), ?: and every assignment operator group right to left, so a = b = c assigns c to b first. Almost all binary operators, including the comma, group left to right.

questionText: Which of the following operators has the LOWEST precedence in C?
explanation: The comma operator is at the very bottom of the precedence table, below the assignment operators, which are below ?:, which in turn is below ||.

questionText:
Assume the ASCII character set. What is the output of the following statement?
printf("%d %c %x", 'A', 66, 255);
explanation: In C a character constant such as 'A' has type int, so %d prints its code 65. %c prints the character whose code is 66 (B), and %x prints 255 in lowercase hexadecimal, ff.

questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("%.3f", 2.0 / 3);
explanation: 2.0 / 3 is a double division giving 0.666666...; %.3f keeps three decimals and rounds using the next digit (6), so 0.667 is printed.

questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("[%6s][%-6s]", "Kath", "Kath");
explanation: A width of 6 for a 4-letter string adds 2 spaces: on the left by default (right-justified), and on the right when the - flag is given (left-justified).

questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("%e", 1234.5678);
explanation: %e writes one digit before the point, 6 digits after it (the default precision, rounded) and an exponent of at least two digits: 1234.5678 = 1.2345678 x 10^3, printed as 1.234568e+03.
'A' + 2 is 67, the code of C. %c prints C, %d prints the code 67, and c + 32 = 99 printed with %c is the lowercase letter c, because ASCII lowercase letters are 32 above the uppercase ones.

options: AB on the first line and C on the second line
A on the first line and BC on the second line
A, B and C on three separate lines
explanation: printf writes exactly its text, while puts writes its string followed by a newline. So A and B share the first line, the newline comes after B, and C starts the second line.
%s skips leading whitespace and then stops at the first whitespace character, so only Ram is stored and Bahadur stays in the input buffer. A whole line needs fgets or a %[^\n] scanset.

questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("%%d = %d", 5);
explanation: %% is the conversion that prints one percent sign, so %%d prints the two characters %d. The following %d is a real conversion and prints the argument 5.

questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("[%+d|% d|% d]", 25, 25, -25);
explanation: The + flag always prints a sign (+25). The space flag puts a blank where the plus sign would go for a non-negative value ( 25), while a negative value simply shows its minus sign (-25).

questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("%#o %#x %#X", 16, 31, 31);
explanation: The # flag adds the base prefix: a leading 0 for octal (16 is 20 in octal, printed 020) and 0x or 0X for hexadecimal (31 is 1f). %X makes both the digits and the X uppercase.

questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("[%.4d|%6.3d]", 42, 7);
explanation: For integer conversions the precision is the minimum number of digits, filled with leading zeros: %.4d gives 0042. In %6.3d the value first becomes 007 and is then right-justified with spaces in a field of 6.

questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("[%*.*f]", 9, 3, 3.14159);
explanation: Each * takes its value from the argument list, so the width is 9 and the precision 3. 3.14159 rounded to 3 decimals is 3.142 (5 characters), right-justified in 9 columns with 4 leading spaces.

questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("[%.2s|%5.3s]", "Nepal", "Nepal");
explanation: For %s the precision is the maximum number of characters printed: %.2s gives Ne. %5.3s takes the first 3 characters, Nep, and right-justifies them in a width of 5 by adding 2 spaces.
Converting -1 to a 32-bit unsigned int gives 2^32 - 1 = 4294967295, with all 32 bits set. %u prints it in decimal and %x prints the 8 hexadecimal digits ffffffff.
printf returns the number of characters it wrote. The opening bracket, the 5-column field '   42' and the closing bracket make 1 + 5 + 1 = 7 characters, so n = 7.

questionText:
What happens when the following statement is executed?
printf("%d", 10, 20);
options: It prints 10; the extra argument is evaluated but ignored
Compile error: too many arguments to printf
explanation: The C standard says that when the format is used up, any remaining arguments are evaluated but otherwise ignored. A compiler may warn, but the program compiles and prints 10.

questionText:
Assume the ASCII character set. What is the output of the following statement?
printf("%d", putchar('A') + 1);
explanation: The argument putchar('A') + 1 is evaluated before printf runs: putchar prints A and returns the character written as an int, 65. Adding 1 gives 66, which printf then prints after the A.
getchar returns one character per call until the newline ends the loop. The 8 characters typed before Enter include 2 spaces, which are not counted, so n = 8 - 2 = 6.
The first %d stores 7. The blank skips the space, then the second %d meets x, which cannot start a number, so scanf stops, leaves b unchanged (2) and returns 1, the number of items stored.
The * in %*d suppresses assignment, so 20 is read and thrown away. x gets 10 and y gets 30, and scanf returns 2 because a suppressed conversion is not counted.
%d reads 5 and stops at the space. %c does not skip whitespace, so a receives that space. The blank before the second %c skips any whitespace (here none), so b gets x and y is left unread.
sprintf formats into buf instead of the screen and returns the number of characters stored, not counting the terminating '\0'. The string 12+30=42 has 8 characters, so n = 8.
fgets keeps the newline when it fits in the buffer, so s holds exam followed by '\n' and '\0'. strlen counts the 4 letters plus the newline, giving 5.

questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("[%-06d|%06.2d|%+06d]", 42, 42, 42);
explanation: With the - flag the 0 flag is ignored, so %-06d left-justifies with spaces. For integer conversions a precision also cancels the 0 flag, so %06.2d pads 42 with spaces. %+06d prints the sign first and fills zeros after it: +00042.

questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("%g|%g|%g", 0.00012, 123456.0, 1234567.0);
explanation: %g keeps 6 significant digits and uses e-style only when the decimal exponent X is below -4 or at least 6. 0.00012 (X = -4) and 123456 (X = 5) are printed in fixed style with trailing zeros removed; 1234567 has X = 6, so it becomes 1.23457e+06.

questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("%d", printf("%d", printf("ABC")));
explanation: The innermost printf runs first, printing ABC and returning 3. The middle printf prints 3 and returns 1 (it wrote one character). The outer printf prints that 1, so the screen shows ABC31.

A field width in scanf limits how many characters a conversion may read: %2d takes 12 and %3d takes 345. The last %d has no width, so it reads the remaining digits 67 and stops at the space, leaving 89 in the buffer.
%i reads an integer the way a C constant is written: a leading 0 means octal (010 = 8) and 0x means hexadecimal (0x1A = 26). %d always reads decimal, so the third 010 is stored as 10.

The scanset %9[^,] reads up to 9 non-comma characters, giving pen, and each literal comma in the format matches a comma in the string. qty = 12 and price = 7.5, so sscanf returns 3 and 12 x 7.5 = 90.00 is printed.

snprintf never writes more than sizeof s = 6 bytes, so s receives 5 characters, NEC-2, plus '\0'. It returns the length the complete text would have had, NEC-2024 = 8 characters, which lets the caller detect truncation.

fgets(a, 5, stdin) stores at most 5 - 1 = 4 characters, Kath, and leaves the rest of the line in the buffer. The second call continues from there and stores the next 4, mand; the u and the newline are still unread.

questionText: Why is the & operator needed in scanf("%d", &n)?
options: & converts the typed characters into an integer
& tells scanf to skip leading whitespace
& is needed only when n has not been initialised
scanf needs the address of n so that it can store the converted value in n
explanation: C passes arguments by value, so without & scanf would receive only a copy of n's value. Passing &n gives scanf the location of n, through which it writes the number it read.

questionText: Which input function was removed from the C11 standard because it cannot limit the number of characters it stores and so can overflow the array?
explanation: gets(s) keeps storing characters until a newline no matter how large s is, which causes buffer overflows. It was deprecated in C99 and removed in C11; fgets(s, n, stdin) is the bounded replacement.

questionText: Which printf conversion specifier is intended for printing the value of a pointer (an address)?
explanation: %p prints a void * value in an implementation-defined form, usually hexadecimal. Passing a pointer to %x or %u is a type mismatch (undefined behaviour) that visibly breaks where pointers are wider than int, and %a is for hexadecimal floating-point numbers.

questionText: Which format specifier prints an unsigned int in hexadecimal using the uppercase letters A to F?
explanation: %x and %X both print unsigned hexadecimal: %x uses a-f and %X uses A-F, so 255 prints as ff and FF respectively. %o prints octal, and there is no %H conversion.

questionText: How does sprintf() differ from printf()?
options: sprintf writes the formatted text to the standard error stream
sprintf writes the formatted text into a character array instead of to stdout
sprintf ignores format specifiers and copies the text as it is
sprintf automatically adds a newline after the text
explanation: sprintf(buf, format, ...) follows the same format rules as printf but stores the result, with a terminating '\0', in buf and returns the number of characters stored. Output to stderr is done with fprintf(stderr, ...).

questionText: Which of the following output functions automatically writes a newline after the string it prints?
explanation: puts(s) writes s followed by '\n'. fputs(s, stdout) and printf("%s", s) write exactly the string, and putchar writes a single character.

questionText: Which call is equivalent to getchar()?
explanation: getchar() is defined to behave like getc(stdin): it reads the next character from the standard input stream and returns it as an int, or EOF when no input is left.

questionText: Given float f; double d; which statement about reading and printing these variables is correct?
options: Both scanf and printf accept %f for f and d alike, because float is promoted to double in both
printf needs %lf for d; printing d with %f shows only its float part
scanf needs %f for f and %lf for d, but printf("%f", ...) prints either one correctly
scanf needs %lf for f and %f for d
explanation: A float passed to printf is promoted to double, so printf's %f always receives a double (%lf is accepted as a synonym). scanf receives pointers, which are not promoted, so it must be told whether it is storing a float (%f) or a double (%lf).

questionText: Why should the value returned by getchar() be stored in an int variable rather than a char?
options: getchar must be able to return EOF as well as every possible character value, and a char cannot represent all of these distinct results
Characters always occupy 4 bytes in C, so a char is too small for any character
putchar cannot print a value stored in a char variable
Assigning the result of getchar to a char is a compile error in C
explanation: getchar returns an unsigned char value converted to int (0 to 255 with 8-bit chars) or EOF, which is negative. Stored in a char, EOF is either never matched (unsigned char) or confused with the byte 0xFF (signed char), which breaks loops such as while ((c = getchar()) != EOF).

questionText:
char line[80];
What does scanf("%79[^\n]", line); do?
options: It reads one word, stopping at the first space or newline
It reads the whole line and stores the newline at the end of line
It skips every character up to the newline and stores nothing
It reads up to 79 characters, including spaces, and stops before the newline, which stays in the input buffer
explanation: [^\n] is a scanset that accepts every character except a newline, so spaces are stored too, and 79 limits the count so line cannot overflow. Unlike fgets, this conversion does not consume the newline; it remains in the buffer.

questionText: A program shows progress with printf("Working...") (no newline) and reports errors with fprintf(stderr, ...). Why can an error message appear on a terminal before "Working..." does?
options: stdout is buffered, so text without a newline can wait in the buffer, while stderr is not buffered and is written at once
stderr has a higher priority, so the operating system interrupts stdout to print it
printf output without \n is discarded and never appears
fprintf is faster because it does not parse its format string
explanation: On a terminal stdout is line-buffered, so "Working..." stays in the buffer until a newline, fflush(stdout) or normal program exit. stderr is never fully buffered (in practice it is unbuffered), so an error message is written immediately and can overtake it.

questionText:
long long big = 9000000000LL;
In printf("%lld", big), what does the ll in the conversion specification indicate?
options: That the value is left-justified in its field
That the value is printed with a minimum width of two columns
That the corresponding argument has type long long int
That the value is printed in scientific (long) notation
explanation: ll is a length modifier: it tells printf, and likewise scanf, that the argument is a long long int (unsigned long long with %llu). Other length modifiers are h for short, l for long and L for long double (%Lf); left-justification is the - flag and width is a plain number.

questionText: Which statement about field width and precision in printf is correct?
options: A width smaller than the number of digits truncates the number to that many digits
A width smaller than the output never truncates it, but a precision on %s can cut a string short
In %.3d the precision keeps only the last 3 digits of the number
A field width has no effect on %s conversions
explanation: The width is only a minimum, so printf("%2d", 12345) still prints 12345. For %s the precision is a maximum, so %.3s prints at most 3 characters, while for %d it is a minimum digit count filled with zeros.

questionText: Which statement about EOF is correct?
options: EOF is the character '\0' stored at the end of every file
EOF is defined as 0 so that loops such as while (c) stop at the end of input
EOF is a negative int constant defined in stdio.h, returned by input functions at end of input or on a read error
EOF is a special byte written to disk after the last character of every text file
explanation: EOF is a macro for a negative integer (commonly -1) that getchar, getc, scanf and similar functions return when no more input is available or an error occurs. It is not a character stored in the file; '\0' is the string terminator.

questionText: Which statement about scanf format strings is NOT correct?
options: A literal character in the format, such as the / in "%d/%d", may be missing from the input without affecting the later conversions
A whitespace character in the format matches any amount of whitespace in the input, including none
%c does not skip leading whitespace, unlike %d, %f and %s
%*d reads an integer but neither stores it nor counts it in the return value
explanation: Ordinary characters in the format must match the input exactly; if the / is missing, scanf stops there, the remaining conversions are not performed and the return value shows how many succeeded. The other three statements are standard scanf rules.

questionText:
What is the output of the following statement?
printf("[%-5d|%05.1f]", 42, 3.14159);
explanation: %-5d left-justifies 42 in a 5-column field, giving '42   '. %05.1f rounds to one decimal (3.1) and zero-pads to a width of 5, giving '003.1'.

options: '\n' (the newline left in the input buffer)
explanation: scanf("%d") consumes the digits 25 but leaves the Enter key's newline in the buffer; getchar() then returns that '\n' immediately instead of waiting for new input.

The body prints n and then adds 2, so it prints 0, 2 and 4. After printing 4, n becomes 6 and the test 6 < 5 is false, so the loop stops.

An else pairs with the nearest unmatched if, here if (b > 0), whatever the indentation suggests. Since a > 0 is false, the whole inner if-else is skipped and only Z is printed.
x = 0 is an assignment, not a comparison: it stores 0 in x and the condition has the value 0 (false). So the else branch runs, and then x, which is now 0, is printed.

options: Compile error: an if cannot end with a semicolon
explanation: The semicolon right after if (x > 5) is an empty statement that forms the whole body of the if. The printf("big ") after it is an ordinary statement, so it always runs, and then 3 is printed.
No case matches 5, so control goes to default wherever it is written. There is no break after default, so execution falls through into case 2, prints 2 and then breaks, giving D2.
i goes 10 -> 7 -> 4 -> 1 -> -2, one step per iteration. After the 4th iteration i = -2 fails the test i > 0, so c = 4 and i = -2.
The while loop tests first: 5 < 5 is false, so its body never runs and a stays 5. The do-while runs its body once before testing, so b becomes 6, and then 6 < 5 ends it.
The semicolon after the for header makes an empty loop body, so the loop only counts i up to 6. The indented s += i is outside the loop and runs once with i = 6, giving s = 6.
i takes the values 1, 3, 9, 27 and 81; the next value 243 fails i <= 100. That is 5 iterations, i.e. floor(log3 100) + 1 = 4 + 1.
For i = 1 to 5 the inner loop runs 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 times, so c = 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 5 x 6 / 2 = 15.
i is incremented first, so the rest of the body sees i = 1 to 5. For odd i, i % 2 is 1 and continue jumps back to the test, skipping printf, so only the even values 2 and 4 are printed.
The comma operator lets the header initialise and update two variables. The pairs (i, j) = (0, 10), (2, 8) and (4, 6) each give one iteration; then (6, 4) fails i < j, so c = 3, i = 6 and j = 4.
