explanation: Sharing the bits keeps the words short, but a branch word issues no control signals, so routines take extra cycles. Two explicit address fields in every word are the drawback of a different technique.

questionText: A datapath has 64 control signals. A horizontal format uses a 64-bit control field. A vertical format activates exactly one signal per microinstruction, using a code that must also allow 'no operation'. For a routine of 10 steps, each activating 3 signals at once, how many control-field bits does each format use (address fields ignored)?
explanation: Horizontal: 10 words × 64 bits = 640. Vertical: 65 codes need ceil(log2 65) = 7 bits and each step needs 3 words, so 30 × 7 = 210 bits; 6-bit codes would give 180, and one word per step 70.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of microprogrammed control over hardwired control?
options: Easier modification or extension of the instruction set
A systematic design that simplifies complex control units
Higher operating speed with the same technology
Design errors can be corrected by changing the microcode
explanation: Microprogrammed control is slower, because every step needs a control-memory read. Its benefits are flexibility, a systematic design and easy correction.

questionText: A vertical microinstruction has a single micro-operation field that encodes 100 distinct micro-operations plus a no-operation code. How many bits does this field need?
explanation: 101 codes are needed, and 2^6 = 64 < 101 ≤ 128 = 2^7, so 7 bits are required. One bit per micro-operation (100 bits) would be the horizontal choice.

questionText: Why do most RISC processors use hardwired control?
options: They have too many instructions to fit into a control memory
Their simple, fixed-format instructions complete in about one clock, and reading a control memory for each step would lengthen that clock
Hardwired control is easier to modify when instructions are added
Microprogrammed control cannot be combined with any form of pipelining
explanation: RISC designs aim at about one instruction per cycle with a short cycle time, and hardwired decoding avoids the control-memory access delay. Large, irregular instruction sets are where microprogramming pays off.

questionText: A microinstruction has 40 control bits, a 6-bit condition-select field and two explicit next-address fields (one used when the condition is true, the other when it is false) for a 4K-word control memory. How long is the microinstruction?
explanation: Each address field needs log2 4096 = 12 bits, so the word is 40 + 6 + 2 × 12 = 70 bits. With a single address field it would be 58 bits.

questionText: Mano's EXCHANGE routine contains the microinstruction ACTDR, DRTAC U JMP NEXT. Why does it swap AC and DR correctly?
options: F1 executes before F2, so DR is copied into AC first and AC into DR afterwards
The sequencer inserts a hidden temporary register between F1 and F2
Only DRTAC executes; ACTDR is ignored because both use the bus
Both transfers are triggered by the same clock edge, so each register receives the other's old contents
explanation: DRTAC (F1 = 100) and ACTDR (F2 = 101) are in different fields and take effect together at the end of the clock period, when both registers still hold their old values. If they ran one after the other, both registers would end up with the same value.

questionText: Which pair of micro-operations cannot be specified together in one of Mano's 20-bit microinstructions because they are coded in the same field?
explanation: READ (100) and ACTDR (101) are both F2 codes, and a field holds only one code. INCPC is in F3 while PCTAR and DRTAR are in F1, so the other pairs are legal; READ, INCPC is in fact the second word of the fetch routine.

questionText: A control memory of 16 KiB (1 KiB = 1024 bytes) holds 64-bit microinstructions. How many microinstructions does it hold, and how wide must CAR be?
explanation: 16 KiB = 16 × 1024 × 8 = 131,072 bits, and 131,072 / 64 = 2048 words, so CAR needs log2 2048 = 11 bits. Dividing the byte count by 64 without converting to bits gives 256.

questionText: Mano's mapping 0 xxxx 00 gives each opcode four consecutive control words. What is done if a new instruction's routine needs six microinstructions?
options: The routine starts at its mapped address and continues, through a jump, in free words elsewhere in control memory
The instruction cannot be implemented in this control unit
The mapping hardware automatically allocates eight words to that opcode
The extra microinstructions are placed in main memory
explanation: The first words sit at the mapped address, and a JMP in the last of them transfers to spare control words (for example above the fetch and INDRCT words), where the routine is completed and returns to FETCH.

questionText: An ADD instruction with I = 0 reaches control address 0, where Mano's microinstruction is NOP I CALL INDRCT. What does the sequencer do?
explanation: With the condition false, CALL behaves like a branch not taken: CAR is simply incremented and the SBR load signal stays inactive. Only when I = 1 does it store 1 in SBR and jump to 67.

questionText: What does the mapping process in a microprogrammed control unit do?
options: Converts a virtual address into a physical main-memory address
Converts the opcode of a machine instruction into the starting address of its routine in control memory
Assigns each micro-operation to a field of the microinstruction
Copies the control memory into a cache at start-up
explanation: After fetch, the opcode bits are transformed, by a fixed bit arrangement or a mapping ROM, into a control-memory address, so the sequencer can jump to that instruction's microroutine.

questionText: In Mano's 128-word control memory the fetch routine is placed at address 64. Why?
options: Address 64 is the reset address of every control ROM
Addresses 0–63 are reserved for the interrupt cycle
A routine that starts at a power of two runs faster
The mapping 0 xxxx 00 puts every opcode routine in addresses 0–63, so 64–127 are free for fetch and shared subroutines
explanation: With a 0 in the top bit of the mapped address, all 16 opcodes × 4 words fall in the lower half of control memory. The upper half, starting at 64, holds FETCH and INDRCT.

questionText: In a microprogrammed CPU, how is one machine-language instruction carried out?
options: By a routine of one or more microinstructions read from control memory
By one machine-language subroutine stored in main memory
By a single state of a hardwired sequence counter
explanation: Each machine instruction is interpreted by its own microroutine: after the shared fetch routine, the mapped routine issues the control words that perform the instruction.

questionText: In Mano's microinstruction format, what is the AD field used for when BR = 10 (RET)?
options: It is added to SBR to form the return address
It is not used, because CAR is loaded from SBR
explanation: RET selects the SBR input of the sequencer multiplexer whatever the condition, so the address field is ignored; in the binary microprogram the AD field of such a word is simply 0000000.

questionText: Which statement about Mano's microprogrammed control unit is NOT correct?
options: With BR = CALL and a false condition, CAR is simply incremented
With BR = MAP, the next address comes from the opcode whatever the CD field selects
Enlarging the control memory from 128 to 256 words requires wider F1, F2 and F3 fields
The U condition is always 1, so U JMP is an unconditional branch
explanation: More control words need one more address bit, in CAR and the AD field (7 to 8 bits); the F fields depend only on the micro-operations they encode. The other three statements describe the sequencer correctly.

questionText: Which fields of Mano's 20-bit microinstruction go to the next-address logic (sequencer) rather than being decoded into datapath micro-operations?
explanation: CD selects the status bit to test, BR chooses the kind of address transition and AD supplies the branch address, while the F fields are decoded into register-transfer signals.

questionText: A control memory holds 2K microinstructions of 48 bits each. What is its capacity in KiB (1 KiB = 1024 bytes)?
explanation: 2048 × 48 = 98,304 bits = 12,288 bytes = 12 KiB. Dividing the bit count by 1024 without first converting to bytes gives 96.

questionText: An instruction set of 40 instructions needs execute routines averaging 6 microinstructions each, plus a shared 3-word fetch routine and a 2-word effective-address subroutine. The number of control-memory words must be a power of two. Each microinstruction has 36 control bits, a 3-bit condition field, a 2-bit branch field and a next-address field. What is the minimum control memory size?
explanation: Words needed = 40 × 6 + 3 + 2 = 245, rounded up to 256, so the address field is 8 bits and a word is 36 + 3 + 2 + 8 = 49 bits: 256 × 49 = 12,544 bits. Not rounding up gives 245 × 49 = 12,005, and dropping the address field gives 256 × 41 = 10,496.

questionText: A microprogrammed control unit has a control memory of 128 words, each 20 bits long. The control address register (CAR) must be:
explanation: 128 = 2^7, so 7 address bits select any of the 128 microinstructions. The 20-bit word length does not affect the address width.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT one of the four status conditions selected by the CD field of Mano's 20-bit microinstruction?
explanation: The CD field selects U (always 1), I (DR(15)), S (AC(15)) or Z (AC = 0). The E flip-flop belongs to the basic computer's hardwired design, not to the microprogrammed example.

questionText: A processor must support 100 distinct operations. What is the minimum width of its opcode field?
explanation: The opcode needs ⌈log2 100⌉ bits: 2^6 = 64 is too few and 2^7 = 128 ≥ 100, so 7 bits are required.

questionText: A register-to-register instruction names one of 120 operations and three operands chosen from a file of 32 registers. What is the minimum instruction length?
explanation: Opcode = ⌈log2 120⌉ = 7 bits and each register field = log2 32 = 5 bits, so the length is 7 + 3 × 5 = 22 bits.

questionText: A word-addressable memory holds 1M words of 32 bits (1M = 2^20). Each instruction occupies one word and has four fields: an opcode, a mode field selecting one of 5 addressing modes, a register field naming one of 30 registers, and a direct memory address. How wide is the opcode field, and how many opcodes can it encode?
explanation: Address = 20 bits, mode = ⌈log2 5⌉ = 3 bits, register = ⌈log2 30⌉ = 5 bits. Opcode = 32 − 20 − 3 − 5 = 4 bits, which encodes 2^4 = 16 operations.

questionText: A 16-bit fixed-length register-immediate instruction has a 5-bit opcode, one register field for a file of 8 registers, and a two's-complement immediate that uses all the remaining bits. What range of constants can the immediate hold?
explanation: Register field = log2 8 = 3 bits, so the immediate has 16 − 5 − 3 = 8 bits. An 8-bit two's-complement field covers −2^7 to 2^7 − 1, i.e. −128 to +127.

questionText: A computer has 20-bit instructions and 7-bit memory address fields. Two-address instructions use all the remaining bits as their opcode, and 50 two-address instructions are defined. Using expanding opcodes, what is the maximum number of one-address instructions?
explanation: Two-address opcode = 20 − 2 × 7 = 6 bits = 64 patterns, of which 64 − 50 = 14 are free. Each free pattern is extended by the released 7-bit address field: 14 × 2^7 = 1792 one-address instructions.

questionText: A computer has 16-bit instructions and 4-bit address fields; three-address instructions have a 4-bit opcode. With expanding opcodes it defines 14 three-address, 30 two-address and 20 one-address instructions. What is the maximum number of zero-address instructions?
explanation: Three-address: 16 − 14 = 2 free patterns give 2 × 2^4 = 32 two-address codes; 32 − 30 = 2 free give 32 one-address codes; 32 − 20 = 12 free give 12 × 2^4 = 192 zero-address instructions.

questionText: What is the main idea of an expanding-opcode scheme?
options: Instructions that need fewer address bits use the freed bits to extend the opcode, so more operations fit in a fixed instruction length
Every instruction has the same opcode width, and extra operations are supplied by a second instruction word
The opcode is expanded at run time by the microprogram into several microinstructions
The opcode grows with the size of main memory so that more addresses can be reached
explanation: An instruction with fewer address fields has spare bits; unused short-opcode patterns act as escapes that are extended by those bits, giving many more opcodes without lengthening the instruction.

questionText: In a single-accumulator CPU, how many explicit address fields does an ADD instruction need?
options: None; both operands are on a stack
Two; one for each source operand
Three; two sources and a result
One; the accumulator is an implied source and destination
explanation: An accumulator machine executes ADD X as AC ← AC + M[X]: the accumulator is implied, so only the memory address X is written in the instruction.

questionText: Which CPU organisation allows arithmetic instructions with no address field at all?
explanation: In a stack machine ADD, MUL and similar instructions take their operands from the top of the stack and push the result, so they are zero-address; only PUSH and POP carry an address.

questionText: Which statement about three-address instructions is correct?
options: They give the shortest programs for arithmetic expressions but need long instruction words to hold three addresses
They give the longest programs because each instruction does less work
They need no temporary registers or locations for any expression
They are the format used by stack machines for PUSH and POP
explanation: Naming two sources and a destination lets each instruction finish a whole operation, so programs are short, but three address fields make the binary instruction long.

questionText: An accumulator machine provides LOAD M, STORE M, ADD M, SUB M and MUL M, each with one memory address; AC is the implied operand and destination. What is the minimum number of instructions that computes X = (A − B) × (C + D), with all five variables in memory?
explanation: One partial result must be parked in memory because AC cannot hold both A − B and C + D: LOAD A, SUB B, STORE T, LOAD C, ADD D, MUL T, STORE X is 7 instructions.

questionText: X = (A + B) × (C + D) is coded four ways, with A, B, C, D and X in memory: three-address using R1 and R2 (3 instructions), two-address using R1 and R2 (6), one-address using a temporary T (7), and zero-address with the stack held in CPU registers (8). Counting only operand accesses to memory, not instruction fetches, which program makes the most?
options: None; all four programs make exactly 5 accesses
explanation: The three-, two- and zero-address programs each read A, B, C, D once and write X once (5 accesses). The one-address program also stores and reloads T, so each of its 7 instructions touches memory once: 7 accesses.

questionText: A stack machine has 8-bit opcodes and 16-bit memory addresses; PUSH and POP carry one address while ADD and MUL carry none. What is the size of the program PUSH A; PUSH B; ADD; PUSH C; PUSH D; ADD; MUL; POP X?
explanation: The four PUSH and one POP are 8 + 16 = 24 bits each and the three arithmetic instructions are 8 bits each: 5 × 24 + 3 × 8 = 120 + 24 = 144 bits = 18 bytes.

questionText: Which postfix (reverse Polish) sequence does a stack computer evaluate for X = (A + B) × (C − D) / E, with × and / of equal precedence applied left to right?
explanation: A + B and C − D become A B + and C D −; their product is A B + C D − ×, and dividing it by E appends E /. The other strings compute different expressions, e.g. (A + B) × (C − D / E).

questionText: X = A + B × (C − D × E) is converted to postfix by the standard algorithm, keeping the operands in their original order, and run on a zero-address machine (one PUSH per operand, one instruction per operator, then POP X). How many instructions does the program have, and what is the largest number of entries on the stack at any moment?
explanation: The postfix form is A B C D E × − × +: 5 PUSH + 4 operators + POP X = 10 instructions. All five operands are pushed before the first operator (D × E) can run, so the stack reaches 5 entries.

questionText:
On a stack machine, SUB and MUL pop the top two entries and push (second entry op top entry). With A = 10, B = 4 and C = 3 in memory, what value does this program store in X?
PUSH A
PUSH B
SUB
PUSH C
MUL
POP X
explanation: The stack holds 10, 4; SUB leaves 10 − 4 = 6; PUSH C gives 6, 3; MUL leaves 18; POP X stores 18, i.e. X = (A − B) × C.

questionText:
In a two-address machine the first operand is both a source and the destination (ADD R1, B means R1 ← R1 + M[B], and MOV copies the second operand into the first). With A = 2, B = 3 and C = 4, what does this program leave in X?
MOV R1, A
ADD R1, B
MOV R2, R1
MUL R1, C
SUB R1, R2
MOV X, R1
explanation: R1 = 2, then 2 + 3 = 5; R2 = 5; R1 = 5 × 4 = 20; R1 = 20 − 5 = 15; X ← 15. The program computes (A + B) × C − (A + B).

questionText: A two-word instruction occupies addresses 600 and 601 of a word-addressable memory, and its second word holds the address field 350. The PC is incremented after each word is fetched. What is the effective address in relative mode?
explanation: After both words are fetched PC = 602, so EA = PC + address field = 602 + 350 = 952.

questionText: The address field of a LOAD instruction is 300, and memory holds M[300] = 450 and M[450] = 900. What value is loaded into the accumulator if the instruction uses indirect addressing?
explanation: Indirect: EA = M[300] = 450 and the operand is M[450] = 900. Direct mode would load 450 and immediate mode would load 300.

questionText: A two-word LOAD AC instruction is stored at 250–251 (word-addressable) with address field 500 in word 251; after the fetch PC = 252. R1 = 400 and the index register XR = 100. Memory holds M[400] = 700, M[500] = 800, M[600] = 900, M[752] = 650 and M[800] = 300. Which addressing mode loads the value 900 into AC?
explanation: Indexed: EA = XR + 500 = 600, operand M[600] = 900. Relative gives EA = 752 (650), indirect gives EA = M[500] = 800 (300), register indirect gives EA = 400 (700), and direct would load M[500] = 800.

questionText: Memory is byte-addressable and operands are 4-byte words. R3 = 1000 before LOAD R1, (R3)+ (autoincrement) is executed twice in succession. What effective address does the second execution use, and what does R3 hold afterwards?
explanation: Autoincrement uses the register as the EA and then adds the operand size, 4. First execution: EA = 1000, R3 → 1004; second: EA = 1004, R3 → 1008.

questionText: A stack grows toward lower addresses in a byte-addressable memory with 4-byte words, and SP points to the top item. PUSH is MOV −(SP), Rx (autodecrement) and POP is MOV Rx, (SP)+ (autoincrement). Starting with SP = 5000, the program performs three pushes and then one pop. What is SP at the end?
explanation: Each push subtracts 4 before writing and each pop adds 4 after reading: SP = 5000 − 3 × 4 + 4 = 4992.

questionText: A program assembled as if it started at address 0 is loaded at address 24000, and its base register is set to 24000. An instruction in base-register mode has displacement 1350. What is its effective address?
explanation: EA = base register + displacement = 24000 + 1350 = 25350. Only the base register changes when the program is relocated.

questionText: A loop body contains LOAD R1, 2000(XR) (indexed mode) in a byte-addressable memory. XR starts at 0 and is increased by 4 at the end of every iteration. What effective address does the instruction use in the 6th iteration?
explanation: Before the 6th iteration XR has been increased 5 times, so XR = 5 × 4 = 20 and EA = 2000 + 20 = 2020.

questionText: An x86-style memory operand uses EA = base + index × scale + displacement. With base register = 1000, index register = 6, scale = 4 and displacement = 20, what is the effective address?
explanation: EA = 1000 + 6 × 4 + 20 = 1000 + 24 + 20 = 1044. Only the index is scaled; the displacement is added unscaled.

questionText: A 3-byte PC-relative branch instruction starts at address 750 in a byte-addressable memory and must jump to address 700. The offset is added to the PC after the whole instruction has been fetched. What signed offset must the assembler place in the instruction?
explanation: When the offset is added, PC = 750 + 3 = 753, so offset = target − PC = 700 − 753 = −53.

questionText: In a byte-addressable RISC with 32-bit instructions, a branch computes target = (PC + 4) + 4 × offset, where PC is the address of the branch and offset is a signed count of words. A branch at address 40000 has offset −3. What is its target address?
A one-word instruction LOAD @A uses indirect addressing. Counting the instruction fetch, how many memory accesses does it make in total?
explanation: One access fetches the instruction, one reads M[A] to obtain the effective address, and one reads the operand at that address: 3 accesses.

questionText: Once the instruction has been fetched, which addressing mode needs no further memory access to obtain its operand?
explanation: In register mode the operand is already in a CPU register. Direct, register indirect and indexed modes all form an effective address in memory and must read it.

questionText: Which addressing mode lets a branch work unchanged wherever the program is loaded in memory (position-independent code)?
explanation: A PC-relative branch stores the distance from the current PC, which stays the same when the whole program moves; absolute addresses would all need patching.

questionText: Which statement about immediate addressing is NOT correct?
options: The operand is part of the instruction itself
No memory access beyond the instruction fetch is needed for the operand
The largest constant is limited by the width of the operand field
The effective address is the value in the address field
explanation: EA = address field describes direct addressing. In immediate mode the field is the operand itself, so no extra access is needed, but the constant's range is limited by the field width.

questionText: Which of the following is a program control instruction?
explanation: Program control instructions change the PC or test conditions for doing so: branch, jump, call, return, compare and test. XCHG and PUSH are data transfer, and ROL is a data manipulation (shift) instruction.

questionText: How does CMP R1, R2 differ from SUB R1, R2?
options: CMP subtracts R1 from R2 instead of R2 from R1
CMP changes R1 but does not affect the flags
CMP performs R1 − R2 only to set the status flags and discards the difference, leaving R1 unchanged
CMP performs a logical AND instead of a subtraction
explanation: Compare subtracts so that C, S, Z and V are ready for a following conditional branch, but it stores no result; TEST does the same with a logical AND.

questionText: An 8-bit register holds 1100 1010. What does it hold after an exclusive-OR with the mask 1111 0000?
explanation: XOR with 1 complements a bit and XOR with 0 leaves it unchanged, so the high nibble 1100 becomes 0011 and the low nibble 1010 is kept: 0011 1010.

questionText: Which single operation sets bits 7 and 0 of an 8-bit register to 1 while leaving bits 6 to 1 unchanged?
explanation: OR with 1 forces a bit to 1 and OR with 0 keeps it. AND with 1000 0001 would clear bits 6 to 1, and XOR would clear bits 7 and 0 if they were already 1.

questionText: An 8-bit register holds the signed value 1011 0100 (−76). What does it hold after one arithmetic shift right?
explanation: SHRA moves every bit one place right and copies the sign bit into the MSB: 1101 1010 = −38 = −76 / 2. A logical shift right would insert 0 and give 0101 1010.

questionText: An 8-bit register holds 0110 0101 (+101). After one arithmetic shift left, what are the register contents and the overflow condition?
options: 1100 1010; overflow, because the sign bit changed
0100 1010; no overflow, because the sign bit is kept
explanation: SHLA shifts left and inserts 0 at the LSB: 1100 1010. The sign bit changed from 0 to 1 because 2 × 101 = 202 exceeds +127, so overflow is set.

questionText: The carry flag is C = 1 and an 8-bit register holds R = 0100 0001. What are R and C after one rotate right through carry (RORC)?
explanation: RORC shifts right, moves the old carry (1) into the MSB and the old LSB (1) into C, giving R = 1010 0000 and C = 1.

questionText: An 8-bit ALU adds 0110 0100 and 0011 0010. C is the carry out of bit 7, Z is set for a zero result, S is bit 7 of the result and V flags signed overflow. Which flag values result?
explanation: 0110 0100 + 0011 0010 = 1001 0110 (100 + 50 = 150). No carry leaves bit 7 (C = 0), bit 7 is 1 (S = 1), two positive operands gave a negative result (V = 1), and the result is non-zero (Z = 0).

questionText: With the same flag definitions (C = carry out of bit 7, Z = zero, V = signed overflow), an 8-bit ALU adds 1111 0000 and 0001 0000. Which flags are set, and is the 8-bit result correct as an unsigned sum and as a signed sum?
options: C = 1, Z = 1, V = 1: wrong both as unsigned and as signed
C = 0, Z = 1, V = 0: correct both as unsigned and as signed
C = 1, Z = 1, V = 0: wrong as unsigned (240 + 16 = 256 does not fit), correct as signed (−16 + 16 = 0)
C = 1, Z = 0, V = 0: correct as unsigned, wrong as signed
explanation: 1111 0000 + 0001 0000 = 1 0000 0000, so the register holds 0000 0000 with C = 1 and Z = 1. Unsigned 240 + 16 = 256 overflows 8 bits (C = 1), but signed −16 + 16 = 0 is exact, so V = 0.

questionText: After CMP A, B on signed two's-complement numbers, which flag condition means A < B?
explanation: A − B is negative when A < B, but overflow inverts the sign bit, so the reliable test is S ⊕ V = 1. C = 0 is the unsigned 'lower' test when C = 1 means no borrow.

questionText: A CPU performs CMP A, B by forming A + B' + 1 in 8 bits, with A = 0110 0100 (+100) and B = 1100 1110 (−50). Which flags result, and is 'branch if less than (signed)', which tests S ⊕ V = 1, taken?
options: S = 1, V = 0; the branch is taken
S = 1, V = 1; the branch is taken
S = 0, V = 0; the branch is not taken
S = 1, V = 1; the branch is not taken
explanation: A + B' + 1 = 0110 0100 + 0011 0001 + 1 = 1001 0110, so S = 1; two positive addends gave a negative result, so V = 1 (+150 does not fit). S ⊕ V = 0, so A ≥ B and the branch is not taken, which is right because +100 > −50.

questionText: Two unsigned 8-bit numbers, 200 and 100, are added. Which status flag shows that the true sum does not fit in 8 bits?
explanation: 300 exceeds 255, so a carry leaves bit 7 and C = 1 while the register keeps 300 − 256 = 44. V reports signed overflow, a different condition (here −56 + 100 = 44, so V = 0).

questionText: A CPU keeps a memory stack that grows toward lower addresses, with SP pointing to the top item. Which microoperation sequence correctly implements CALL to a subroutine at effective address EA?
options: PC ← EA; SP ← SP − 1; M[SP] ← PC
M[SP] ← PC; SP ← SP + 1; PC ← EA
SP ← SP − 1; M[SP] ← PC; PC ← EA
explanation: The return address (the PC, already pointing at the next instruction) must be pushed before PC is overwritten, and a push onto a downward-growing stack decrements SP first. PC ← M[SP]; SP ← SP + 1 is the RETURN sequence.

questionText: Which of the following is a difference between a program interrupt and a subroutine call?
options: An interrupt is started by a hardware or internal signal rather than by an instruction, and the CPU saves its status (PSW) as well as the return address
An interrupt always returns to the instruction that caused it, while a call returns to the next instruction
A subroutine call saves every CPU register automatically, while an interrupt saves nothing
An interrupt transfers control to the address in the current instruction's address field
explanation: A subroutine call is an instruction whose address field gives the target and which saves only the PC. An interrupt is triggered by a signal, its service-routine address comes from hardware, and the CPU state (PSW) is saved too.

questionText: An accumulator machine has 3-byte instructions (1-byte opcode, 2-byte address) and 4-byte data words. It runs LOAD A; ADD B; STORE T; LOAD C; ADD D; MUL T; STORE X. Counting both instruction fetches and data transfers, how many bytes move between the CPU and memory?
explanation: Code: 7 instructions × 3 bytes = 21 bytes fetched. Data: each instruction reads or writes one 4-byte word, 7 × 4 = 28 bytes. Total = 21 + 28 = 49 bytes.

questionText: In a load/store architecture such as MIPS or RISC-V, which instructions are allowed to read or write data memory?
options: Every arithmetic and logic instruction, through memory operands
Only the LOAD and STORE instructions
Any instruction that uses indirect addressing
explanation: In a load/store (RISC) design, ALU instructions work only on registers and immediates; LOAD brings a word from memory into a register and STORE writes it back.

questionText: Three of these instruction-set families are RISC designs. Which one is the CISC design?
explanation: The VAX, with hundreds of instructions, variable-length encoding and many memory addressing modes, is the classic CISC machine; ARM, MIPS and SPARC are RISC designs.

questionText: Which type of control unit is typical of a RISC processor?
options: Microprogrammed control with a writable control store
explanation: Simple, uniform RISC instructions can be decoded by fast combinational logic, so RISC uses hardwired control; microprogramming suits large, complex CISC instruction sets.

questionText: Why is a CISC program for a task usually shorter, in number of instructions, than the RISC program for the same task?
options: CISC compilers delete more instructions during optimisation
A single CISC instruction can do more work, such as fetching memory operands and computing in one step
CISC processors have more registers, so fewer loads are needed
Every CISC instruction is shorter in bytes than every RISC instruction
explanation: Complex instructions with memory operands combine what RISC does with separate loads, ALU operations and stores, so the instruction count IC is lower even though each instruction takes more cycles.

questionText: Which statement about RISC is NOT correct?
options: Most RISC instructions complete at a rate of one per clock cycle in a pipeline
A RISC program always contains fewer instructions than the equivalent CISC program
RISC relies on an optimising compiler for register allocation and instruction scheduling
RISC instructions have a fixed length and few formats
explanation: RISC programs usually contain more instructions than CISC programs, because each instruction does less; RISC wins through a lower CPI and a faster clock, not a lower instruction count.

questionText: How do fixed-length instructions with fixed field positions make a RISC pipeline simpler?
options: They let each instruction access memory several times without stalling
They remove the need for a program counter
The next instruction's address is known during fetch, and register fields sit in the same bits of every format, so registers can be read while the opcode is decoded
They let the processor skip the decode stage entirely
explanation: With every instruction one word long, fetch simply adds the word size to the PC, and fixed register-field positions let register reading overlap decoding, so every instruction passes through the same short stages.

questionText: Studies of compiled high-level-language programs that led to the Berkeley RISC design found which fact that motivated overlapped register windows?
options: Programs rarely used local scalar variables
Procedure calls and returns were the most time-consuming operations, largely because of saving registers and passing parameters
explanation: Weighted by the machine instructions and memory references they cause, calls and returns cost the most, and most operands were local scalars; keeping those in register windows removes most call overhead.

questionText: With overlapped register windows, where does a calling procedure place the parameters for the procedure it calls?
options: In its outgoing (common) registers, which become the callee's incoming registers when the window pointer moves
In the global registers only, which every procedure shares
On the memory stack, because windows cannot share registers
In the callee's local registers, which the caller writes before the call
explanation: Adjacent windows overlap: the caller's outgoing registers are physically the same as the callee's incoming registers, so a call just advances the current-window pointer and no parameter is copied.

questionText: In a circular register file of overlapped windows, what happens when a call is made and no free window is left?
options: A window-overflow trap saves the oldest window's registers to memory so that its window can be reused
The call is refused and the program is aborted
The newest window is overwritten without being saved
The processor switches to microprogrammed mode and uses the memory stack
explanation: The overflow trap spills the oldest activation's window to memory; a later return into that procedure raises an underflow trap that reloads it.

questionText: A register file is organised as a circular buffer of 8 overlapped windows (as in Stallings and SPARC, one window is kept free because the newest window's outgoing registers would otherwise overlap the oldest window's incoming registers). At most how many procedure activations can be held in registers at once before a window-overflow trap is needed?
explanation: The ring closes on itself: the outgoing registers of the newest window would overlap the incoming registers of the oldest, so an N-window file holds N − 1 = 7 activations.

questionText: A register file of 224 registers consists of 8 global registers plus overlapped windows, each window having 12 local registers and 6 registers common with each adjacent window. How many windows does the file have?
explanation: Total = (L + C)W + G, so W = (224 − 8) / (12 + 6) = 216 / 18 = 12. Dividing by L + 2C = 24 would count each overlap twice and give 9.

questionText: With 16 global registers, 8 local registers per window and 8 registers common to each pair of adjacent windows, how many registers can one procedure address at any time?
explanation: Window size = G + L + 2C = 16 + 8 + 2 × 8 = 40: the globals, the locals, the incoming registers shared with the caller and the outgoing registers shared with the callee.

questionText: A designer wants each procedure to see 32 registers, 8 of them global, with the number of local registers equal to the number of common registers shared with each neighbour. If the file has 8 windows, how many physical registers are needed?
explanation: 32 = G + L + 2C = 8 + 3C gives C = L = 8. Total = (L + C)W + G = 16 × 8 + 8 = 136, the SPARC organisation.

questionText: Each window has 10 local registers and 6 registers common with each neighbour, and registers are 32 bits wide. A window-overflow trap stores the local and incoming registers of the oldest window. If a program triggers 25 overflow traps, how many bytes do the traps write to memory?
explanation: Each trap saves L + C = 16 registers × 4 bytes = 64 bytes, so 25 traps write 25 × 64 = 1600 bytes (400 is the count of words, not bytes).

questionText: A program executes 2.5 million instructions with an average CPI of 2 on a processor whose clock period is 0.5 ns. What is its CPU time?
A program's instruction mix is ALU 50% (CPI 1), loads 20% (CPI 4), stores 10% (CPI 3) and branches 20% (CPI 2). What is its average CPI?
explanation: CPI = 0.5 × 1 + 0.2 × 4 + 0.1 × 3 + 0.2 × 2 = 0.5 + 0.8 + 0.3 + 0.4 = 2.0. The plain mean of the class CPIs (2.5) ignores how often each class occurs.

questionText: A processor runs at 800 MHz with an average CPI of 1.6. What is its MIPS rating?
A benchmark performs 60 million floating-point operations and runs in 0.4 s. What is its MFLOPS rating?
explanation: MFLOPS = FP operations / (time × 10^6) = 60 × 10^6 / (0.4 × 10^6) = 150.

questionText: Instruction classes A, B and C need 1, 2 and 3 cycles on a 1 GHz processor. Code sequence 1 executes 6M A, 1M B and 2M C instructions; sequence 2 executes 3M A, 2M B and 2M C. Which statement is correct?
options: Sequence 1 has the higher MIPS rating, but sequence 2 runs faster
Sequence 1 has the higher MIPS rating and also runs faster
Sequence 2 has the higher MIPS rating and runs faster
Both take the same time because they use the same instruction classes
explanation: Sequence 1: 14M cycles = 14 ms for 9M instructions (643 MIPS). Sequence 2: 13M cycles = 13 ms for 7M instructions (538 MIPS). Sequence 2 is faster despite its lower MIPS rating.

questionText: A CISC machine runs a program as 20 million instructions with CPI 4 at 400 MHz. A RISC machine runs the same program as 30 million instructions with CPI 1.25 at 250 MHz. Which statement is correct?
options: The RISC machine is about 2.13 times faster
The RISC machine is about 1.33 times faster
The CISC machine is 1.5 times faster because it executes fewer instructions
Both machines take the same time
explanation: CISC: 20M × 4 / 400 MHz = 0.2 s. RISC: 30M × 1.25 / 250 MHz = 0.15 s. The ratio 0.2 / 0.15 = 1.33 favours RISC; 2.13 compares cycle counts and ignores the different clock rates.

questionText: The RISC version of a program executes 1.4 times as many instructions as the CISC version, whose average CPI is 3.5. Both machines use the same clock. What is the largest average CPI the RISC machine may have and still be at least as fast?
explanation: At equal clock the RISC machine needs 1.4 × IC × CPI_R ≤ IC × 3.5, so CPI_R ≤ 3.5 / 1.4 = 2.5.

questionText: A CISC machine executes a program as 10 million instructions with CPI 3 at 600 MHz. A RISC machine needs 15 million instructions with CPI 1.2 for the same program. What is the minimum RISC clock frequency needed to match the CISC execution time?
explanation: CISC time = 10M × 3 / 600 MHz = 50 ms. The RISC machine needs 15M × 1.2 = 18M cycles in 50 ms, so f = 18 × 10^6 / 0.05 s = 360 MHz.

questionText: A microprogrammed CISC processor executes each machine instruction as an average of 6 microinstructions, each taking one 10 ns clock cycle. What is its MIPS rating?
explanation: Each machine instruction takes 6 × 10 ns = 60 ns, so the rate is 1 / 60 ns = 16.7 × 10^6 instructions per second, i.e. 16.7 MIPS.

questionText: On a RISC machine, loads are 25% of executed instructions and take 3 cycles; every other instruction takes 1 cycle. A better data cache cuts the load time to 2 cycles. What is the overall speedup, with the same instruction count and clock?
explanation: Old CPI = 0.25 × 3 + 0.75 × 1 = 1.5; new CPI = 0.25 × 2 + 0.75 × 1 = 1.25. Speedup = 1.5 / 1.25 = 1.20; 1.5 is only the speedup of the loads themselves.

questionText: A program runs 10 million instructions at CPI 1.2 on a 500 MHz processor. Adding a complex instruction cuts the instruction count by 10% but raises the average CPI to 1.4 at the same clock. What is the new CPU time?
explanation: Old: 10M × 1.2 / 500 MHz = 24 ms. New: 9M × 1.4 / 500 MHz = 25.2 ms, about 5% slower, so the complex instruction does not pay off.

questionText: A program of 8 million instructions takes 12 ms on a 1.5 GHz processor. What is its average CPI?
A load/store machine with three-register ALU instructions (for example ADD R1, R1, R2) computes X = (A + B) × (C + D), with A, B, C, D and X in memory. What is the minimum number of instructions?
explanation: Four LOADs bring A to D into registers, two ADDs and one MUL work on registers, and one STORE writes X: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8, because only LOAD and STORE may touch memory.

questionText: For X = (A + B) × (C + D), a RISC program has 8 fixed 32-bit instructions. A CISC version uses 3 memory-to-memory three-address instructions (ADD T, A, B; ADD X, C, D; MUL X, T, X), each with a 1-byte opcode and three 2-byte addresses. How many times larger is the RISC code in bytes?
explanation: RISC code = 8 × 4 = 32 bytes; CISC code = 3 × (1 + 3 × 2) = 21 bytes. The ratio 32 / 21 = 1.52; 2.67 compares instruction counts rather than bytes.

questionText: A designer's feature list for a new processor contains the four items below. Which one comes from the RISC tradition rather than from classic CISC?
options: Memory-to-memory arithmetic with many addressing modes
A large register file organised as overlapped register windows
explanation: Large windowed register files come from RISC (Berkeley RISC, SPARC). Classic CISC machines have relatively few registers, many addressing modes, variable-length formats and microprogrammed control.

questionText: What is the main advantage of microprogrammed control over hardwired control?
options: It is always faster, because microinstructions are fetched in parallel
It removes the need for any sequencing logic
The instruction set can be changed or extended by rewriting the control memory instead of redesigning the logic
explanation: A microprogrammed unit stores its control signals as microinstructions, so complex instructions are easy to add or correct; the price is speed, because every step reads the control memory.

questionText: Why does a RISC design depend heavily on an optimising compiler?
options: The compiler must translate each instruction into microcode at run time
The compiler must choose among hundreds of complex instructions for each statement
The compiler must keep variables in the large register file and reorder instructions to fill delay slots and avoid pipeline stalls
The compiler must insert memory-to-memory instructions for arithmetic
explanation: RISC hardware stays simple by leaving register allocation and instruction scheduling (including load-delay and branch-delay slots) to the compiler.

questionText: In a pipelined RISC with delayed branches (no annul option), what happens to the instruction immediately after a branch, in the delay slot?
options: It is always executed, whether or not the branch is taken
It is executed only if the branch is not taken
It is discarded and replaced by a bubble
explanation: A delayed branch takes effect one instruction late, so the delay-slot instruction always executes; the compiler places a useful instruction there, or a NOP if none is available.

questionText:
A RISC uses delayed branches with one delay slot (no annulling). What value does this code store in X?
MOV   R1, #5
BR    L            ; unconditional delayed branch
ADD   R1, R1, #3
ADD   R1, R1, #10
L: STORE X, R1
explanation: MOV sets R1 = 5; the ADD #3 in the delay slot executes before the jump takes effect, giving R1 = 8; ADD #10 is skipped, so X = 8.

questionText: Why is the average CPI of a classic CISC processor well above 1?
options: Many instructions access memory several times and run as multi-step microroutines
Its clock period is shorter than that of a RISC processor
It has too many registers to read in one cycle
explanation: A memory-to-memory instruction must fetch several operands and store a result, and a microprogrammed unit spends one cycle per microinstruction, so one instruction takes many cycles.

questionText: Which statement about MIPS as a performance measure is NOT correct?
options: The MIPS rating depends on the instruction mix of the program being run
A machine with a higher MIPS rating always runs a given program faster
MIPS cannot fairly compare machines with different instruction sets
explanation: MIPS ignores how much work each instruction does: a machine or code sequence can execute more, simpler instructions per second and still take longer, so higher MIPS does not guarantee a shorter time.

questionText: A scientific program executes 200 million instructions, 50 million of which are floating-point operations, with an average CPI of 1.5 on a 1 GHz processor. What is its MFLOPS rating?
explanation: Time = 200M × 1.5 / 1 GHz = 0.3 s, so MFLOPS = 50 × 10^6 / (0.3 × 10^6) = 166.7. The MIPS rating would be 200 / 0.3 = 666.7.

questionText: Compared with CISC, which factor of CPU time = IC × CPI × T does a RISC instruction set usually increase?
explanation: Simpler instructions mean more of them per program, so IC rises; RISC then lowers CPI to about 1 and allows a shorter clock period.

questionText: Which pairing of a CPU-time factor with what mainly determines it is correct?
options: Clock cycle time — the compiler and the program's instruction mix
Instruction count — the instruction set architecture and the compiler
Instruction count — the transistor technology alone
Clock cycle time — the number of instructions in the program
explanation: The number of instructions executed depends on the instruction set and on how the compiler translates the program; the clock cycle time is set by hardware technology and organisation.

questionText: How do modern x86 processors achieve RISC-like pipelining while keeping the CISC instruction set?
options: Hardware decoders translate each x86 instruction into simple fixed-length micro-operations that a RISC-style core executes
They execute every x86 instruction in microcode without pipelining
They require programs to be recompiled into ARM code
They restrict x86 programs to instructions that access memory once
explanation: Since the Pentium Pro, x86 front ends crack instructions into micro-ops that a pipelined, superscalar core schedules like RISC instructions; only rare complex instructions fall back to microcode.

questionText: What is the purpose of compressed 16-bit instruction encodings such as ARM Thumb and the RISC-V C extension?
options: To increase the number of addressable registers
To add memory-to-memory arithmetic to RISC
To improve code density, reducing program memory size and instruction-fetch bandwidth
To replace hardwired control with microcode
explanation: Fixed 32-bit RISC instructions waste space; 16-bit encodings of common instructions shrink programs, which matters in embedded systems with small memories and caches.

questionText: Which set of addressing modes is typical of a RISC instruction set?
options: Memory indirect, autoincrement deferred and scaled index with displacement
Direct memory operands for every arithmetic instruction
Register, immediate and register plus displacement
explanation: RISC keeps a few simple modes: register operands, small immediates, and base register plus displacement for LOAD and STORE. The richer memory modes belong to CISC machines such as the VAX.

questionText: Why do RISC processors provide a large number of general-purpose registers?
options: Because microcode needs one register for each microinstruction
Because variable-length instructions need extra registers for decoding
Because a large register file shortens every instruction's opcode
Because only loads and stores reach memory, keeping operands and local variables in registers cuts memory traffic and speeds procedure calls
explanation: In a load/store machine every operand must be in a register before use, so many registers (or register windows) let the compiler keep variables there and avoid loads, stores and register saving at calls.

questionText: A program takes 10 s on machine A and 15 s on machine B. How many times faster is A than B?
explanation: Performance is the reciprocal of execution time, so A is 15 / 10 = 1.5 times as fast as B.

questionText: A superscalar RISC core running at 2 GHz executes 3.6 billion instructions in 1.5 s. What is its average CPI?

A circular register file has 6 overlapped windows and holds at most W − 1 procedure activations. Each overflow trap saves exactly one window and no window is saved in advance. Starting from main with only main's window in use, the program makes 8 nested calls without any return, so 9 activations exist at the deepest point. How many window-overflow traps occur?
explanation: The file holds W − 1 = 5 activations, so activations 6, 7, 8 and 9 each force one trap: 9 − 5 = 4. Assuming all 6 windows usable would wrongly give 3.

questionText: The 'semantic gap' argument used to justify CISC designs refers to:
options: The delay between issuing a load and receiving its data
The difference in speed between registers and main memory
The difference between high-level-language operations and machine instructions, which designers tried to close with complex instructions and many addressing modes
The unused opcode space left in a fixed-length instruction format
explanation: CISC designers argued that instructions resembling high-level statements would simplify compilers and shorten programs; RISC studies showed those instructions were rarely used.

questionText: A RISC processor uses overlapped register windows with 10 global registers, 8 windows, 10 local registers per window and 6 registers common to adjacent windows. The total number of registers in the file is:
explanation: N = (L + C)W + G = (10 + 6) × 8 + 10 = 138, the Berkeley RISC I organisation. Each procedure sees L + 2C + G = 32 registers.

questionText: The same program compiles to 0.8 million instructions on a CISC machine (average CPI 3) and to 1.2 million instructions on a RISC machine (average CPI 1.2). Both run at 500 MHz. Which statement is correct?
options: The CISC machine is faster by a factor of 1.5 because it executes fewer instructions
The two machines take the same time
The RISC machine is faster by a factor of about 2.5
The RISC machine is faster by a factor of about 1.67
explanation: T = IC × CPI / f. CISC: 0.8M × 3 / 500M = 4.8 ms; RISC: 1.2M × 1.2 / 500M = 2.88 ms. Ratio 4.8 / 2.88 = 1.67 in favour of RISC despite 50 percent more instructions.

questionText: Flynn's taxonomy classifies computer architectures according to:
options: The number of processors and the number of memory modules
The number of concurrent instruction streams and data streams
The word length and the clock frequency of the processor
Whether memory is shared by all processors or distributed among them
explanation: Flynn classifies machines by how many instruction streams and how many data streams are processed at the same time, giving SISD, SIMD, MISD and MIMD. Shared versus distributed memory is a later subdivision of MIMD, not Flynn's criterion.

questionText: A quad-core processor in which each core fetches its own instructions and works on its own data belongs to which of Flynn's classes?
explanation: Each core has its own instruction stream and its own data stream, so the machine is multiple-instruction, multiple-data. Multicore CPUs, multiprocessors and clusters are all MIMD.

questionText: According to Mano, a uniprocessor that obtains its parallelism from an instruction pipeline and multiple functional units belongs to which of Flynn's classes?
options: SISD, because there is still one instruction stream operating on one data stream
MIMD, because several instructions are in execution at the same time
SIMD, because one control unit drives all the pipeline stages
MISD, because several stages work on the same data item
explanation: Mano states that an SISD computer may achieve parallel processing by means of multiple functional units or pipeline processing. Overlapping the phases of one instruction stream does not create extra instruction or data streams, so the machine remains SISD.

questionText: Which statement about a SIMD array processor is correct?
options: Each processing element fetches and decodes its own instruction stream from a shared memory
It is a single arithmetic pipeline whose stages work on successive elements of a vector
A master control unit broadcasts each instruction to many processing elements, each with its own local memory, which execute it on different data
All processing elements operate on one shared data item with different instructions
explanation: In Mano's SIMD array processor identical processing elements with local memories execute the same broadcast instruction in lockstep on different data. Independent instruction streams would be MIMD, a single pipeline is a vector processor, and one data item with many instructions is MISD.

questionText: A 6-stage pipeline has a clock period of 5 ns and no stalls. How long does it take to complete 50 tasks?
explanation: T = (k + n − 1)τ = (6 + 50 − 1) × 5 ns = 55 × 5 = 275 ns. 1500 ns is the non-pipelined time (50 × 6 × 5 ns), 250 ns forgets the k − 1 fill cycles and 55 is the number of clock cycles, not the time.

questionText: In the space-time diagram of a 4-segment pipeline (one clock per segment, no stalls), task T1 enters segment 1 in clock cycle 1. In which clock cycle does task T6 complete segment 4?
explanation: Task Ti enters segment 1 in cycle i and leaves segment k in cycle i + k − 1, so T6 finishes in cycle 6 + 4 − 1 = 9. Cycle 24 would be the non-pipelined finish (6 × 4).

questionText: A 5-stage pipeline with equal stage delays processes 20 tasks without stalls. What is its efficiency (the fraction of the ideal speedup k that is achieved)?
explanation: E = n/(k + n − 1) = 20/24 ≈ 0.833, equivalently S/k with S = 100/24 ≈ 4.17. 0.800 comes from using k + n instead of k + n − 1, and 4.17 is the speedup itself.

questionText: A 5-stage pipeline with a 4 ns clock processes a batch of 10 tasks with no stalls. What is the throughput measured over the whole batch?
explanation: Time = (5 + 10 − 1) × 4 ns = 56 ns, so H = 10/56 ns ≈ 178.6 × 10^6 tasks/s. 250 million is the ideal 1/τ reached only for very long batches, 50 million is the non-pipelined rate 1/(5 × 4 ns) and 166.7 million counts k + n cycles.

questionText: The four stages of a pipeline have delays of 40, 30, 60 and 50 ns, and each interstage latch adds 10 ns. What is the minimum clock period?
explanation: τ = max(τ_i) + d = 60 + 10 = 70 ns. 60 ns forgets the latch, 55 ns uses the average stage delay (45 + 10) and 190 ns adds a single latch delay to the sum of the four stage delays (180 + 10).

questionText: A non-pipelined unit takes 100 ns per instruction. It is split into 4 stages with delays of 20, 25, 30 and 25 ns, and a 5 ns latch is added after each stage. Ignoring hazards, what speedup does the pipeline give for 200 instructions?
explanation: τ = 30 + 5 = 35 ns; pipelined time = (4 + 199) × 35 = 7105 ns; non-pipelined time = 200 × 100 = 20 000 ns; S = 20 000/7105 ≈ 2.82. Ignoring the latch gives 3.28, and the equal-stage formula nk/(k + n − 1) gives 3.94.

questionText: A task needs 40 ns in a non-pipelined unit that has no latches. In a 4-stage pipeline the stage delays are 10, 8, 12 and 10 ns and each latch adds 2 ns. What is the maximum speedup obtainable for a very long stream of tasks?
explanation: τ = 12 + 2 = 14 ns, and for n → ∞ the speedup tends to t_n/τ = 40/14 ≈ 2.86. 3.33 forgets the latch (40/12), 3.43 wrongly adds four latch delays to the non-pipelined time (48/14), and 4 holds only for balanced stages with no latch overhead.

questionText: A four-segment floating-point adder pipeline has segment delays of 60, 70, 100 and 80 ns and interface registers with a 10 ns delay. How long does it take to add 100 pairs of numbers, with no stalls?
explanation: τ = 100 + 10 = 110 ns; T = (4 + 100 − 1) × 110 ns = 103 × 110 = 11 330 ns ≈ 11.33 µs. 31.0 µs is the non-pipelined time 100 × (60 + 70 + 100 + 80) ns, 10.30 µs forgets the register delay and 11.00 µs forgets the fill cycles.

questionText: A 5-stage pipeline has stage delays of 20, 25, 20, 30 and 25 ns and a 5 ns latch after each stage. The non-pipelined unit takes 120 ns per instruction. When the pipeline is clocked at its minimum clock period, what is the latency of a single instruction in it?
explanation: Every stage occupies one full clock τ = 30 + 5 = 35 ns, so an instruction needs kτ = 5 × 35 = 175 ns from entry to exit: pipelining raises latency while it improves throughput. 145 ns adds the latches to the raw delays but ignores that each stage must wait for the whole clock, and 35 ns is the clock period.

questionText: A non-pipelined processor takes 50 ns per instruction. It is pipelined either into 5 or into 10 equal stages, and each latch adds 2 ns. For a very long instruction stream with no hazards, how many times faster is the 10-stage design than the 5-stage design?
explanation: 5 stages: τ = 50/5 + 2 = 12 ns; 10 stages: τ = 50/10 + 2 = 7 ns. For a long stream the time per instruction is τ, so the ratio is 12/7 ≈ 1.71, not 2, because the latch overhead does not shrink. 7.14 is the 10-stage speedup over the non-pipelined processor (50/7) and 0.58 inverts the ratio.

questionText: A 5-stage pipeline with equal stages and no stalls must reach a speedup of at least 4 over the non-pipelined unit. What is the minimum number of tasks n in the batch?
A 4-stage pipeline with equal stages and a 20 ns clock processes 36 tasks without stalls. What are its efficiency and its throughput?
explanation: Cycles = 4 + 36 − 1 = 39. E = n/(k + n − 1) = 36/39 ≈ 0.923 and H = 36/(39 × 20 ns) = 36/780 ns ≈ 46.2 × 10^6 tasks/s. 50.0 million is the ideal 1/τ, the 0.900 and 45.0 pair counts k + n = 40 cycles, and 0.250 and 12.5 million are non-pipelined figures.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT a reason why the actual speedup of a k-stage pipeline is less than k?
options: The k − 1 cycles needed to fill the pipeline
Using separate instruction and data caches
Unequal stage delays, since the clock must suit the slowest stage
The delay of the latches between stages
explanation: Fill time, stage imbalance and latch overhead all pull the speedup below k. Separate instruction and data caches remove a structural hazard, so they help the pipeline approach its ideal rather than limiting it.

questionText: Pipelining an instruction unit mainly improves:
options: Throughput: more instructions are completed per unit time, although the latency of each instruction is not reduced
The latency of each individual instruction, which becomes k times shorter
The number of instructions in the program, which decreases
The hit ratio of the instruction cache
explanation: Overlapping instructions raises the completion rate towards one per clock, but each instruction still passes through all k stages, and the latch overhead makes its latency slightly longer than before.

questionText: Which statement about the registers (latches) placed between pipeline stages is correct?
options: They shorten the latency of a single task by storing partial results
They are needed only in arithmetic pipelines, not in instruction pipelines
They remove all data hazards because every result is stored in them
They hold each stage's result for the next stage, so every stage can work on a different task in the same clock, but their delay is added to the clock period
explanation: Pipeline registers isolate the stages so that k tasks can be in progress at once; the price is the latch delay d in τ = max τ_i + d. Data hazards still need forwarding or stalls even though results pass through the latches.

questionText: In a four-segment floating-point adder pipeline, which segment shifts the mantissa of the number with the smaller exponent to the right?
options: Segment 3: add or subtract the mantissas
explanation: Segment 1 subtracts the exponents to find their difference, segment 2 shifts the smaller-exponent mantissa right by that difference, segment 3 adds the aligned mantissas and segment 4 normalises the result.

questionText: In the classic 5-stage RISC pipeline IF–ID–EX–MEM–WB, in which stage does a load instruction read the data cache?
explanation: EX computes the effective address, MEM reads the data cache at that address and WB writes the loaded value into the destination register. IF reads the instruction cache, not the data cache.

questionText: In Mano's four-segment instruction pipeline (FI, DA, FO, EX), if there is only one memory, which two segments can need memory in the same clock cycle and so conflict?
explanation: FI fetches a new instruction while FO of an earlier instruction fetches its operand from memory, so both need memory at once. Mano notes that separate instruction and data memories remove this conflict.

questionText: In Mano's three-segment RISC pipeline (I: instruction fetch, A: ALU operation, E: execute), what does the delayed-load technique do?
options: The compiler places a no-operation, or an independent instruction, after a load whose result is needed by the next instruction, instead of relying on a hardware interlock
The hardware delays every load by one extra cycle so that the data cache can be refreshed
The compiler moves the load after the instruction that uses its result
The processor fetches the operands of two loads in the same cycle
explanation: In Mano's RISC pipeline a loaded value is not yet available to the very next instruction, so the compiler detects the conflict and inserts a no-op (or schedules an unrelated instruction) in that slot; this software solution is called delayed load.

questionText: A conditional branch is not resolved until the EX stage, but the instructions that follow it have already been fetched. The resulting problem is a:
explanation: A control hazard arises when the PC changes after instructions on the wrong path have already entered the pipeline; they must be flushed, or the branch handled by prediction or delayed branching.

questionText:
For the instruction sequence below, which list of dependences is complete and correct?

I1: LOAD R1, 0(R2)
I2: ADD  R3, R1, R4
I3: SUB  R1, R5, R6
options: RAW I1→I2 on R1; WAR I2→I3 on R1; WAW I1→I3 on R1
RAW I1→I2 on R1; RAW I2→I3 on R1; WAW I1→I3 on R1
WAR I1→I2 on R1; RAW I2→I3 on R1; WAW I1→I3 on R1
explanation: I2 reads R1 written by I1 (RAW), I3 writes R1 that I2 reads (WAR), and I1 and I3 both write R1 (WAW). No other register is shared: R3 is written by I2 and not used again.

questionText: In a simple in-order 5-stage pipeline where operands are read only in ID and results are written only in WB, which data hazards can occur?
options: RAW, WAR and WAW can all occur
Only RAW; WAR and WAW cannot occur because reads and writes happen in fixed stages in program order
Only WAW, because two instructions can write the same register
Only WAR, because a later instruction may write before an earlier one reads
explanation: Every instruction reads its operands in ID before any later instruction reaches WB, and writes happen in program order in WB, so only true (RAW) dependences cause hazards. WAR and WAW hazards appear with out-of-order completion, for example with long floating-point pipelines.

questionText:
A 5-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) has no forwarding; the register file is written in the first half of a clock and read in the second half, and the hazard is handled by stalling the dependent instruction in ID. How many stall cycles occur between the two instructions below?

ADD R1, R2, R3
SUB R4, R1, R5
explanation: ADD writes R1 in WB in cycle 5, so SUB can read R1 in ID no earlier than cycle 5 instead of cycle 3: 2 stall cycles. Forwarding from the EX/MEM register would remove them.

questionText:
A 5-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) has full forwarding and a hazard-detection unit, and there are no other stalls. How many clock cycles are needed for the sequence below, from the first IF to the last WB?

LW  R1, 0(R2)
ADD R3, R1, R4
SUB R5, R3, R6
explanation: The ideal time is 5 + 3 − 1 = 7 cycles. The load-use dependence LW→ADD costs one stall because the loaded value is ready only after MEM, while ADD→SUB is covered by forwarding with no stall, giving 8 cycles (11 without forwarding).

questionText:
A 5-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) has no forwarding; the register file is written in the first half and read in the second half of a clock, and hazards are handled by stalling in ID. How many cycles does the sequence take, from the first IF to the last WB?

I1: ADD R1, R2, R3
I2: SUB R4, R1, R5
I3: AND R6, R1, R7
I4: OR  R8, R4, R6
explanation: I1 writes R1 in cycle 5, so I2 reads it then and executes in cycle 6 (2 stalls); R1 is then ready for I3, which executes in cycle 7 and writes R6 in cycle 9. I4 must read R6 in cycle 9 and executes in cycle 10 (2 more stalls), so its WB is in cycle 12, against 8 cycles with no hazards.

questionText: Operand forwarding (bypassing) removes many RAW stalls by:
options: Writing every result to memory so that later instructions can load it
Having the compiler insert no-operation instructions between dependent instructions
Routing a result from a pipeline register straight to the ALU input of a following instruction before it is written to the register file
Predicting the value that the earlier instruction will produce
explanation: Forwarding adds multiplexers at the ALU inputs fed from the EX/MEM and MEM/WB registers, so a result can be used in the very next cycle instead of waiting for write-back. Inserting no-ops is a software remedy that keeps the lost cycles rather than removing them.

questionText: Why does a load followed immediately by an instruction that uses the loaded register still need one stall cycle in a 5-stage pipeline with full forwarding?
options: The register file cannot be read and written in the same cycle
The loaded data is available only at the end of MEM, but the dependent instruction needs it at the start of its EX in that same cycle
Loads use the instruction cache, which causes a structural hazard
The branch predictor must first check the address of the load
explanation: An ALU result exists at the end of EX, one cycle before the next instruction's EX, so it can be forwarded; a load result exists only after MEM, which coincides with the next instruction's EX, so one bubble is unavoidable unless the compiler schedules an independent instruction there.

questionText: In a pipeline with an ideal CPI of 1, 20% of the instructions are branches and every branch causes a 2-cycle stall. What is the effective CPI?
explanation: CPI = 1 + f_branch × penalty = 1 + 0.20 × 2 = 1.4. 1.2 uses a 1-cycle penalty, 1.6 wrongly counts 3 cycles per branch and 3.0 adds the full penalty to every instruction.

questionText: A 5-stage pipeline with an ideal CPI of 1 uses predict-not-taken. 25% of instructions are branches and 60% of branches are taken; each taken branch costs 3 cycles, not-taken branches cost nothing, and there are no other stalls. What is its speedup over a non-pipelined version of the same datapath that takes 5 clock cycles per instruction at the same clock?
explanation: CPI = 1 + 0.25 × 0.60 × 3 = 1.45, so S = 5/1.45 ≈ 3.45. Penalising every branch gives CPI 1.75 and S = 2.86; penalising the not-taken branches instead (0.40) gives CPI 1.30 and S = 3.85.

questionText: In Stallings' six-stage instruction pipeline (FI, DI, CO, FO, EI, WO), a conditional branch is resolved at the end of its EI stage and turns out to be taken. With no branch prediction, how many instructions fetched after the branch must be discarded?
explanation: While the branch moves from FI to the end of EI, the four following instructions enter FI, DI, CO and FO behind it; all four are on the wrong path and are flushed, a penalty of 4 cycles (Stallings' example: a branch at I3 to I15 discards I4 to I7).

questionText: Which technique for dealing with conditional branches keeps a small, very fast memory of the most recently fetched instructions in sequence, so that a short loop can be executed again without fetching from memory?
explanation: Stallings lists multiple streams, prefetch of the branch target, the loop buffer, branch prediction and delayed branch. The loop buffer holds the last few sequential instructions, so a backward branch to a target inside it is served from the buffer; a branch target buffer instead stores branch addresses with their targets and prediction bits.

questionText: A loop-closing branch is taken 9 times and then not taken once each time the loop runs, and the loop is run many times. In steady state, how many mispredictions per run of the loop does a 1-bit predictor make, and how many does a 2-bit saturating-counter predictor make?
explanation: The 1-bit predictor misses at the loop exit and again at the first branch of the next run, because the exit flipped its bit. The 2-bit counter only drops from strongly to weakly taken at the exit and still predicts taken on re-entry, so it misses once per run.

questionText: What is stored in a branch target buffer (BTB)?
options: The instructions placed in the delay slots of all branches
Both the taken and not-taken paths of every branch in the program
The addresses of recently executed branch instructions together with their target addresses and prediction history
The return addresses of subroutine calls saved on the stack
explanation: The BTB is a small associative memory looked up with the address of the instruction being fetched; on a hit the predicted target is fetched at once, so a correctly predicted taken branch costs no cycles.

questionText: A pipeline with an ideal CPI of 1 has a single unified memory port. 30% of instructions are loads or stores, and each data access stalls instruction fetch for 1 cycle. How many times faster is the same pipeline with separate instruction and data caches, at the same clock?
explanation: With one port CPI = 1 + 0.30 × 1 = 1.30; with split caches the structural hazard disappears and CPI = 1, so the split design is 1.30/1 = 1.30 times faster. 1.43 misuses 1/(1 − 0.3) and 0.77 inverts the ratio.

questionText: A pipelined processor runs at 800 MHz and, because of stalls, its effective CPI is 1.6. What is its instruction throughput?
explanation: Throughput = f/CPI = 800 × 10^6/1.6 = 500 × 10^6 instructions per second = 500 MIPS. 800 MIPS is the stall-free ideal and 1280 MIPS multiplies by the CPI instead of dividing.

questionText: Why do vector processors use interleaved main memory?
options: So that the vector instruction can be decoded while memory is idle
To keep instructions and data in separate memories and so avoid structural hazards
To reduce the access time of each individual memory module
So that consecutive elements lie in different modules whose accesses overlap, letting memory deliver about one operand per clock to the pipeline
explanation: Interleaving does not make any module faster; with m modules on consecutive addresses, m accesses proceed in parallel and a new word can be delivered every clock once the stream is under way.

questionText: A vector pipeline needs one operand every 10 ns, and each memory module has a cycle time of 80 ns. With consecutive elements in consecutive modules (low-order interleaving), what is the minimum number of modules?
explanation: Each module can start a new access only every 80 ns, so 80/10 = 8 modules working in rotation are needed to deliver one word every 10 ns.

questionText: How many multiply-add operations are needed to multiply two 20 × 20 matrices?
explanation: The product has n^2 = 400 elements, each an inner product of n = 20 terms, so n^3 = 20^3 = 8000 multiply-add operations are needed. 400 counts only the inner products, 16 000 counts the multiplications and additions separately and 7600 counts only the additions.

questionText: 90% of a program's execution time can be parallelised perfectly and the rest is serial. According to Amdahl's law, what speedup is obtained on 10 processors?
explanation: S = 1/((1 − f) + f/p) = 1/(0.10 + 0.90/10) = 1/0.19 ≈ 5.26. 9.00 simply multiplies 0.9 × 10, and 1.10 swaps the serial and parallel fractions.

questionText: 4% of a program is strictly sequential and the rest can be parallelised perfectly. What is the maximum speedup with an unlimited number of processors?
options: Unlimited, because it grows with the number of processors
explanation: S_max = 1/(1 − f) = 1/0.04 = 25, because the serial 4% never shrinks. 1.04 is 1/0.96, which uses the parallel fraction instead of the serial one.

questionText: An enhancement makes one part of a program run 8 times faster, and the whole program becomes 3 times faster. What fraction of the original execution time did the enhanced part take?
Which statement correctly distinguishes a superscalar processor from a superpipelined one?
options: A superscalar processor issues several instructions per clock to multiple parallel pipelines, while a superpipelined processor splits its stages into shorter ones so that it can be clocked faster
A superscalar processor always has more pipeline stages than a superpipelined one
A superpipelined processor issues several instructions per clock, while a superscalar one issues one
Both terms describe SIMD vector units operating on whole arrays
explanation: Superscalar designs replicate pipelines and issue independent instructions in parallel; superpipelining gets more overlap from many short stages and a shorter cycle. Both exploit instruction-level parallelism within one instruction stream.

questionText: A 5-segment pipeline in which every segment takes one clock cycle processes 200 tasks. The speedup over a non-pipelined unit performing the same tasks is closest to:
explanation: Pipelined cycles = k + n − 1 = 5 + 199 = 204; non-pipelined = 200 × 5 = 1000. S = 1000/204 ≈ 4.90, just below the ceiling of k = 5.

questionText: In an instruction pipeline, instruction I2 tries to read register R1 before the preceding instruction I1 has written its result into R1. This is a:
explanation: A read that must wait for an earlier write is a read-after-write, or true data, dependency. It is normally cured by operand forwarding or a one-cycle stall.

questionText: Moving down the memory hierarchy from CPU registers towards magnetic tape, which of the following does NOT happen?
options: The frequency of access by the processor increases
explanation: Going down the hierarchy the access time and capacity rise and the cost per bit falls, while the processor accesses the lower levels less often, not more. That falling access frequency is what lets the small fast levels serve most references.

questionText: A loop counter i is read and updated in every iteration of a loop. Keeping i in a register or in the cache after its first use exploits which property of programs?
explanation: Temporal locality means that a location referenced now is likely to be referenced again soon; the repeated use of the same variable i is the classic example. Spatial and sequential locality concern neighbouring addresses such as successive array elements or instructions.

questionText: A two-level storage system has 1 GB of level-1 memory costing $10 per GB and 99 GB of level-2 memory costing $0.10 per GB. What is the average cost per GB of the whole system?
explanation: Average cost C_s = (C1 S1 + C2 S2) / (S1 + S2) = (10 × 1 + 0.10 × 99) / (1 + 99) = 19.9 / 100 = $0.199 per GB, close to the price of the large cheap level. Averaging the two prices ($5.05) ignores the sizes of the levels.

questionText: A single dynamic RAM (DRAM) storage cell consists of:
options: A cross-coupled flip-flop of about six transistors
A floating-gate transistor that traps charge
A fusible link that is blown during programming
explanation: A DRAM cell stores the bit as charge on a capacitor reached through one access transistor, which makes it dense and cheap but forces periodic refresh. Six-transistor flip-flops are SRAM cells, floating gates are EPROM/flash cells and fuses are PROM cells.

questionText: Which statement about SRAM and DRAM is NOT correct?
options: SRAM needs periodic refresh because the charge in its flip-flop slowly leaks away
DRAM is denser and cheaper per bit because each cell needs only one transistor and one capacitor
Both SRAM and DRAM are volatile
SRAM is faster than DRAM, which is why it is used for cache memory
explanation: SRAM keeps each bit in a bistable flip-flop that holds its state as long as power is applied, so it needs no refresh. It is DRAM whose capacitor charge leaks and must be refreshed every few milliseconds; the other three statements are true.

questionText: Why is the cycle time of a DRAM longer than its access time?
options: The DRAM must wait for the next refresh period after every access
The data must pass through an ECC circuit before they can be sent to the processor
The column address can be decoded only after the data of the previous access have been removed from the bus
A read discharges the cells of the selected row, so the row must be restored and the bit lines precharged before the next access can begin
explanation: Access time is the delay from address to data out, whereas cycle time is the minimum interval between the starts of two accesses. The DRAM read is destructive, so the sense amplifiers write the row back and the bit lines are precharged after the data appear, which makes the cycle time exceed the access time.

questionText: A 256M × 1 DRAM chip multiplexes its row and column addresses over the same pins using RAS and CAS, with equal numbers of row and column address bits. How many address pins does it need?
explanation: 256M = 2^28 cells need a 28-bit address. With 2^14 rows × 2^14 columns, the 14-bit row address is latched by RAS and then the 14-bit column address by CAS over the same 14 pins, halving the pin count.

questionText: A DDR SDRAM module has a 64-bit data bus and a 200 MHz bus clock. What is its peak transfer rate? (1 GB/s = 10^9 bytes per second)
explanation: DDR moves data on both clock edges: 200 × 10^6 × 2 transfers/s × 8 bytes = 3.2 × 10^9 bytes/s = 3.2 GB/s (the DDR-400 or PC-3200 rating). Ignoring the double data rate gives 1.6 GB/s, and 25.6 is the figure in gigabits per second.

questionText: A DRAM has 8192 rows, each of which must be refreshed every 64 ms, and one row refresh keeps the chip busy for 50 ns. What fraction of the time is the DRAM busy refreshing, and what is the interval between row refreshes if they are spread evenly (distributed refresh)?
explanation: Refresh work per period = 8192 × 50 ns = 409.6 µs, and 409.6 µs / 64 ms = 0.0064 = 0.64% of the time. Spread evenly, the rows are refreshed every 64 ms / 8192 = 7.8125 µs, about 7.8 µs.

questionText: How is a conventional EPROM erased?
options: Electrically, one byte at a time, while the chip stays in the circuit
Electrically, one block at a time, by commands from the processor
By exposing the chip to ultraviolet light through its quartz window, which erases the whole chip
It cannot be erased, because its bit pattern is fixed by a photomask
explanation: An EPROM is erased by ultraviolet light, typically for several minutes, and the entire chip is cleared at once. Electrical byte erase describes EEPROM, electrical block erase describes flash, and a fixed photomask describes mask ROM.

questionText: Which statement correctly distinguishes flash memory from EEPROM?
options: Flash is erased electrically a whole block at a time, whereas EEPROM can be erased and rewritten a byte at a time
Flash is erased by ultraviolet light, whereas EEPROM is erased electrically
Flash is volatile, whereas EEPROM is non-volatile
Flash can be programmed only once, whereas EEPROM can be rewritten many times
explanation: Both are electrically erasable and non-volatile. Flash gives up byte-level erasure in exchange for a smaller, denser cell and erases a block (sector) at a time, which is why it replaced EEPROM for bulk storage.

questionText: Which statement about NOR and NAND flash is correct?
options: NOR flash allows random byte reads and execute-in-place, so it suits program code; NAND flash is denser and is read and written in pages, so it suits bulk storage such as SSDs
NAND flash allows execute-in-place and random byte reads, while NOR flash is used in SSDs because it is denser
NOR and NAND flash differ only in their supply voltage
