NAND flash can be erased one byte at a time, whereas NOR flash can only be erased as a whole chip
explanation: NOR cells sit in parallel on the bit lines, giving fast random reads so the processor can execute firmware directly from the chip. NAND cells form series strings, giving a smaller cell and higher density, with page reads and writes and block erase, which makes NAND the medium for SSDs, USB drives and memory cards.

questionText: Which of the following memories retains its contents when the power is removed?
explanation: Flash stores charge on an insulated floating gate that stays for years without power, so it is non-volatile. SRAM, DRAM and SDRAM (a synchronous DRAM) all lose their contents when power is removed.

questionText: A QLC NAND flash cell stores 4 bits. How many distinct charge (threshold-voltage) levels must the cell be able to hold and distinguish?
explanation: n bits per cell need 2^n distinguishable levels: SLC 2, MLC 4, TLC 8 and QLC 2^4 = 16. More levels raise the density but shrink the margin between levels, which lowers endurance and speed.

questionText: An SSD controller receives a request to overwrite a logical page that already holds data. What normally happens?
options: The page is erased and rewritten in place, because flash can be erased one page at a time
The new data are written to a free, already erased page, the old page is marked invalid, and garbage collection later erases whole blocks to reclaim space
The whole SSD is erased and then rewritten with the new data
The data are kept only in the SSD's DRAM cache and never reach the flash
explanation: Flash cannot be rewritten in place: a page must be erased before it is programmed again, and erasure works only on whole blocks of many pages. The controller therefore maps the logical page to a fresh physical page and reclaims stale pages later, while wear levelling spreads the writes evenly.

questionText: A byte is stored with a 12-bit Hamming SEC code whose check bits occupy bit positions 1, 2, 4 and 8. On a read, the syndrome C8 C4 C2 C1 is 0101. Assuming at most one bit is in error, which statement is correct?
options: Check bits C4 and C1 are both in error
Bit position 5, which holds a data bit, is in error and is corrected by inverting it
Bit position 10, which holds a data bit, is in error
There is no error, because the syndrome contains an even number of 1s
explanation: Read as a binary number, the syndrome is the position of the flipped bit: 0101 = 5. Position 5 is not a power of two, so it is a data bit, and inverting it restores the word; reading the syndrome in reverse bit order would wrongly give 1010 = 10.

questionText: An ECC memory module protects each 64-bit data word with a SEC-DED (single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting) Hamming code. How many bits are stored per word?
explanation: SEC needs k check bits with 2^k ≥ 64 + k + 1: k = 6 gives 64 < 71 (fails) and k = 7 gives 128 ≥ 72. One more overall parity bit adds double-error detection, so 64 + 7 + 1 = 72 bits are stored; 71 bits would give SEC only.

questionText: On a multi-platter magnetic disk, the set of tracks that lie at the same radius on all recording surfaces is called a:
explanation: All heads move together on one arm, so the tracks under them at one arm position form a cylinder and can be read without another seek. A sector is part of one track, a cluster is a file-system allocation unit, and a zone is a band of adjacent tracks in multiple-zone recording.

questionText: A server disk spins at 15,000 rpm. What is its average rotational latency?
explanation: 15,000 rpm = 250 revolutions per second, so one revolution takes 1/250 s = 4 ms. On average the wanted sector is half a revolution away: 4 / 2 = 2 ms.

questionText: A disk drive has 4 platters, both surfaces of each used for data, with 20,000 tracks per surface, 500 sectors per track and 512 bytes per sector. What is its capacity? (1 GB = 10^9 bytes)
explanation: Capacity = surfaces × tracks per surface × sectors per track × bytes per sector = 8 × 20,000 × 500 × 512 = 40,960,000,000 bytes = 40.96 GB. Counting only 4 surfaces gives 20.48 GB.

questionText: A disk has an average seek time of 4 ms, rotates at 10,000 rpm and has 500 sectors per track. What is the average time to read one randomly located sector? (Ignore controller overhead.)
explanation: One revolution takes 60 / 10,000 s = 6 ms, so the average rotational latency is 3 ms and one sector passes the head in 6 / 500 = 0.012 ms. T = 4 + 3 + 0.012 = 7.012 ms; using a full revolution as the latency gives 10.012 ms.

questionText: A disk spins at 12,000 rpm and every track holds 256 KB. What is its maximum sustained transfer rate when reading whole tracks? (1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB)
explanation: 12,000 rpm = 200 revolutions per second, and one full track passes the head in each revolution: 256 KB × 200 = 51,200 KB/s = 50 MB/s. Forgetting to divide the rpm by 60 gives 3000 MB/s, and 400 is the rate in megabits per second.

questionText: A magnetic disk uses constant angular velocity (CAV) with the same number of sectors on every track. Which statement is correct?
options: Outer tracks hold more bits than inner tracks, so the transfer rate is higher on the outer tracks
The disk slows down whenever the head moves to the outer tracks
Outer tracks are longer but hold the same number of bits, so their bit density is lower and capacity is wasted; multiple-zone recording addresses this
The innermost tracks cannot be used because their bit density would be too high
explanation: With CAV and equal sectors per track, a sector is easy to locate by track and sector number, but the outermost track stores no more than the innermost one. Multiple-zone recording divides the surface into zones and gives the outer zones more sectors per track to raise the capacity.

questionText: A disk has 16 recording surfaces, 1024 tracks per surface, 256 sectors per track and 512 bytes per sector, and rotates at 6000 rpm. What are its capacity and its maximum data transfer rate? (1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB, 1 GB = 1024 MB)
explanation: Capacity = 16 × 1024 × 256 × 512 = 2^31 bytes = 2 GB. One track holds 256 × 512 B = 128 KB and passes the head 6000 / 60 = 100 times per second, so the rate is 12,800 KB/s = 12.5 MB/s; not dividing the rpm by 60 gives 750 MB/s.

questionText: A disk has an average seek time of 5 ms, rotates at 10,000 rpm and has 400 sectors of 512 bytes per track. A file of 1600 sectors occupies 4 complete adjacent tracks. Assuming the track-to-track seek time is negligible and that each track needs an average rotational latency before reading starts, how long does it take to read the file sequentially?
explanation: One revolution = 60 / 10,000 s = 6 ms, the average latency is 3 ms, and a full track is read in one revolution. First track: 5 + 3 + 6 = 14 ms; each of the other 3 tracks: 3 + 6 = 9 ms; total = 14 + 3 × 9 = 41 ms. Charging the full seek to every track gives 4 × 14 = 56 ms.

questionText: A disk has an average seek time of 5 ms, rotates at 10,000 rpm and has 400 sectors per track. The 1600 sectors of a file are scattered at random over the disk, so every sector needs its own seek and rotational latency. How long does it take to read the whole file?
explanation: Per sector: 5 ms seek + 3 ms average latency (half of 6 ms) + 6 / 400 = 0.015 ms transfer = 8.015 ms. For 1600 sectors: 1600 × 8.015 ms = 12,824 ms ≈ 12.82 s. Using a full revolution as the latency gives 17.62 s.

questionText: Compared with a magnetic hard disk, which components of the access time are essentially absent in a solid-state drive (SSD)?
options: Rotational latency only; an SSD still has a seek time
Seek time only; an SSD still has a rotational latency
explanation: An SSD has no moving arm and no spinning platters, so there is no mechanical seek and no wait for a sector to rotate under a head. Only the controller overhead, the flash read time and the transfer time remain.

questionText: Which statement correctly describes constant linear velocity (CLV) recording as used on a CD-ROM?
options: The disc spins at a constant rpm, so the outer part of the track holds fewer bits per millimetre
Data are recorded on concentric tracks that all have the same number of sectors
The spiral track passes the laser at a constant speed, so the disc spins faster when the head reads near the centre than near the outer edge
The laser head moves at a constant speed while the disc stays stationary
explanation: With CLV the bit density is uniform along the single spiral track, which maximises the capacity. To keep the linear speed constant, the rotation rate must fall as the head moves outwards (roughly 500 rpm at the centre to 200 rpm at the edge for a 1× CD); constant rpm with lower outer density describes CAV.

questionText: Why can a Blu-ray disc hold much more data per layer than a CD or a DVD of the same diameter?
options: It spins at constant angular velocity, so its outer tracks hold more data
It uses a shorter-wavelength (405 nm blue-violet) laser, which allows smaller pits and a narrower track pitch
It stores the data magnetically instead of as pits and lands
It records data on both surfaces of the disc at the same time
explanation: The smallest spot a laser can be focused to scales with its wavelength (CD 780 nm, DVD 650 nm, Blu-ray 405 nm), and Blu-ray also uses a lens with a larger numerical aperture. Smaller pits on a tighter spiral raise the capacity from about 0.7 GB (CD) and 4.7 GB (DVD) to 25 GB per layer.

questionText: Which storage medium offers only sequential access, so that the time to reach a record depends strongly on where it is stored?
explanation: Tape must be wound past all the data in between to reach a record, which is sequential access. A disk gives direct access (seek to a track, then wait for the sector), and RAM gives random access with the same access time for every location.

questionText: A tape drive needs on average 30 s to position the tape at the start of a file and then transfers data at 300 MB/s. How long does it take to read a 6 GB file? (1 GB = 1000 MB)
explanation: For a sequential-access device T_N = T_A + n / R = 30 s + 6000 MB / (300 MB/s) = 30 + 20 = 50 s. Omitting the positioning time gives 20 s, and reading the rate as 300 Mbit/s gives 30 + 160 = 190 s.

questionText: Which RAID level stripes data blocks across several disks but stores no redundant information at all?
explanation: RAID 0 only stripes, giving high throughput and 100% usable capacity, but the failure of any one disk loses the data of the array. RAID 1 mirrors, and RAID 4 and RAID 5 add parity.

questionText: Two 4 TB disks are configured as a RAID 1 mirrored pair. Which statement about the array is correct?
options: It provides 8 TB of usable space and survives the failure of either disk
It provides 4 TB of usable space and survives the failure of either disk
It provides 4 TB of usable space but cannot survive any disk failure
It provides 2 TB of usable space and survives the failure of both disks
explanation: RAID 1 writes every block to both disks, so the usable space equals one disk: 2 × 4 TB / 2 = 4 TB. Because each disk holds a complete copy, the array keeps working if either disk fails.

questionText: Which RAID level uses block-level striping with all parity blocks on one dedicated disk, so that this parity disk becomes a bottleneck when many small writes occur?
explanation: RAID 4 uses large (block) strips and a single parity disk that every write must update, so small writes queue up on it. RAID 5 removes the bottleneck by rotating the parity over all disks, and RAID 3 uses bit- or byte-level strips with parallel access.

questionText: Which RAID level stripes data at the bit level and uses a Hamming code, stored on several check disks, to correct errors?
explanation: RAID 2 spreads very small strips over synchronised disks and computes a Hamming code across corresponding bits, which needs several check disks. Since drives already have internal error correction it is not used in practice; RAID 3 needs only a single parity disk.

questionText: Five 2 TB disks form a RAID 5 array. What is its usable capacity, and how many simultaneous disk failures can it survive?
explanation: RAID 5 uses one disk's worth of space for distributed parity: (5 − 1) × 2 TB = 8 TB. The parity can rebuild any single failed disk, but a second failure before the rebuild finishes loses data; 6 TB with two-failure tolerance would be RAID 6.

questionText: Six 4 TB disks are configured as RAID 6. What is the usable capacity?
explanation: RAID 6 keeps two independent check blocks (P and Q) in every stripe, which costs two disks' worth of space: (6 − 2) × 4 TB = 16 TB. In return it survives any two simultaneous disk failures; 20 TB would be RAID 5 and 24 TB RAID 0.

questionText: An array is to be built from four identical disks and must survive the failure of any one disk. Which RAID level gives the largest usable capacity?
explanation: With 4 disks RAID 5 keeps 3 disks of data (75%), while mirrored pairs (RAID 10) and RAID 6 keep only 2 disks of data (50%). RAID 0 keeps all 4 disks but cannot survive any failure, so it does not meet the requirement.

questionText: In a RAID 5 stripe the data blocks and the parity block hold (one byte of each shown, in hexadecimal) D0 = 5A, D1 = 3C, D2 = F0 and P = 96. The application overwrites D1 with 0F. Using the read-modify-write method, what is the new parity byte and how many disk accesses does this small write need?
options: A5; 2 accesses (write new D1 and new P)
A5; 4 accesses (read old D1 and old P, then write new D1 and new P)
99; 4 accesses (read old D1 and old P, then write new D1 and new P)
33; 3 accesses (read old D1, then write new D1 and new P)
explanation: P_new = P_old ⊕ D1_old ⊕ D1_new = 96 ⊕ 3C ⊕ 0F = AA ⊕ 0F = A5, which matches 5A ⊕ 0F ⊕ F0 = A5. The old data and old parity must be read before the new data and parity are written, so one small write costs 2 reads + 2 writes = 4 accesses.

questionText: In a virtual memory system, a page fault occurs when:
options: The required block is not in the cache and must be fetched from main memory
The TLB has no entry for the page, although the page is in main memory
Two processes try to access the same physical frame at the same time
The referenced page is not in main memory, so it must be brought in from secondary storage
explanation: A page fault is raised when the page-table entry shows that the page is not resident; the operating system then loads it from disk or SSD. A cache miss and a TLB miss are far cheaper events that need no transfer from secondary storage.

questionText: The translation lookaside buffer (TLB) is best described as:
options: A buffer that holds dirty cache lines until they are written back to main memory
The area of the disk that holds pages swapped out of main memory
A register that holds the starting address of the page table
A small, fast cache of recently used page-table entries that speeds up virtual-to-physical address translation
explanation: Without a TLB every memory reference would need an extra memory access to read the page table; the TLB keeps recent translations so most references are translated almost instantly. The swap area and the page-table base register are separate structures.

questionText: A system uses 1 KB pages (1 KB = 1024 bytes) and byte addresses. Virtual page 4 of a process is mapped to physical frame 9. Which physical address corresponds to virtual address 5000 (decimal)?
explanation: Page number = 5000 div 1024 = 4 and offset = 5000 − 4 × 1024 = 904. Page 4 is in frame 9, so the physical address = 9 × 1024 + 904 = 9216 + 904 = 10120.

questionText: A system has 32-bit virtual byte addresses, 4 KB pages (1 KB = 1024 bytes) and a single-level page table with 4-byte entries. How many bits form the virtual page number, and how large is the full page table of one process?
explanation: The offset is log2(4096) = 12 bits, so the page number has 32 − 12 = 20 bits and the table has 2^20 entries. Its size is 2^20 × 4 bytes = 4 MB (1 MB = 1024 KB); forgetting the 4-byte entry size gives 1 MB.

questionText: Main memory access time is 100 ns and servicing a page fault takes 8 ms. If one memory access in 100,000 causes a page fault, what is the effective access time, using EAT = (1 − p) × memory access time + p × page-fault service time? (Ignore TLB and cache effects.)
explanation: EAT = (1 − p) × 100 ns + p × 8 ms with p = 10^-5: 0.99999 × 100 + 10^-5 × 8,000,000 ns = 99.999 + 80 ≈ 180 ns. Even such rare faults slow memory by about 80%, because each costs 80,000 normal accesses; writing 8 ms as 8,000 ns gives the 100.08 ns distractor.

questionText: Main memory access time is 200 ns, a page fault takes 10 ms to service, and EAT = (1 − p) × 200 ns + p × 10 ms, where p is the page-fault rate. To keep the slowdown caused by page faults below 5% (EAT below 210 ns), p must be below about:
explanation: Require (1 − p) × 200 + p × 10,000,000 < 210 ns, so p × 9,999,800 < 10 and p < 1.0 × 10^-6: at most about one fault per 1,000,000 accesses. Writing 10 ms as 1,000,000 ns gives the 1-in-100,000 distractor.

questionText: A paged system has a TLB with a lookup time of 10 ns and a hit ratio of 90%, a main-memory access time of 100 ns and a single-level page table held in main memory. The TLB is searched first; on a TLB miss the page-table entry is read from memory before the data access. Ignoring page faults and caches, what is the effective memory access time?
explanation: TLB hit: 10 + 100 = 110 ns; TLB miss: 10 + 100 (page-table entry) + 100 (data) = 210 ns. EAT = 0.9 × 110 + 0.1 × 210 = 99 + 21 = 120 ns, compared with 200 ns if there were no TLB at all.

questionText: A hard disk rotates at 7200 rpm. Its average rotational latency is approximately:
explanation: 7200 rpm is 120 revolutions per second, so one revolution takes 8.33 ms. The average wait is half a revolution, 4.17 ms.

questionText: The minimum number of check bits required by a Hamming single-error-correcting code for 16 data bits is:
explanation: The condition is 2^k ≥ m + k + 1. For m = 16, k = 4 gives 16 < 21 (fails) and k = 5 gives 32 ≥ 22, so 5 check bits are needed.

questionText: A program makes 2000 memory references, of which 1840 are found in the cache. What is the hit ratio?
explanation: Hit ratio h = hits / total references = 1840 / 2000 = 0.92. The miss ratio is 1 − h = 160 / 2000 = 0.08.

questionText: A cache has an access time of 5 ns, main memory has an access time of 80 ns, and the hit ratio is 0.95. Both are accessed simultaneously, so a hit takes 5 ns and a miss takes 80 ns in total. What is the average access time?
explanation: Simultaneous model: t_avg = h t_c + (1 − h) t_m = 0.95 × 5 + 0.05 × 80 = 4.75 + 4 = 8.75 ns. Charging the cache time again on a miss (the hierarchical model) would give 5 + 0.05 × 80 = 9.00 ns.

questionText: A processor looks in its cache (2 ns) first and accesses main memory (60 ns) only after a miss has been detected (hierarchical, look-through access). The hit ratio is 0.9. What is the average access time?
explanation: Every access spends t_c and each miss adds t_m: t_avg = t_c + (1 − h) t_m = 2 + 0.1 × 60 = 8.0 ns, the same as 0.9 × 2 + 0.1 × (2 + 60). The simultaneous model would give 0.9 × 2 + 0.1 × 60 = 7.8 ns.

questionText: A cache with an access time of 10 ns and a main memory with an access time of 50 ns are accessed simultaneously, so a miss costs 50 ns in total. What hit ratio is needed for an average access time of 18 ns?
explanation: 18 = 10h + 50(1 − h) = 50 − 40h, so h = 32 / 40 = 0.80. With the hierarchical model, 18 = 10 + 50(1 − h), the answer would be 0.84 instead.

questionText: A cache holds 32 KB of data in lines of 64 bytes (1 KB = 1024 bytes). How many lines does it have?
explanation: Lines m = cache size / line size = 32 × 1024 / 64 = 32,768 / 64 = 512. Taking 1 KB as 1000 bytes gives 500, and treating the 64-byte line as 64 bits gives 4096.

questionText: In a byte-addressable memory, a cache uses 128-byte blocks. How many address bits form the word (byte-offset) field?
explanation: The offset must select one of the 128 bytes of a block, so it needs log2(128) = 7 bits. Treating the 128 bytes as 1024 bits would wrongly give 10 bits.

questionText: A 64 KB, 8-way set-associative cache uses 64-byte blocks (1 KB = 1024 bytes). How many sets does it have?
explanation: Lines = 65,536 / 64 = 1024, and sets = lines / ways = 1024 / 8 = 128, so the set field is 7 bits wide. 1024 is the number of lines, not the number of sets.

questionText: How many tag comparisons are made in parallel on each access to a 4-way set-associative cache that has 256 sets?
explanation: The set field selects one set, and only the 4 tags stored in that set are compared with the tag of the address, so 4 comparators are needed. A fully associative cache with the same 1024 lines would need 1024 comparisons, and a direct-mapped cache only 1.

questionText: A cache has 8 lines and is organised as 8-way set-associative. This organisation is equivalent to:
options: A cache without a tag field
explanation: With k = 8 ways and 8 lines there is v = 8 / 8 = 1 set, so any block can be placed in any line, which is fully associative mapping. At the other extreme, k = 1 (8 sets of one line) is direct mapping.

questionText: Which cache mapping function needs no replacement algorithm?
explanation: In direct mapping each block can go to exactly one line (block mod lines), so on a miss the block in that line is simply replaced and there is no choice to make. Associative and set-associative mappings must choose a victim using LRU, FIFO, LFU or random replacement.

questionText: With fully associative mapping, the cache interprets a main-memory address as:
options: A tag field, a line field and a word field
A tag field, a set field and a word field
A line field and a word field only
A tag field and a word (offset) field only
explanation: A block may be placed in any line, so there is nothing to index: the whole block number is the tag and is compared with the tags of all lines at once. Tag | line | word is direct mapping and tag | set | word is set-associative mapping.

questionText: A direct-mapped cache has 128 lines. Into which line is main-memory block number 300 placed?
explanation: Direct mapping uses line = block mod lines = 300 mod 128 = 300 − 256 = 44. The quotient 300 div 128 = 2 is the tag stored with the line.

questionText: A direct-mapped cache stores 16 KB of data in 32-byte lines, and the processor uses 32-bit byte addresses (1 KB = 1024 bytes). What are the widths of the tag, line and word fields?
explanation: Word = log2(32) = 5 bits; lines = 16,384 / 32 = 512, so line = 9 bits; tag = 32 − 9 − 5 = 18 bits. Using log2 of the cache size in bytes (14) as the line field is a common slip.

questionText: A fully associative cache of 64 KB with 16-byte lines is used with 24-bit byte addresses (1 KB = 1024 bytes). How many bits wide is each tag?
explanation: Fully associative mapping has no line or set field, so tag = address bits − word bits = 24 − log2(16) = 24 − 4 = 20 bits. A direct-mapped cache of the same size (4096 lines, 12 line bits) would need only 8 tag bits.

questionText: A byte-addressable machine has 16-bit addresses, a 2 KB direct-mapped cache and 16-byte blocks, so an address is split as tag 5 | line 7 | word 4. Into which cache line is address 3A7C (hexadecimal) placed, and what tag is stored with it?
explanation: 3A7C = 00111 0100111 1100 in binary, so the tag is 00111 = 7, the line is 0100111 = 39 and the word is 1100 = 12. Equivalently, block = 3A7 hex = 935, line = 935 mod 128 = 39 and tag = 935 div 128 = 7.

questionText: A word-addressable main memory has 2^24 words of 32 bits. A direct-mapped cache holds 16K words (K = 1024) in blocks of 8 words. What are the widths of the tag, line and word fields of the address?
explanation: The address selects a word, so it has 24 bits and the word field is log2(8) = 3 bits. Lines = 16K / 8 = 2048, giving 11 line bits, and tag = 24 − 11 − 3 = 10 bits; a 5-bit offset would apply only to byte addressing.

questionText: A 4 KB direct-mapped cache with 32-byte blocks is used with 16-bit byte addresses (1 KB = 1024 bytes). Which address maps to the same cache line as address 1240 (hexadecimal) but belongs to a different memory block?
explanation: There are 4096 / 32 = 128 lines, so an address splits as tag 4 | line 7 | word 5. 1240 hex is block 146, line 146 mod 128 = 18, tag 1; 3240 hex is block 402, line 402 mod 128 = 18, tag 3, so it competes for the same line. 1250 is inside the same block as 1240, and 1340 and 1640 map to lines 26 and 50.

questionText: A direct-mapped cache splits a 32-bit address as tag 16 | line 10 | word 6. The same cache, with the same total size and block size, is reorganised as 4-way set-associative. What are the new field widths?
explanation: The 1024 lines in groups of 4 give 256 sets, so the set field is 8 bits; the block size is unchanged, so the word field stays 6 bits and tag = 32 − 8 − 6 = 18 bits. Each doubling of associativity moves one bit from the index to the tag.

questionText: A 4-way set-associative cache holds 32 KB of data in 64-byte blocks, and the processor uses 32-bit byte addresses (1 KB = 1024 bytes). For address 1234ABCD (hexadecimal), which set is selected and which tag is compared?
explanation: Lines = 32,768 / 64 = 512 and sets = 512 / 4 = 128, so the fields are word 6, set 7 and tag 19 bits. Tag = address >> 13 = 91A5, set = (address >> 6) mod 128 = 2F and offset = 0D; using 8 set bits, as for 256 sets, would give set AF and tag 48D2.

questionText: A direct-mapped, write-through cache holds 32 KB of data in 64-byte lines for a processor with 32-bit byte addresses, and each line has one valid bit (1 KB = 1024 bytes). What is the total number of storage bits in the cache, including tags and valid bits?
explanation: Lines = 32,768 / 64 = 512 (9 line bits), word = 6 bits and tag = 32 − 9 − 6 = 17 bits. Each line stores 64 × 8 = 512 data bits + 17 tag bits + 1 valid bit = 530 bits, so the total is 512 × 530 = 271,360 bits, about 3.5% more than the 262,144 data bits.

questionText: A 2-way set-associative write-back cache holds 64 KB of data in 64-byte blocks for 32-bit byte addresses (1 KB = 1024 bytes). Each line stores a tag, a valid bit and a dirty bit (ignore replacement bits). How many bytes do the tags and status bits occupy in total?
explanation: Lines = 65,536 / 64 = 1024 and sets = 512 (9 bits), word = 6 bits, so tag = 32 − 9 − 6 = 17 bits. Overhead = 1024 × (17 + 1 + 1) = 19,456 bits = 2432 bytes; a direct-mapped cache would need only 16 tag bits (2304 bytes), and leaving out the status bits gives 2176 bytes.

questionText: The first reference ever made to a block always misses, whatever the size or organisation of the cache. Such a miss is called a:
explanation: Compulsory misses occur because a block must be brought into the cache at its first use; only larger blocks or prefetching reduce them. Capacity misses come from a working set larger than the cache, and conflict misses from blocks competing for the same line or set.

questionText: Which category of cache misses is eliminated completely by making a cache fully associative while keeping its size and block size unchanged?
explanation: Conflict misses happen when blocks collide in one line or set while other lines are still usable; a fully associative cache can place a block anywhere, so they disappear. Compulsory and capacity misses depend on first use and on the cache size, not on placement.

questionText: Which statement about cache size is NOT correct?
options: Doubling the cache size always halves the miss rate
A larger cache reduces capacity misses
Once the cache holds the program's working set, extra capacity gives diminishing returns
A larger cache tends to be slightly slower because of more address decoding and longer wires
explanation: The miss rate falls as the cache grows, but with diminishing returns rather than in proportion; once the working set fits, doubling the size barely helps. The other three statements are standard design trade-offs.

questionText: An array of 1024 four-byte integers, aligned to a block boundary, is read once in order a[0], a[1], …, a[1023]. The cache starts empty, is large enough to hold the whole array and uses 32-byte blocks. What is the miss rate of these reads?
explanation: Each 32-byte block holds 8 integers, so only the first access to each block misses: 1024 / 8 = 128 misses out of 1024 reads = 12.5%. Dividing by the 4096 bytes instead of the 1024 reads gives 3.125%, and 16-byte blocks would give 25%.

questionText: Two arrays A and B of 4-byte integers start at byte addresses 0 and 8192. A loop reads A[0], B[0], A[1], B[1], …, A[255], B[255]. The cache is 8 KB (1 KB = 1024 bytes) with 32-byte blocks and starts empty. What are the miss rates if the cache is direct-mapped, and if it is 2-way set-associative with LRU (same size and block size)?
explanation: The 8192-byte offset is a multiple of the 8 KB cache size, so A[i] and B[i] fall in the same direct-mapped line and evict each other on every access: 100% misses. In the 2-way cache both blocks fit in one set, so only the first access to each 32-byte block (one in 8 elements) misses: 12.5%.

questionText: Which replacement algorithm may evict a heavily used block simply because it was the first of the blocks in its set to be loaded?
explanation: FIFO replaces the block that has been in the set longest, using only the order of loading and ignoring how often or how recently the block was used. LRU would keep a block that is being referenced repeatedly.

questionText: Which statement about random replacement is correct?
options: It always gives a higher hit ratio than LRU
It can be used only with direct-mapped caches
It needs a counter in each line that is incremented on every reference
It picks the victim at random among the lines of the set, needs almost no bookkeeping hardware, and in simulations is only slightly worse than LRU
explanation: Random replacement ignores the usage history, so it needs no age bits or counters, and simulation studies show its hit ratio is only slightly below that of usage-based algorithms. A per-line reference counter describes LFU.

questionText: How can LRU replacement be implemented in a 2-way set-associative cache?
options: With a 2-bit counter per line that counts its accesses, replacing the line with the smaller count
With a single bit per set that records which of its two lines was referenced more recently; on a miss the other line is replaced
By always replacing the line that was loaded first, using a pointer in each set
It cannot be done in hardware, so the operating system must choose the victim
explanation: With only two lines per set, one bit of state is enough to remember which line was used less recently (Stallings describes it as a USE bit in each line, set when the line is referenced while the other line's bit is cleared). The access counter describes LFU and the load-order pointer describes FIFO, neither of which is LRU.

questionText: A direct-mapped cache has 4 lines and starts empty. The processor references main-memory blocks in the order 0, 1, 4, 1, 0, 5, 1, 4, 2, 0. How many of these references are hits?
explanation: Line = block mod 4, so blocks 0 and 4 share line 0 and blocks 1 and 5 share line 1: 0 M, 1 M, 4 M, 1 H, 0 M, 5 M, 1 M, 4 M, 2 M, 0 M. Only one reference hits; a 2-way LRU cache of the same size would score 4 hits.

questionText: A 2-way set-associative cache with 4 sets and 16-byte blocks uses LRU replacement and starts empty. The processor reads byte addresses (hexadecimal) 000, 040, 004, 080, 010, 048, 000, 0C0, 014, 08C. How many hits occur, and which blocks does set 0 hold at the end?
explanation: Block = address div 16 gives 0, 4, 0, 8, 1, 4, 0, 12, 1, 8, and set = block mod 4 puts all but block 1 in set 0. LRU: 0 M, 4 M, 0 H, 8 M (4 out), 1 M, 4 M (0 out), 0 M (8 out), 12 M (4 out), 1 H, 8 M (0 out), so 2 hits leave blocks 12 and 8 in set 0 (FIFO would score 3 hits).

questionText: A fully associative cache with 3 lines starts empty. The processor references blocks 3, 4, 2, 3, 4, 5, 3, 4, 5, 1. How many hits occur with LRU and with FIFO replacement respectively?
explanation: LRU: 3 M, 4 M, 2 M, 3 H, 4 H, 5 M (2 out), 3 H, 4 H, 5 H, 1 M, giving 5 hits. FIFO: 5 M evicts 3, the oldest block, then 3 M evicts 4 and 4 M evicts 2, followed by 5 H and 1 M, giving only 3 hits because FIFO discarded blocks still in use.

questionText: In a write-back cache, when is a modified word copied to main memory?
options: When its cache line is replaced and the line's dirty bit is set
Immediately, on every write to the cache
Only when the program that wrote it terminates
On every clock cycle, by a background controller
explanation: Write-back updates only the cache and sets the line's dirty (update) bit; main memory is written only when a dirty line is evicted. Writing memory on every write is write-through.

questionText: Under a write-allocate policy, what happens on a write miss?
options: The word is written directly to main memory and the block is not loaded into the cache
The block containing the address is loaded into the cache and the write is then performed in the cache
The write is cancelled and retried after another block has been evicted
The whole cache is flushed to main memory before the write
explanation: Write-allocate (fetch on write) brings the block in so that later accesses to it hit; it pairs naturally with write-back. Writing straight to memory without loading the block is no-write-allocate, also called write-around.

questionText: A program writes the same cached variable 500 times and then its cache line is evicted. The line was already in the cache before the first write, and there is no write buffer or write combining. How many main-memory write operations occur with write-through and with write-back respectively?
explanation: Write-through sends every write to memory: 500 writes. Write-back only sets the dirty bit on each write and copies the block to memory once, when the dirty line is evicted: 1 write.

questionText: Which statement about cache write policies is correct?
options: Write-through needs a dirty bit in every line to know which lines must be copied back
With write-through, main memory always holds a current copy of every cached word, so a DMA device reading memory never sees stale data
Write-back causes more memory traffic than write-through when the same word is written many times
With write-back, an I/O module can safely read main memory directly without any cache-coherence measure
explanation: Write-through updates memory on every write, keeping it valid for I/O modules and other bus masters at the cost of extra traffic. The dirty bit belongs to write-back, which writes each modified block once on eviction and can leave memory stale, so DMA needs snooping or a cache flush.

questionText: A cache uses write-through with no-write-allocate and initially does not contain the block holding address X. The processor performs: write X, read X, read X, write X, read X. How many cache misses occur, and how many would occur with write-allocate instead?
explanation: With no-write-allocate the first write misses and updates memory only, the next read misses and loads the block, and the remaining three accesses hit: 2 misses. With write-allocate the first write already loads the block, so only that access misses.

questionText: A direct-mapped, write-back, write-allocate cache has 4 lines and starts empty. The processor issues these accesses (operation and block number): R0, W0, R4, W4, R0, W5, R1, R8. How many cache misses occur, and how many dirty blocks are written back to main memory during the sequence?
explanation: Line = block mod 4: R0 M; W0 H (dirty); R4 M, write back 0; W4 H (dirty); R0 M, write back 4; W5 M, allocated in line 1 and dirty; R1 M, write back 5; R8 M, but block 0 in line 0 is clean, so no write-back. That gives 6 misses and 3 write-backs.

questionText: A write-back, write-allocate cache with 64-byte blocks serves 1,000,000 references with a miss rate of 2%. Every miss replaces a valid block, and 30% of the replaced blocks are dirty. How many bytes are transferred between the cache and main memory? (Ignore any other traffic.)
explanation: Misses = 0.02 × 1,000,000 = 20,000, each fetching 64 bytes: 1,280,000 bytes. Dirty victims = 0.3 × 20,000 = 6000, each written back as 64 bytes: 384,000 bytes, so the total is 1,664,000 bytes (writing back every victim would give 2,560,000).

questionText: The cache size is kept fixed while the block (line) size is increased step by step from very small to very large. Which statement is correct?
options: The hit ratio rises steadily, because every miss brings in more data
The hit ratio does not change; only the miss penalty changes
The hit ratio first rises because of spatial locality, then falls as fewer lines fit and useful blocks are evicted sooner, while the miss penalty keeps growing
The miss penalty falls, because fewer misses need to be serviced
explanation: Larger blocks prefetch neighbouring words (spatial locality), but with a fixed size the number of lines drops, raising conflict and capacity misses, and each miss must transfer more bytes. The hit ratio therefore peaks at a moderate block size, 32 to 128 bytes in typical designs.

questionText: On a cache miss, main memory needs 20 clock cycles before the first data appear; the 64-byte block is then transferred over an 8-byte-wide bus, one transfer per cycle. What is the miss penalty?
explanation: Miss penalty = latency + (block size / bus width) × cycles per transfer = 20 + (64 / 8) × 1 = 20 + 8 = 28 cycles. Paying the 20-cycle latency again for each of the 8 transfers would give 8 × 21 = 168 cycles.

questionText: Why do most processors use split level-1 caches (a separate instruction cache and data cache)?
options: Because a split cache always has a higher hit ratio than a unified cache of the same total size
Because instructions and data use different address widths
So that the pipeline can fetch an instruction and access data in the same cycle without competing for one cache
Because data must never be cached, only instructions
explanation: A split (Harvard-style) L1 removes the structural hazard between the instruction-fetch stage and the memory-access stage. A unified cache of the same size balances its contents automatically and usually hits slightly more often, which is why L2 and L3 are unified.

questionText: In a two-level cache, 5% of all processor references miss in L1, and 20% of the references that reach L2 miss there as well. What is the global miss rate of L2, the fraction of all processor references that must go to main memory?
explanation: Global L2 miss rate = L1 miss rate × L2 local miss rate = 0.05 × 0.20 = 0.01 = 1%. The 20% is L2's local miss rate, and 4% (0.05 × 0.8) is the fraction of all references that hit in L2.

questionText: Which statement about the design of a two-level cache hierarchy is correct?
options: L1 should be larger than L2 because it is closer to the processor
L1 is kept small and fast to minimise the hit time, while L2 is larger and often more associative to minimise the accesses that go to main memory
An L2 cache is useful only if it is faster than the L1 cache
Once an L2 cache is added, the L1 hit ratio no longer affects the average access time
explanation: L1 sits on the processor's critical path, so its hit time limits the clock cycle; L2 exists to catch L1 misses before they pay the full memory penalty, so its size and associativity matter more than its speed.

questionText: L1 hit time is 1 cycle and 4% of references miss in L1. L2 hit time is 10 cycles and its local miss rate is 25%. Main memory takes 100 cycles. Using AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty at each level, what is the average memory access time?
explanation: L1 miss penalty = L2 hit time + L2 local miss rate × memory time = 10 + 0.25 × 100 = 35 cycles, so AMAT = 1 + 0.04 × 35 = 2.4 cycles. Without the L2 cache it would be 1 + 0.04 × 100 = 5.0 cycles.

questionText: A processor has a base CPI of 1.2 with a perfect cache. Each instruction makes on average 1.5 memory references (one instruction fetch and 0.5 data references), 2% of all references miss in the cache, and the miss penalty is 50 cycles. What is the effective CPI?
explanation: Memory-stall cycles per instruction = references per instruction × miss rate × miss penalty = 1.5 × 0.02 × 50 = 1.5, so CPI = 1.2 + 1.5 = 2.7, 2.25 times slower than with a perfect cache. Counting only the instruction fetches gives 1.2 + 1.0 = 2.2.

questionText: A 4-way set-associative cache of 8 KB uses 32-byte blocks in a system with 32-bit byte addresses. The number of tag bits in the address is:
explanation: Lines = 8192 / 32 = 256; sets = 256 / 4 = 64, so the set field is 6 bits and the word field is log2(32) = 5 bits. Tag = 32 − 6 − 5 = 21 bits.

questionText: In Vahid and Givargis's classification, which memory has its bits set by masks during chip fabrication, giving it the lowest write ability and the highest storage permanence?
explanation: Mask-programmed ROM connections are fixed when the chip is fabricated, so it can never be rewritten (lowest write ability) and its bits never change unless the chip is damaged (highest permanence). OTP ROM is programmed once by the user with a ROM programmer, while EPROM and flash can be erased and rewritten.

questionText: Which memory sits at the low end of the storage-permanence scale, starting to lose its bits almost immediately after they are written unless it is refreshed?
explanation: A DRAM cell stores its bit as charge on a tiny capacitor that leaks away within milliseconds, so every row must be refreshed periodically. SRAM holds data without refresh as long as power is applied, and NVRAM and EEPROM are nonvolatile.

questionText: Which group lists only in-system programmable memories, i.e. memories that the embedded processor itself can write without the chip being removed from the board?
options: Mask ROM, OTP ROM, EEPROM and flash
OTP ROM, EPROM, NVRAM and SRAM
explanation: In-system programmable memories are those in the high and middle range of write ability: RAM, NVRAM, EEPROM and flash. Mask ROM is fixed at fabrication, and OTP ROM and EPROM need an external programmer.

questionText: Which statement about one-time programmable (OTP) ROM is correct?
options: It is erased by exposing the die to ultraviolet light through a quartz window
The user programs it once by having a ROM programmer blow fuses; it cannot be erased, so its write ability is very low and its storage permanence very high
It can be rewritten byte by byte by the processor while installed in the system
Its contents are defined by the metal masks used when the chip is fabricated
explanation: An OTP ROM ships blank, and a ROM programmer blows the fuses where connections should not exist; a blown fuse cannot be restored. Being cheaper than erasable parts and hard to change by accident, it is common in final products. UV erasure describes EPROM, in-system byte writes describe EEPROM, and mask-defined contents describe mask ROM.

questionText: Vahid lists typical uses of ROM in an embedded system. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
options: Holding the stack and the local variables of running tasks
Storing the program of a general-purpose processor
Storing constant data such as lookup tables
Implementing a combinational circuit directly as a truth table
explanation: A ROM is not written during normal operation, so it holds programs, constant data and the truth tables of combinational functions. The stack and local variables change constantly and must live in RAM.

questionText: On Vahid's write-ability scale, which memories lie in the middle range, where the embedded processor itself can write the memory but much more slowly than it can read it?
explanation: The high end is RAM, written quickly by the processor; the middle range is EEPROM and flash, written in-system but slowly; the lower range is EPROM and OTP ROM, which need an external programmer; the low end is mask ROM, written only during fabrication.

questionText: A program changes a single byte inside a flash block that already holds data. Why can this take much longer than rewriting one byte of EEPROM?
options: Flash must be exposed to ultraviolet light before any byte can be rewritten
The whole block must be read out, erased and written back with the modified byte, because flash can erase only whole blocks
Flash can be written only by an external programmer after the chip is removed
Each flash write must wait until a DRAM-style refresh cycle has finished
explanation: Programming can only change bits from 1 to 0; restoring 1s needs an erase, and flash erases whole blocks. Updating one byte in place therefore means copying the block, erasing it and reprogramming it, whereas EEPROM can erase and rewrite the single word.

questionText: Which memory keeps its contents after external power is removed and can still be written as fast as it is read, with no limit on the number of writes?
options: Battery-backed NVRAM (SRAM with its own battery)
explanation: Battery-backed NVRAM is SRAM with a permanently connected battery, so writes run at SRAM speed with unlimited cycles and the data survive power loss. Flash and EEPROM are nonvolatile but write slowly and wear out, and DRAM is volatile.

questionText: What is pseudo-static RAM (PSRAM)?
options: An SRAM with its own battery so that it becomes nonvolatile
An SRAM whose contents are copied into EEPROM when power fails
A DRAM with a built-in refresh controller, so that to the processor it behaves like an SRAM
A mask ROM whose contents are copied into SRAM at power-up
explanation: PSRAM uses dense one-transistor DRAM cells but refreshes itself internally, giving a low-cost, high-density substitute for SRAM. Battery-backed SRAM and SRAM paired with EEPROM or flash are the two forms of NVRAM.

questionText: An embedded product needs (i) calibration constants that are changed a few times a year in the field, one byte at a time, (ii) a large nonvolatile area for storing photos, and (iii) firmware for a product made in millions of units that will never be updated. Which assignment is the best match?
explanation: EEPROM suits small data rewritten occasionally word by word, flash suits large nonvolatile data such as photos (dense, fast block erase), and mask ROM gives the lowest unit cost for high-volume code that never changes because its mask NRE is spread over millions of units.

questionText: Which list orders memories correctly from HIGHEST to LOWEST storage permanence?
explanation: Mask ROM keeps its bits for the life of the product, flash retains data without power for about ten years, SRAM keeps data only while powered, and DRAM loses data within milliseconds unless refreshed.

questionText: Many EEPROMs provide a READY/BUSY output. What is it used for during in-system programming?
options: It shows that the EEPROM is being refreshed, as a DRAM would be
It tells the processor that an internal erase-and-program cycle lasting milliseconds is still in progress, so the next write must wait
It signals that the ultraviolet erase of the chip has finished
It requests the system bus so that the EEPROM can perform a DMA transfer
explanation: EEPROM writes are slow because each word is erased and then programmed with an internally generated higher voltage. The on-chip controller holds BUSY until the write finishes, and the processor polls this pin (or a status bit) before the next write.

questionText: A memory is organised as 16K × 4 (K = 1024). How many address lines and data lines does it have, and what is its capacity in bits?
explanation: 16K = 2^14 words need log2(16,384) = 14 address lines; each word has 4 bits, so there are 4 data lines and 16,384 × 4 = 65,536 bits (64 Kbit).

questionText: A combinational circuit with 6 inputs and 3 outputs is to be implemented directly as a ROM truth table (the inputs drive the address lines and the outputs are the data lines). What is the minimum ROM size?
explanation: Every input combination needs its own ROM word: 2^6 = 64 words, each holding the 3 output bits, so 64 × 3 = 192 bits.

questionText: A 32K × 8 SRAM chip (K = 1024) has separate address pins, 8 bidirectional data pins, three control inputs (CS, OE, WE), one supply pin and one ground pin. What is the minimum number of pins?
explanation: 32K = 2^15 words need 15 address pins; adding 8 data, 3 control and 2 power pins gives 15 + 8 + 3 + 2 = 28, the familiar 28-pin 32K × 8 SRAM package.

questionText: A memory chip has 11 address inputs and 16 data lines (K = 1024). What is its capacity?
explanation: 11 address inputs select 2^11 = 2048 words and each word has 16 bits, so the chip holds 2048 × 16 = 32,768 bits = 4096 bytes = 4 KB (a 2K × 16 organisation).

questionText: A 64-Kbit static RAM is sold in two organisations, 64K × 1 and 8K × 8 (K = 1024), each with one bidirectional data pin per data bit. How many address-plus-data pins does each organisation need?
explanation: 64K × 1 needs 16 address + 1 data = 17 pins; 8K × 8 needs 13 address + 8 data = 21 pins. The bit count is the same, but the wider organisation trades address pins for data pins.

questionText: A 4K × 32 memory is built from 4K × 8 chips. How many chips are needed, how many address lines does the composed memory use, and is a chip-select decoder required?
options: 4 chips, 12 address lines, a 2-to-4 decoder on the two highest address lines
explanation: Only the width grows (8 → 32 bits), so 32 / 8 = 4 chips sit side by side, sharing A11–A0 (2^12 = 4096 words) and one chip select; each supplies 8 of the 32 data bits and no decoder is needed.

questionText: A 64K × 8 memory is built from 16K × 8 chips on a 16-bit address bus A15–A0, with each chip holding one contiguous quarter of the addresses. Which address lines go to every chip, and which drive the chip-select decoder?
options: A15–A0 to every chip; no decoder is needed
A11–A0 to every chip; A15–A12 to a 4-to-16 decoder
A13–A0 to every chip; A15–A14 to a 2-to-4 decoder
A14–A0 to every chip; A15 to a 1-to-2 decoder
explanation: Each 16K chip needs log2(16,384) = 14 lines, A13–A0, shared by all chips. There are 64K / 16K = 4 chips, so the remaining two lines A15–A14 feed a 2-to-4 decoder whose outputs drive the four chip selects.

questionText: A 64K × 16 memory is built from 16K × 4 chips using a decoder on the high-order address bits. How many chips are needed, and how many chips does each decoder output enable at the same time?
options: 16 chips; each decoder output enables 1 chip
16 chips; each decoder output enables 4 chips
8 chips; each decoder output enables 2 chips
4 chips; each decoder output enables 4 chips
explanation: Rows = 64K / 16K = 4 and columns = 16 / 4 = 4, so 4 × 4 = 16 chips. A 2-to-4 decoder selects a row, and all 4 chips of that row share its output because together they supply the 16-bit word.

questionText: A 2 MB memory organised as 2M × 8 (M = 2^20) is to be built from 256K × 4 chips (K = 2^10), ignoring any address multiplexing. How many chips are needed, what decoder selects a row, and how many address lines go to every chip?
options: 16 chips, a 3-to-8 decoder, 18 lines to every chip
8 chips, a 3-to-8 decoder, 18 lines to every chip
16 chips, a 4-to-16 decoder, 17 lines to every chip
16 chips, a 3-to-8 decoder, 21 lines to every chip
explanation: Rows = 2M / 256K = 8 and columns = 8 / 4 = 2, so 16 chips. The memory needs 21 address lines (2^21 words): 18 of them (A17–A0, 2^18 = 256K) go to every chip, and the top 3 (A20–A18) drive a 3-to-8 decoder that selects one row of two chips.

questionText: A byte-addressable 16 MB memory (MB = 2^20 bytes) with a 32-bit data bus is built from 1M × 8 chips arranged in rows of four chips, one chip per byte lane; A1–A0 generate the byte enables. Which address lines connect to every chip, and which drive the row decoder?
options: A19–A0 to every chip; A23–A20 to a 4-to-16 decoder
A21–A2 to every chip; A23–A22 and A1–A0 to a 4-to-16 decoder
A19–A0 to every chip; A21–A20 to a 2-to-4 decoder
A21–A2 to every chip; A23–A22 to a 2-to-4 decoder
explanation: 16 MB needs 24 byte-address bits. A1–A0 choose the byte lane, each 1M-word chip needs 20 lines (A21–A2), and 16 chips / 4 per row = 4 rows are selected by A23–A22 through a 2-to-4 decoder.

questionText: A 4096-byte memory is to be built from 256 × 8 RAM chips. How many chips are needed, how many address lines are common to all chips, and what size of decoder generates the chip selects?
explanation: 4096 / 256 = 16 chips, and 4096 bytes need 12 address lines. Each chip uses log2(256) = 8 of them (A7–A0) in common, and the remaining 4 (A11–A8) feed a 4-to-16 decoder, one output per chip.

questionText: How many 64-Kbit RAM chips organised as 8K × 8 are needed to build 256 KB of byte-organised memory (K = 1024), and how many address inputs does the chip-select decoder need?
explanation: 256 KB = 256K × 8 = 2,097,152 bits and one chip holds 65,536 bits, so 32 chips, each 8 bits wide, stacked as 256K / 8K = 32 rows. Selecting one of 32 rows needs log2 32 = 5 decoder inputs (a 5-to-32 decoder).

questionText: An 8-bit, byte-addressable system must fill the address range 0000H–7FFFH with RAM built from 4K × 4 chips (K = 1024). How many chips are needed, and how are they arranged?
explanation: 0000H–7FFFH spans 8000H = 32,768 bytes = 32K × 8. Rows = 32K / 4K = 8 and columns = 8 / 4 = 2, so 16 chips; each row of two chips covers 4 KB (1000H addresses) and supplies both 4-bit halves of the byte.

questionText: In a byte-addressable system, a memory chip is selected for addresses 8000H through 9FFFH. What is its capacity (KB = 1024 bytes)?
explanation: Size = 9FFFH − 8000H + 1 = 2000H = 8192 bytes = 8 KB.

questionText: A 16 KB RAM (KB = 1024 bytes) in a byte-addressable system starts at address 4000H. What is its last address?
explanation: 16 KB = 4000H bytes, so the last address is 4000H + 4000H − 1 = 7FFFH; 8000H is the first address after the RAM.

questionText: Four 8K × 8 chips are mapped one after another from address 0000H in a byte-addressable system, chip 0 first. What address range does chip 2 occupy?
explanation: Each chip spans 8K = 2000H addresses: chip 0 at 0000H–1FFFH, chip 1 at 2000H–3FFFH and chip 2 at 4000H–5FFFH.

questionText: In a system with a 16-bit address bus, a 3-to-8 decoder (74LS138, permanently enabled) has its inputs C B A connected to A15 A14 A13, and each output selects one 8 KB memory chip. Which address range does output Y5 select?
explanation: Y5 is active when A15 A14 A13 = 101 while A12–A0 range over 8 KB, so the range runs from 1010 0000 0000 0000 = A000H to 1011 1111 1111 1111 = BFFFH.

questionText: A 74LS138 decoder has C B A = A13 A12 A11 and is enabled only when A15 = 0 and A14 = 1 (address bus A15–A0). Each output selects a 2 KB chip whose address inputs are A10–A0. Which address range does output Y3 select?
explanation: The enables require A15 A14 = 01 and Y3 requires A13 A12 A11 = 011, so the address is 0101 1xxx xxxx xxxx: from 0101 1000 0000 0000 = 5800H to 0101 1111 1111 1111 = 5FFFH.

questionText: A small computer has four 128 × 8 RAM chips (RAM 1 at 0000H–007FH, RAM 2 at 0080H–00FFH, and so on up to 01FFH) and one 512 × 8 ROM at 0200H–03FFH, fully decoded on address lines A9–A0. Which lines select one of the four RAM chips, and which line separates RAM from ROM?
options: A1–A0 select the RAM chip; A9 = 0 selects RAM and A9 = 1 selects ROM
A9–A8 select the RAM chip; A7 separates RAM from ROM
A8–A7 select the RAM chip; A9 = 0 selects RAM and A9 = 1 selects ROM
A8–A7 select the RAM chip; A9 = 1 selects RAM and A9 = 0 selects ROM
explanation: Each RAM chip uses A6–A0 (128 = 2^7) and the four chips occupy consecutive 80H blocks, so A8 A7 = 00, 01, 10, 11 pick RAM 1–4. The ROM uses A8–A0 (512 = 2^9), and A9 is 0 throughout 0000H–01FFH (RAM) and 1 throughout 0200H–03FFH (ROM).

questionText: An 8085 system (16-bit address bus, byte-addressable) needs 16 KB of ROM starting at 0000H built from 4K × 8 EPROMs, followed immediately by 8 KB of RAM built from 2K × 8 SRAMs (K = 1024). What is the RAM address range, and how many memory chips are used in total?
explanation: ROM: 16 KB / 4 KB = 4 EPROMs covering 0000H–3FFFH. RAM: 8 KB / 2 KB = 4 SRAMs from 4000H to 4000H + 2000H − 1 = 5FFFH. Total 4 + 4 = 8 chips.

questionText: In a 64 KB byte-addressable space, ROM occupies 0000H–3FFFH and RAM occupies 8000H–FFFFH, with nothing else decoded. How much memory is installed, and how much address space is unused (KB = 1024 bytes)?
explanation: ROM: 3FFFH − 0000H + 1 = 4000H = 16 KB; RAM: FFFFH − 8000H + 1 = 8000H = 32 KB. Installed = 48 KB, leaving 64 − 48 = 16 KB (4000H–7FFFH) unused.

questionText: An 8 KB memory chip uses address lines A12–A0, and its chip select is driven by A15 alone (selected when A15 = 0); A14 and A13 are not decoded. In a 16-bit address space, at how many different address ranges (images) does the chip appear?
explanation: Two address lines (A14 and A13) are ignored, so each location answers to 2^2 = 4 addresses: the chip appears at 0000H–1FFFH, 2000H–3FFFH, 4000H–5FFFH and 6000H–7FFFH.

questionText: A 2 KB chip uses A10–A0, and its chip select is A15 AND (NOT A14), with A13–A11 not decoded, on a 16-bit address bus. Over which total address range does the chip respond, and how many images does it have?
explanation: The chip is selected when A15 A14 = 10, i.e. anywhere in 8000H–BFFFH (16 KB). Three lines (A13–A11) are ignored, so the 2 KB chip repeats 2^3 = 8 times: 8000H–87FFH, 8800H–8FFFH, …, B800H–BFFFH.

questionText: Which statement about partial address decoding is NOT correct?
options: It uses fewer decoding gates than full decoding
Each device appears at several mirrored (fold-back) address ranges
Every memory location still has exactly one unique address
Later expansion is harder because the mirror images already occupy address space
explanation: Partial decoding ignores some high-order address lines, so each location answers to 2^m addresses, where m is the number of ignored lines; a unique address for every location is the property of full decoding. Partial decoding saves logic but wastes address space and complicates expansion.

questionText: In linear-select decoding, each of several high-order address lines is wired directly to the chip select of one memory chip, with no decoder. What is its main drawback?
options: It wastes most of the address space, and an address with two select lines active enables two chips at once, causing bus contention on a read
It needs a large multi-level decoder, which makes it the most expensive scheme
It gives every location a unique address but needs more address lines than the CPU has
It can be used only with ROM chips, never with RAM
explanation: Linear select needs no decoder at all, which is its advantage. But each line serves only one chip, most address combinations are unusable or mirrored, and software must never activate two select lines together, or two chips will drive the data bus at once.

questionText: When several memory chips are stacked to increase the number of words, their data lines are wired together. Why does this not cause a conflict?
options: The data lines are ORed together, so every chip may drive the bus at once
Each chip drives a different bit position of the data word
The decoder converts the outputs of all chips into one serial stream
The chips have tri-state outputs, and only the chip whose chip select is active drives the bus while the others stay in the high-impedance state
explanation: A deselected chip's output buffers float (high impedance), so exactly one chip, chosen by the decoder through its chip select, places data on the shared bus. Different bit positions per chip describe width expansion, not depth expansion.

questionText: A design needs a 2K × 4 memory, but the only chip available is 8K × 8 (K = 1024). Following Vahid's approach, how is the larger chip used?
options: It cannot be used, because the chip must match the required size exactly
Connect A10–A0 to the system, hold the two unneeded high-order address inputs (A12, A11) at a fixed level, and leave four data lines unused
Use four 8K × 8 chips in parallel so that the widths match
Connect only A3–A0, because 4 data bits are needed
explanation: When the available memory is larger than required, the unneeded high-order address bits are simply ignored (held constant) and the extra data lines are left unused; the chip then behaves as a 2K × 4 memory, and the remaining cells are wasted.

questionText: Which statement about memory composition is NOT correct?
options: Increasing the number of words needs a decoder on the high-order address lines
Chips connected side by side to widen the word share all address lines and the chip select
Doubling the word width from 8 to 16 bits needs one extra address line and a 1-to-2 decoder
Chips needed = (words required / words per chip) × (bits required / bits per chip)
explanation: Width expansion only places chips side by side; all of them are selected together and the number of address lines does not change. Extra address lines and a decoder are needed only when the number of words grows.

questionText: On a typical SRAM chip, what is the difference between chip select (CS) and output enable (OE)?
options: CS chooses between read and write, while OE selects the row address
CS and OE are two names for the same pin
OE is used only during writes, to latch the data into the cells
CS activates the chip for any read or write access, while OE turns on its output buffers so that the selected chip drives the data bus during a read
explanation: Chip select (chip enable) decides whether the chip takes part in the current cycle, output enable controls its tri-state data outputs during reads, and the separate write enable decides whether the cycle is a write.

questionText: Four 8-bit-wide memory chips are placed side by side to form a 32-bit word, and each chip has a cycle time of 50 ns. What is the maximum data bandwidth of the composed memory (MB = 10^6 bytes)?
explanation: All four chips are accessed in the same cycle, so every 50 ns delivers 4 bytes: 4 B / 50 ns = 80 × 10^6 B/s = 80 MB/s (640 Mbit/s). One chip alone would give 20 MB/s.

questionText: A 64-word memory is built from four 16-word modules using low-order interleaving, i.e. the two least significant address bits select the module. In which module, and at which word within that module, is address 29 (decimal) stored?
explanation: 29 = 011101 in binary. Low-order interleaving uses the two LSBs (01) as the module number and the upper four bits (0111 = 7) as the word within the module. High-order (block) selection would instead give module 1, word 13.

questionText: An EEPROM needs 5 ms for each internal write cycle and can write either a single byte or a whole 64-byte page per cycle. Ignoring bus transfer time, how long does it take to store 256 bytes (starting on a page boundary) byte by byte, and how long using page writes?
options: 1.28 s byte by byte; 5 ms with page writes
1.28 s byte by byte; 20 ms with page writes
1.28 s byte by byte; 320 ms with page writes
20 ms byte by byte; 1.28 s with page writes
explanation: Byte mode: 256 cycles × 5 ms = 1280 ms = 1.28 s. Page mode: 256 / 64 = 4 pages × 5 ms = 20 ms, which is why EEPROM drivers group writes into pages.

questionText: A data logger erases and rewrites one flash block every minute, and each block is rated for 100,000 erase cycles. Approximately how long will the flash last if wear levelling spreads the erasures evenly over 64 blocks (1 year = 365 days)?
explanation: Available erasures = 64 × 100,000 = 6.4 × 10^6; at one per minute that is 6.4 × 10^6 min ÷ (60 × 24 × 365 min per year) ≈ 12.2 years. Without wear levelling one block would wear out after 100,000 min ≈ 69 days.

questionText: A 4-to-16 decoder drives the chip selects of 4K × 8 memory chips, one chip per decoder output (K = 1024). What is the largest memory that can be built this way, and how many address lines does it use?
explanation: 16 outputs select 16 chips of 4 KB, giving 16 × 4 KB = 64 KB. Each chip needs 12 lines (A11–A0) and the decoder adds 4 inputs (A15–A12), so 16 address lines in total; the 16 decoder outputs are chip selects, not address lines.

questionText: Which of the following memories has the highest write ability according to Vahid's classification?
explanation: Write ability rises from mask ROM (not writable) through EPROM (external programmer) and EEPROM (slow in-system writes) to SRAM and DRAM, which the processor writes at full speed without limit.

questionText: An 8K × 8 memory is to be built from 2K × 8 chips. How many high-order address lines must be connected to the chip-select decoder?
explanation: 8K needs 13 address lines and each 2K chip uses 11 of them (A0–A10). The remaining 2 lines (A11–A12) feed a 2-to-4 decoder that selects one of the four chips.

questionText: To obtain a 2K × 16 memory from 2K × 8 chips, the correct arrangement is:
options: Two chips in parallel sharing all address lines and chip select; no decoder needed
Two chips selected alternately by a 1-to-2 decoder on the highest address line
Four chips, two per row, with a 2-to-4 decoder on the two highest address lines
One chip, because 2K × 8 already provides the required 2K words
explanation: Only the width changes (8 to 16 bits) while the number of words stays 2K, so the two chips are accessed together: same A0–A10, same CS, one supplying data bits 0–7 and the other bits 8–15.

questionText: A processor allows 120 ns from address output to data sampling in one bus cycle and runs at 25 MHz (40 ns clock). A memory with 200 ns access time is attached. The minimum number of wait states required is:
explanation: The shortfall is 200 − 120 = 80 ns; each wait state adds one 40 ns clock, so ceil(80 / 40) = 2 wait states are needed.

questionText: In programmed I/O the CPU repeatedly reads the interface's status register until the flag bit shows that the device is ready. What is this waiting called?
explanation: The CPU stays in a loop testing the flag and does no useful work until it changes, which is busy waiting or polling. Cycle stealing and burst are DMA modes, and handshaking is a two-wire timing protocol between two units.

questionText: Which method of I/O data transfer needs the least additional hardware in the computer?
explanation: Programmed I/O needs only a status flag in the interface that software tests. Interrupts add request lines and priority logic, DMA adds a controller with address, count and control registers, and an IOP is a complete processor.

questionText: A printer must be polled 2,000 times per second, and each poll costs 250 clock cycles on a 100 MHz CPU. What percentage of CPU time is spent polling the printer?

Under programmed I/O each 16-bit word costs the CPU 40 clock cycles (status test, read, store and pointer update) on a 200 MHz processor. Ignoring all other work, what is the highest data rate the CPU can sustain (1 MB = 10^6 bytes)?
explanation: Words per second = 200 × 10^6 ÷ 40 = 5 × 10^6; with 2 bytes per word that is 10 × 10^6 B/s = 10 MB/s. 5 MB/s forgets that a word is 2 bytes, and 80 is the rate in megabits per second.

questionText: A network interface buffers incoming data in a 16-byte FIFO and receives 2 MB/s (1 MB = 10^6 bytes). The CPU polls it just often enough never to overflow: every poll finds a full FIFO and empties it at a cost of 400 clock cycles on a 500 MHz CPU. What percentage of CPU time does this take?
explanation: Polls per second = 2 × 10^6 ÷ 16 = 125,000; cycles per second = 125,000 × 400 = 5 × 10^7; fraction = (5 × 10^7) ÷ (5 × 10^8) = 10%. Polling once per 4-byte word instead would give 40%.

questionText: When does a CPU normally check for, and accept, a pending enabled interrupt request?
options: Immediately, in the middle of the current bus cycle
At the end of the current instruction's execute phase, before the next fetch
Only when the running program executes a return instruction
At the start of every memory read cycle
explanation: The interrupt is tested after the execute phase of each instruction, so the interrupted instruction is always complete and only the PC and status need saving. DMA requests, by contrast, may be granted between bus cycles.

questionText: A device transfers 12,500 bytes per second, one byte at a time. Under program-controlled I/O the CPU busy-waits for every byte; under interrupt-driven I/O each byte costs only a 5 µs interrupt overhead (the transfer itself is negligible). By what factor does interrupt-driven I/O reduce the CPU time spent per byte?
explanation: Interval per byte = 1 ÷ 12,500 s = 80 µs, all of which is wasted in busy waiting; interrupt I/O costs 5 µs, so the gain is 80 ÷ 5 = 16. 6.25 is the interrupt overhead as a percentage of the interval (5 ÷ 80).

questionText: Each interrupt from a device costs 10 µs of CPU time in total (context save, service and restore), and the device raises 40,000 interrupts per second. What percentage of CPU time does the device consume?
explanation: CPU time per second = 40,000 × 10 µs = 0.4 s, i.e. 40% of the CPU. 60% is the time left for other programs.

questionText: A 1 KB block (1 KB = 1024 bytes) is read with one interrupt per byte. Each interrupt costs 2 µs to save the context, 3 µs to run the service routine and 1 µs to restore. How much CPU time does the whole block cost?
explanation: Per byte: 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 µs; for 1024 bytes: 1024 × 6 µs = 6144 µs = 6.144 ms. Counting only the routine gives 3.072 ms, forgetting the restore gives 5.12 ms, and counting bits (8192) gives 49.152 ms.

questionText: A 50 MHz CPU checks for interrupts only at the end of an instruction. Its longest instruction takes 20 clock cycles, the interrupt acknowledge cycle takes 4 cycles, and the hardware then pushes 6 registers at 2 cycles each before the first ISR instruction. What is the worst-case interrupt latency?
explanation: Worst case = 20 + 4 + 6 × 2 = 36 cycles; at 20 ns per cycle that is 36 × 20 ns = 0.72 µs. Leaving out the instruction gives 0.32 µs, leaving out the pushes 0.48 µs, and one cycle per push 0.60 µs.

questionText: In Mano's basic computer, what happens during the interrupt cycle?
options: The return address (PC) is stored in memory location 0, PC is set to 1 and IEN is cleared
PC is pushed onto a stack, PC is loaded with a vector supplied by the device and IEN is set
The accumulator is stored in location 0 and PC is set to 0
PC is stored in location 1, PC is set to 0 and IEN is set
explanation: The interrupt cycle is RT0: AR ← 0, TR ← PC; RT1: M[AR] ← TR, PC ← 0; RT2: PC ← PC + 1, IEN ← 0. The return address is saved in location 0, execution continues at location 1 (which holds a branch to the ISR) and further interrupts are disabled.

questionText: A program attempts to divide by zero and the processor responds with an interrupt. How is this interrupt classified?
explanation: Internal interrupts, also called traps, arise from erroneous use of an instruction or data, such as overflow, divide by zero or an invalid opcode. External interrupts come from devices and timers, and software interrupts are requested deliberately by an instruction.

questionText: What is a software interrupt normally used for?
options: Switching from user mode to supervisor mode to request an operating-system service
Signalling that a peripheral has finished a transfer
Reporting an imminent power failure that cannot be masked
Handing the system bus to a DMA controller
explanation: A software interrupt is initiated by an instruction in the program, most commonly a supervisor-call instruction that switches the CPU to supervisor mode so the OS can perform a service. Device completion is an external interrupt and power failure uses a non-maskable interrupt.

questionText: Which kind of interrupt input is normally reserved for catastrophic events such as an impending power failure, because the program cannot disable it?
explanation: A non-maskable interrupt bypasses the interrupt-enable flag and the mask register, so it is always recognised; that makes it suitable for power-fail or memory-parity emergencies.

questionText: In a vectored interrupt system, where does the CPU obtain the starting address of the interrupt service routine?
options: From a fixed memory location that is the same for every device
From the interrupting device, which places a vector address on the data bus during the interrupt acknowledge cycle
From the program counter value saved on the stack
From the DMA controller's address register
explanation: With vectored interrupts the source supplies its own vector (VAD) during the acknowledge cycle, so the CPU branches directly to that device's routine. A fixed branch location for all devices describes a non-vectored interrupt.

questionText: Five devices, D1 (nearest the CPU) to D5, are daisy-chained on the interrupt acknowledge line. D2 and D4 have pending requests when the CPU acknowledges. Which statement is correct?
options: D4 places its vector because the acknowledge enters the chain from the far end
D1 blocks the acknowledge because it is the device nearest the CPU
Both D2 and D4 place their vectors on the bus and the CPU accepts the lower one
D2 places its vector address on the bus and sets its PO to 0, so D3, D4 and D5 receive PI = 0
explanation: D1 has no request, so with PI = 1 and RF = 0 it passes PO = 1. D2 has PI = 1 and RF = 1, so it enables its VAD and sets PO = 0; every device after it, including D4, sees PI = 0 and waits.

questionText: Which is a disadvantage of daisy-chain priority interrupt compared with the parallel priority scheme?
options: It needs a separate interrupt request line and mask bit for every device
Priorities are fixed by the physical position of the devices and cannot be changed by software
It cannot supply a vector address to the CPU
Devices far from the CPU always receive the fastest service
explanation: In a daisy chain the device nearest the CPU always wins, so priority is set by wiring; a low-priority device can also be delayed indefinitely. The parallel scheme, which does use one request line and mask bit per device, lets software alter priorities through the mask register.

questionText: In a parallel priority interrupt unit, what is the purpose of the mask register?
options: It stores the vector address supplied by the device
It holds the return address of the interrupted program
It lets the program enable or disable each interrupt request individually
It counts how many times each device has interrupted
explanation: Each interrupt register bit is ANDed with its mask bit before the priority encoder, so software can disable or re-enable individual sources and thereby change the effective priority set.

questionText: A 4-input priority encoder with I0 as the highest priority produces x = I0'I1', y = I0'I1 + I0'I2' and IST = I0 + I1 + I2 + I3. What are its outputs when I0 I1 I2 I3 = 0 0 1 1?
explanation: x = I0'I1' = 1·1 = 1; y = I0'I1 + I0'I2' = 1·0 + 1·0 = 0; IST = 1 because at least one request is present. Code 10 selects I2, the highest-priority active input; 11 would wrongly select I3.

questionText: Four devices use a parallel priority interrupt with I0 the highest priority. Requests are pending on I1, I2 and I3, and the mask register (1 = enabled) holds M0 M1 M2 M3 = 1 0 1 1. The priority encoder output xy forms the vector as VAD = 40h + 4 × xy. Which vector address does the CPU receive?
explanation: Masking removes I1, leaving I2 and I3; I2 has the higher priority, so xy = 10 (binary) = 2 and VAD = 40h + 4 × 2 = 48h. Ignoring the mask would select I1 (44h), and forgetting the factor 4 gives 42h.

questionText: Eight devices share one interrupt line, and the service routine identifies the source by testing device flags in priority order at 0.4 µs per test; a device's routine starts as soon as its flag test succeeds. If only the lowest-priority device (tested last) is requesting, how much time is spent testing flags before its routine starts?
explanation: The routine tests all eight flags, the last one successfully: 8 × 0.4 µs = 3.2 µs. Counting only the seven failed tests gives 2.8 µs; this delay is why software polling is the slowest priority method.

questionText: Why is interrupt-driven I/O unsuitable for a high-speed disk that delivers a word every few hundred nanoseconds?
options: The save, service and restore overhead is paid for every word and can exceed the interval between words
Disk interfaces cannot generate interrupt requests
Interrupt-driven I/O needs more main memory than DMA
An interrupt can be recognised only once per program
explanation: With one interrupt per word the CPU spends its time entering and leaving service routines; when that overhead approaches or exceeds the word interval the CPU is swamped or data is lost. DMA moves the whole block with one interrupt at the end.

questionText: What does a CPU do when a DMA controller activates the bus request (BR or HOLD) line?
options: It saves its registers on the stack and jumps to a DMA service routine
It completes the current bus cycle, places its buses in the high-impedance state and asserts bus grant (BG or HLDA)
It aborts the current instruction and restarts it after the transfer
It sends the starting address and word count to the controller over the data bus
explanation: The CPU finishes the bus cycle in progress, floats its address, data and read/write lines and answers with bus grant; the controller then becomes bus master. The registers are programmed earlier, not at the bus request.

questionText: Which pairs of signals does a DMA controller use to coordinate with the CPU and with the I/O device respectively?
options: DMA request and DMA acknowledge with the CPU; bus request and bus grant with the device
Bus request and bus grant with the CPU; DMA request and DMA acknowledge with the device
Interrupt request and interrupt acknowledge with the CPU; a strobe with the device
Read and write with the CPU; bus request and bus grant with the device
explanation: The controller asks the CPU for the buses with BR and waits for BG; with the device it exchanges DMA request (the device is ready) and DMA acknowledge (the transfer is being made). An interrupt goes to the CPU only when the count reaches zero.

questionText: How many DMA transfers are needed to move an 8 KB buffer (1 KB = 1024 bytes) over a 16-bit data bus, one bus-width word per transfer?
explanation: 8 KB = 8192 bytes; a 16-bit bus moves 2 bytes per transfer, so 8192 ÷ 2 = 4096 transfers. 8192 counts bytes, 2048 assumes a 32-bit bus and 65,536 counts bits.

questionText: A DMA controller must be able to address any byte of a 64 MB byte-addressable memory (1 MB = 2^20 bytes) and hold word counts up to 5000. What are the minimum widths of its address and word-count registers?
explanation: 64 MB = 2^6 × 2^20 = 2^26 bytes, so 26 address bits; 5000 lies between 2^12 = 4096 and 2^13 = 8192, so 13 count bits. 29 bits would count bits instead of bytes, and 12 bits holds only up to 4095.

questionText: A DMA controller's address register is loaded with 1000h and its word-count register with 200 (decimal). Memory is byte-addressable and each transfer moves one 32-bit word, so the address increases by 4 and the word count decreases by 1 per transfer. What do the two registers hold after 120 transfers?
explanation: Address = 1000h + 120 × 4 = 1000h + 480 = 1000h + 1E0h = 11E0h; count = 200 − 120 = 80. Incrementing by 1 gives 1078h, and adding 480 as if it were hexadecimal gives 1480h.
