questionText: Which sequence correctly orders a DMA input transfer?
options: Controller interrupts CPU → CPU loads address and count → device raises DMA request → words move → controller releases bus

CPU loads address, count and control registers → device raises DMA request → controller gets bus grant → words move with address incremented and count decremented → controller interrupts CPU at count zero
Device raises DMA request → CPU copies each word to the controller → controller writes memory → CPU decrements the count
CPU asserts bus request → controller grants the bus → CPU loads address and count → words move → device interrupts the controller
explanation: The CPU first programs the controller through programmed I/O and carries on; the device's DMA request makes the controller ask for and receive the bus, the data moves directly between device and memory, and the only interrupt comes when the word count reaches zero.

questionText: Which statement correctly contrasts the points at which a CPU can respond to a DMA request and to an interrupt?
options: Both are recognised only at the end of an instruction
An interrupt can be taken after any bus cycle, while a DMA request waits for the end of the program
A DMA request is recognised only when the interrupt enable flag IEN is 1
A DMA request can be granted after any bus cycle, even mid-instruction, whereas an interrupt is recognised only at the end of an instruction
explanation: Granting the bus does not disturb the program state, so the CPU can pause at any DMA breakpoint between bus cycles; an interrupt changes the flow of control and is therefore taken only at an instruction boundary.

questionText: A DMA controller in burst mode moves 4000 bytes over a 16-bit data bus, one bus-width word per 250 ns memory cycle. For how long is the CPU kept off the bus?
explanation: Transfers = 4000 ÷ 2 = 2000; time = 2000 × 250 ns = 500 µs. Counting bytes gives 1 ms; assuming a 32-bit or 64-bit bus gives 250 µs or 125 µs.

questionText: Which DMA mode moves a whole block in one continuous bus tenure, giving the highest transfer rate but keeping the CPU off the bus until the block is finished?
explanation: In burst mode the controller keeps the bus until the word count reaches zero, so the block moves at memory speed while the CPU cannot use the bus. Cycle stealing interleaves single words with CPU cycles, and transparent DMA uses only idle cycles.

questionText: Which statement about cycle-stealing DMA is NOT correct?
options: The controller takes the bus for one word and then returns it to the CPU
The CPU saves its registers before each stolen cycle and restores them afterwards
The CPU may be delayed by one memory cycle for each word transferred
For a whole block it is slower than burst mode because the bus changes hands for every word
explanation: A stolen cycle only pauses the CPU's bus activity; no context is saved because no program switch occurs. The other statements are true: one word per grant, one lost cycle per word, and extra request/grant overhead per word.

questionText: Which statement about transparent (hidden) DMA is correct?
options: It halts the CPU for the whole block but hides the transfer from the operating system
It uses the CPU registers to hold the data, so no DMA controller is needed
It is the fastest DMA mode because it needs no bus arbitration
It transfers only in bus cycles the CPU is not using, so the CPU is never slowed, but its rate is the lowest of the DMA modes
explanation: Transparent DMA needs logic that detects idle bus cycles (for example while the CPU decodes or executes internally) and uses only those, so there is no slowdown at all; the price is the slowest transfer rate.

questionText: A cycle-stealing DMA controller transfers 32-bit words from a device producing 10 MB/s (1 MB = 10^6 bytes), and each stolen memory cycle lasts 80 ns. By what fraction is the CPU slowed, assuming it would otherwise use every bus cycle?
explanation: Words per second = 10 × 10^6 ÷ 4 = 2.5 × 10^6, so one word every 400 ns; slowdown = 80 ns ÷ 400 ns = 20%. Treating each byte as a transfer gives 80%, and 16-bit or 64-bit words give 40% or 10%.

questionText: In cycle-stealing mode the CPU slowdown must not exceed 10%. Each stolen memory cycle takes 50 ns and moves one 32-bit word. What is the highest device data rate the DMA controller can serve (1 MB = 10^6 bytes)?
explanation: Allowed stolen time is 0.1 s per second, so words per second = 0.1 ÷ 50 ns = 2 × 10^6; with 4 bytes per word that is 8 × 10^6 B/s = 8 MB/s. 2 MB/s forgets the 4 bytes per word, and 64 is the rate in megabits per second.

questionText: A system bus has a 100 ns cycle and the CPU uses 60% of all bus cycles. What is the maximum rate at which a transparent-mode DMA controller can move words?
explanation: Bus cycles per second = 1 ÷ 100 ns = 10^7; transparent DMA may use only the 40% the CPU leaves idle, so 0.4 × 10^7 = 4 × 10^6 words/s. 6 × 10^6 uses the busy fraction and 10^7 assumes the whole bus.

questionText: A 256-word block is moved by DMA. Acquiring the bus (bus request to bus grant) takes 3 clock cycles, releasing it takes 1 cycle and each word transfer takes 2 cycles. How many clock cycles of bus activity does the block need in burst mode and in cycle-stealing mode (bus acquired and released for every word)?
options: 512 in burst mode and 1536 in cycle stealing
516 in burst mode and 1024 in cycle stealing
516 in burst mode and 1536 in cycle stealing
1536 in burst mode and 516 in cycle stealing
explanation: Burst: 3 + 256 × 2 + 1 = 516 cycles. Cycle stealing: 256 × (3 + 2 + 1) = 1536 cycles, because the handover overhead is repeated for every word. Leaving out the handover in burst mode gives 512.

questionText: A device produces data at 256 KB/s into a DMA controller's buffer (1 KB = 1024 bytes). Each time 4 KB has accumulated, the controller bursts it into memory over a 32-bit bus at one word per 100 ns memory cycle. For what percentage of the time is the CPU denied the bus?
explanation: Burst = (4096 ÷ 4) × 100 ns = 102.4 µs; filling the buffer takes 4 KB ÷ 256 KB/s = 15.625 ms; blocked fraction = 102.4 µs ÷ 15,625 µs = 0.66%. Counting bytes gives 2.62%, a 16-bit bus 1.31%, and 99.34% is the time the CPU keeps the bus.

questionText: A DMA controller's 16-bit byte-count register allows at most 65,536 bytes per programming. At minimum, how many times must it be programmed (acquiring the bus once each time in burst mode) to move a 20,000 KB file (1 KB = 1024 bytes)?
explanation: File = 20,000 × 1024 = 20,480,000 bytes; 20,480,000 ÷ 65,536 = 312.5, which must be rounded up to 313. Rounding down leaves bytes unmoved, 306 comes from 1 KB = 1000 bytes, and 625 assumes only 32,768 bytes per programming.

questionText: A disk streams data at 8 MB/s into memory by DMA in 16 KB blocks (1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB). Each block costs the 500 MHz CPU 1000 cycles to set up the controller and 500 cycles for the completion interrupt. What fraction of CPU time is spent on the disk?
explanation: Blocks per second = 8 MB/s ÷ 16 KB = 8192 KB ÷ 16 KB = 512; cycles = 512 × (1000 + 500) = 768,000 per second; fraction = 768,000 ÷ (500 × 10^6) = 0.154%. Using only the set-up gives 0.102% and only the completion 0.051%.

questionText: An interrupt service routine moves 1000 bytes from a device to memory. After two set-up instructions (initialise address, initialise count) it loops: load byte from device; store byte to memory; increment address; decrement count; branch if count ≠ 0. Load and store take 2 clock cycles each and every other instruction 1 cycle. A DMA controller would need 50 cycles of initialisation plus 2 cycles per byte. What is the approximate speed-up of the DMA design?
explanation: Program: 2 + 1000 × (2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1) = 7002 cycles; DMA: 50 + 1000 × 2 = 2050 cycles; speed-up = 7002 ÷ 2050 ≈ 3.42. Ignoring both overheads gives 3.50, and counting load and store as 1 cycle gives 2.44.

questionText: In a single-bus, detached DMA configuration each word is first read from the I/O module into the DMA module and then written to memory, one bus cycle each. How much bus time is used to move 1500 words if one bus cycle is 80 ns?
explanation: Each word crosses the bus twice: 1500 × 2 × 80 ns = 240 µs. 120 µs would apply to an integrated or I/O-bus configuration where each word uses the system bus once.

questionText: A DMA controller writes a disk block into main memory while the CPU has a write-back data cache. Which problem can occur, and what is a standard remedy?
options: The address register may overflow, so the block must always be split into 256-byte pieces
The CPU loses its program counter, so it must be saved before every DMA transfer
Main memory becomes read-only during DMA, so the CPU must wait for the completion interrupt
The cache may still hold old copies of those memory words, so the affected lines must be invalidated or the cache must snoop the DMA writes
explanation: DMA updates memory behind the cache, so any cached copy of that region becomes stale; the OS invalidates those lines before reading the buffer, or cache hardware snoops the bus and invalidates matching lines. For DMA output from memory, dirty lines must first be written back.

questionText: What is a channel called that serves one high-speed device at a time, staying dedicated to it until its whole I/O operation is finished?
explanation: A selector channel connects to one fast device, such as a disk, for the whole transfer before it can select another. A multiplexer channel interleaves many slow devices.

questionText: A channel must serve three devices with data rates of 10 KB/s, 20 KB/s and 50 KB/s. What minimum rate must it support if it is a multiplexer channel with all three active at once, and if it is a selector channel serving one device at a time?
options: 80 KB/s as a multiplexer channel and 50 KB/s as a selector channel
50 KB/s as a multiplexer channel and 80 KB/s as a selector channel
80 KB/s as a multiplexer channel and 80 KB/s as a selector channel
26.7 KB/s as a multiplexer channel and 50 KB/s as a selector channel
explanation: A multiplexer channel interleaves all active devices, so it needs their sum: 10 + 20 + 50 = 80 KB/s. A selector channel handles one device at a time, so it needs only the fastest rate, 50 KB/s; 26.7 KB/s is merely the average.

questionText: Which statement about communication between the CPU and an I/O processor (IOP), as described by Mano, is NOT correct?
options: The CPU first tests the I/O path and then issues a start I/O instruction
The IOP reads its commands from main memory
The CPU executes each channel command itself and passes every data word to the IOP
When finished, the IOP interrupts the CPU, which then checks a status word the IOP stored in memory
explanation: The point of an IOP is that it fetches and executes the I/O program (channel commands) itself and moves the data by DMA-style cycle stealing, leaving the CPU free. The other three statements follow Mano's CPU–IOP sequence.

questionText: In a daisy-chain priority interrupt scheme, which device has the highest priority?
options: The device with the lowest vector address
The device physically closest to the CPU in the chain
The device that requested the interrupt first
The device whose bit is set in the mask register
explanation: The interrupt acknowledge signal travels serially through the chain; the first device with a pending request blocks it, so the device nearest the CPU always wins. Priority is fixed by wiring, not by software.

questionText: A DMA controller transfers a 4 KB block in burst mode over a 32-bit data bus. If each memory cycle takes 100 ns, how long does the transfer occupy the bus?
explanation: 4 KB = 4096 bytes = 1024 words of 4 bytes, so 1024 memory cycles × 100 ns = 102.4 µs. Using bytes instead of words gives the wrong 409.6 µs.

questionText: In Flynn's classification, into which class does a shared-memory multiprocessor fall, given that each of its processors runs its own instruction stream on its own data?
explanation: Multiple processors each executing their own instruction stream on their own data form a multiple-instruction, multiple-data (MIMD) machine. SIMD describes array and vector processors that apply one instruction to many data items.

questionText: According to Mano, which kind of multiprocessor can tolerate a higher degree of interaction between tasks?
options: A cluster of computers linked by a local area network
explanation: Tightly coupled processors exchange data through shared memory quickly, so they cope with frequent interaction; loosely coupled systems, which communicate by messages, are most efficient when interaction between tasks is minimal.

questionText: Which statement correctly distinguishes a multicomputer from a multiprocessor?
options: A multicomputer has several CPUs on one chip sharing a single cache
A multiprocessor has only one CPU but several I/O processors
In a multicomputer each node has private memory and the nodes communicate by message passing, whereas a multiprocessor's CPUs share main memory
In a multicomputer all nodes share one global address space with uniform access time
explanation: A multicomputer is a set of complete computers (processor plus private memory) joined by a network and cooperating by messages; a multiprocessor's processors share one main memory and one operating system.

questionText: One CPU of a multiprocessor fails, yet the system keeps running at reduced performance on the remaining CPUs. Which characteristic of multiprocessors does this illustrate?
explanation: Because the processors are interchangeable and share memory and I/O, the failure of one leaves the others able to carry on; this fault tolerance is one of the main benefits of multiprocessors.

questionText: How many crosspoint switches does a crossbar contain if it connects 16 processors to 32 memory modules?
explanation: A crossbar has one crosspoint at every processor–module intersection: 16 × 32 = 512. Adding the counts (48) or squaring either one (256, 1024) is wrong.

questionText: What is the main limitation of a time-shared common bus in a multiprocessor?
options: Every memory module needs a separate port for each processor
It needs N × M crosspoint switches
Processors cannot share any memory over it
Only one processor can transfer over the bus at a time, so contention grows as processors are added
explanation: All units share one path, so while one transfer is in progress every other processor must wait; the bus is the cheapest interconnection but becomes the bottleneck. Separate ports belong to multiport memory and N × M crosspoints to the crossbar.

questionText: In a bus-based multiprocessor each processor keeps the shared bus busy for 15% of the time on average. What is the largest number of processors the bus can support without the total demand exceeding 100%?
explanation: N_max = floor(1 ÷ 0.15) = floor(6.67) = 6; six processors use 90% of the bus while seven would demand 105%. Rounding up to 7 overloads the bus.

questionText: Each processor of a bus-based SMP issues 80 × 10^6 memory references per second and its private cache has a hit ratio of 97.5%. Every miss moves a 32-byte block over a 64-bit bus with a 10 ns bus cycle. Ignoring all other traffic, how many processors can the bus support before it saturates?
explanation: Misses = 80 × 10^6 × 0.025 = 2 × 10^6 per second; bus time per miss = (32 ÷ 8) × 10 ns = 40 ns; one processor uses 2 × 10^6 × 40 ns = 8% of the bus, so floor(1 ÷ 0.08) = floor(12.5) = 12. A 32-bit bus would give 6, and 40 is just 1 ÷ miss ratio.

questionText: In a multiprocessor where every processor has a local bus with its own local memory and I/O, connected through a system bus controller to a common system bus, what is the system bus mainly used for?
options: Reaching the shared memory and communicating with the other processors
Fetching every instruction of every processor
Carrying the local cache's tag comparisons
Connecting the processor to its own local memory
explanation: Local memory and local I/O are reached over the local bus, which keeps most traffic off the common bus; only accesses to the shared memory on the system bus, and hence interprocessor communication, need the system bus.

questionText: A multiport memory system connects 4 processors to 8 memory modules. How many ports does each memory module need, and how many separate processor–module paths are there?
explanation: Every module has one port for each processor, so 4 ports per module, and every processor has its own bus to every module: 4 × 8 = 32 paths. Adding 4 + 8 = 12 counts units, not connections.

questionText: In a multiport memory system, how are simultaneous requests from several processors to the same memory module resolved?
options: By a daisy chain running through all the processors
By the destination tags of an omega network
By the operating system's round-robin scheduler
By fixed priorities assigned to the module's ports
explanation: Mano's multiport memory resolves access conflicts inside each module by giving its ports fixed priorities; the processor on the highest-priority port wins.

questionText: Which interconnection gives each processor its own separate address, data and control buses into every memory module?
explanation: In multiport memory each module has one port per processor, each with its own address, data and control lines; that gives a high transfer rate at the cost of much wiring and control logic.

questionText: According to Mano, what does each crosspoint of a crossbar switch contain?
options: A small cache holding recently used memory words
Multiplexers and arbitration logic that set up the path and resolve simultaneous requests for the same module
A complete processor that forwards messages
Only a fixed wire joining one processor permanently to one module
explanation: Each switch point examines the address on the processor bus to see whether its module is addressed, connects the path through multiplexers and resolves multiple requests for that module on a priority basis.

questionText: A crossbar connects 8 processors to 4 memory modules. What is the maximum number of simultaneous processor–memory transfers, and how many crosspoints does it have?
explanation: Crosspoints = 8 × 4 = 32. Each module can serve only one processor at a time, so at most min(8, 4) = 4 transfers proceed at once, with the other processors waiting.

questionText: How many stages and how many 2×2 switches does a 16×16 omega network need?
explanation: Stages = log₂16 = 4, each with 16 ÷ 2 = 8 switches, so 4 × 8 = 32 switches. 64 counts one switch per line per stage.

questionText: A 64×64 network is built either as a crossbar or as an omega network of 2×2 switches. Counting each 2×2 switch as 4 crosspoints, how many crosspoints does each design need (omega versus crossbar)?
explanation: Omega: log₂64 = 6 stages × 32 switches = 192 switches, × 4 = 768 crosspoints; crossbar: 64 × 64 = 4096. 192 forgets the 4 crosspoints per switch, and 128 counts the crossbar as N + M.

questionText: A 2×2 interchange switch connects its upper input to its lower output and its lower input to its upper output. What is this setting called?
explanation: The four states of a 2×2 switch are straight, exchange (cross), upper broadcast and lower broadcast; swapping the two lines is the exchange state.

questionText: In an 8-line perfect-shuffle connection, to which line is line 6 (binary 110) connected?
explanation: The perfect shuffle rotates the line number left by one bit: 110 becomes 101 = 5. Rotating right gives 011, flipping the last bit (the exchange) gives 111, and shifting left without wrapping the MSB round gives 100.

questionText: In an 8×8 omega network with destination-tag routing (destination bits used from the MSB in stages 1 to 3, 0 = upper output, 1 = lower output), processor 111 requests memory module 011. Which switch outputs does the request take in stages 1, 2 and 3?
explanation: Only the destination 011 matters: bit 0 → upper at stage 1, bit 1 → lower at stage 2, bit 1 → lower at stage 3. Reading the destination from the LSB gives lower, lower, upper, and following the source bits gives lower, lower, lower.

questionText: In an 8×8 omega network (perfect shuffle before each stage, destination-tag routing with the destination bits used from the MSB in stages 1 to 3, 0 = upper output, 1 = lower output), which pair of simultaneous requests cannot both be connected because they need the same link?
explanation: The line after stage i is the source shifted left i places with the first i destination bits shifted in. For P1 (001) → M5 (101) and P3 (011) → M4 (100) the stage-1 lines are 011 and 111, but after stage 2 both are on line 110, so they collide; the other pairs use different lines at every stage.

questionText: Each 2×2 switch of an 8×8 omega network is set either straight or exchange. How many different settings of the whole network are possible, each giving a different permutation of the 8 inputs?
explanation: There are 3 × 4 = 12 switches with 2 settings each, so 2^12 = 4096 permutations, far fewer than the 8! = 40,320 possible ones; 16,777,216 = 4^12 wrongly counts the broadcast states as permutations.

questionText: Which one of these claims about an N×N omega network is false?
options: There is exactly one path from each source to each destination
It is non-blocking, so any permutation of connections can be set up in one pass
Each switch can set itself from one bit of the destination address
explanation: Because the path between a source and a destination is unique and there are only 2^((N/2)log₂N) settings, some request patterns conflict inside the network, so the omega network is blocking. The other statements are true.

questionText: Why is an omega network described as self-routing?
options: Each processor stores a routing table for every possible destination
Messages are flooded to every output and discarded by the wrong modules
Each switch sets itself from one bit of the destination tag carried by the request, so no central controller is needed
The operating system reprograms the switches before every transfer
explanation: At stage i a switch looks at bit i of the destination (counted from the MSB) and chooses its upper output for 0 or its lower output for 1, so the route is fixed by the destination address alone.

questionText: Which statement best describes a single-stage shuffle-exchange network?
options: A crossbar with N × N crosspoints that never blocks
A shared bus on which every processor snoops the others' transfers
A binary n-cube in which each node links to the nodes differing in one bit
One stage of perfect-shuffle wiring followed by exchange switches, through which data recirculate up to log₂N times to reach their destination
explanation: Each pass through the stage rotates the line number left (shuffle) and may flip its last bit (exchange); after log₂N passes every bit of the line number can be set to the destination bit. Unrolling those passes into separate stages gives the omega network.

questionText: A hypercube multicomputer has 128 processors. What is its dimension, and how many links does each node have?
explanation: 2^n = 128 gives n = 7, and a node in an n-cube has one neighbour per address bit, so 7 links. 127 links per node would describe a fully connected network.

questionText: How many communication links does a 6-dimensional hypercube have in total?
explanation: Links = n × 2^(n−1) = 6 × 32 = 192, since each of the 64 nodes has 6 links and each link is shared by two nodes. 384 = 6 × 64 counts every link twice.

questionText: In a 4-dimensional hypercube, what is the minimum number of hops between nodes 0110 and 1011?
explanation: The distance is the number of 1 bits in 0110 XOR 1011 = 1101, which is 3. 5 is the difference of the decimal values 11 − 6, and 4 is the diameter.

questionText: A message travels from node 1010 to node 0111 in a 4-cube using e-cube routing, which corrects the differing address bits starting with the lowest-numbered dimension. Which path does it follow?
explanation: 1010 XOR 0111 = 1101, so dimensions 0, 2 and 3 differ; correcting bit 0, then bit 2, then bit 3 gives 1011, 1111, 0111. The second path corrects the highest dimension first, and the last one changes two bits in one hop, which is not a link.

questionText: In a 5-dimensional hypercube, how many nodes are exactly 2 hops away from a given node?
explanation: A node 2 hops away differs in exactly 2 of the 5 address bits, and there are C(5, 2) = 10 ways to choose them. 20 counts each pair of bits twice (ordered pairs).

questionText: What is the bisection width (number of links cut when the machine is split into two equal halves across one dimension) of a 6-dimensional hypercube?
explanation: Splitting across one dimension leaves two 5-cubes joined by one link per pair of matching nodes: 2^(6−1) = 32 links. 64 is the node count and 192 is the total number of links.

questionText: Which statement about a hypercube (binary n-cube) multiprocessor is NOT correct?
options: All processors share one global memory that they reach through the cube links
Each node has its own local memory and nodes cooperate by message passing
Two nodes are directly linked when their addresses differ in exactly one bit
The diameter grows only as log₂ of the number of nodes
explanation: The hypercube is a loosely coupled structure: each node is a processor with private memory and I/O, and data move between nodes as messages. The other three statements are standard properties of the n-cube.

questionText: How many point-to-point links are needed to connect 12 processors in a fully connected network?
explanation: Each pair of processors needs one link: 12 × 11 ÷ 2 = 66. 132 counts every link twice, and 11 is the number of links per node.

questionText: How many links does an 8 × 8 two-dimensional mesh without wraparound connections have?
explanation: Each of the 8 rows has 7 horizontal links and each of the 8 columns has 7 vertical links: 2 × 8 × 7 = 112. 128 = 2N is the count for a torus, which adds wraparound links.

questionText: Sixteen processors are connected as a ring, as a 4 × 4 mesh without wraparound, and as a 4-dimensional hypercube. What are the diameters of the three networks, in that order?
explanation: Ring: ⌊16/2⌋ = 8; 4 × 4 mesh: 2(4 − 1) = 6 hops corner to corner; 4-cube: n = 4. 15 is the diameter of a 16-node linear array, and 16 is the hypercube's node count.

questionText: How does a NUMA multiprocessor differ from a UMA multiprocessor?
options: NUMA has no shared address space, so processors exchange messages
In UMA each processor can reach only its own private memory
NUMA is simply another name for a loosely coupled cluster
In NUMA all memories form one shared address space, but a processor reaches remote memory more slowly than its local memory
explanation: Both UMA and NUMA are shared-memory designs; in UMA every word takes the same time from every processor, while in NUMA the latency depends on whether the word is in the processor's own node or a remote one.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a symmetric multiprocessor (SMP) as defined by Stallings?
options: Only one master processor runs the operating system kernel while the others run user tasks as slaves
Two or more similar processors of comparable capability share main memory and I/O
Memory access time is approximately the same for every processor
The system is controlled by a single integrated operating system
explanation: In an SMP all processors can perform the same functions, including running the OS, which is what makes it symmetric; a master–slave arrangement is asymmetric multiprocessing.

questionText: What distinguishes a cache-only memory architecture (COMA)?
options: Each node's local memory acts as a large cache, and data migrate to whichever node uses them without a fixed home location
It has no caches at all, only a central shared memory
Each processor has a private cache but no access to other nodes' memory
Every memory access goes to one global cache shared over a bus
explanation: In COMA the distributed memories behave as attraction memories: a block is not tied to one home node but moves to and is replicated in the nodes that reference it.

questionText: In a NUMA multiprocessor a local memory access takes 100 ns and a remote access 400 ns. If 80% of a program's references are local, what is its average memory access time?
explanation: t_avg = 0.8 × 100 + 0.2 × 400 = 80 + 80 = 160 ns. 250 ns is the plain average, 340 ns swaps the fractions, and 180 ns wrongly adds the local time to every remote access.

questionText: On a NUMA machine a local access takes 100 ns and a remote access 600 ns. What minimum fraction of references must be local for the average access time to be no more than 150 ns?
explanation: 100p + 600(1 − p) ≤ 150 gives 600 − 500p ≤ 150, so p ≥ 450 ÷ 500 = 0.9 = 90%. 10% is the largest remote fraction allowed, not the local one.

questionText: Which statement about the cache coherence problem is correct?
options: Coherence problems arise only with write-through caches
Coherence is guaranteed if all caches use the same block size
A write-back cache cannot cause coherence problems because memory is updated later
Write-through keeps main memory up to date, but other caches may still hold the old value, so write-through alone does not ensure coherence
explanation: With write-through the writer's cache and memory are consistent, but copies in other processors' caches are not updated; with write-back even memory is stale. Some protocol, such as snooping or a directory, is needed in both cases.

questionText: Memory location X holds 10. Processors P1 and P2 each read X into their private write-back caches, and there is no coherence protocol. P1 then writes 15 to X, after which P2 reads X again. What does P2 read, and what does main memory hold at that moment?
options: P2 reads 15 from P1's cache, and memory holds 10
P2 reads 10 from its own cache, and memory still holds 10
explanation: P1's write-back cache updates only its own copy (now dirty), so memory keeps 10 until that line is evicted, and P2 hits on its stale copy of 10. Memory would hold 15 only with write-through, and P2 would see 15 only if a coherence protocol invalidated or updated its copy.

questionText: Which of the following does NOT cause a cache coherence problem in a shared-memory multiprocessor?
options: Two processors writing to the same shared variable
A process migrating from one processor to another
Several processors reading the same read-only program code
A DMA device writing memory behind the caches
explanation: Coherence problems come from sharing writable data, process migration and I/O that modifies memory; copies of read-only code are never written, so they always stay identical.

questionText: 5% of a program is strictly sequential and the rest parallelises perfectly. According to Amdahl's law, what is the maximum speed-up obtainable with any number of processors?
explanation: As N grows without limit, S = 1 ÷ ((1 − f) + f/N) approaches 1 ÷ (1 − f) = 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20. 1.05 is 1 ÷ 0.95, which inverts the parallel fraction instead of the serial one.

questionText: A program is 90% parallelisable. According to Amdahl's law, what is the parallel efficiency when it runs on 8 processors?
explanation: S = 1 ÷ (0.1 + 0.9/8) = 1 ÷ 0.2125 = 4.71, so E = S/N = 4.71 ÷ 8 = 58.8%. 91.3% comes from the scaled (Gustafson) speed-up 0.1 + 0.9 × 8 = 7.3, and 13.7% from swapping the serial and parallel parts.

questionText: What fraction of a program must be parallelisable for it to reach a speed-up of 12 on 16 processors, according to Amdahl's law?
Which statement about Amdahl's law is NOT correct?
options: The speed-up can never exceed 1/(1 − f), however many processors are used
If the whole program is parallelisable (f = 1), the speed-up equals N
Parallel efficiency S/N always increases as more processors are added
A small serial fraction severely limits the speed-up on large machines
explanation: For f < 1, S grows more slowly than N, so the efficiency S/N falls as processors are added; for example with f = 0.9 it drops from 0.53 at N = 10 to 0.09 at N = 100. The other statements follow directly from S = 1 ÷ ((1 − f) + f/N).

questionText: A hypercube interconnection of dimension 4 has how many processor nodes, and what is the maximum number of hops between any two nodes?
explanation: An n-cube has 2^n nodes and a diameter of n, because two nodes can differ in at most n address bits; for n = 4 that is 16 nodes and 4 hops.

questionText: Which interconnection structure allows every processor to be connected to a different memory module at the same time, at the cost of one switch point for every processor-module pair?
explanation: A crossbar places a switch with arbitration logic at each of the N×M crosspoints, so all combinations of simultaneous, non-blocking connections are possible; the omega network is cheaper but blocking.

questionText: 80% of a program can be executed in parallel and the rest is strictly sequential. According to Amdahl's law, what speed-up is obtained on 4 processors?
explanation: S = 1 / ((1 − 0.8) + 0.8/4) = 1 / (0.2 + 0.2) = 2.5. Even with infinitely many processors the speed-up could not exceed 1/0.2 = 5.

questionText: In a shared-memory multiprocessor, a sending processor places a request for another processor in a reserved area of common memory, with status bits showing whether the area holds a message and for which processor it is meant. What is this area called?
explanation: Mano calls this memory area a mailbox: the sender writes the message and the status bits, and the receiver checks it by polling or after an interprocessor interrupt. A directory entry records cached copies of a block, not messages.

questionText: A processor has just left a message in the mailbox of processor P3 and wants P3 to handle it immediately rather than at its next periodic check of the mailbox. What should it use?
options: A DMA transfer from its own cache to P3's cache
An interprocessor interrupt directed to P3
A bus request at the highest arbitration priority
A cache flush of the mailbox line
explanation: An interprocessor interrupt forces the target processor to run a handler at once, so it need not poll its mailbox; bus arbitration only decides who uses the bus next.

questionText: Which is an advantage of communicating through shared memory rather than by message passing?
options: Processors exchange data with ordinary load and store instructions, without packaging and routing messages
No synchronization between the processors is ever needed
It scales more easily to thousands of processors
Each processor can keep all of its data private
explanation: Shared variables are read and written directly, which is fast and simple to program. The price is the need for locks and cache coherence and limited scalability, where message passing over a network is stronger.

questionText: In which multiprocessor operating-system organisation does one designated processor always execute the operating-system functions, while the others only run user programs and must ask it for OS services?
options: Separate operating system for each processor
explanation: Mano lists three organisations: master-slave (one processor runs the OS), separate OS (each processor has its own copy, suited to loosely coupled systems) and distributed OS, where OS routines float from processor to processor but each function runs on only one at a time.

questionText: A node of a message-passing multiprocessor sends a 4,000-byte message to a neighbour. The software start-up time is 20 µs and the link bandwidth is 50 MB/s (1 MB = 10^6 bytes). How long does the transfer take?
explanation: T = t_startup + L/B = 20 µs + 4,000 B / (50 × 10^6 B/s) = 20 + 80 = 100 µs. Leaving out the start-up gives 80 µs, and misreading 50 MB/s as 50 Mbit/s gives 20 + 640 = 660 µs.

questionText: A 2,000-byte message crosses 4 links (hops) of a message-passing network, each with a bandwidth of 100 MB/s (1 MB = 10^6 bytes); ignore start-up time. With store-and-forward routing each node receives the whole message before forwarding it; with cut-through routing only a header delay of 0.2 µs is added per hop. What are the two transfer times?
options: 80 µs with store-and-forward, 20.8 µs with cut-through
20 µs with store-and-forward, 20.8 µs with cut-through
80 µs with store-and-forward, 80.8 µs with cut-through
640 µs with store-and-forward, 160.8 µs with cut-through
explanation: One link transmission takes 2,000 / 10^8 = 20 µs. Store-and-forward repeats it on every link: 4 × 20 = 80 µs; cut-through pipelines the message through the nodes: 20 + 4 × 0.2 = 20.8 µs.

questionText: Two processors update the same shared variable with separate load, modify and store instructions, and the final value depends on how their instructions happen to interleave in time. What is this situation called?
explanation: When the outcome of unsynchronised read-modify-write sequences depends on timing it is a race condition; putting the update in a critical section protected by a lock removes it.

questionText: A shared counter holds 5. Processors P1 and P2 each execute the sequence LOAD R, count; ADD R, 1; STORE count, R exactly once, without any lock. Which final values of count are possible?
explanation: If the two sequences do not overlap the result is 7; if both load 5 before either stores, both store 6 and one increment is lost. The value cannot stay 5 because at least one store of 6 or 7 always happens.

questionText: Processor P1 executes Mano's test-and-set instruction TSL SEM, which leaves the tested (old) value of SEM in processor register R, while SEM = 0 (Mano's convention: 0 = resource free, 1 = busy). What are SEM and R afterwards, and what does P1 do?
options: SEM = 1, R = 0; P1 enters the critical section
SEM = 1, R = 1; P1 waits and retries
SEM = 0, R = 1; P1 enters the critical section
SEM = 0, R = 0; P1 waits and retries
explanation: TSL performs R ← M[SEM] and M[SEM] ← 1 in one locked operation, so R receives the old value 0 and SEM becomes 1. R = 0 tells P1 that the resource was free and now belongs to it, so it enters the critical section; R = 1 would mean another processor holds it.

questionText: In Mano's description of semaphores in a multiprocessor, what is the hardware lock?
options: A processor-generated signal that prevents other processors from using the system bus while it is active
A bit in each cache line that stops the line from being replaced
A key register that must match before a processor may write to memory
A watchdog timer that aborts a critical section that runs too long
explanation: The hardware lock is asserted while the test-and-set instruction executes, so no other processor can take the bus between the read and the write of the semaphore.

questionText: A counting semaphore S with initial value 2 guards two identical printers. wait(S) decrements S and blocks the caller if the result is negative; signal(S) increments S and wakes one blocked process if the result is 0 or less, so a negative S equals minus the number of blocked processes. The processes perform, in order: wait, wait, wait, wait, signal, wait, signal. What is S at the end, and how many processes are blocked?
explanation: S goes 2 → 1 → 0 → −1 → −2 (two blocked), then signal gives −1 (one woken), wait gives −2 and the last signal gives −1. One process is still waiting for a printer.

questionText: The atomic instruction CAS(addr, expected, new) writes new into M[addr] only if M[addr] equals expected, and always returns the old value of M[addr]. M[addr] = 7 and a processor executes CAS(addr, 5, 9). What happens?
options: It returns 7 and M[addr] stays 7, so the update has failed
explanation: The comparison 7 = 5 fails, so memory is not changed and the caller receives the current value 7; it would normally retry with 7 as the new expected value.

questionText: A shared counter c = 10. Three processors each execute the atomic fetch-and-add FAA(c, 1), which returns the old value of c and adds 1 to it. Which outcome is guaranteed?
options: All three receive 10 and c ends at 11
All three receive 10 and c ends at 13
The processors receive 10, 11 and 12 in some order, and c ends at 13
The values received depend on timing, and c may end at 11, 12 or 13
explanation: Each FAA is indivisible, so the three updates are serialised: every caller receives a different old value and no increment is lost, whatever the order.

questionText: Which synchronization mechanism makes each processor wait at a given point of a parallel program until every participating processor has reached that point?
options: A binary semaphore guarding a critical section
explanation: A barrier is usually a shared counter incremented atomically by each arrival plus a release flag set when the count reaches the number of processors; it separates phases of a parallel algorithm.

questionText: With fixed-priority daisy-chain bus arbitration, the processor at the far end of the chain may wait indefinitely because processors nearer the arbiter keep requesting the bus. What is this problem called?
explanation: No rule forbids the low-priority unit from using the bus, yet it is postponed indefinitely: that is starvation. Dynamic schemes such as the rotating daisy chain, LRU or FIFO arbitration prevent it.

questionText: Processor A holds lock L1 and waits for L2, while processor B holds L2 and waits for L1. Which rule, applied to all code, prevents this situation?
options: Every processor releases its lock as soon as it is granted the bus
Locks are implemented with test-and-test-and-set instead of test-and-set
Every processor acquires the locks in one fixed global order, for example L1 before L2
Each processor waits with exponential backoff before retrying
explanation: A fixed acquisition order makes circular wait impossible, and circular wait is one of the four conditions needed for deadlock. The spin-lock refinements only reduce bus traffic.

questionText: Why does a test-and-test-and-set spin lock produce far less bus traffic than one that simply repeats the test-and-set instruction?
options: It locks the bus for the whole time the lock is held, so no other traffic can occur
It keeps the lock in a processor register instead of memory
Waiting processors spin by reading their cached Shared copy of the lock and attempt the atomic test-and-set only when they see it free
It lets several processors enter the critical section together, so fewer have to wait
explanation: Every test-and-set is a read-modify-write that needs exclusive ownership of the line, so repeating it keeps generating bus transactions. Ordinary reads hit in the local cache until the holder's release write invalidates the copies.

questionText: Processor P0 holds a spin lock for 2 µs while 4 other processors wait for it. With plain test-and-set, each waiter retries every 100 ns and every retry is one bus transaction. With test-and-test-and-set, each waiter takes one read miss to load the lock line and then spins in its own cache. How many bus transactions do the waiters cause while P0 holds the lock?
explanation: Test-and-set: 2 µs / 100 ns = 20 retries per waiter, 4 × 20 = 80 transactions. Test-and-test-and-set: one read miss per waiter, 4 transactions, then local cache hits until the release.

questionText: Each iteration of a parallel loop spends 40 µs on private work and then 10 µs in a critical section protected by one lock. Ignoring lock overhead, what is the maximum total throughput with any number of processors, and at how many processors is that bound first reached?
explanation: Only one processor can be in the critical section at a time, so at most 1 / 10 µs = 100,000 iterations/s. One processor alone completes 1 / 50 µs = 20,000 iterations/s, so 100,000 / 20,000 = 5 processors saturate the lock.

questionText: A job takes 800 ms on one processor. On 8 processors the work divides perfectly, but lock and barrier waiting adds 20 ms. Using S = T1 / (T1/N + T_sync), what is the speed-up?
explanation: S = 800 / (800/8 + 20) = 800 / 120 = 6.67. Ignoring T_sync gives the ideal 8, and 8 × 800/820 = 7.80 wrongly adds the overhead to the one-processor time.

questionText: Eight processors share a bus under time-slice arbitration, with 50 ns slots given in a fixed round-robin order whether or not a processor needs the bus. A processor needs the bus immediately after its own slot has ended. How long must it wait for its next slot to begin?
explanation: The slots of the other seven processors come first, each 50 ns long even if they are idle: 7 × 50 = 350 ns. 400 ns is the full round including its own slot.

questionText: Four processors are connected in a rotating daisy chain in the order P0 → P1 → P2 → P3 → back to P0. P1 has just released the bus, and P0 and P3 now request it at the same time. Which processor gets the bus, and which processor has the lowest priority in this arbitration?
options: P0 gets the bus; P3 has the lowest priority
P0 gets the bus; P1 has the lowest priority
P3 gets the bus; P0 has the lowest priority
P3 gets the bus; P1 has the lowest priority
explanation: In a rotating daisy chain the priority order starts at the unit after the last bus master: P2, P3, P0, P1. P2 is not requesting, so P3 wins, and P1, which just used the bus, is last; a fixed daisy chain would have chosen P0.

questionText: Six processors share a bus. Each generates 2.5 × 10^6 bus transactions per second, and every transaction occupies the bus for 40 ns. What is the bus utilisation?
explanation: One processor uses 2.5 × 10^6 × 40 × 10^-9 = 0.10 of the bus time, so six use 6 × 0.10 = 0.60, that is 60 %.

questionText: Each processor in a bus-based multiprocessor keeps the shared bus busy 8 % of the time when running alone. Ignoring queueing effects, what is the largest number of processors whose total bus demand does not exceed 100 %?
explanation: N × 0.08 ≤ 1 gives N ≤ 12.5, so 12 processors (96 %); a 13th would demand 104 % of the bus.

questionText: Each processor issues 2 × 10^8 memory references per second, and 98.5 % of them hit in its private cache. Every miss occupies the shared bus for 25 ns. What fraction of bus time does one processor use, and what is the largest number of processors whose total demand does not exceed the bus capacity?
explanation: Misses = 2 × 10^8 × 0.015 = 3 × 10^6 per second; bus share = 3 × 10^6 × 25 ns = 0.075. Then N ≤ 1/0.075 = 13.3, so 13 processors; 14 would need 105 % of the bus.

questionText: In each bus cycle, each of 4 processors independently requests the bus with probability 0.3. What is the probability that two or more processors request in the same cycle, so that arbitration must make at least one of them wait?
explanation: P(no request) = 0.7^4 = 0.2401 and P(exactly one) = 4 × 0.3 × 0.7^3 = 0.4116, so P(two or more) = 1 − 0.2401 − 0.4116 = 0.348. 0.760 is the probability of at least one request.

questionText: In the MESI protocol, which state means that the line is valid only in this cache and has been written, so the copy in main memory is out of date?
explanation: Modified means dirty and exclusive: the cache must write the line back, or supply it, before anyone else uses it. An Exclusive line is also the only cached copy, but it still equals memory.

questionText: Under MESI, processor P1 read-misses on block X and no other cache holds X. In which state is X loaded into P1's cache?
explanation: No other cache responds to the snoop, so this is the only cached copy and it equals memory: Exclusive. If another cache had held X, both copies would end up Shared.

questionText: Which MESI state change takes place without any transaction on the shared bus?
options: Shared to Modified when the local processor writes the line
Exclusive to Modified when the local processor writes the line
Invalid to Exclusive when the local processor reads the line
Invalid to Modified when the local processor writes the line
explanation: A line in E is known to be the only cached copy, so the write needs nobody's permission. S to M must broadcast an invalidate, and both transitions out of I need a bus read (BusRd or read-with-intent-to-modify).

questionText: Cache C2 holds block X in the Modified state. Processor P1 then read-misses on X. With the MESI protocol as described by Stallings, what happens?
options: C2 supplies X and writes it back to memory, then changes to Shared; P1 loads X as Shared
C2 keeps X as Modified and P1 reads the stale value from memory
C2 invalidates its copy and P1 loads X as Exclusive
C2 changes to Exclusive and P1 loads X as Modified
explanation: The snooping C2 must not let P1 read stale memory, so it provides the dirty line, memory is updated, and both caches end with clean Shared copies.

questionText: Caches C1 and C3 hold block Y in the Shared state. Processor P2, whose cache does not contain Y, writes to Y. Under MESI, what are the states of Y in C1, C2 and C3 afterwards?
explanation: P2's write miss issues a read-with-intent-to-modify; C1 and C3 snoop it and invalidate their copies, and P2 loads the line and writes it, so only C2 holds Y, in Modified.

questionText: Three processors have write-back MESI caches, and block X is initially only in memory. The accesses are: P1 reads X, P2 reads X, P3 writes X, P1 reads X. What are the final states of X in the caches of P1, P2 and P3? Assume Stallings' MESI rules: a read miss loads E only if no other cache holds the block, otherwise S; a cache that snoops another processor's read of its M block writes it back to memory and changes to S; a snooped read-with-intent-to-modify or invalidate makes every other copy I, an M copy being written back first.
explanation: P1 loads E; P2's read makes both S; P3's write miss (RWITM) invalidates P1 and P2 and leaves P3 in M; P1's read miss makes P3 write X back and drop to S, and P1 loads S.

questionText: Two processors have write-back MESI caches, and block A is initially only in memory. The accesses are: P1 reads A, P1 writes A, P1 writes A, P2 reads A, P2 writes A. Counting each read miss (BusRd), read-with-intent-to-modify and invalidate as one bus transaction, and write-backs separately, how many bus transactions and write-backs occur? Assume Stallings' MESI rules: a read miss loads E only if no other cache holds the block, otherwise S; a cache that snoops another processor's read of its M block writes it back to memory and changes to S; a snooped read-with-intent-to-modify or invalidate makes every other copy I, an M copy being written back first.
explanation: P1's read is a BusRd (E); its two writes are silent (E to M, then an M hit); P2's read is a BusRd that makes P1 write back and go to S; P2's write is an invalidate (S to M). That is 3 transactions and 1 write-back.

questionText: Three processors have write-back MESI caches, and block X is initially only in memory. The accesses are: P1 writes X, P2 reads X, P3 reads X, P3 writes X, P1 reads X, P2 writes X. Counting each BusRd, read-with-intent-to-modify and invalidate as one bus transaction, how many bus transactions and write-backs occur, and what is the final state of X in P2's cache? Assume Stallings' MESI rules: a read miss loads E only if no other cache holds the block, otherwise S; a cache that snoops another processor's read of its M block writes it back to memory and changes to S; a snooped read-with-intent-to-modify or invalidate makes every other copy I, an M copy being written back first.
options: 6 bus transactions, 1 write-back; P2 holds X as Modified
6 bus transactions, 2 write-backs; P2 holds X as Modified
5 bus transactions, 2 write-backs; P2 holds X as Exclusive
6 bus transactions, 3 write-backs; P2 holds X as Shared
explanation: Steps: RWITM (P1 M); BusRd with P1 writing back (P1, P2 S); BusRd (all S); invalidate (P3 M); BusRd with P3 writing back (P1, P3 S); RWITM (P2 M, others I). Every access uses the bus once, giving 6 transactions and 2 write-backs.

questionText: Three processors have write-back MESI caches, and block X is initially only in memory. The accesses are: P2 reads X, P1 reads X, P2 writes X, P2 writes X, P3 writes X, P1 reads X, P3 reads X. What are the final states of X in P1, P2 and P3, and how many times is X written back to memory? Assume Stallings' MESI rules: a read miss loads E only if no other cache holds the block, otherwise S; a cache that snoops another processor's read of its M block writes it back to memory and changes to S; a snooped read-with-intent-to-modify or invalidate makes every other copy I, an M copy being written back first.
explanation: P2 E; P1 read makes both S; P2's first write invalidates P1 (P2 M) and the second hits; P3's write miss makes P2 write back and go to I (P3 M); P1's read makes P3 write back and both become S; P3's read hits. Final S, I, S with 2 write-backs.

questionText: Under a write-update (write-broadcast) coherence protocol, what happens when a processor writes to a line that other caches also hold?
options: An invalidation is broadcast and every other copy is discarded
The new data is broadcast on the bus and every cache holding the line updates its copy
Only the writer's copy changes; the others keep the old value until the next context switch
The writer stalls until every other cache has evicted the line
explanation: Write-update keeps all copies valid by sending the written word to them. Write-invalidate, as in MESI, instead removes the other copies so that the writer holds the only one.

questionText: For which access pattern does a write-invalidate protocol generate much less bus traffic than a write-update protocol?
options: One processor writes a value once and several processors read it immediately afterwards
One processor writes the same block many times before any other processor reads it
Several processors only read a block that nobody ever writes
Each processor uses only data that no other processor ever caches
explanation: Write-invalidate pays one invalidation and then writes locally, whereas write-update broadcasts every write. For write-once, read-by-many data write-update does better, and in the last two cases neither protocol generates coherence traffic.

questionText: Block Z is held in the Shared state by the caches of P1, P2 and P3. P1 then writes Z six times in a row, after which P2 and P3 each read Z once. Count one bus transaction for each invalidation, each update broadcast and each read miss (a write-back that services a miss is part of that miss). How many bus transactions does a write-invalidate protocol need, compared with a write-update protocol?
explanation: Write-invalidate: one invalidation on the first write, five local hits, then read misses by P2 and P3, giving 3. Write-update: six update broadcasts, after which both reads hit, giving 6.

questionText: Processors P1 and P2 repeatedly update two different variables, a and b, that lie in the same 64-byte cache block. Their MESI caches show heavy invalidation traffic although no data is actually shared. What is the problem, and what is a remedy?
options: True sharing; protect a and b with one common lock
Capacity misses; double the cache size
Deadlock; acquire the locks in a fixed order
False sharing; place a and b in different cache blocks, for example by padding
explanation: Coherence works on whole blocks, so each write to a invalidates P2's copy of the block that also holds b, and vice versa. Separating the variables into different blocks stops the ping-pong.

questionText: In the software coherence scheme that uses a centralised global table set up by the compiler (Mano), each memory block is marked read-only (RO) or read-write (RW). Which rule applies?
options: RO blocks may be copied into all caches, but an RW block may be in only one cache
RW blocks may be copied into all caches, but an RO block may be in only one cache
Both RO and RW blocks may be in every cache, and the table is consulted only on a write
Neither RO nor RW blocks may be cached; the table replaces the caches
explanation: Copies of read-only data can never disagree, so they may be cached everywhere; allowing each writable block in only one cache means it can never have two different cached values.

questionText: A 256-processor NUMA machine connects its nodes through a point-to-point switching network with no shared bus. Which cache coherence approach is appropriate?
options: Write-through caches with no coherence mechanism
explanation: Snooping needs a broadcast medium that every cache can watch. Without a bus, and at this scale, a directory records the sharers of each block and sends invalidations only to them.

questionText: Which statement about snoopy cache coherence is NOT correct?
options: Every cache controller must observe every transaction on the shared bus
It is well suited to a small bus-based symmetric multiprocessor
It scales easily to hundreds of processors because invalidations are sent only to the caches that hold the block
MESI is an example of a snoopy write-invalidate protocol
explanation: Snooping broadcasts every coherence transaction to all caches, so bus bandwidth and snoop load limit it to modest processor counts. Sending invalidations only to the sharers is what a directory does.

questionText: In a 32-processor system with a full-map directory, block B is cached in the Shared state by P4, P9 and P20. P7 now writes B. To how many caches must the directory send invalidation messages?
explanation: The presence bits identify exactly the three sharers, P4, P9 and P20, so three invalidations are sent. A snooping bus would instead broadcast to all 31 other caches.

questionText: A full-map directory keeps one presence bit per processor and one dirty bit for every memory block. For 16 processors and 32-byte blocks, how much storage does the directory add, as a percentage of main-memory capacity?
explanation: Each entry has 16 + 1 = 17 bits for 32 × 8 = 256 data bits, so the overhead is 17/256 = 6.64 %. Forgetting the dirty bit gives 6.25 %, and comparing bits with bytes gives 53.1 %.

questionText: A NUMA machine has 64 processors and 4 GiB of main memory with 128-byte blocks. A full-map directory stores 64 presence bits and 1 dirty bit for every block. How much storage does the directory need (1 MiB = 2^20 bytes)?
explanation: Blocks = 2^32 / 2^7 = 2^25; directory = 65 × 2^25 bits = 65 × 2^22 bytes = 260 MiB, about 6.3 % of memory. Without the dirty bit it would be 256 MiB, and 2,080 is the size in mebibits.

questionText: A 256-processor system compares a full-map directory (one presence bit per processor plus a dirty bit) with a limited-pointer directory that stores up to 4 processor numbers plus a dirty bit for each block. How many bits does each entry need, and how much smaller is the limited-pointer entry?
options: 257 bits versus 1,025 bits, about four times larger
explanation: Full map: 256 + 1 = 257 bits. Limited pointer: 4 × log2 256 + 1 = 4 × 8 + 1 = 33 bits, so the entry is 1 − 33/257 = 87 % smaller.

questionText: Why must the test-and-set instruction used for a semaphore be executed as an indivisible read-modify-write cycle?
options: So that the semaphore can be stored in a processor register instead of memory
So that the instruction executes faster than a normal memory write
So that no other processor can read the semaphore between its test and its update, which would let two processors enter the critical section
So that the interrupt system is disabled for the whole critical section
explanation: If another processor could access the semaphore between the read and the write, both could see it as free and both would set it, breaking mutual exclusion; the bus is locked for the duration of the instruction to prevent this.

questionText: In a loosely coupled multiprocessor, inter-processor communication is achieved mainly through
options: shared variables in a common global memory
message passing over a communication network
a common cache shared by all processors
explanation: Loosely coupled processors have private memories and no global shared memory, so they exchange information as packets (messages) routed over links or a switching network.

questionText: Which dynamic bus arbitration algorithm allots the bus to each processor for a fixed-length interval in a round-robin sequence, regardless of whether it needs the bus?
explanation: Time-slice arbitration divides bus time into equal fixed slots given to each processor in turn; FIFO serves by arrival, LRU favours the longest-idle unit and the rotating daisy chain moves the top priority after each use.

questionText: A snoopy cache coherence protocol relies on which mechanism?
options: Every cache controller monitoring the shared bus for writes to lines it holds
A central directory in memory that lists which caches hold each line
Marking all shared data as non-cacheable
Flushing every cache at each context switch
explanation: Snoopy protocols (write-invalidate such as MESI, or write-update) work because every cache watches the broadcast bus and reacts to writes from other processors; the directory approach is the alternative for non-bus interconnects.

questionText: In a CMOS logic gate, when does a pMOS transistor conduct (act as a closed switch)?
options: When its gate input is logic 1 (high)
When its gate input is logic 0 (low)
Only while the clock is high
Only when its source and drain are both at logic 1
explanation: A pMOS transistor conducts when its gate is low, while an nMOS transistor conducts when its gate is high. CMOS gates pair a pMOS pull-up network with an nMOS pull-down network so that exactly one of them conducts for each input combination.

questionText: The function F(a, b, c) = a'b'c + a'bc + ab'c + abc is minimised with a Karnaugh map. What is the simplest sum-of-products form?
explanation: The four minterms (1, 3, 5, 7) are exactly the cells where c = 1, so they form one group of four in which a and b both change, giving F = c.

questionText: Which of the following register-transfer (RT) level components is sequential rather than combinational?
explanation: A counter stores its present count in flip-flops and changes it on clock edges, so its output depends on stored state. Multiplexers, decoders and comparators have outputs that depend only on their present inputs.

questionText: Which combinational component converts an n-bit binary code into 2^n output lines, exactly one of which is active?
explanation: A decoder activates the single output selected by its n-bit input, for example to produce one-hot register load enables or state signals. An encoder performs the reverse mapping.

questionText: In a datapath, register R can be loaded from five different sources through one multiplexer. What is the minimum number of select lines the controller must drive for that multiplexer?
explanation: A k-input multiplexer needs ceil(log2 k) select lines: ceil(log2 5) = ceil(2.32) = 3. Two lines can choose among only four sources, and five lines would be a one-hot select.

questionText: What does register-transfer level (RTL) design describe?
options: A circuit as registers plus the combinational operations that transform and move data between them in each clock cycle
The layout of transistors and wires on the chip
Only the Boolean equations of combinational gates, with no storage elements
The instruction set seen by an assembly-language programmer
explanation: At RT level a design is expressed as registers, functional units, multiplexers and buses, and what is transferred between registers in each clock cycle, as in an FSMD. Gate-level and layout descriptions come later in the flow.

questionText: Which statement about Moore and Mealy finite-state machines is NOT correct?
options: In a Moore machine the outputs are a function of the present state only
A Moore machine's outputs change as soon as an input changes, even between clock edges
A Mealy machine's outputs can respond to an input change within the same clock cycle
For the same behaviour, a Mealy machine often needs fewer states than a Moore machine
explanation: Because a Moore machine's outputs depend only on the stored state, they change only after a clock edge updates the state register. It is the Mealy machine whose outputs follow input changes between clock edges.

questionText: An FSM must output 1 whenever the last three input bits are 1, 0, 1, with overlapping allowed (the input 10101 gives two detections). What are the minimum numbers of states for a Mealy and for a Moore implementation?
explanation: A Mealy machine needs the states 'nothing useful seen', 'seen 1' and 'seen 10', and produces the 1 on the transition that completes 101. A Moore machine needs one more state, 'seen 101', whose output is 1, giving 4.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of a custom single-purpose processor over a general-purpose processor running the same function?
options: The ability to run a different program after the product has shipped
explanation: A custom single-purpose processor is hard-wired for one algorithm, so it can be fast, small and power-efficient for that task but cannot be reprogrammed. Flexibility, like low NRE cost, is the strength of the general-purpose processor.

questionText: In Vahid and Givargis's RT-level method, which sequence correctly orders the design steps of a custom single-purpose processor?
options: Write the program, convert it to an FSMD, create the datapath, then derive the controller FSM from the FSMD and the datapath
Build the controller FSM, write the program, create the datapath, then derive the FSMD
Create the datapath, write the program, convert it to an FSMD, then choose the state encoding
Convert to an FSMD, write the program, derive the controller, then create the datapath
explanation: The behaviour is captured as a program and turned into an FSMD; a datapath is allocated for its variables and operations; only then is the controller FSM obtained by replacing actions with control signals and conditions with status signals.

questionText: What distinguishes a finite-state machine with datapath (FSMD) from a plain FSM?
options: An FSMD has no clock and changes state asynchronously
An FSMD can have only Moore-type outputs
An FSMD adds declared variables, so its states can contain arithmetic actions on them and its transitions can test conditions on them
An FSMD always uses one-hot state encoding, while an FSM uses binary encoding
explanation: An FSMD extends the FSM model with variables and data operations: states carry actions such as x = x - y and transitions carry conditions such as x < y. It is the intermediate model between a program and the datapath-plus-controller implementation.

questionText: Using Vahid's templates for converting a program into an FSMD (each assignment gets its own state; a loop gets a condition state and a join state), how many states does the fragment 'while (c) { a = a + 1; }' produce?
explanation: The loop becomes a condition state that tests c, one state for a = a + 1 that returns to the condition state, and a join state reached when c is false: 3 states.

questionText: Using Vahid's program-to-FSMD templates (one state per assignment; a branch gets a condition state whose paths all end in a join state), how many states does 'if (c) a = b; else a = d;' produce?
explanation: One condition state tests c, one state performs a = b, one performs a = d, and both paths meet in a join state: 4 states. The join state can later be removed during FSMD optimisation.

Three loops give 3 condition states and 3 join states, and the five assignments (sum = 0, i = 0, the two body statements and s_o = sum) give 5 more: 11 states. ceil(log2 11) = 4 flip-flops, because 3 bits provide only 8 codes.

questionText: Why do Vahid's program-to-FSMD templates create join states such as 5-J and 6-J in the GCD FSMD?
options: They give every loop and branch one common exit point where the separate paths meet, so the templates can be chained mechanically; they perform no action and are usually removed during optimisation
They hold the arithmetic actions of the loop body
They synchronise the controller with a second clock domain
They store the return address of the loop so that it can be repeated
explanation: A join state is an empty state where the paths of a branch, or the exit of a loop, come together. Because it does no work, its outgoing transition can be folded into the states before it, which is how 5-J and 6-J disappear in the optimised GCD FSMD.

questionText: Why can state 1 of Vahid's unoptimised GCD FSMD, generated from the outer while (1), be eliminated during FSMD optimisation?
options: Its only transition condition is the constant 1, so it always goes to the same next state and performs no action
It performs the subtraction, which can be moved into the datapath
It is equivalent to the output state d_o = x
It is needed only for simulation, because while (1) cannot be synthesised
explanation: State 1 tests a condition that is always true and has no action, so the transitions into it can go straight to its successor. The same reasoning removes the join states whose only job is to pass control on.

questionText: Two consecutive FSMD states are to be merged into one state, in which both assignments complete at the same clock edge using the register values from the start of that state. Which pair of assignments CANNOT be merged without changing the result?
options: x = a + b; y = a - b
explanation: In a merged state y would be computed from the old value of x, not from a + b, so y = x + 1 must stay in a later state. The other pairs have no data dependency and can share one state, as x = x_i and y = y_i do in the optimised GCD FSMD.

options: sum = 10, the same as the C program
explanation: In the merged state sum adds the old i: 0 + 0, then + 1, + 2 and + 3, giving 6 when i reaches 4, instead of 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. Because sum reads the new i, the assignments are dependent and must stay in separate states, or the merged state must compute sum = sum + i + 1.

questionText: A straight-line FSMD passes through 11 states once each. One state contains a multiplication with an 18 ns delay; every other state needs at most 6 ns. Design A clocks at 18 ns so that the multiply fits in one state. Design B separates the multiply into 3 states and clocks at 6 ns. What are the execution times of A and B?
explanation: A: 11 states x 18 ns = 198 ns. B: the multiply now takes 3 states, so 10 + 3 = 13 states x 6 ns = 78 ns, about 2.5 times faster; 11 x 6 = 66 ns forgets the two extra states.

Registers: sum, i and s for the output. Functional units: a less-than comparator for i < n_i and two adders (sum + i and i + 1). sum and i are each written from the constant 0 and from an adder, so each needs a 2-to-1 multiplexer, while s is loaded only from sum.

questionText: A datapath has four registers, each with a load enable. Three registers are fed through 2-to-1 multiplexers and the fourth through a 4-to-1 multiplexer, and an ALU performs 8 functions selected by a binary code. How many control bits must the controller supply in every state?
explanation: Load enables 4 + multiplexer selects 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 5 + ALU function code ceil(log2 8) = 3, giving 4 + 5 + 3 = 12 control bits.

questionText: In the GCD datapath, register x is loaded through a 2-to-1 multiplexer that selects either the input x_i or the subtractor output x - y. To carry out the FSMD action x = x - y, what must the controller do in that state?
options: Set x_sel to choose x_i and set x_ld = 1
Set x_sel to choose the subtractor output and set x_ld = 0
Set x_sel to choose the subtractor output and set x_ld = 1, keeping y_ld = 0
Set d_ld = 1 so that the result appears on d_o
explanation: The multiplexer must route x - y to the input of x, and the load enable must be 1 so that x captures it at the clock edge; y_ld stays 0 so y keeps its value. This is how each FSMD action is replaced by control-signal settings in the controller.

questionText: In the GCD processor the comparator output x_lt_y goes from the datapath to the controller, and x_ld goes from the controller to the datapath. What are these two signals called?
options: x_lt_y is a status signal and x_ld is a control signal
x_lt_y is a control signal and x_ld is a status signal
Both are data signals on the result bus
explanation: Status signals report conditions from the datapath to the controller (x_lt_y, x_neq_y). Control signals are set by the controller to steer the datapath: register loads such as x_ld and multiplexer selects such as x_sel.

questionText: In Vahid's GCD datapath the output d_o is driven by a separate register d, loaded by d_ld in the output state, rather than directly by register x. Why?
options: Because a register such as x cannot drive an output port
So that d_o holds the finished result steadily while x and y are reloaded and changed by the next computation
Because register d performs the final subtraction
So that the controller needs fewer states
explanation: Register x changes throughout every computation, so connecting it to d_o would expose intermediate values. Register d captures the result once, in the output state, so d_o shows only finished results.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT an input to the combinational (next-state and output) logic of a custom processor's controller?
options: The present-state bits from the state register
Status signals from the datapath, such as x_lt_y
External control inputs, such as go_i
The full n-bit data value held in datapath register x
explanation: The controller sees data only through 1-bit status signals produced by comparators in the datapath; the data words themselves stay in the datapath. Its inputs are the present state, the status signals and external control inputs.

questionText: The unoptimised GCD controller has 13 states in a binary-encoded state register, 3 inputs (go_i, x_neq_y, x_lt_y) and 5 control outputs (x_sel, y_sel, x_ld, y_ld, d_ld). Its combinational logic is implemented as a ROM addressed by the state bits and the inputs, whose words hold the next state and the control outputs. What is the ROM size?
explanation: State bits = ceil(log2 13) = 4, so the address has 4 + 3 = 7 bits and the ROM has 2^7 = 128 words. Each word holds 4 next-state bits + 5 outputs = 9 bits, so the ROM holds 128 x 9 = 1152 bits.

questionText: A 4-state Moore controller uses binary state codes Q1Q0: S0 = 00 (wait), S1 = 01 (load x from x_i), S2 = 10 (x = x - y) and S3 = 11 (output). The load signal x_ld must be 1 in S1 and S2 only. Which expression gives x_ld?
explanation: x_ld = Q1'Q0 + Q1Q0', which is Q1 XOR Q0. Q1 + Q0 would also assert x_ld in S3 (11), and Q0 alone would assert it in S3 but not in S2.

questionText: The GCD processor works on 8-bit unsigned inputs x_i and y_i, and its datapath uses 8-bit unsigned registers and subtractors with no borrow or sign handling. Why can the subtraction results never be negative?
options: The controller clears a borrow flag after every subtraction
The registers are made twice the input width so that negative values fit
The subtractor saturates at zero whenever the result would be negative
Each subtraction takes the smaller value from the larger (y - x only when x < y, x - y only when x > y), so no result is ever negative
explanation: The FSMD subtracts only after the comparator has shown which operand is smaller, so the result is never negative and never exceeds the larger input. That is why unsigned registers of the input width are enough.

questionText: Which statement about one-hot state encoding of an N-state controller is correct?
options: It uses N flip-flops, one per state, which usually makes the next-state and output logic simpler and faster
It needs ceil(log2 N) flip-flops, the fewest possible
It leaves no unused state codes
It is another name for Gray encoding
explanation: One-hot sets exactly one of N flip-flops to 1, so each output is simply the OR of the flip-flops of the states that assert it and the next-state logic is shallow. The cost is N flip-flops instead of ceil(log2 N), with 2^N - N codes unused.

questionText: A controller's states are visited mostly in one fixed sequence. Which state encoding assigns codes so that consecutive states differ in only one bit, reducing flip-flop switching and hence dynamic power?
options: Output encoding, where the state codes are chosen equal to the output values
explanation: In Gray encoding successive codes differ in exactly one bit, so each common transition toggles a single flip-flop. Binary counting can toggle several bits at once, for example 011 to 100.

questionText: A controller with 5 states is given a 3-bit binary state register. In how many different ways can distinct 3-bit codes be assigned to the 5 states (the reason synthesis tools use heuristics instead of trying every encoding of a large FSM)?
explanation: The first state can take any of 8 codes, the next any of the remaining 7, and so on: 8 x 7 x 6 x 5 x 4 = 6720 assignments. 5! = 120 counts only the orderings, and C(8, 5) = 56 ignores which state receives which code.

questionText:
A Moore controller has the state table below (next state for input x = 0 and x = 1, and the output z). After state minimisation, how many states remain?

State  x=0  x=1  z
A      B    C    0
B      D    E    0
C      F    E    0
D      A    G    1
E      A    G    1
F      D    E    0
G      B    C    0
explanation: Splitting by output gives {A, B, C, F, G} and {D, E}; successor groups then split the first block into {A, G} (both successors with z = 0), {B, F} (both with z = 1) and {C} (one of each). A further pass changes nothing, so {A, G}, {B, F}, {C} and {D, E} remain: 4 states.

questionText: An FSMD has three states. S1 computes t1 = a + b and t2 = c + d, S2 computes t3 = t1 + t2, and S3 computes t4 = t3 + a, t5 = t3 + b and t6 = t3 + c. Additions in the same state need separate adders, but adders may be shared between states. What is the minimum number of adders, compared with one-to-one allocation?
options: 6 instead of 6, because no sharing is possible
explanation: The minimum equals the largest number of additions in any one state: max(2, 1, 3) = 3. One-to-one allocation uses one adder per operation, 6, so sharing saves 3 adders at the cost of multiplexers on the adder inputs.

questionText: An FSMD passes through states S1 to S8 in order. Each variable is live from the state that writes it to the last state that reads it, inclusive: a S1-S3, b S2-S4, f S3-S5, c S4-S6, d S5-S8, e S7-S8. Two variables may share a register only if their live ranges have no state in common. What is the minimum number of registers?
explanation: At most 3 variables are live in the same state (a, b, f in S3; b, f, c in S4; f, c, d in S5), so 3 registers are needed, and 3 suffice: R1 = a, c, e; R2 = b, d; R3 = f. One-to-one allocation would use 6.

questionText: Which pair of operations in an FSMD can be bound to a single shared subtractor?
options: a - b and c - d, both in state S3
y - x in state S6 and x - y in state S7
x - y and x + y, both in state S4
Any two subtractions, whatever states they are in
explanation: A functional unit can be shared only by operations that are never needed in the same clock cycle, i.e. operations in different states; the GCD subtractions y - x and x - y qualify. Two subtractions in the same state need two subtractors.

questionText: A datapath uses an adder in state S2 and a subtractor in state S5. The designer replaces both with one ALU that can add or subtract. Which statement is correct?
options: The ALU needs no extra control, because it detects from its inputs which operation is needed
