A manager walks the ifInOctets column (i) with GetNext requests only, and (ii) with GetBulk requests using non-repeaters = 0 and max-repetitions = 10. Counting the request that shows the column has ended, how many requests does each walk need?
explanation: GetNext returns one row per request, and the 25th request returns an OID beyond the column, which ends the walk. Each GetBulk returns 10 bindings: rows 1-10, rows 11-20, then rows 21-24 plus 6 bindings past the column, so 3 requests.

questionText: A GetBulkRequest lists three variables, sysUpTime, ifInOctets and ifOutOctets, with non-repeaters = 1 and max-repetitions = 10. Assuming the interface table has more than 10 rows and the reply fits in one message, how many variable bindings does the response contain?
explanation: The first variable (the non-repeater) is returned once, and each of the R = 2 remaining variables is repeated M = 10 times: N + M x R = 1 + 10 x 2 = 21. 30 treats all three as repeaters, and 11 repeats only one of them.

questionText: An administrator's SNMP manager sets ifAdminStatus.5 on a switch to down(2), shutting interface 5. Which SNMP operation does it use?
explanation: SetRequest writes a new value to a MIB object, here the interface's administrative status. Get and GetNext only read values, and a Trap is an unsolicited alert from the agent to the manager.

questionText: What is the difference between an SNMP Trap and an InformRequest?
options: A Trap is sent by the manager and an Inform by the agent
An Inform is acknowledged by the receiving manager with a Response and is retransmitted if no reply arrives; a Trap is sent once and never acknowledged
A Trap uses UDP port 161 and an Inform uses TCP port 162
An Inform reads a value from the agent, while a Trap writes one
explanation: Both are notifications sent to the manager, normally to UDP port 162; Inform, introduced in SNMPv2, adds acknowledgement and retries so that events are not silently lost. Reading and writing values are done with Get and Set.

questionText: Why does SNMP use UDP rather than TCP?
options: UDP guarantees that every trap reaches the manager
Each poll is one small request and reply, the manager handles timeouts and retries itself, and a connectionless protocol keeps working when the network is congested or failing
explanation: With no handshake or connection state, a manager can poll thousands of agents cheaply, and management traffic still gets through when links are overloaded. The price is that lost messages must be caught by the manager's own timers, which is why Inform was added for notifications.

questionText: An attacker captures an SNMPv2c SetRequest that a manager sends to a router. What can the attacker most likely do next?
options: Read the read-write community string in plain text from the packet and use it to change the router's settings
Nothing, because SNMPv2c encrypts every message with AES
Only read the router's uptime, because Set messages hide their contents
Nothing, because community strings are hashed before they are sent
explanation: SNMPv1 and v2c send the community string, their only credential, unencrypted in every message, so one captured Set exposes write access. SNMPv3 at the authPriv level prevents this.

questionText: Which SNMPv3 security level provides both authentication of messages and encryption of their contents?
explanation: SNMPv3's User-based Security Model has three levels: noAuthNoPriv (user name only), authNoPriv (HMAC authentication) and authPriv (authentication plus AES or DES encryption). Privacy without authentication is not defined.

questionText: MRTG polls a 32-bit ifInOctets counter 300 s apart and reads 4,294,000,000 and then 2,000,000. Assuming the counter wrapped exactly once, what is the average inbound rate over the interval?
explanation: Delta = 2^32 - 4,294,000,000 + 2,000,000 = 2,967,296 octets, so the rate = 8 x 2,967,296 / 300 = 79,128 bit/s. Using only the second reading gives 53.3 kbit/s, forgetting the factor 8 gives 9.9 k, and taking |C2 - C1| gives 114.5 Mbit/s.

questionText: A monitoring tool polls a 32-bit octet counter every 60 s. The counter's increase can be measured correctly only if it stays below 2^32 octets between polls. At full load, on which of these interfaces is the 32-bit counter still usable: 100 Mbps, 400 Mbps and 1 Gbps (1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s)?
options: All three, because the tool corrects for counter wraps
explanation: Wrap time = 2^32 x 8 / rate: 343.6 s at 100 Mbps, 85.9 s at 400 Mbps and 34.4 s at 1 Gbps, so only the 1 Gbps counter passes 2^32 octets within 60 s and needs the 64-bit ifHCInOctets counter. Using a 300 s interval would leave only 100 Mbps, and forgetting the factor 8 would wrongly rule out all three.

questionText: Users complain that a 100 Mbps link is slow for a few seconds at a time, yet its MRTG graph never shows more than 60 Mbps. What is the most likely explanation?
options: MRTG plots 5-minute averages, so short bursts at the full 100 Mbps are averaged away
MRTG counts only packets, not bytes, so it under-reports traffic
The link cannot be the problem, because a 60 % peak average proves there is always spare capacity
SNMP counters stop counting while the link is congested
explanation: Each point is the octet-counter change over the 5-minute poll interval divided by 300 s, so a 20-second burst at line rate barely moves the average. Shorter polling intervals, or flow and packet tools, reveal such micro-bursts.

questionText: Over a 300 s interval, the counters of a 100 Mbps full-duplex interface rise by 2,250,000,000 (ifInOctets) and 750,000,000 (ifOutOctets). Taking 1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s, what are the inbound and outbound utilisations?
explanation: Inbound = 8 x 2.25 x 10^9 / 300 = 60 Mbps = 60 % and outbound = 8 x 0.75 x 10^9 / 300 = 20 Mbps = 20 %, since each direction of a full-duplex link has its own 100 Mbps. Adding them (80 %) treats the link as half duplex, 7.5 % forgets the factor 8, and 57.2 % uses 1 Mbps = 2^20 bit/s.

questionText: In PRTG Network Monitor, what is a sensor?
options: A hardware probe that must be plugged into every switch
One monitored measurement on a device, such as the traffic on one switch port, a ping time or a disk's free space
The SNMP community string of a device
explanation: PRTG organises monitoring as devices with sensors, each sensor collecting one set of values with its own graphs and alert limits. Licences are counted in sensors, and the free edition allows 100.

questionText: PRTG must monitor CPU load and disk usage on Windows servers on which SNMP is not installed. Which data source does it normally use?
options: Packet sniffing on a mirror port
explanation: WMI exposes Windows performance and configuration data to authorised remote queries, so PRTG's WMI sensors need no SNMP agent. NetFlow and packet sniffing describe network traffic, not a server's CPU or disks.

questionText: In Cisco Packet Tracer, which mode lets a student step through a ping hop by hop and open each PDU to see its OSI-layer details?
explanation: Simulation mode pauses the clock and records events in the Event List, so each packet can be advanced and inspected layer by layer. Realtime mode runs like a live network, and promiscuous and monitor modes belong to packet capture on real interfaces.

questionText: A student has no lab equipment but wants to build a three-router network, configure OSPF with IOS commands and check that it works. Which tool fits best?
explanation: Packet Tracer simulates Cisco routers, switches and end devices, including a large subset of IOS commands, so designs can be tested without hardware. Wireshark, MRTG and PRTG observe real networks and cannot build one.

questionText: Which Wireshark capture filter (BPF syntax) records only DNS traffic to or from the host 10.0.0.5?
explanation: Capture filters use BPF primitives such as host, net, port, tcp and udp, combined with and, or and not; port 53 covers DNS over both UDP and TCP. ip.addr == 10.0.0.5 && dns is a valid display filter, but it cannot be used as a capture filter.

questionText: Which Wireshark display filter shows only the first segment of each TCP connection attempt (SYN set, ACK not set)?
explanation: tcp.flags.syn == 1 alone also matches the server's SYN-ACK, so the ACK bit must be tested as well. tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0 is capture-filter (BPF) syntax, and the last option is valid in neither.

questionText: An analyst runs Wireshark in promiscuous mode on a PC connected to an ordinary port of a switched Ethernet LAN. Which traffic can she capture?
options: Every frame on the LAN, because promiscuous mode makes the switch copy all traffic to her port
Only frames addressed to her own MAC address, because promiscuous mode has an effect only on hubs
Only frames the switch sends to her port: her own traffic plus broadcasts, multicasts and flooded unknown-unicast frames; to see other hosts' traffic she needs a SPAN (mirror) port or a tap
All traffic on the LAN, but only the headers and never the payloads
explanation: Promiscuous mode only stops her own network card from discarding frames addressed to other MACs; the switch still forwards each known unicast frame only to its destination's port. Port mirroring (SPAN) or a tap delivers copies of other hosts' traffic.

questionText: What does Wireshark's 'Follow TCP Stream' do?
options: It starts a new capture that records only new TCP connections
It traces the route of a TCP connection hop by hop, like traceroute
It decrypts the TLS records of an HTTPS session without needing any keys
It filters the capture to one TCP connection (tcp.stream eq N) and shows its reassembled payload as a conversation in both directions
explanation: It applies the display filter tcp.stream eq N and shows the bytes of that connection in order, client and server data in different colours, which makes protocols such as HTTP, SMTP or FTP easy to read. Encrypted TLS payloads stay unreadable unless the session keys are supplied.

questionText: Which statement about Wireshark's colouring rules is correct?
options: They are display-filter expressions that paint matching rows in the packet list, for example highlighting TCP retransmissions, and they do not change what is captured or saved
They decide which packets are captured and which are dropped
They encrypt the packets of different protocols with different keys
They can be set only in tcpdump, before the capture starts
explanation: Each rule pairs a display filter with foreground and background colours; the default 'Bad TCP' rule, for instance, marks retransmissions, duplicate ACKs and zero windows. Colouring affects only how the rows are shown.

questionText: Which tcpdump command captures traffic to or from port 443 on interface eth0, without resolving addresses to names, and saves it to a file for later analysis in Wireshark?
explanation: -i chooses the interface, -n turns off name resolution, -w writes raw packets to a pcap file and port 443 is the BPF filter. -r reads an existing file, tcp.port == 443 is display-filter syntax, and -c 443 would stop after 443 packets of any kind.

questionText: What does a NetFlow record, exported by a router to a collector, contain?
options: A full copy of every packet, including its payload
Only the total octet counters of each interface, as SNMP gives
A summary of one flow: its key fields (source and destination IP and port, protocol, ToS, input interface) with packet and byte counts and start and end times
A copy of the router's routing table
explanation: The router groups packets that share the key fields into flows and exports one record per flow over UDP, so a collector can show which hosts and applications use the bandwidth. No payload is exported, which keeps the data small.

questionText: Which statement about Wireshark is NOT correct?
options: It can read passwords sent by unencrypted protocols such as Telnet or HTTP
It decodes protocols layer by layer, from the Ethernet frame up to the application data
It can open capture files saved by tcpdump
It can block or modify packets passing through the interface in real time, like a firewall
explanation: Wireshark is a passive analyser: it copies packets from the capture driver (libpcap or Npcap) and never alters or blocks the live traffic. It does decode hundreds of protocols, show plaintext credentials and read tcpdump's pcap files.

questionText: An SNMP agent sends an unsolicited Trap message to the network management station. On which port does the manager receive it?
explanation: Agents listen for Get/Set requests on UDP 161; traps are sent to the manager on UDP 162.

questionText: Which Wireshark display filter shows only packets whose TCP source or destination port is 80?
explanation: tcp.port == 80 is display-filter syntax; port 80 is BPF capture-filter syntax, and the other two are invalid.

questionText: MRTG reads a router interface's ifInOctets counter twice, 60 seconds apart, and the counter has increased by 7,500,000. If the interface speed is 10 Mbps, what is the inbound utilisation?
Which kind of encryption is faster, and is therefore used to encrypt bulk data?
options: Neither; bulk data is protected only by hashing
explanation: Symmetric ciphers such as AES use cheap bit operations, often in hardware, while public-key operations need modular arithmetic on 2048-bit numbers and are roughly 100 to 1000 times slower. Hybrid systems such as TLS and PGP therefore use public-key methods only to set up a symmetric session key.

questionText: AES is an example of:
explanation: AES (Rijndael) uses the same secret key to encrypt and decrypt 128-bit blocks, with 128, 192 or 256-bit keys. DES and 3DES are also symmetric, while RSA and ECC are asymmetric.

questionText: What is the RSA algorithm mainly used for in practice?
options: Encrypting large files faster than AES can
Public-key encryption of short values, such as a session key, and digital signatures
Converting IP addresses into MAC addresses
Scanning a host for open TCP ports
explanation: RSA is slow, so it protects only short values: a random symmetric key (as in PGP) or a message hash when signing. The bulk data is then encrypted with a symmetric cipher such as AES.

questionText: What is the primary purpose of the Diffie-Hellman key exchange?
options: To allocate IP addresses to hosts
To let two parties agree on a shared secret key over an insecure network without ever sending the key itself
explanation: Each side sends only g^x mod p, and both compute the same g^(ab) mod p, which an eavesdropper could find only by solving the discrete logarithm problem. Plain Diffie-Hellman does not authenticate the parties, so it is combined with signatures or certificates to stop a man-in-the-middle.

questionText: According to Kerckhoffs's principle, a cryptosystem should remain secure even if:
options: The key is known to the attacker, as long as the algorithm stays secret
Everything about it except the key, including the algorithm, is known to the attacker
The attacker can read the plaintext before it is encrypted
Every user in the world shares the same key
explanation: Security must rest on the secrecy of the key alone, because algorithms leak and can be reverse-engineered, and public algorithms such as AES are better studied. Relying on a secret algorithm is 'security through obscurity', the opposite idea.

questionText: Using a Caesar cipher with key k = 3 (each letter shifted three places forward), what is the ciphertext of NEPAL?
explanation: C = (P + 3) mod 26: N to Q, E to H, P to S, A to D and L to O, giving QHSDO. KBMXI shifts backwards (that is decryption), while RITEP and PGRCN use shifts of 4 and 2.

questionText: How many useful (non-identity) keys does a Caesar cipher have, and how many keys does a general monoalphabetic substitution cipher have?
explanation: A Caesar key is a shift of 1 to 25, since a shift of 0 or 26 changes nothing. A monoalphabetic key is any permutation of the 26 letters, so there are 26! = 4.0 x 10^26 keys, yet the cipher still falls quickly to letter-frequency analysis.

questionText: Encrypt NETWORK with the Vigenere cipher using the key KEY (A = 0, ..., Z = 25; the key is repeated as needed).
explanation: Add KEYKEYK mod 26: N+K = 13+10 = 23 (X), E+E = 8 (I), T+Y = 43 mod 26 = 17 (R), W+K = 32 mod 26 = 6 (G), O+E = 18 (S), R+Y = 41 mod 26 = 15 (P), K+K = 20 (U). YJSHTQV counts A as 1, DAVMKTA subtracts the key (decryption) and XIRWORK forgets to repeat the key.

questionText: The plaintext SECURITY is encrypted with a rail-fence cipher of depth 2 (letters written alternately on two rails, then read rail by rail). What is the ciphertext, and what kind of cipher is this?
explanation: Rail 1 holds letters 1, 3, 5 and 7 (S, C, R, T) and rail 2 letters 2, 4, 6 and 8 (E, U, I, Y), giving SCRTEUIY. The letters are unchanged and only their order moves, which makes it a transposition cipher; SREUIYCT is what 3 rails would give.

questionText: A Playfair cipher uses the key MONARCHY, whose 5 x 5 matrix rows are MONAR, CHYBD, EFGIK, LPQST and UVWXZ (I and J share a cell). What is the ciphertext of SPOOF, splitting the double letter with X?
explanation: The pairs are SP, OX, OF: SP lies in one row, so each letter moves right (TQ); OX forms a rectangle, so each letter takes the corner in its own row and the other letter's column (AV); OF lies in one column, so each letter moves down (HP). TQVAHP swaps the rectangle corners, QLAVVH moves left and up (decryption), and TQAVNG treats the column pair like a row.

questionText: Alice wants to send Bob a message that only Bob can read, using public-key encryption. Which key does she encrypt it with?
explanation: Only the holder of the matching private key, Bob, can decrypt what was encrypted with Bob's public key. Encrypting with Alice's private key makes a signature that anyone can undo with her public key, so it gives no confidentiality.

questionText: A company of 50 employees wants every pair of employees to be able to talk privately. How many secret keys are needed with pairwise symmetric encryption, and how many individual keys (public plus private) with public-key cryptography?
explanation: Symmetric: one key per pair, n(n - 1)/2 = 50 x 49 / 2 = 1,225. Public-key: each employee has one public and one private key, 2n = 100 keys, and a new employee adds only 2 keys instead of 50.

questionText: Which statement correctly contrasts block ciphers and stream ciphers?
options: A block cipher uses a public key, while a stream cipher uses a private key
A stream cipher needs the data padded to a multiple of its block size, while a block cipher never needs padding
A block cipher encrypts fixed-size blocks (128 bits for AES), while a stream cipher XORs the data with a keystream bit by bit or byte by byte, as ChaCha20 does
Block ciphers are used only for hashing, and stream ciphers only for key exchange
explanation: Both kinds are symmetric. A block cipher in ECB or CBC mode may need padding, while a stream cipher (or a block cipher in CTR mode) needs none, but it must never reuse a keystream, that is, the same key with the same nonce.

questionText: What are the effective key length and the block size of DES?
explanation: DES takes a 64-bit key of which 8 bits are parity, leaving 56 effective key bits, and encrypts 64-bit blocks in 16 Feistel rounds. A 56-bit key is small enough to search exhaustively today.

questionText: AES-256 encrypts data in blocks of what size, and with how many rounds?
explanation: The AES block is always 128 bits; only the key length changes the number of rounds: 10 for AES-128, 12 for AES-192 and 14 for AES-256. Rijndael itself allowed larger blocks, but the AES standard (FIPS 197) fixes the block at 128 bits.

questionText: A key-search machine tests 10^12 DES keys per second. How long does it take, in the worst case, to try every 56-bit DES key?
explanation: 2^56 = 7.2 x 10^16 keys, and 7.2 x 10^16 / 10^12 = 7.2 x 10^4 s = 20.0 h. On average the key is found halfway (about 10 h); 214 days would be the time for a full 64-bit key and 2.3 years the time at only 10^9 keys per second.

questionText: Why is ECB mode unsuitable for encrypting an image, or any data with repeated patterns?
options: ECB needs a new secret key for every block
ECB ciphertext cannot be decrypted without the IV, which is lost with the image
Identical plaintext blocks encrypt to identical ciphertext blocks under the same key, so the patterns stay visible in the ciphertext
ECB turns the block cipher into a public-key cipher, which is too slow for images
explanation: ECB encrypts every block independently, with no IV and no chaining, so an encrypted bitmap still shows the outline of the picture. CBC, CTR or GCM with a fresh IV or nonce hide such patterns.

questionText: Which statement about the CBC and CTR modes of operation is correct?
options: CTR XORs each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block, so it is sequential; CBC encrypts counter values, so it can run in parallel

CBC XORs each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encrypting it, so encryption is sequential; CTR encrypts successive counter values to make a keystream, so blocks can be encrypted in parallel
Neither mode needs an IV or a nonce, because the key alone makes each block unique
CTR needs the plaintext padded to a multiple of the block size, while CBC does not
explanation: In CBC, C_i = E_K(P_i XOR C_i-1) with a random IV as C_0, and the last block is padded. In CTR, C_i = P_i XOR E_K(nonce || i), which needs no padding and allows parallel encryption, but a nonce must never be reused with the same key.

questionText: A 1,030-byte message is encrypted with AES in CBC mode using PKCS#7 padding. How long is the ciphertext, not counting the IV?
explanation: AES blocks are 16 bytes and 1,030 = 64 x 16 + 6, so PKCS#7 adds 10 padding bytes to fill a 65th block: 65 x 16 = 1,040 bytes. 1,030 ignores the padding, 1,032 uses 8-byte DES blocks, and 1,056 also counts the 16-byte IV.

questionText: What are the digest sizes of MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256, respectively?
explanation: MD5 gives 128 bits and SHA-1 160 bits, and both are broken for collision resistance; SHA-256, from the SHA-2 family, gives 256 bits and is the current standard. SHA-512 is the family member with a 512-bit digest.

questionText: A cryptographic hash function makes it computationally infeasible to find ANY two different messages that produce the same digest. What is this property called?
explanation: Preimage resistance means a digest cannot be inverted to a message, and second-preimage resistance means that for a GIVEN message no other message with the same digest can be found. Collision resistance lets the attacker choose both messages, and by the birthday paradox it costs only about 2^(n/2) trials for an n-bit hash.

questionText: Why is elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC) often preferred to RSA in phones, smart cards and TLS?
options: It is a symmetric cipher, so it is as fast as AES
It needs no private key, only a public one
It gives the same security with much smaller keys: a 256-bit ECC key is about as strong as a 3,072-bit RSA key
Its security rests on factoring, which is harder for curves than for integers
explanation: ECC rests on the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem, for which no sub-exponential attack is known, so keys and signatures are short and operations are fast. It is still public-key cryptography, with a private and a public key.

questionText: Alice and Bob share a secret key and attach an HMAC-SHA256 tag to every message. What does a valid tag prove to Bob?
options: That the message was kept confidential in transit
That Alice cannot later deny sending it, because only she knows the key
Nothing more than a plain SHA-256 hash, since anyone can compute the tag
That the message was not altered and came from someone holding the shared key; it gives no non-repudiation, because Bob could have made the same tag
explanation: A MAC provides integrity and data-origin authentication but no confidentiality, since the message travels in clear unless it is also encrypted. Both parties hold the key, so a third party cannot tell which of them made a tag; non-repudiation needs a digital signature.

questionText: In RSA with p = 13 and q = 17, what are n and φ(n)?
explanation: n = p x q = 13 x 17 = 221 and φ(n) = (p - 1)(q - 1) = 12 x 16 = 192. 220 is n - 1, which is the totient only when n itself is prime.

questionText: An RSA key has φ(n) = 192. Which of these values can be chosen as the public exponent e?
explanation: e must satisfy 1 < e < φ(n) and gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1 so that its inverse d exists. 192 = 2^6 x 3, so 3, 12 and 16 all share a factor with it, while gcd(11, 192) = 1.

questionText: In RSA with p = 7, q = 19 and e = 5, what is the private exponent d?
explanation: φ(n) = 6 x 18 = 108, and the extended Euclidean algorithm gives 1 = 2 x 108 - 43 x 5, so d = -43 mod 108 = 65 (check: 5 x 65 = 325 = 3 x 108 + 1). 80 is the inverse modulo n = 133, 53 the inverse modulo n - 1 = 132, and 43 drops the minus sign.

questionText: A public RSA key is (e = 5, n = 91). What is the ciphertext of the message m = 4?
explanation: c = m^e mod n = 4^5 mod 91 = 1,024 mod 91 = 1,024 - 11 x 91 = 23. Reducing modulo φ(n) = 72 gives the wrong 16, 1,024 forgets the reduction, and 20 multiplies instead of raising to a power.

questionText: Bob's RSA key uses p = 5, q = 17 and e = 5. He receives the ciphertext c = 3. What plaintext m does he recover?
explanation: φ(n) = 4 x 16 = 64 and d = 13 (5 x 13 = 65 = 64 + 1), so m = 3^13 mod 85 = 63; re-encrypting, 63^5 mod 85 = 3 confirms it. 73 wrongly uses e as the exponent, 19 reduces modulo φ(n) instead of n, and 27 comes from the sign error d = -13 mod 64 = 51.

questionText: Alice and Bob run Diffie-Hellman with the public values p = 19 and g = 2. Alice's secret is a = 5 and Bob's is b = 7. What shared key K do they both compute?
explanation: A = 2^5 mod 19 = 13 and B = 2^7 mod 19 = 14 are sent in clear; Alice computes K = 14^5 mod 19 = 10 and Bob K = 13^7 mod 19 = 10, both equal to 2^35 mod 19. 13 and 14 are only the public values, and 11 is 2^(5+7) mod 19, which wrongly adds the exponents.

questionText: Why does the security of RSA rest on the difficulty of factoring the modulus n?
options: Factoring n reveals the plaintext directly, without any need for d
The public exponent e is hidden inside n, and factoring n reveals it
φ(n) is published with the public key, so n itself must be kept secret
Anyone who finds p and q can compute φ(n) = (p - 1)(q - 1) and then d = e^(-1) mod φ(n), recovering the private key
explanation: The public key (e, n) is public, and φ(n) is the only missing piece needed to compute d. Multiplying p and q is easy, but no known classical algorithm can factor a 2048-bit n in practical time.

questionText: In RSA with p = 5, q = 11 and public exponent e = 3, the private exponent d is:
How many secret keys are needed so that each pair among 10 users can communicate using symmetric encryption?
explanation: Each pair needs its own key: n(n − 1)/2 = 10 × 9 / 2 = 45.

questionText: In SSL/TLS and other public-key infrastructures, what does a certificate authority (CA) do?
options: It encrypts all the data exchanged between the browser and the web server
It checks the identity of an applicant and issues a digital certificate, signed with the CA's private key, that binds the applicant's name to its public key
It routes packets between the client and the server
It scans downloaded files for viruses
explanation: A CA vouches for public keys: after checking the applicant, it signs a certificate binding the subject's name to its key, and it can later revoke that certificate. Browsers verify the CA's signature, but the CA takes no part in encrypting the session.

questionText: In an RSA digital signature, which key is used to sign (that is, to 'encrypt') the hash of the message?
options: A symmetric key shared with the receiver
explanation: Only the sender holds the private key, so only the sender can produce S = H(M)^d mod n, while anyone can check it with the sender's public key. Encrypting with the receiver's public key would give confidentiality, not a signature.

questionText: Which security service does a digital signature on its own NOT provide?
explanation: The message travels next to its signature in readable form, so anyone can read it; to hide it, it must also be encrypted. A signature does provide integrity, origin authentication and non-repudiation.

questionText: What does an X.509 public-key certificate essentially bind together?
options: A user name and the user's password
A domain name and its IP address
The subject's identity and the subject's public key, under the issuing CA's signature
A private key and the MAC address of the computer that stores it
explanation: A certificate states that a public key belongs to a named subject and is signed by the issuing CA, so anyone who trusts the CA can trust the key. Binding names to addresses is the job of DNS, and private keys never appear in certificates.

questionText: Which PGP step converts the binary output of signing, compression and encryption into printable ASCII characters so that the message can pass through e-mail systems?
explanation: Radix-64 (base64) maps every 3 bytes to 4 printable characters, making the data about 33 % larger, so that text-only mail systems carry it unchanged. Segmentation only splits long messages to fit mail size limits.

questionText: How does PGP traditionally let a user decide that a public key really belongs to its claimed owner?
options: Through a web of trust, in which users sign one another's keys and each user decides how far to trust each introducer
Through a single worldwide root CA run by the IETF
Through the MX record of the owner's mail domain
Through the TLS certificate of the owner's mail server
explanation: PGP is decentralised: keys are signed by other users, and a key is accepted when it carries signatures from introducers the user trusts enough. S/MIME, by contrast, relies on X.509 certificates issued by CAs.

questionText: Which ITU-T standard defines the format of the public-key certificates used by TLS and S/MIME?
explanation: X.509 defines public-key certificates (version 3 adds extensions) and certificate revocation lists. X.25 is an old packet-switching WAN standard, X.400 a message-handling (e-mail) standard and X.800 the OSI security architecture.

questionText: An OpenPGP version 4 key has a 160-bit fingerprint (a SHA-1 hash of the key), and its long key ID is the low-order 64 bits of that fingerprint. Written in hexadecimal, how many digits long are the fingerprint and the key ID?
explanation: Each hex digit carries 4 bits, so the fingerprint has 160 / 4 = 40 digits and the key ID 64 / 4 = 16 digits. 20 and 8 are the lengths in bytes, not in hex digits.

questionText: Why does a sender sign a hash of the message rather than the message itself?
options: Hashing encrypts the message, so the signed message also becomes confidential
Signing the whole message would reveal the private key to the receiver
The receiver cannot recompute the hash, so the hash itself proves the sender's identity
The hash is short and of fixed length, so the slow private-key operation runs once on a few bytes and the signature has a fixed size, while any change to the message still changes the hash
explanation: Public-key operations are slow and RSA can only process values smaller than n, so signing a 32-byte SHA-256 digest is far cheaper than signing megabytes of data. Because the hash is collision resistant, a signature on the digest effectively covers the whole message.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT a field of an X.509 v3 certificate?
options: Validity period (not before and not after)
explanation: A certificate is public and carries only the subject's public key, together with the serial number, issuer, subject, validity period, extensions and the CA's signature. The private key never leaves its owner.

questionText: Which statement correctly distinguishes a CRL from OCSP?
options: A CRL lists every valid certificate a CA has issued, while OCSP lists only the revoked ones
A CRL is sent by an applicant to request a new certificate, while OCSP returns the signed certificate

A CRL is a list of the serial numbers of revoked certificates, signed and published periodically by the CA; OCSP lets a client ask a responder about one certificate and receive a signed good, revoked or unknown answer
Both are encryption algorithms that protect certificates in transit
explanation: Both report revocation, which is needed when a private key is stolen or a certificate is mis-issued before it expires. A CRL must be downloaded in full and can be hours old, while OCSP (RFC 6960) answers for one certificate at a time; the request for a new certificate is a CSR.

questionText: A web server sends its certificate L, issued by the intermediate CA I, together with I's certificate, which was issued by the root CA R. R's self-signed certificate is in the browser's trust store. How does the browser check the signatures in this chain?
options: It checks L's signature with I's public key, and I's signature with R's public key taken from its trust store
It checks L's signature with the server's private key, which is sent during the handshake
It checks L's signature with L's own public key, since every certificate is self-signed
It asks R to decrypt L with R's private key during every connection
explanation: Each certificate is signed by its issuer, so it is verified with the public key in the issuer's certificate, step by step up to a root the browser already trusts. Only the root is self-signed, and the CAs take no part in the connection itself.

questionText: PGP sends a message that is both signed and encrypted. In which order does the sender apply the operations?
explanation: The signature is computed on the original message; message and signature are then ZIP-compressed, encrypted with the session key and finally radix-64 encoded for transport, and the receiver reverses the steps. Signing before compressing lets the uncompressed message and its signature be stored and checked later, independently of the compression algorithm.

questionText: Why does PGP compress the message before encrypting it rather than after?
options: Radix-64 conversion accepts only compressed input
Compression removes redundancy, which shortens the data to be encrypted and sent and leaves less structure for cryptanalysis, whereas ciphertext looks random and would hardly compress
The signature must be computed over the compressed data
ZIP compression is itself a form of encryption, so the session key can be shorter
explanation: Good ciphertext is statistically random, so compressing after encryption would save almost nothing. Compressing first saves bandwidth and removes redundancy an attacker could exploit; the signature, however, is made before compression.

questionText: Alice sends one PGP-encrypted message to three recipients, Bob, Carol and Dave. How is it encrypted?
options: The message is encrypted three times, each copy with a different recipient's public key
The message is encrypted once with Alice's private key, so that all three can decrypt it with her public key
The message is encrypted once with a random session key, and that session key is encrypted separately with each recipient's public key
The three recipients must first agree on a shared password, which PGP uses as the key
explanation: The hybrid design encrypts the bulk data only once with a fast symmetric cipher, and each recipient's public key protects only the short session key, which that recipient unlocks with his own private key. Encrypting with Alice's private key would give no confidentiality, because her public key is public.

questionText: How does PGP protect the private keys stored on a user's own computer?
options: They are kept in the private-key ring, each encrypted with a symmetric key derived from a hash of the user's passphrase
They are stored in plain text, because the user's disk is considered private
They are encrypted with the user's own public key
They are uploaded to a public key server, which keeps them secret
explanation: The private-key ring holds the user's own key pairs with every private key encrypted under a key derived from the passphrase, so a stolen key file alone is not enough. The public-key ring holds other users' public keys and trust information, and key servers store only public keys.

questionText: Bob uses GnuPG's default rule: a key is valid if it is signed by at least 1 key whose owner he trusts fully, or by at least 3 keys whose owners he trusts marginally. He trusts Carol fully and Dave, Erin and Frank marginally, and he has verified all four of their keys himself. Key K1 is signed by Dave and Erin; K2 by Carol; K3 by Dave, Erin and Frank; K4 by Dave and by Grace, whom Bob does not know. Which keys does Bob accept as valid?
explanation: K2 has one fully trusted signature and K3 three marginal ones, so both are valid. K1 has only two marginal signatures, and on K4 Grace's signature counts for nothing, leaving a single marginal one.

questionText: Bob checks a signed message. He hashes the message he received, and applying Alice's public key to the attached signature gives a different value. What should he conclude?
options: The message is authentic but was compressed on the way
The signature is invalid: the message or the signature was altered, or it was not made with Alice's private key; Bob cannot tell which, so he rejects the message
Only the confidentiality of the message has been lost; its integrity is intact
Alice's private key must have been stolen, so her certificate should be revoked
explanation: A mismatch means the check failed, but it cannot show whether the message was changed, the signature was damaged or a different key was used; in every case the message is not accepted as coming from Alice. A mismatch alone is no evidence that her key was stolen.

questionText: Which statement correctly compares S/MIME with PGP?
options: S/MIME can only sign messages and cannot encrypt them
PGP needs an X.509 certificate from a CA for every key, while S/MIME uses a web of trust
S/MIME uses X.509 certificates issued by CAs and carries signed or encrypted content as MIME parts built with CMS, whereas PGP traditionally relies on a web of trust with OpenPGP keys
S/MIME encrypts only the hop between two mail servers, like STARTTLS
explanation: Both sign and encrypt the message itself end to end; they differ mainly in their trust model and message format. S/MIME's CA-based PKI suits organisations and corporate mail clients, while OpenPGP is common among individuals and for signing software.

questionText: Why should MD5 and SHA-1 no longer be used as the hash in digital signatures?
options: Practical collision attacks exist, so an attacker can prepare two different documents with the same digest, have the harmless one signed, and reuse that signature on the other
Their digests are too long for RSA to sign
They are keyed hashes, so the verifier would need the signer's secret key
They are much slower than SHA-256
explanation: A signature covers only the digest, so two messages with equal digests share one signature. MD5 collisions take seconds to find and a SHA-1 collision was published in 2017, so signatures now use SHA-256 or stronger.

questionText: Why is it good practice to use separate key pairs for signing and for encryption, as PGP does with subkeys and X.509 does with the key-usage extension?
options: Because RSA cannot mathematically use one key pair for both purposes
Because a signing private key must be published, while an encryption private key is kept secret

Because an encryption private key may need to be backed up or escrowed so that data can still be recovered, while copies of a signing key would undermine non-repudiation; the two keys can also be replaced on different schedules
Because encryption keys must always be ten times longer than signing keys
explanation: If the key that decrypts stored data is lost, the data is lost too, so that key is often backed up; a signing key should exist only with its owner, so that a signature proves who signed. Separate keys let each be handled correctly and limit the damage if one is compromised.

questionText: On 15 April 2026 a browser connects to https://pay.shop.example. The server's certificate lists shop.example and www.shop.example as its Subject Alternative Names, is valid from 1 March 2026 to 30 May 2026, chains to a trusted root and is not revoked. What does the browser do?
options: It accepts the certificate, because the chain, the dates and the revocation status are all in order
It rejects the certificate as expired
It rejects the certificate, because an intermediate CA may not issue server certificates
It rejects the certificate, because pay.shop.example is not among the names it certifies
explanation: The host name must match a Subject Alternative Name, and pay.shop.example is not listed; a wildcard entry *.shop.example would have covered it. The dates (15 April lies between 1 March and 30 May) and the chain are fine, but one failed check is enough to reject the certificate.

questionText: Alice's RSA public key is (e = 3, n = 55). Bob receives a message whose hash value is h = 17. Which of these is a valid signature by Alice on that hash?
explanation: Verification computes S^e mod n and compares it with h: 8^3 = 512 = 9 × 55 + 17, so 8^3 mod 55 = 17 matches. The others fail: 18^3 mod 55 = 2, 27^3 mod 55 = 48 and 13^3 mod 55 = 52 (18 is h^3 mod 55, obtained by wrongly applying the public key to the hash).

questionText: A signature scheme must offer 128-bit security against an attacker who searches for hash collisions. What is the smallest digest length that achieves this?
explanation: A birthday attack finds a collision after about 2^(n/2) hash computations, so 2^(n/2) = 2^128 gives n = 256 bits, as with SHA-256. A 128-bit digest resists collisions only up to about 2^64 work.

questionText: Alice's RSA key uses p = 7, q = 11 and the public exponent e = 13. She signs a message whose hash value, reduced modulo n, is h = 18. What is her signature S?
explanation: n = 77, φ(n) = 6 × 10 = 60 and d = 13^(−1) mod 60 = 37 (13 × 37 = 481 = 8 × 60 + 1), so S = 18^37 mod 77 = 39, and the check 39^13 mod 77 = 18 confirms it. 46 = 18^13 mod 77 uses the public exponent, 15 uses an inverse taken modulo n, and 48 reduces modulo φ(n) instead of n.

questionText: Alice signs with textbook RSA, without hashing or padding, and her public key is (e = 5, n = 91). An attacker has seen her signatures on the messages 2 and 5, which are s(2) = 32 and s(5) = 31. Without knowing her private key, what valid signature can he produce for the message 10?
explanation: Textbook RSA is multiplicative: s(2) × s(5) = 2^d × 5^d = 10^d (mod n), so s(10) = 32 × 31 mod 91 = 992 − 910 = 82, and 82^5 mod 91 = 10 verifies. 63 adds the two signatures instead of multiplying them, 69 = 32 × 5 mod 91 multiplies a signature by a message, and 56 reduces 992 modulo φ(n) = 72 instead of n. This forgery is why real schemes sign a padded hash (PKCS #1 v1.5 or PSS) instead of the raw message.

questionText: Alice's RSA key pair is (e = 3, d = 7, n = 33) and Bob's public key is (e = 5, n = 91). Using textbook RSA, Alice signs the hash value h = 9 with her private key and then encrypts the signature with Bob's public key. What value does she send?
explanation: Sign: S = 9^7 mod 33 = 15; encrypt: C = 15^5 mod 91 = 71. Bob recovers S = 71^29 mod 91 = 15 with his private key (d = 29) and checks 15^3 mod 33 = 9; 15 alone is the unencrypted signature, 81 = 9^5 mod 91 encrypts the hash without signing it, and 8 = 15^3 mod 91 uses Alice's exponent instead of Bob's.

questionText: A PGP user signs with a 2048-bit RSA key. How long is the raw signature, and how many characters does it take after radix-64 encoding? Take the signature to be exactly as long as the modulus, and ignore packet headers, line breaks and the checksum.
explanation: An RSA signature is a number below n, so it occupies 2048 / 8 = 256 bytes; radix-64 then gives 4 × ceil(256 / 3) = 4 × 86 = 344 characters, including padding. 342 forgets that the output comes in whole groups of 4, and 32 bytes is the size of a SHA-256 digest, not of the signature.

questionText: A PGP message and its signature together total 12,000 bytes. ZIP compresses them to 35 % of that size, encryption with the session key keeps the length unchanged, and the 256-byte RSA-encrypted session key is then prepended. Ignoring packet headers, line breaks and the checksum, how long is the result after radix-64 encoding?
explanation: Compressed: 0.35 × 12,000 = 4,200 bytes; adding the session key: 4,200 + 256 = 4,456 bytes; radix-64: 4 × ceil(4,456 / 3) = 4 × 1,486 = 5,944 bytes. 5,600 forgets the session key, 4,456 forgets the encoding and 16,344 skips the compression.

questionText: A signature system uses a weak 80-bit hash, and an attacker can compute 10^9 hashes per second. Roughly how long does a birthday attack need to find a collision, and how long does it take to find a message matching one given digest (a second preimage)?
options: About 18 minutes for a collision; about 38 million years for a second preimage
About 38 million years for a collision; about 18 minutes for a second preimage
explanation: A collision needs about 2^(n/2) = 2^40 ≈ 1.1 × 10^12 hashes, which is 1,100 s or about 18 minutes; a second preimage needs about 2^80 ≈ 1.2 × 10^24 hashes, which is 1.2 × 10^15 s or about 38 million years. This gap is why a hash used for signatures needs twice as many bits as the target security level.

questionText: To verify Alice's digital signature on a message, Bob uses:
explanation: Alice signs with her private key, so anyone verifies with Alice's public key.

questionText: In PGP confidentiality, the message body is encrypted with a one-time session key, and that session key is then encrypted with:
explanation: PGP is hybrid: a symmetric session key protects the data and the receiver's public key protects the session key, so only the receiver can recover it.

questionText: What does VPN stand for?
explanation: A VPN is a virtual private network: an encrypted tunnel across a shared public network that lets remote hosts or sites behave as if they were on one private network.

questionText: Which of the following best describes a VPN?
options: A hardware firewall that blocks incoming connections
A secure, encrypted connection (a tunnel) across an untrusted network such as the Internet
explanation: A VPN wraps private traffic in encrypted, authenticated packets so that it can cross the Internet safely; IPsec and TLS-based VPNs are the common types. A firewall may terminate VPN tunnels, but it is not itself a VPN.

questionText: At which layer does IPsec provide security?
explanation: IPsec protects the IP packets themselves, so TCP, UDP, ICMP and every application above them are covered without any change to the applications. TLS, by contrast, sits above TCP and protects one connection at a time.

questionText: Which protocol suite is most commonly used to build secure site-to-site VPNs between the gateways of two offices?
explanation: IPsec, with ESP in tunnel mode and IKE for key exchange, is the standard for gateway-to-gateway VPNs. FTP transfers files, BGP exchanges routes between autonomous systems and SMTP carries e-mail, and none of them provides this security.

questionText: What does SSL/TLS add to a TCP connection?
options: Authentication of the server (and optionally the client), plus encryption and integrity protection of the data
Packet sequencing and retransmission of lost segments
Flow control between the sender and the receiver
explanation: TLS adds the security services: certificate-based authentication, confidentiality and integrity. Sequencing, retransmission and flow control are already done by TCP underneath, and SSL itself is obsolete, so today this means TLS 1.2 or 1.3.

questionText: Which statement about SSL and TLS is correct today?
options: SSL 3.0 is newer and stronger than TLS 1.2
All SSL versions, and also TLS 1.0 and 1.1, are deprecated; secure connections should use TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3
HTTPS still requires SSL 3.0 for compatibility
SSL and TLS are unrelated protocols with different purposes
explanation: TLS 1.0 (1999) was the IETF's successor to Netscape's SSL 3.0. SSL 2.0 and 3.0 are prohibited (RFC 6176 and RFC 7568; POODLE broke SSL 3.0), and RFC 8996 deprecated TLS 1.0 and 1.1 in 2021.

questionText: Which transport protocol and port does IKE use to negotiate IPsec security associations when there is no NAT on the path?
explanation: IKE runs over UDP port 500; when a NAT is detected, IKE and ESP move to UDP port 4500 (NAT traversal). Port 443 is HTTPS, 53 is DNS and 22 is SSH.

questionText: What does the STARTTLS command do in SMTP, IMAP and POP3?
options: It upgrades a connection that began in plain text on the protocol's normal port to TLS, before any credentials or message data are sent
It opens a second connection on a dedicated TLS-only port
It encrypts the message end to end, so that no mail server can read it
It starts an IPsec tunnel between the two mail servers
explanation: With STARTTLS the two sides first talk in clear (for example SMTP on port 587 or 25) and then run the TLS handshake on the same connection. It protects only that hop, and an active attacker who strips the STARTTLS offer can force plain text unless TLS is required.

questionText: TLS needs a reliable, in-order byte stream and therefore runs over TCP. Which protocol gives the same kind of security to UDP-based applications, such as WebRTC or some VPN clients?
explanation: DTLS adapts TLS to datagrams by adding explicit sequence numbers and coping with loss and reordering itself. SSH secures remote logins over TCP, S/MIME secures e-mail messages, and L2TP is a tunnelling protocol with no encryption of its own.

questionText: Which option correctly matches each security protocol with the layer at which it protects traffic?
options: IPsec: transport layer; TLS: network layer; WPA2: application layer; PGP: data link layer
IPsec: data link layer; TLS: application layer; WPA2: network layer; PGP: transport layer
IPsec: network layer; TLS: data link layer; WPA2: physical layer; PGP: transport layer
IPsec: network layer; TLS: just above TCP, below the application; WPA2: data link layer (Wi-Fi); PGP: application layer
explanation: IPsec protects IP packets, TLS protects a TCP byte stream just above the transport layer, WPA2 encrypts Wi-Fi frames at the data link layer, and PGP protects the message itself at the application layer. Lower-layer protection covers all traffic between two points, while higher-layer protection travels end to end with the data.

questionText: An attacker records many TLS 1.2 sessions with a server and, years later, steals the server's RSA private key. Which of the recorded sessions can he now decrypt?
options: Every recorded session, whatever key exchange was used
None, because TLS never uses the certificate's key for anything
Only the sessions that used ECDHE key exchange
The sessions that used RSA key transport, in which the client encrypted the pre-master secret with the server's RSA public key; sessions that used ephemeral (EC)DHE stay safe
explanation: With RSA key transport the stolen key decrypts the recorded pre-master secret and hence every session key. With ephemeral (EC)DHE the RSA key only signs the handshake and the DH secrets are discarded, which is forward secrecy; TLS 1.3 therefore allows only (EC)DHE.

questionText: Which of the following was removed from TLS in version 1.3?
options: Static RSA key transport, in which the client encrypts a pre-master secret with the server's RSA public key
explanation: TLS 1.3 removed static RSA and static DH key exchange, CBC and RC4 ciphers, compression and renegotiation, keeping only AEAD ciphers and (EC)DHE. Certificates are still used, but only to sign the handshake.

questionText: In the TLS 1.2 cipher suite TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, which component authenticates the server?
options: ECDSA, the signature algorithm of the key in the server's certificate
explanation: The server signs its ephemeral ECDHE parameters with the ECDSA private key that matches its certificate, which proves its identity. ECDHE agrees the keys, AES-256-GCM encrypts and authenticates the records, and SHA-384 is the hash used by the key-derivation function (PRF).

questionText: What is the purpose of the Finished messages at the end of a TLS handshake?
options: They close the TCP connection once the handshake is over
Each side sends a MAC, computed with the new keys, over the entire handshake transcript, so that any tampering with earlier handshake messages, such as a cipher-suite downgrade, is detected
They carry the server's certificate chain
They tell the certificate authority that the session has started
explanation: The hello messages travel before any keys exist, so an attacker could try to alter them; the Finished messages prove that both sides saw the same handshake and hold the same keys. Without 0-RTT or False Start, the client sends application data only after it has verified the server's Finished.

questionText: On public Wi-Fi an attacker intercepts a user's connection to https://bank.example and presents his own self-signed certificate for bank.example. What normally defeats this attack?
options: Nothing needs to, because TLS encryption alone stops the attacker from reading the data
The TCP checksum detects the forged certificate

The browser cannot chain the certificate to a trusted root CA, so it shows an error and does not continue; the attack works only if the user clicks through the warning or a rogue root certificate has been installed
The access point's WPA2 encryption blocks the attacker's certificate
explanation: The attacker terminates the TLS connection himself, so encryption alone would protect nothing; it is the certificate check that ties the keys to the real bank. HSTS makes browsers refuse to let users click through such errors on sites that use it.

questionText: Why does IPsec AH fail when a NAT device sits between the two peers, while ESP with NAT traversal works?
options: AH packets are larger than the NAT device's MTU
NAT devices drop every encrypted packet

AH's integrity check covers the addresses in the outer IP header, which NAT rewrites, so the check fails; ESP does not authenticate the outer header, and NAT traversal wraps ESP in UDP port 4500 so that the NAT has ports to translate
AH runs over TCP, which NAT cannot translate
explanation: AH authenticates the unchanging fields of the IP header, including the addresses, so any address translation makes every packet look forged. ESP's ICV covers only the ESP header, payload and trailer, and the UDP wrapper gives the NAT a port pair to work with.

questionText: Two IPsec gateways exchange ESP-protected traffic in both directions. How many ESP security associations do they need, and how does a receiver find the SA an arriving packet belongs to?
options: Two SAs, one for each direction; the receiver finds the SA from the SPI in the ESP header (together with the destination address and protocol)
One SA, found from the pair of IP addresses
Four SAs, one per host and direction, found from the TCP port numbers
Two SAs, found from the IKE port number 500
explanation: An SA is one-way, so two-way traffic needs a pair, each with its own SPI chosen by the receiving side. The receiver looks the SPI up in its Security Association Database to get the keys and algorithms for that packet.

questionText: An observer on the Internet captures a packet of a site-to-site VPN that uses ESP in tunnel mode. What can he read?
options: The inner hosts' IP addresses and TCP port numbers, but not the data
Nothing at all, not even the outer IP header
The two gateways' IP addresses, the SPI, the sequence number and the packet's length, but not the inner addresses, the port numbers or the data
Everything, because ESP in tunnel mode only authenticates the packet
explanation: The new outer IP header and the ESP header (SPI and sequence number) must stay in clear for routing and SA lookup, while the whole original packet, including its header and ports, is encrypted. Only the size and timing of packets still leak, which allows limited traffic analysis.

questionText: In IKEv2, what happens in the first two exchanges, IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH?
options: IKE_SA_INIT sends each peer's password in clear, and IKE_AUTH checks it against a RADIUS server

IKE_SA_INIT negotiates algorithms and runs a Diffie-Hellman exchange with nonces to create the IKE SA; IKE_AUTH then authenticates the peers (with certificates or a pre-shared key) under that protection and sets up the first child SA for ESP or AH
IKE_SA_INIT creates the ESP SA directly, without any Diffie-Hellman exchange
Both exchanges are TCP handshakes on port 443
explanation: The four messages (two round trips) first establish shared keys and then prove identities inside the encrypted IKE SA, so the identities are hidden from passive observers. Further child SAs and rekeying use CREATE_CHILD_SA exchanges (RFC 7296).

questionText: A company links its Kathmandu and Pokhara offices over the Internet so that any host at one site can reach any host at the other, with the two gateways doing all the encryption. Which IPsec configuration fits best?
options: AH in transport mode between every pair of hosts
ESP in transport mode between the two gateways only
AH in tunnel mode, because AH encrypts the whole packet
ESP in tunnel mode between the two gateways, as a site-to-site VPN
explanation: Tunnel mode lets the gateways wrap every packet between the sites in a new header addressed gateway to gateway, so the hosts need no IPsec software, and ESP supplies the encryption. Transport mode between the gateways would protect only traffic addressed to the gateways themselves, and AH never encrypts.

questionText: A salesperson's IPsec VPN client often fails on hotel networks, while the company's SSL/TLS VPN client works there. What is the most likely reason?
options: The SSL/TLS VPN does not encrypt the traffic, so the hotel firewall lets it through
The SSL/TLS VPN uses TCP port 22, which hotels always open
The SSL/TLS VPN runs over port 443 like ordinary HTTPS, which hotel firewalls and NATs almost always allow, whereas IPsec needs UDP 500 and 4500 or IP protocol 50, which are often blocked
explanation: Guest networks usually allow web traffic but may block other ports and protocols, and plain ESP has no ports for a NAT to translate. A TLS-based VPN looks like HTTPS to the network and so gets through, while still encrypting everything inside the tunnel.

questionText: A traveller connects to a commercial VPN service before browsing on hotel Wi-Fi. Which statement is correct?
options: No one, including the VPN provider, can see which sites the traveller visits

The hotel network sees only encrypted traffic to the VPN server and websites see the VPN server's address, but the VPN provider can see the traffic leaving its server, so the traveller must trust the provider
Websites still see the traveller's hotel IP address
HTTPS is no longer needed, because the VPN encrypts the traffic all the way to each website
explanation: The tunnel ends at the VPN server, which decrypts and forwards the traffic, so beyond it the data is protected only by what the application itself uses, such as HTTPS. A VPN therefore moves trust from the local network to the VPN provider rather than removing it.

questionText: What does the 8-byte ESP header that follows the IP header contain?
options: The 32-bit Security Parameter Index (SPI) and the 32-bit sequence number
The source and destination port numbers
The Pad Length and Next Header fields
The initialisation vector and the integrity check value
explanation: The SPI identifies the SA and the sequence number provides anti-replay protection. Padding, Pad Length and Next Header form the encrypted ESP trailer, the IV (when the cipher needs one) starts the payload, and the ICV comes last.

questionText: IPsec AH in transport mode with HMAC-SHA1-96 is applied to a 1,000-byte IPv4 packet. The AH header has 12 bytes of fixed fields (Next Header, Payload Length, Reserved, SPI, Sequence Number) followed by the 96-bit ICV. What is the size of the protected packet?
explanation: The ICV is 96 / 8 = 12 bytes, so AH adds 12 + 12 = 24 bytes and transport mode keeps the original IP header: 1,000 + 24 = 1,024 bytes. 1,012 forgets the ICV, 1,044 adds a new 20-byte IP header as in tunnel mode, and 1,108 counts the ICV as 96 bytes.

questionText: The RTT between a client and a server is 60 ms; processing and transmission times are ignored, and neither TLS False Start nor 0-RTT is used. Counting from the moment the client sends its TCP SYN, when can the client send its first byte of application data with (i) a full TLS 1.2 handshake, (ii) a resumed TLS 1.2 session (abbreviated handshake) and (iii) a full TLS 1.3 handshake?
explanation: TCP takes 1 RTT (60 ms), after which the ClientHello goes out. A full TLS 1.2 handshake then needs 2 more RTTs (180 ms), while an abbreviated TLS 1.2 resumption and a full TLS 1.3 handshake each need 1 (120 ms); only TLS 1.3 0-RTT resumption could send data with the ClientHello at 60 ms.

questionText: A gateway protects a 1,000-byte IPv4 packet with ESP in tunnel mode, using AES-CBC (16-byte IV, 16-byte blocks) and HMAC-SHA-256-128 (16-byte ICV). The encrypted part (inner packet, padding, 1-byte Pad Length and 1-byte Next Header) must be a whole number of blocks. How long is the resulting packet, including the new 20-byte IPv4 header?
explanation: Encrypted part: 1,000 + 2 = 1,002 bytes, padded up to 1,008 (63 blocks, 6 padding bytes); total = 20 (new IP) + 8 (SPI and sequence) + 16 (IV) + 1,008 + 16 (ICV) = 1,068 bytes. 1,062 forgets the padding, 1,048 the new IP header and 1,052 the ICV.

questionText: A VPN uses ESP in tunnel mode with a new 20-byte IPv4 header, the 8-byte ESP header, a 16-byte IV, a 16-byte ICV and AES blocks of 16 bytes (the encrypted part includes the 2-byte trailer). The path MTU is 1,492 bytes (PPPoE). What is the largest TCP MSS the inner hosts can use without fragmentation, assuming 20-byte inner IPv4 and TCP headers without options?
explanation: Room for the encrypted part: 1,492 − 20 − 8 − 16 − 16 = 1,432 bytes, rounded down to whole blocks = 1,424; the largest inner packet is 1,424 − 2 = 1,422 bytes, so MSS = 1,422 − 40 = 1,382 bytes. 1,390 skips the rounding to whole blocks, 1,398 leaves out the IV and 1,452 ignores IPsec altogether.

questionText: A server sends a 100,000-byte file over TLS 1.3 with AES-128-GCM, filling each record with the maximum 16,384 bytes of plaintext. Each record adds a 5-byte header, a 1-byte inner content type and a 16-byte authentication tag, with no padding. How many bytes of TLS records are sent?
explanation: ceil(100,000 / 16,384) = 7 records (six of 16,384 bytes and one of 1,696), each with 5 + 1 + 16 = 22 bytes of overhead, so 100,000 + 7 × 22 = 100,154 bytes. 100,147 forgets the content-type byte, 100,035 counts only the headers and 100,022 ignores the 16,384-byte record limit.

questionText: A 1,000-byte HTTP request is sent over TLS 1.3 (22 bytes of record overhead), TCP and IPv4 (20-byte headers each, no options). The resulting packet then goes through an ESP tunnel using AES-GCM: a new 20-byte IPv4 header, the 8-byte ESP header, an 8-byte IV and a 16-byte ICV, with padding only to make inner packet + padding + 2-byte trailer a multiple of 4 bytes (GCM needs no block padding). How long is the packet on the Internet?
explanation: Inner packet = 1,000 + 22 + 20 + 20 = 1,062 bytes; 1,062 + 2 = 1,064 is already a multiple of 4, so no padding; total = 20 + 8 + 8 + 1,064 + 16 = 1,116 bytes. 1,124 pads to 16-byte blocks as for CBC, 1,096 leaves out the new IP header and 1,108 the IV.

questionText: An ESP receiver uses an anti-replay window of 64 packets. The highest sequence number received so far is 1000, and every number from 937 to 1000 has arrived except 950 and 960. Packets with these sequence numbers now arrive, in this order and all with valid ICVs: 950, 1000, 1040, 960, 1020. Which does the receiver accept?
options: 950, 1040 and 1020 are accepted; 1000 and 960 are dropped
950, 1040, 960 and 1020 are accepted; only 1000 is dropped
Only 1040 is accepted, because every packet numbered below the highest one seen is dropped
All five are accepted, because each has a valid ICV
explanation: 950 lies in the window 937–1000 and is new, so it is accepted; 1000 is a duplicate; 1040 is new and moves the window to 977–1040. 960 now falls left of the window and is dropped even though it never arrived before, while 1020 is inside the window and new, so it is accepted.

questionText: Which IPsec protocol provides encryption of the payload?
explanation: ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) provides confidentiality plus optional integrity; AH gives integrity and authentication only.

questionText: In which IPsec mode is the entire original IP packet encapsulated and given a new IP header?
explanation: Tunnel mode protects the whole original packet inside a new outer header and is used by site-to-site VPN gateways; main and aggressive are IKE phase-1 modes.

questionText: How many round trips does a full TLS 1.3 handshake take before application data can be sent (excluding TCP setup)?
explanation: TLS 1.3 completes a full handshake in 1 RTT versus 2 RTT for TLS 1.2; 0-RTT is possible only when resuming a previous session.

questionText: What does WEP stand for in wireless LAN security?
explanation: WEP means Wired Equivalent Privacy: it aimed to give a wireless link privacy comparable to a wired one, but its design is broken and it must not be used.

questionText: Which wireless security standard is the most secure?
explanation: WPA3 (2018) is the newest and strongest: it uses SAE instead of a plain pre-shared key, adds forward secrecy and protected management frames, and resists offline dictionary attacks. WEP is broken and WPA is weak.

questionText: What is the main purpose of a firewall in a network?
options: To resolve domain names into IP addresses
To encrypt every TCP connection end to end
To store the MAC addresses of every host on the LAN
To monitor and control incoming and outgoing traffic according to a security policy
explanation: A firewall sits at a network boundary and allows or blocks traffic by a set of rules, so that only authorised traffic passes and the events are logged. Encryption, address tables and name resolution are the jobs of TLS/IPsec, switches and DNS.

questionText: At which OSI layers can firewalls operate?
options: At several layers, depending on the type of firewall
explanation: A packet filter works at layers 3-4, a proxy gateway at layer 7, a circuit-level gateway at layer 5 and a next-generation firewall across layers 3-7. So the layer depends on the firewall's type, not a single fixed layer.

questionText: Which encryption does WPA2 use, and how does it differ from WPA?
options: WPA2 uses AES in CCMP mode, replacing the RC4-based TKIP that WPA introduced
WPA2 uses RC4 with TKIP, while WPA used DES
WPA2 uses WEP's RC4 with a longer key
WPA2 and WPA both use AES, differing only in key length
explanation: WPA2 (IEEE 802.11i) mandates AES-CCMP, a modern block-cipher mode giving confidentiality and integrity. WPA was an interim scheme that kept RC4 but added TKIP so that it could run on existing WEP hardware.

questionText: What is an evil-twin attack on a wireless network?
options: Sending forged deauthentication frames to disconnect clients
Guessing the Wi-Fi passphrase from a captured handshake
An attacker's access point that advertises the same SSID as a legitimate one, so that clients associate with it and their traffic can be intercepted
Flooding the channel with radio noise to cause a denial of service
explanation: An evil twin impersonates a trusted network by copying its SSID (and often its captive portal), luring clients into connecting and enabling a man-in-the-middle. It is a rogue AP aimed specifically at mimicking a known network.

questionText: Which statement about hiding the SSID and filtering by MAC address is correct?
options: Together they make a network as secure as WPA2
They are weak measures: the SSID still appears in client probe requests, and MAC addresses are sent in clear and easily spoofed
They are required by the WPA3 standard
explanation: Neither measure encrypts anything. A hidden SSID is revealed whenever a client looks for the network, and an attacker can sniff an allowed MAC address and clone it, so real security still comes from WPA2 or WPA3.

questionText: What is the difference between an IDS and an IPS?
options: An IDS encrypts traffic, while an IPS decrypts it
An IDS works only on wireless networks and an IPS only on wired ones
An IDS is hardware and an IPS is always software
An IDS detects and alerts on suspicious traffic, usually out of band, while an IPS sits inline and can block or drop the malicious traffic in real time
explanation: Both look for attacks by signatures or anomalies, but their placement and response differ: an IDS watches a copy of the traffic and raises alerts, whereas an inline IPS can stop the traffic, at the risk of blocking legitimate flows on a false positive.

questionText: Why is WEP considered insecure, beyond simply having a short key?
options: It uses AES, which is too slow for wireless links
It requires a RADIUS server that most home routers lack
Its 24-bit IV soon repeats so keystreams are reused, RC4 has weak-key IVs that leak the key, and its unkeyed linear CRC-32 lets an attacker alter frames undetected
It encrypts the SSID, which breaks client discovery
explanation: WEP's failures are structural: IV reuse exposes the keystream, the Fluhrer-Mantin-Shamir attack recovers the key from weak IVs, and the CRC-32 integrity check can be forged. Together these let tools break WEP within minutes.

questionText: A study guide says WEP's main weakness is simply 'weak encryption keys that can be cracked easily'. Which more precise statement captures the real flaw?
options: The real flaw is the 24-bit IV: it is so small that IVs and keystreams repeat, and because it is sent in clear as the first bytes of the RC4 key, RC4's key-scheduling weakness reveals the key, however long the secret key is
WEP has no encryption at all, so frames travel in clear text
WEP keys expire after a few seconds and cannot be renewed
WEP uses AES-128, which has since been broken
explanation: Even a 104-bit WEP key falls quickly, because the fault lies in the tiny clear-text IV, which makes keystreams repeat and exposes RC4's weakness to the FMS and PTW key-recovery attacks, not in the length of the secret. WEP does encrypt (with RC4), and it never used AES.

questionText: How do WPA2/WPA3 Personal (PSK) and Enterprise modes differ?
options: Personal uses AES and Enterprise uses RC4
Personal encrypts the traffic and Enterprise leaves it in clear
Enterprise works only on wired networks
Personal shares one passphrase for the whole network, while Enterprise authenticates each user separately through 802.1X with EAP and a RADIUS server
explanation: Both modes use the same AES-based encryption; they differ in authentication. Enterprise gives each user or device its own credentials via 802.1X/EAP and a RADIUS server, so access can be revoked individually without changing a shared passphrase.

questionText: What is the purpose of the WPA2/WPA3 4-way handshake?
options: To scan for the least congested Wi-Fi channel
To let the client and access point confirm they share the master key and to derive fresh per-session keys, using exchanged nonces, and to install the group key
To assign the client an IP address
To negotiate the maximum data rate of the link
explanation: The 4-way handshake runs after association: it proves both sides know the pairwise master key without sending it, mixes in nonces so each session gets a unique transient key, and delivers the group key for broadcasts. Channel selection, addressing and rates are separate.

questionText: What advantage does WPA3's SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) have over the WPA2-Personal handshake?
options: Each password guess needs a fresh interaction with the access point, defeating offline dictionary attacks on captured handshakes, and it provides forward secrecy
It lets the network run without encryption
It removes the need for any password
explanation: With WPA2-Personal an attacker who captures the 4-way handshake can try unlimited guesses offline. SAE makes every guess require a new online exchange with the AP and derives session keys so that a later password compromise does not expose earlier traffic.

questionText: A basic packet-filtering firewall makes its decisions primarily using information from which OSI layers?
options: The network and transport layers (IP addresses, protocol, and TCP/UDP port numbers)
explanation: A packet filter inspects layer-3 and layer-4 header fields, source and destination IP addresses, the protocol, and the port numbers, to allow or deny each packet. Reading message content would need an application-layer (proxy) firewall.

questionText: How does a stateful inspection firewall improve on a stateless packet filter?
options: It encrypts the packets it forwards
It keeps a table of active connections, so it can allow inbound packets only when they belong to a session already started from the trusted side
It works at the physical layer for higher speed
It stores a copy of every packet permanently for auditing
explanation: A stateless filter judges each packet alone, so allowing replies means opening ports permanently. A stateful firewall remembers connections in a state table and lets return traffic through only while its session is active.

questionText: Which firewall type inspects the actual content of an application protocol, so that it can, for example, block specific HTTP requests or filter FTP commands?
explanation: An application-level gateway works at layer 7 and understands the protocol it relays, so it can inspect and filter the content itself. A circuit-level gateway only validates the TCP session and relays bytes without looking inside.

questionText: What is the role of a web application firewall (WAF)?
options: It replaces TLS by encrypting web pages
It assigns IP addresses to web clients
It sits in front of web applications and filters HTTP requests to block attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting
It caches web pages to speed up delivery
explanation: A WAF understands HTTP and web-application behaviour, so it can spot and block malicious requests aimed at the application layer, which a network firewall that only checks addresses and ports cannot. It complements, rather than replaces, TLS.

questionText: Why is network address translation (NAT) often said to give a firewall-like side effect, even though it is not a firewall?
options: By mapping many private addresses to one public address, it has no entry for unsolicited inbound connections, so outside hosts cannot reach internal hosts directly unless a port is forwarded
It encrypts the payload of every packet that crosses it
It authenticates every user before allowing traffic
It inspects the application-layer content of each packet
explanation: NAT keeps a table of connections started from inside; an unsolicited packet from outside matches no entry and is dropped. This blocks direct inbound access as a by-product, but NAT applies no security policy and inspects no content, so it is not a true firewall.

questionText: Where should the publicly reachable web, mail and DNS servers be placed, and why?
options: Inside the ISP's network, so the company need not protect them
On the internal LAN with the workstations, for easier management
Directly on the Internet with no firewall, to maximise performance
In a DMZ, a perimeter network separated from the internal LAN, so that a compromised public server cannot directly reach the internal hosts
explanation: Public servers must accept connections from outside, so they are the most exposed. Putting them in a DMZ between an outer and inner firewall means that if one is breached, the attacker is still separated from the internal network.

questionText: A signature-based IDS/IPS and an anomaly-based one differ in a key way. Which statement is correct?
options: Signature-based detection catches brand-new (zero-day) attacks that anomaly-based detection misses

Signature-based detection matches known attack patterns, so it misses new attacks; anomaly-based detection flags deviations from a learned baseline, so it can catch new attacks but raises more false alarms
Anomaly-based detection needs a database of known attack signatures
Both methods can only be used in an IDS, never in an IPS
explanation: A signature engine is accurate on known threats but blind to anything not yet in its database, while an anomaly engine can notice novel behaviour at the cost of more false positives. Either method can run in a detecting IDS or a blocking IPS.

questionText: A network uses only MAC-address filtering and a hidden SSID, with open (unencrypted) Wi-Fi. What is the security result?
options: Weak: an attacker sniffs the SSID from probe traffic, copies an allowed MAC address seen in clear, and reads all traffic because there is no encryption
Strong, because two independent controls are combined
Adequate for confidential data, because the SSID is hidden
Secure against eavesdropping but not against denial of service
explanation: None of these measures encrypts the air link, so anyone in range reads the frames; the SSID leaks in management frames and MAC addresses are trivial to spoof. Only WPA2 or WPA3 encryption gives real protection.

questionText:
A firewall evaluates rules top to bottom, first match wins, with an implicit default deny at the end:
R1 ALLOW src 192.168.1.0/24 any TCP 443
R2 ALLOW src any dst 203.0.113.10 TCP 80
R3 ALLOW src 192.168.1.10 dst 192.168.2.0/24 TCP 22
R4 DENY src any any TCP 23
What happens to a packet from 192.168.1.50 to 192.168.2.20 on TCP port 22?
explanation: R1 needs port 443, R2 needs destination 203.0.113.10, R3 needs source 192.168.1.10 (not .50) and R4 needs port 23, so none matches. With first-match evaluation the packet falls through to the implicit default deny.

questionText: Using the same rule set (R1 ALLOW 192.168.1.0/24 -> any TCP 443; R2 ALLOW any -> 203.0.113.10 TCP 80; R3 ALLOW 192.168.1.10 -> 192.168.2.0/24 TCP 22; R4 DENY any -> any TCP 23; then default deny), how is a packet from 192.168.1.50 to 203.0.113.10 on TCP port 80 handled?
explanation: R1 requires port 443, so it does not match a port-80 packet; the next rule, R2, allows any source to reach 203.0.113.10 on TCP 80, so the packet is allowed there. First-match means later rules are not consulted.

questionText: An administrator adds, at the bottom of a first-match rule set, R5 DENY src 192.168.1.0/24 dst 203.0.113.10 TCP 80, intending to stop internal users reaching the DMZ web server, but R2 ALLOW src any dst 203.0.113.10 TCP 80 already sits above it. What is the effect, and how should it be fixed?
options: R5 works as intended, because a DENY rule always overrides an ALLOW
R5 blocks all traffic to 203.0.113.10, including from outside
Both rules fire, so the packets are logged twice but still allowed
R5 is never reached, because R2 matches those packets first; the specific DENY must be placed above the broad ALLOW
